one_way_hebrew: PSALM 2 QUOTATION: The second half — וְכִכְלִי יוֹצֵר תְּנַפְּצֵם ('and like a potter's vessel you shall shatter them') — is nearly VERBATIM from Psalm 2:9b (כִּכְלִי יוֹצֵר תְּנַפְּצֵם). The Hebrew Revelation preserves the Psalm's exact words.

The first half uses יְנַהֵג (yenaheg — 'shall lead/drive', H5090) where Psalm 2:9a has תְּרֹעֵם (tero'em — 'you shall break them', from root רעע H7489). The Hebrew Revelation CHANGES the Psalm: instead of 'break them' (destruction), it says 'lead them' (shepherding). This is a deliberate theological reinterpretation — the rod of iron becomes an instrument of governance, not annihilation. Significantly, the Greek ποιμανεῖ ('shall shepherd') aligns with the Hebrew Revelation's 'lead' rather than with the Psalm's 'break' — suggesting the Greek follows the Hebrew Revelation's reading, not the MT of Psalm 2.

Uses שֵׁבֶט (shevet — 'rod/scepter/tribe', H7626) — a word with triple meaning in Hebrew: (1) a rod/staff, (2) a royal scepter, (3) a tribe of Israel. This triple meaning is uniquely Hebrew and untranslatable. Greek ῥάβδῳ ('rod') captures only one meaning.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'lead them' (ינהג — govern/shepherd). Greek: 'shepherd them' (ποιμανεῖ). Close — both deviate from Psalm 2's 'break them.'
Hebrew: 'you shall shatter them' (תנפצם — 2nd person). Greek: 'they shall be broken' (συντριβήσεται — passive). Different voice.
translation_notes: 'Lead' for yenaheg — not 'break.' The Hebrew Revelation reinterprets Psalm 2's destruction as governance.
'Rod' for shevet carries the triple Hebrew meaning of staff, scepter, and tribe.
textual_notes: Psalm 2:9 (MT) — תְּרֹעֵם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל כִּכְלִי יוֹצֵר תְּנַפְּצֵם. The LXX of Psalm 2:9 reads ποιμανεῖς ('you will shepherd') instead of 'break,' reading תרעם as from רעה (shepherd) not רעע (break). The Hebrew Revelation's ינהג (lead) represents yet a third reading — neither breaking nor shepherding but leading/driving.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַשַּׁחַר (ha-shachar — 'the dawn/daybreak', H7837) where Greek has τὸν ἀστέρα τὸν πρωϊνόν ('the morning star'). The Hebrew gives the DAWN ITSELF — the breaking of light over darkness — not a single star. A back-translator from Greek would write כּוֹכַב הַבֹּקֶר ('star of the morning'), not shachar. The Hebrew is grander: the overcomer receives not a star but dawn — the end of all darkness. Isaiah 14:12 uses the related phrase הֵילֵל בֶּן שָׁחַר ('Helel, son of the Dawn') — the fallen aspirant who sought to climb above God. The true dawn belongs to the overcomer.
Uses אָבִי (avi — 'my Father', H1) — the intimate possessive form expressing filial relationship. The speaker claims sonship to the one from whom authority was received.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the dawn' (השחר — the breaking of daylight). Greek: 'the morning star' (τὸν ἀστέρα τὸν πρωϊνόν — a specific celestial object). Different gift: all-encompassing dawn vs. a single star.
Hebrew has 'so I will give him the dawn' as a direct continuation. Greek has 'And I will give him the morning star' as a separate sentence/verse.
translation_notes: 'Dawn' for shachar — not 'morning star.' The Hebrew envisions the gift as the breaking of cosmic light, not a single point of light.

Note: The source text has [28] marking a verse division within this text. The content before [28] ('as I received from my Father') and after ('so I will give him the dawn') correspond to standard verses 27b-28.
textual_notes: Isaiah 14:12 — 'How you are fallen from heaven, Helel son of the Dawn (בן שחר)!' The dawn (shachar) that the fallen one lost is now given to the overcomer. Malachi 3:20 (Hebrew; 4:2 English) — 'The sun of righteousness shall rise (וזרחה) with healing in its wings' — uses a related sunrise/dawn image for eschatological vindication.

one_way_hebrew: The recurring formula uses singular עֵדָה (edah — 'assembly') throughout the chapter, never the plural. Greek alternates between singular ἐκκλησία (in individual letters) and plural ἐκκλησίαις (in the ears formula of some manuscripts). The Hebrew's consistent singular edah presents each assembly as a singular covenantal community.

As noted in v6: the Hebrew uses dual אָזְנַיִם (oznayim — 'ears') and the present participle שׁוֹמֵעַ (shome'a — 'hears' as a fact), while Greek uses singular οὖς ('ear') and the imperative ἀκουσάτω ('let him hear' as a command). The Hebrew structure declares: having ears entails hearing. The Greek structure commands: having an ear, choose to hear.

3.summary: Revelation 3 in Hebrew contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The most striking are: (1) The five-verse פתח (patach) wordplay chain across vv7-8-20, where 'key' (mafteach), 'opener' (poteach), 'open opening' (petach patuach), and 'opening' (petach) all share one Hebrew root — a structural feature IMPOSSIBLE in Greek where κλείς, θύρα, and ἀνοίγω share no root. (2) The use of חַבְרוּתַת הַשָּׂטָן ('fellowship of the Adversary,' v9) instead of 'synagogue of Satan' — a distinctly rabbinic term no back-translator would choose. (3) The use of תְּשׁוּבָה ('returning,' vv3,19) instead of a calque of Greek metanoia ('mind-change'). (4) The use of שֶׁמֶן ('oil,' v18) for eye-anointing instead of Greek κολλούριον ('eye-salve') — with the verb מָשַׁח (mashach, root of Messiah). (5) The אָמֵן/נֶאֱמָן root-wordplay in v14 connecting the divine title 'Amen' to the attribute 'Faithful' through the shared root אמן. (6) The Song of Songs 5:2 echo in v20 — 'voice' + 'knock' (דופק) + 'open' (פתח). (7) The fixed OT word-pair עני ואביון ('poor and destitute,' v17) where Greek has five separate descriptors. (8) The use of ירק ('spit,' v16) — an act of Torah rejection — where Greek has 'vomit.' (9) The consistent use of עֵדָה (edah — Torah congregation) throughout for 'assembly.' The chapter also shows the Hebrew as systematically more concise than Greek, with Greek adding the 'pillar in the temple' clause (v12), the entire dining scene (v20), and multiple expansions (vv14,17,18). These patterns collectively point to Hebrew as the prior text from which the Greek was independently rendered.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵדָה (edah, H5712 — 'assembly/congregation') — the specific Torah word for the congregation of Israel (Num 1:2, 16:2, 27:17, Josh 22:20). Greek has ἐκκλησία (ekklesia — 'church/assembly'). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as אקלסיה or use קהל (qahal — 'assembly'), NOT the Torah-specific term edah. This word choice ties each assembly directly to Israel's wilderness congregation. Used consistently throughout the chapter.

Uses כֹּה אָמַר (ko amar — 'thus says') — the exact prophetic oracle formula used hundreds of times in the Hebrew prophets: כה אמר יהוה (Isa 43:1, 44:2, 45:1; Jer 2:2; Ezek 2:4, etc.). Greek τάδε λέγει is a simple rendering, but a back-translator from Greek would not necessarily reconstruct this specific prophetic formula. The Hebrew author naturally frames the messages to the assemblies as prophetic oracles.

Hebrew has הָרוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה ('the spirits of YHWH') WITHOUT 'seven' before 'spirits.' Greek has τὰ ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ ('the seven spirits of God'). Two deviations: (1) Hebrew uses YHWH where Greek uses 'God,' and (2) Hebrew omits 'seven' before 'spirits' while keeping 'seven' only before 'stars.' A back-translator from Greek would include 'seven' before both nouns. The Hebrew 'spirits of YHWH' may echo Isaiah 11:2 where the attributes of the 'Spirit of YHWH' are enumerated.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'the seven spirits of God' (τὰ ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ). Hebrew: 'the spirits of YHWH' — no number, and YHWH instead of 'God.'
Greek: Σάρδεσιν (Sardesin). Hebrew: זַארְדִּין (Zardin) — a distinct transliteration suggesting independent transmission, not translation from Greek.
translation_notes: 'Assembly' for edah — preserving the Torah congregation connection rather than using 'church.'
'Stars' for kokhavim (H3556) — the standard OT word for stars (Gen 1:16, 15:5, 37:9).
textual_notes: The כה אמר formula appears in all three letters of this chapter (v1, v7, v14), structuring them as prophetic oracles in the pattern of the Hebrew prophets.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַל תִּישַׁן (al tishan — 'do not sleep', from yashen H3462). Greek has γίνου γρηγορῶν ('become watchful'). The Hebrew frames the problem as SLEEPING, not as failure to watch. Sleep carries OT prophetic weight — Jonah sleeping during the storm (Jonah 1:5-6), the disciples sleeping at Gethsemane. A back-translator from Greek 'be watchful' would use שמר (shamar — to guard/watch), not the sleeping verb.

Uses שְׁלֵימָה (shelemah — 'whole/complete', H8003, from the root שלם — shalom). Greek has πεπληρωμένα ('fulfilled/filled'). The Hebrew root שלם means 'whole/complete/at peace' — it's the root of shalom. A back-translator from Greek 'fulfilled' would use מלא (male — 'filled'), not the theologically loaded shalom root. The Hebrew says their deeds lack wholeness/integrity.

Hebrew: לִפְנֵי יַהְוֶה ('before YHWH'). Greek: ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ μου ('before MY God'). Hebrew uses the divine name YHWH; Greek uses 'my God' with a possessive pronoun. A back-translator from Greek would write לפני אלהי ('before my God'), not use the divine name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'do not sleep' (negative command). Greek: 'be watchful' (positive command). Opposite framing.
Hebrew: 'whole' (שלמה). Greek: 'fulfilled' (πεπληρωμένα). Different concepts — integrity vs. completion.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH.' Greek: 'before my God.'
translation_notes: 'Whole' for shelemah — capturing the shalom/integrity meaning rather than 'complete' or 'fulfilled.'
שֶׁרוֹצֶה (she-rotzeh) literally means 'that desires/wants,' but in later Hebrew usage means 'is about to.' The biblical root רצה (H7521) means 'to delight in/be pleased with.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah, H8666 — 'returning/repentance,' from root שוב shuv — 'to return'). Greek has μετανόησον (metanoeō — 'change your mind'). Teshuvah is THE Hebrew concept of repentance — a physical turning back to YHWH, a directional reorientation (Jer 3:12,14,22; Hos 14:1-2; Joel 2:12). Greek metanoia is a mental change ('after-thinking'). A back-translator from Greek would use a calque like שנוי דעת ('change of mind') or the late Hebrew חרטה (charatah — regret), NEVER the deeply Jewish teshuvah. This word appears again in v19.

Uses כַּגַּנָּב (ka-gannav — 'like THE thief', H1590) with the definite article. Greek has ὡς κλέπτης ('as a thief') WITHOUT the article. The Hebrew definite article suggests a known/proverbial figure — 'the thief' as an archetype. This grammatical distinction could not arise from back-translating the anarthrous Greek.

Uses זְמַן (zeman — 'time/season') for the unknown moment. Greek has ὥραν (hōra — 'hour'). Hebrew zeman is a broader term for appointed time or season (Eccl 3:1, Neh 2:6, Est 9:27); Greek specifies a precise 'hour.' A back-translator from Greek would use שעה (sha'ah — 'hour'), not the broader zeman.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: תשובה ('returning'). Greek: μετανόησον ('change your mind'). Fundamentally different concepts of repentance.
Hebrew: 'at what time' (זמן — season). Greek: 'what hour' (ὥραν — specific hour).
Hebrew: 'like THE thief' (definite). Greek: 'as a thief' (indefinite).
translation_notes: 'Teshuvah' left untranslated — no English word captures the Hebrew concept of physical, directional return to YHWH.
מְקַיֵּים (meqayem — 'upholding/fulfilling') from a later Hebrew form related to root קום (qum, H6965 — to rise/establish). No standard Strong's number for this piel form.
textual_notes: The thief imagery connects to Joel 2:9 — 'they enter through the windows like a thief' (כַּגַּנָּב) — using the same definite article construction. This is an OT prophetic motif.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has שִׁמְךָ נִשְׁמָע ('your name is heard,' שם/שמע). Greek has ὀλίγα ὀνόματα ('a few names,' meaning a few people). These are entirely different statements! Hebrew says 'your name/reputation is known'; Greek says 'you have few names/people.' The Hebrew contains an assonance — שִׁמְךָ (shimkha, 'your name') and נִשְׁמָע (nishma, 'is heard') echo each other phonetically (shin-mem/shin-mem-ayin). This Hebrew wordplay is invisible in Greek and could not arise from back-translation.

Uses תֵּלְכוּ (telkhu — 'shall walk', from halakh H1980). Greek has περιπατήσουσιν (peripatesousin — 'shall walk around'). Both mean 'walk,' but the Hebrew verb הלך is THE verb of following YHWH's ways in the OT — 'walking in his statutes' (Lev 26:3), 'walking before YHWH' (Gen 17:1). The 'walking with me' (עמי) echoes Enoch who 'walked with God' (Gen 5:22,24).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your name is heard' (positive reputation statement). Greek: 'you have a few names' (numerical statement about people). Entirely different meaning.
Hebrew: 'for they are worthy of this' (לזה). Greek: 'for they are worthy' — omits 'of this.'
translation_notes: טִנְּפוּ (tinfu — 'defiled/soiled') is a later Hebrew verb with no standard Strong's number. The biblical equivalent would be טמא (tame — H2930, 'to make unclean').
רְאוּיִם (re'uyim — 'worthy/fitting') is a later Hebrew adjective, no standard Strong's.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוֹדִיעַ (modia — 'make known', hifil of yada H3045). Greek has ὁμολογήσω (homologēsō — 'I will confess/acknowledge'). These are fundamentally different acts: 'making known' (revealing to those who don't yet know) vs. 'confessing/acknowledging' (declaring before those who already know). A back-translator from Greek ὁμολογέω would use הודה (hodah — 'to confess/give thanks'), NOT the causative of ידע (yada).

Uses אֶמְחֶה (emcheh — 'I will blot out', from machah H4229) — the EXACT verb from Exodus 32:32-33 where YHWH says 'Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out (אֶמְחֶנּוּ) of my book.' The Hebrew author uses Moses's precise vocabulary. Greek ἐξαλείψω is equivalent but a back-translator would not necessarily reach for this specific Exodus verb.

Uses תֵּלֵךְ (telekh — 'shall walk', from halakh H1980) for wearing white garments. Greek has περιβαλεῖται (peribaleitai — 'shall be clothed/wrapped'). Hebrew says the overcomer will WALK in white; Greek says the overcomer will be CLOTHED in white. Different verbs entirely — walking implies active movement; being clothed implies passive reception.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'make known' (מודיע, revealing). Greek: 'confess/acknowledge' (ὁμολογήσω, declaring).
Hebrew: 'shall walk in white garments.' Greek: 'shall be clothed in white garments.' Different verbs.
Hebrew: מִסֵּפֶר ('from the scroll' — sefer, a scroll). Greek: ἐκ τῆς βίβλου ('from the book' — biblos). Hebrew specifies a scroll; Greek specifies a codex/book.
translation_notes: 'Scroll' for sefer (H5612) — preserving the ancient format. A sefer in the biblical period was always a scroll, not a bound book.
'Make known' for modia — the causative of 'to know,' implying revelation of something previously hidden.
textual_notes: Exodus 32:32-33 — 'And YHWH said to Moses: Whoever has sinned against me, him will I blot out (אמחנו) from my book (ספרי).' The vocabulary sefer + machah in the same context is an Exodus echo.

one_way_hebrew: Uses SINGULAR הָעֵדָה ('the assembly'). Greek has PLURAL ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('the assemblies/churches'). A back-translator from Greek plural would write העדות (ha-edot — plural). The Hebrew singular addresses each assembly individually as 'the assembly,' reflecting the Torah concept of Israel as one edah.

Hebrew: שׁוֹמֵעַ ('hears' — present participle, stating a fact). Greek: ἀκουσάτω ('let him hear' — imperative, issuing a command). The Hebrew states that the one with ears DOES hear; the Greek commands him TO hear. Different moods entirely.
Uses אָזְנַיִם (oznayim — 'ears', DUAL form, both ears). Greek has οὖς (ous — 'ear', SINGULAR). The Hebrew dual emphasizes hearing with BOTH ears — full attentiveness.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: singular 'assembly.' Greek: plural 'assemblies.'
Hebrew: 'hears' (indicative). Greek: 'let him hear' (imperative).
Hebrew: 'ears' (dual — both ears). Greek: 'ear' (singular).
textual_notes: This refrain appears in all seven letters (Rev 2-3). The formula echoes Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 6:9-10 — the theme of ears that hear and ears that don't.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL WORDPLAY: The Hebrew creates a triple wordplay on the root פתח (patach — 'to open'): מַפְתֵּחַ (mafteach — 'key,' literally 'that which opens'), הַפּוֹתֵחַ (ha-poteach — 'the opener'), and the infinitive לִפְתּוֹחַ (liftoach — 'to open'). In Hebrew, the word 'key' SHARES ITS ROOT with 'open' — the key IS 'the opener.' This wordplay is IMPOSSIBLE in Greek, where κλείς ('key') and ἀνοίγω ('open') share no root. A back-translator could never reconstruct this triple פתח wordplay. This wordplay continues in v8 and v20.

Uses הַנֶּאֱמָן (ha-ne'eman — 'the Faithful One,' from root אמן aman, H539). Greek has ὁ ἀληθινός (ho alēthinos — 'the True One'). Different attributes: faithfulness/trustworthiness vs. truth/genuineness. A back-translator from 'the True One' would use הָאֲמִתִּי (ha-amiti — 'the truthful one') or הַיָּשָׁר (ha-yashar — 'the upright one'), not ne'eman. Note: ne'eman shares root אמן with אָמֵן (Amen) in v14 — a cross-verse wordplay.

Uses הַמַּפְתֵּחַ שֶׁל דָּוִד ('the key of David,' H4668) — a DIRECT quote from Isaiah 22:22: וְנָתַתִּי מַפְתֵּחַ בֵּית דָּוִד עַל שִׁכְמוֹ ('and I will place the key of the house of David upon his shoulder'). The Hebrew uses the identical word מפתח from Isaiah. Greek has τὴν κλεῖν Δαυΐδ ('the key of David'). A back-translator could use מפתח, but the triple פתח wordplay (key-opener-open) reveals an author thinking in Hebrew roots, not translating from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Faithful One' (נאמן). Greek: 'the True One' (ἀληθινός). Different attributes.
Hebrew adds יוּכַל ('is able') — 'no one IS ABLE to shut/open.' Greek has simply οὐδεὶς κλείσει/ἀνοίγει ('no one shall/does shut/open'). Hebrew emphasizes INABILITY.
translation_notes: 'Key' for mafteach (H4668) — this word appears in Isaiah 22:22, Judges 3:25, and 1 Chronicles 9:27. It literally means 'opener' (the tool that opens).
'Opener' and 'shutter' preserve the participial forms that highlight the authority of the key-holder.
textual_notes: Isaiah 22:22 — 'And I will place the key (מפתח) of the house of David upon his shoulder; and he shall open (ופתח), and none shall shut (ואין סגר); and he shall shut (וסגר), and none shall open (ואין פתח).' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Isaiah's vocabulary with the same roots פתח and סגר.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL WORDPLAY: פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ (petach patuach — 'an open opening'). BOTH words are from the SAME root פתח! This is a Hebrew figura etymologica (cognate accusative) that intensifies meaning — the opening is emphatically, inherently open. Greek has θύραν ἀνεῳγμένην ('an opened door') — where 'door' (θύρα) and 'opened' (ἀνοίγω) share NO root. A back-translator from Greek would write דלת פתוחה ('an opened door'), not the wordplay petach patuach. This continues the פתח wordplay chain from v7.

Uses כּוֹפֵר (kofer — 'denying') from the root כפר. In biblical Hebrew, this root means 'to cover/atone' (H3722) — it is the root of כִּפֻּר (kippur, as in Yom Kippur) and כֹּפֶר (kofer — 'ransom/atonement price,' H3724). In later Hebrew, כפר ב came to mean 'to deny/disbelieve in.' The same root thus connects denial and atonement — denying the name is the opposite of receiving atonement. This semantic range is unique to Hebrew. Greek ἠρνήσω ('denied') has no such atonement connection.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: פֶּתַח ('opening,' from root פתח). Greek: θύραν ('door'). Hebrew uses 'opening'; Greek uses 'door.' Different nouns.
Hebrew: כופר ('denying,' root כפר). Greek: ἠρνήσω ('denied,' root ἀρνέομαι). The Hebrew root carries atonement overtones absent from the Greek.
translation_notes: 'Opening' for petach (H6607) rather than 'door' — preserving the root connection with mafteach (key) and poteach (opener) from v7.
'Guarded' for shamarta (H8104) — shamar means to watch over, protect, and keep, as in 'to guard the garden' (Gen 2:15) and 'to guard the commandments' (Deut 5:29).
כּוֹפֵר (kofer) in the 'deny' sense has no standard Strong's number; this usage is post-biblical.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חַבְרוּתַת (chavrutat — 'fellowship/companionship of'), from root חבר (chaver, H2266/H2270 — 'companion/friend'). Greek has συναγωγῆς (sunagōgēs — 'synagogue/gathering'). The Hebrew חברותא (chavruta) is a uniquely Hebraic/Aramaic term for intimate fellowship or study partnership — a concept central to rabbinic culture. A back-translator from Greek 'synagogue' would write בֵּית כְּנֶסֶת (beit knesset — 'house of gathering') or transliterate סינאגוגא, NEVER use the distinctly Jewish relational term chavruta. The choice implies an intimate circle of the Adversary, not merely a 'synagogue.'

Uses הַשָּׂטָן (ha-satan — 'the Adversary,' H7854) WITH the definite article, preserving it as a common noun with article ('the accuser/adversary'), as in Job 1:6-7, 2:1 and Zechariah 3:1-2. Greek has Σατανᾶ (Satana) as a PROPER NAME without article. The Hebrew treats this as a title — 'the adversary' — maintaining OT usage. A back-translator from Greek's proper name would omit the article.

Uses לִתְפַּלֵּל (lehitpalel — 'to pray/bow in prayer,' H6419, hitpael of פלל). This is THE Hebrew word for Jewish prayer — the reflexive of palal ('to judge'), implying self-examination before God. Greek has προσκυνήσωσιν (proskunēsōsin — 'to worship/bow down'). A back-translator from Greek would use לְהִשְׁתַּחֲווֹת (lehishtachavot — 'to prostrate/bow down'), NOT the prayer-specific lehitpalel. The Hebrew implies they will come and PRAY at the feet of the faithful — a far deeper act than mere bowing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חברותת ('fellowship/companionship'). Greek: συναγωγή ('synagogue/gathering'). Different social concepts.
Hebrew: לתפלל ('to pray/bow in prayer'). Greek: προσκυνήσωσιν ('to worship/bow down'). Different acts.
Hebrew: כוזבים ('deceivers/liars,' from כזב). Greek: ψεύδονται ('they lie'). Hebrew uses a noun (they ARE liars); Greek uses a verb (they lie).
translation_notes: 'Fellowship' for chavrutat — capturing the intimate relational concept rather than the institutional 'synagogue.'
'Adversary' for ha-satan — preserving the common noun with article, as in the OT, rather than treating it as a proper name.
'Bow in prayer' for lehitpalel — the hitpael of palal carries both prayer and physical bowing.
וּלְהַכִּיר (ulehakir — 'and to acknowledge,' hifil of nakar H5234) means 'to recognize/identify' — more relational than Greek γνῶσιν ('they will know').
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:14 — 'The sons of those who oppressed you shall come bending low to you, and all who despised you shall bow down (והשתחוו) at the soles of your feet.' The Hebrew Revelation may allude to this Isaiah prophecy but uses the prayer verb instead of the bowing verb.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תִּקְוָתִי (tiqvati — 'my hope,' from tikvah H8615). Greek has ὑπομονῆς μου (hupomonēs mou — 'my patience/endurance'). These are ENTIRELY different concepts: hope (expectation/waiting for something good) vs. patience (enduring hardship). A back-translator from Greek 'patience' would use סַבְלָנוּת (savlanut — 'patience'), אֹרֶךְ אַפַּיִם (erekh apayim — 'long-suffering'), or סֵבֶל (sevel — 'endurance'), NEVER the hope-word tikvah. Furthermore, tikvah in Hebrew ALSO means 'cord/thread' (Josh 2:18, 21 — Rahab's scarlet cord of tikvah). The 'utterance of my cord/hope' carries a dual meaning impossible in Greek.

Uses הַדִּיבּוּר (ha-dibbur — 'the utterance/speech') — from root דבר (davar, H1696). This is the specific word for divine speech, as in the עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדִּבְּרוֹת (Aseret ha-Dibbrot — 'the Ten Utterances/Commandments'). Greek has τὸν λόγον (ton logon — 'the word'). A back-translator from Greek would use דָּבָר (davar — 'word'), not the elevated dibbur. The Hebrew implies guarding a divine utterance, not merely a word.

Uses שָׁמַרְתָּ ... אֶשְׁמוֹר (shamarta ... eshmor — 'you guarded ... I will guard') — the SAME root שמר (shamar, H8104) for both human and divine action, creating a reciprocal bond: 'you guarded my utterance, therefore I guard you.' Greek uses the same root τηρέω (tēreō) for both, but the Hebrew שמר carries the weight of Genesis 2:15 (guarding the garden) and Psalm 121 (YHWH who guards Israel). The Hebrew reciprocity is structural.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: תקותי ('my hope'). Greek: ὑπομονῆς μου ('my patience/endurance'). Fundamentally different concepts.
Hebrew: דיבור ('utterance'). Greek: λόγον ('word'). Different registers of speech.
Hebrew: הָעֵת ('the time/season'). Greek: τῆς ὥρας ('the hour'). Hebrew = broader season; Greek = specific hour.
Greek adds τῆς οἰκουμένης ὅλης ('the whole inhabited world') — Hebrew has simply הָאָרֶץ ('the earth').
translation_notes: 'Utterance' for dibbur — preserving the elevated register of divine speech, distinct from the common 'word' (davar).
'Hope' for tikvah — left as the primary meaning, though the 'cord/thread' secondary meaning enriches the image.
textual_notes: The tikvah/cord connection to Joshua 2:18 is striking: Rahab was saved from destruction by the tikvah (scarlet cord); here the assembly is saved from trial by guarding the 'utterance of my tikvah.' Both involve being protected during judgment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'crown') — the ROYAL crown word from Esther (Est 1:11, 2:17, 6:8). Greek has στέφανον (stephanon — 'wreath/victory crown'). These are fundamentally different types of crowns: keter is a royal diadem of sovereignty (Persian/royal usage); stephanos is a wreath awarded for athletic or military victory. A back-translator from Greek στέφανος would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — 'wreath/garland,' H5850) or transliterate, NOT reach for the royal keter. The Hebrew author gives the overcomer a ROYAL crown, not merely a victor's wreath.

Uses שְׁמוֹר (shemor — 'guard,' from shamar H8104). Greek has κράτει (kratei — 'hold fast/seize'). The Hebrew verb means to watch over and protect (as a sentinel); the Greek verb means to grip or hold onto. A back-translator from Greek would use אחז (achaz — 'to grasp') or החזק (hecheziq — 'to hold fast'), not the guardian-verb shamar.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: כתר ('royal crown'). Greek: στέφανος ('victor's wreath'). Different types of crown.
Hebrew: שמור ('guard/protect'). Greek: κράτει ('hold fast/grip'). Different verbs.
translation_notes: 'Crown' for keter — the royal diadem, not a wreath. This is the crown of Esther and the Persian kings.
בִּמְהֵרָה (bimherah — 'speedily') is a Hebrew liturgical word familiar from Jewish prayer ('bimhera v'yameinu — speedily and in our days'). No standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew OMITS the entire clause about being made a pillar in the temple: Greek has ποιήσω αὐτὸν στῦλον ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ θεοῦ μου, καὶ ἔξω οὐ μὴ ἐξέλθῃ ἔτι ('I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more'). This substantial clause is ABSENT from Hebrew. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, omitting such a vivid and theologically significant image would be inexplicable. Its absence suggests the Greek translator added this pillar imagery — possibly influenced by the actual pillars of the Jerusalem temple (Jachin and Boaz, 1 Kings 7:21).
greek_deviations: Greek adds the entire 'pillar in the temple' clause — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: מֵאֱלֹהַי ('of/from my Elohim') appears three times. Greek also has τοῦ θεοῦ μου ('of my God') three times. Parallel structure preserved, but Hebrew uses the distinctly Hebraic 'Elohim.'
translation_notes: הֶחָדָשׁ (he-chadash — 'the new,' masculine) modifying ירושלים. Jerusalem in Hebrew can take either masculine or feminine agreement.
textual_notes: The three-fold repetition of 'my Elohim' (אלהי) emphasizes the personal covenant relationship. Isaiah 62:2 prophesies: 'You shall be called by a new name (שם חדש) which the mouth of YHWH will designate' — the 'new name' concept has OT roots.

greek_deviations: Same deviations as v6: Hebrew singular 'assembly' vs. Greek plural 'assemblies'; Hebrew indicative 'hears' vs. Greek imperative 'let him hear'; Hebrew dual 'ears' vs. Greek singular 'ear.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL WORDPLAY: אָמֵן (Amen, H543) followed immediately by נֶאֱמָן (ne'eman — 'faithful,' H539). BOTH words derive from the SAME Hebrew root אמן (aman — 'to be firm/established/faithful'). Amen IS 'the faithful one' — the name and the attribute share one root. In Greek, Ἀμήν is a transliterated Hebrew word, and πιστός ('faithful') comes from πείθω ('to persuade'). The root connection is INVISIBLE in Greek. This also connects back to הַנֶּאֱמָן (the Faithful One) in v7 — the same root spans both letters.

Uses PLURAL בְּרִיאוֹת (beriot — 'creations/creatures'). Greek has SINGULAR κτίσεως (ktiseōs — 'creation'). The Hebrew plural implies multiple acts of creation or multiple created orders. A back-translator from Greek singular would use בְּרִיאָה (beriah — singular 'creation'), not the plural.

Hebrew: הָעֵד נֶאֱמָן ('the faithful witness' — two words). Greek: ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστὸς καὶ ἀληθινός ('the faithful AND TRUE witness' — adds 'and true'). The Hebrew is more concise; the Greek adds ἀληθινός ('true'). Hebrew omits 'true' because ne'eman already encompasses both faithfulness and truthfulness in the Hebrew semantic range.
greek_deviations: Greek adds καὶ ἀληθινός ('and true') — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: plural 'creations' (בריאות). Greek: singular 'creation' (κτίσεως).
Greek adds τοῦ θεοῦ ('of God') after 'creation' — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Amen' left untranslated — it is a Hebrew word meaning 'firm/certain/so be it,' functioning here as a divine title: 'The Certain One.'
הַתְּחִלָּה (ha-techillah, H8462 — 'the beginning') appears in Gen 13:3, 41:21, 43:18-20; Ruth 1:22; Neh 11:17.
בְּרִיאוֹת (beriot) is from root ברא (bara, H1254 — 'to create'). The noun form is post-biblical.
textual_notes: Isaiah 65:16 — 'Whoever blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of Amen (אלהי אמן).' Amen as a divine title/attribute has OT precedent.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אוּלַי (ulai — 'perhaps/maybe,' H194). Greek has ὄφελον (ophelon — 'I wish/would that'). These express DIFFERENT attitudes: Hebrew אולי is a tentative suggestion, a gentle 'perhaps' (Gen 18:24, 24:5, Num 22:11); Greek ὄφελον is a strong wish bordering on lament. A back-translator from Greek's strong wish would use מי יתן (mi yitten — 'who would give that...,' the standard Hebrew optative), NOT the mild, exploratory ulai.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: אולי ('perhaps'). Greek: ὄφελον ('I wish'). Different intensity — gentle suggestion vs. strong desire.
translation_notes: קַר (qar, H7119 — 'cold') appears in Prov 25:25, Gen 8:22. חָם (cham, H2525 — 'hot/warm') appears in Gen 8:22, Josh 9:12.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יֹרֵק (yoreq — 'spit,' from yaraq H3417). Greek has μέλλω ἐμέσαι (mellō emesai — 'I am about to VOMIT'). These are completely different bodily acts: spitting is an act of REJECTION and SHAMING in Hebrew culture (Num 12:14 — 'If her father had spat in her face'; Deut 25:9 — spitting in the face of one who refuses levirate duty; Isa 50:6 — 'I did not hide my face from shame and spitting'). Vomiting is an involuntary physiological response. A back-translator from Greek 'vomit' would use הֵקִיא (heqi — 'to vomit,' from root קיא H7006, Lev 18:28, Prov 23:8, Jonah 2:10), NOT the shaming act of spitting. The Hebrew author invokes the Torah's act of public rejection.

Hebrew: present tense יֹרֵק ('I spit' — ongoing/present). Greek: future/imminent μέλλω ἐμέσαι ('I am ABOUT TO vomit'). Hebrew presents the rejection as already underway; Greek presents it as impending. Different temporal framing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spit' (ירק — act of shaming). Greek: 'vomit' (ἐμέω — physiological response). Entirely different imagery.
Hebrew: present tense ('I spit'). Greek: imminent future ('I am about to vomit').
Hebrew lacks any equivalent of χλιαρός ('lukewarm') — Greek inserts this term; Hebrew simply restates 'not cold and not hot.'
translation_notes: 'Spit' for yoreq — preserving the Hebrew act of public rejection/shaming, distinct from vomiting.
The consonantal text ירק could theoretically be read as 'green/vegetable' (yerek), but contextual meaning is clearly 'to spit' (yaraq, as in Lev 15:8).
textual_notes: Numbers 12:14 — 'If her father had surely spit (ירק ירק) in her face, would she not be ashamed seven days?' Leviticus 15:8 — 'If the one with a discharge spits (ירק) on one who is clean.' The spitting verb carries Torah-level significance as an act of rejection.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses the word pair עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן (ani v'evyon — 'poor and destitute,' H6041 + H34) — only TWO descriptors. Greek has FIVE: ταλαίπωρος καὶ ἐλεεινὸς καὶ πτωχὸς καὶ τυφλὸς καὶ γυμνός ('wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked'). The Hebrew עני ואביון is a FIXED OT word pair appearing as a unit in Deut 15:11, 24:14; Ps 35:10, 37:14, 40:17, 70:5, 72:13, 86:1, 109:16,22; Jer 22:16; Ezek 16:49; Amos 8:4. A back-translator from Greek's five-word list would NEVER independently reconstruct this specific two-word OT pairing. The Hebrew is a concise prophetic formula; the Greek is an expanded rhetorical list.

Uses דַּי (dai, H1767 — 'enough/sufficient') — a distinctly Hebrew word. Greek has πεπλούτηκα ('I have become rich'). Hebrew says 'I have enough'; Greek says 'I have become wealthy.' Different claims: sufficiency vs. enrichment.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 2 descriptors — 'poor and destitute' (עני ואביון). Greek: 5 descriptors — 'wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, naked.' Hebrew omits 'blind and naked.'
Hebrew: 'I have enough' (dai). Greek: 'I have become rich' (πεπλούτηκα). Different self-assessments.
Hebrew: 'I have no need of anything' (אינה צורך לשום דבר). Greek: 'I have need of nothing' (οὐδενὸς χρείαν ἔχω). Similar but Hebrew uses later idiom.
translation_notes: 'Destitute' for evyon (H34) — this word specifically denotes one who is needy/lacking/in want. Together with ani ('poor'), it forms the classic OT pair for the oppressed class whom Torah commands Israel to protect.
צוֹרֶךְ (tzorekh — 'need') is a later Hebrew noun with no standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Hosea 12:8 (Hebrew 12:9) — 'And Ephraim said: Surely I have become rich (עשרתי), I have found wealth for myself.' The self-deceived boast of wealth has prophetic precedent. The Laodicean boast echoes Ephraim's.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בַּשֶּׁמֶן (ba-shemen — 'with oil,' H8081). Greek has κολλούριον (kollourion — 'eye-salve'). Shemen is the standard OT anointing oil (Ex 30:25, 1 Sam 16:13). A back-translator from Greek κολλούριον (a specific Greco-Roman medicinal product for eyes) would transliterate the Greek term or describe an eye-salve, NEVER use שמן (shemen — generic oil). The Hebrew author prescribes the biblical anointing substance; the Greek translator converted it to a culturally familiar Greco-Roman remedy. Laodicea was famous for its eye-salve industry — the Greek may reflect local knowledge that the Hebrew original did not possess.

CRITICAL: Uses מָשַׁחְתָּ (mashachta — 'and you shall anoint,' from mashach H4886) — the ROOT of מָשִׁיחַ (Mashiach — 'Messiah/Anointed One'). This is the specific verb for priestly and royal anointing (Ex 30:26, 1 Sam 16:13, 1 Kings 1:39). Greek ἐγχρῖσαι (enchrisai) is from χρίω (chriō) — the root of Χριστός (Christos). BOTH words are 'anoint' roots, but the Hebrew mashach carries the full weight of Torah anointing — kings, priests, and the tabernacle were all 'mashach'd.' The Hebrew reader hears Messianic overtones in 'anoint your eyes.'

Uses עֲצָתִי (atzati — 'my counsel,' from etsah H6098). This is the OT word for divine/wise counsel (Isa 9:6 — 'Wonderful Counselor'; Ps 33:11 — 'the counsel of YHWH stands forever'; Prov 19:21 — 'the counsel of YHWH, it will stand'). Greek: συμβουλεύω ('I advise'). A back-translator would use a verb form; the Hebrew uses the noun 'my counsel,' invoking the prophetic/wisdom tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'with oil' (שמן — anointing oil). Greek: κολλούριον ('eye-salve'). Entirely different substances.
Hebrew: 'my counsel' (noun, עצתי). Greek: 'I counsel' (verb, συμβουλεύω). Different construction.
Greek adds πεπυρωμένον ἐκ πυρός ('refined by fire') after gold — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds ἵνα πλουτήσῃς ('so that you may become rich') — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds καὶ μὴ φανερωθῇ ἡ αἰσχύνη τῆς γυμνότητός σου ('and the shame of your nakedness not be revealed') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew is dramatically more concise.
translation_notes: 'Anoint' for mashach — preserving the Messianic/priestly anointing verb.
'Counsel' for etsah — the specific word for divine/wise counsel in the prophetic tradition.
מַלְבּוּשִׁים (malbushim, H4403 — 'garments/clothing') — from root לבש (lavash — 'to clothe'). Different from בגדים (begadim) used in vv4-5; malbush emphasizes the garment as clothing to put on.
textual_notes: Isaiah 55:1 — 'Come, buy (שברו) wine and milk without money and without price.' The invitation to 'buy from me' echoes Isaiah's free-of-charge invitation. The gold here is spiritual, not commercial.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוֹסֵר (moser — 'chastise/discipline,' from root יסר yasar, H3256) — ONE Hebrew word. Greek has ἐλέγχω καὶ παιδεύω ('I rebuke AND discipline') — TWO words. The Hebrew collapses two Greek concepts into one word. Hebrew מוסר (musar — 'discipline/instruction') is THE central concept of Proverbs (Prov 1:2,7, 3:11, 12:1, 13:24, 15:5). A back-translator from Greek's two words would use two Hebrew words (e.g., מוכיח ומיסר), not collapse them into one.

DIRECT ECHO of Proverbs 3:12 — כִּי אֶת אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב יְהוָה יוֹכִיחַ ('For whom YHWH loves he disciplines'). The Hebrew Revelation uses the same love-discipline pairing. Greek uses φιλῶ (phileō — 'friendship love'), NOT ἀγαπάω (agapaō). Hebrew uses אָהַבְתִּי (ahavti — from ahav, H157), the deep covenant love of the OT. A back-translator from Greek phileō might use חבב (chibev — 'to cherish') or ריע (rea — 'friend'), NOT the covenantal ahav.
Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah) again — the same Hebrew repentance concept from v3. Greek has μετανόησον. See v3 notes.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: one verb מוסר ('chastise'). Greek: two verbs ἐλέγχω καὶ παιδεύω ('rebuke and discipline').
Hebrew: אהבתי (ahavti — 'I have loved,' PAST tense, covenantal love). Greek: φιλῶ (philō — 'I love,' PRESENT tense, friendship love). Different tense and different type of love.
Greek adds ζήλωσον ('be zealous') before 'repent' — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Chastise' for moser — capturing the musar/discipline concept central to Proverbs.
'Teshuvah' left untranslated — see note on v3.
textual_notes: Proverbs 3:11-12 — 'My son, do not despise the discipline (מוסר) of YHWH, nor loathe his reproof; for whom YHWH loves (יאהב) he disciplines.' The Hebrew Revelation directly echoes this Proverbs passage.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The פתח wordplay chain from v7-8 CONTINUES here: הַפֶּתַח (ha-petach — 'the opening') appears TWICE, and יִפְתַּח (yiftach — 'he opens') uses the same root. In v7: מַפְתֵּחַ (key) and פּוֹתֵחַ (opener) and לִפְתּוֹחַ (to open). In v8: פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ (open opening). Now in v20: הפתח ... ויפתח הפתח. This extended five-verse פתח wordplay (vv7-8-20) is a deliberate structural feature ONLY visible in Hebrew. Greek uses three different roots: κλείς (key), θύρα (door), and ἀνοίγω (open) — no wordplay possible.

Uses דֹפֵק (dofek — 'knock,' from dafaq H1849). This EXACT form appears in Song of Songs 5:2 — קוֹל דּוֹדִי דוֹפֵק ('the voice of my beloved knocks'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes the Song of Songs' language of the beloved knocking at the door. A back-translator from Greek κρούω ('knock') could use דפק, but the Song of Songs echo (voice + knock at the opening) would be coincidental rather than deliberate.

Hebrew: לָזֶה אֵלֵךְ ('to this one I will go') — ONLY this. Greek adds: καὶ εἰσελεύσομαι πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ δειπνήσω μετ' αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς μετ' ἐμοῦ ('and I will enter to him and dine with him and he with me'). The ENTIRE dining/fellowship clause is ABSENT from Hebrew. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, omitting such a beloved and vivid image of intimate table fellowship would be inexplicable.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: הפתח ('opening,' from root פתח). Greek: θύραν ('door'). Different nouns, breaking the Hebrew wordplay.
Greek adds the entire clause about dining together (δειπνήσω μετ' αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς μετ' ἐμοῦ) — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: אלך ('I will go' — from halakh). Greek: εἰσελεύσομαι ('I will enter' — from eiserchomai). Hebrew implies walking toward; Greek implies entering into.
translation_notes: 'Opening' for petach — maintaining the consistent פתח translation throughout the chapter (vv7-8-20).
'Knock' for dofek — the Song of Songs verb for the beloved's knock.
לִפְנֵי (lifnei — 'before/in the face of') — more personal than merely 'at.' The speaker stands face-to-face with the opening.
textual_notes: Song of Songs 5:2 — 'I sleep but my heart is awake: the voice of my beloved knocks (דופק). Open (פתחי) to me, my sister, my darling, my dove.' The Hebrew Revelation combines 'voice' + 'knock' + 'open' (פתח), exactly as in Song of Songs.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּסֵּא (kise, H3678 — 'throne/seat') — the standard OT throne word (1 Kings 1:37,46; 2:12,19; Ps 45:6, 89:14, 93:2, 97:2). This is the throne of Solomon, of David, and of YHWH. Greek θρόνος is equivalent, but the Hebrew naturally draws from the OT throne vocabulary.

The parallel structure מְנַצֵּחַ/נִצַּחְתִּי (menatzeach/nitzachti — 'overcomes/I overcame') using the SAME root נצח (natsach, H5329) in both participial and perfect forms creates a Hebrew verbal echo: the overcomer's action mirrors the speaker's completed action. The root נצח in the OT means 'to oversee/direct/be victorious' (used in Psalm titles for the מנצח — director/choirmaster). The overcomer participates in the same נצח as the Mashiach.
translation_notes: 'Sit' for yoshev (H3427) — the verb of enthronement and settled authority (Ps 2:4 — 'He who sits in the heavens laughs'; Ps 110:1 — 'Sit at my right hand').
textual_notes: Psalm 110:1 — 'YHWH said to my lord: Sit (שב) at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' The invitation to sit on the throne echoes the Messianic enthronement psalm.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew OMITS 'to the assemblies' (ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις) which Greek includes. The final refrain of the seven letters in Hebrew ends simply: 'what the spirit says' — without specifying the recipient. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, there would be no reason to drop 'to the assemblies' in this final instance. The omission may indicate that this concluding refrain universalizes the message — the spirit speaks not only to the assemblies but to all who hear.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('to the assemblies') — absent from Hebrew in this final refrain.
Same mood difference as v6 and v13: Hebrew indicative 'hears' vs. Greek imperative 'let him hear.'

4.summary: Revelation 4 in Hebrew is a throne-room vision built entirely from Ezekiel's merkavah (Ezek 1) and Isaiah's seraphim vision (Isa 6), expressed in native Hebrew theological vocabulary. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek. The most powerful are: (1) The verbatim Isaiah 6:3 quotation (קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת) where Greek has 'Lord God Almighty'; (2) The tripartite YHWH-etymological formula הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה ('who was, is, and shall be') using three forms of the root from which the divine name derives, where Greek substitutes 'the coming one' for 'shall be'; (3) The priestly zaraq verb (v10) for the elders 'dashing' their crowns as a sacrificial offering; (4) The menorah-specific nerot ('lamps', v5) vs. Greek 'torches of fire'; (5) The shophar (v1) vs. Greek 'trumpet'; (6) Ezekiel's signature kidmut vocabulary (vv6-7); (7) The שׁוֹר/ox (v7) matching Ezekiel where Greek has 'calf'; and (8) The keter/royal crown (vv4,10) vs. Greek stephanos/victor's wreath. The chapter also uses breastplate gemstone vocabulary (sapphire, jasper, nofech, achlamah) to describe the heavenly throne, linking it to the priestly vestments. The Hebrew merges Ezekiel's four chayyot with Isaiah's six-winged seraphim into a unified throne vision — a theological synthesis that arises naturally in Hebrew but would not emerge from Greek back-translation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שׁוֹפָר (shophar, H7782) — the ram's horn blown at Sinai (Ex 19:16,19, 20:18), on Yom Kippur (Lev 25:9), and at Jericho (Josh 6:4-20). Greek has σάλπιγγος (salpingos — 'trumpet'), a generic brass instrument. A back-translator from Greek would write חֲצוֹצְרָה (chatsotsrah, H2689 — the silver trumpet of Numbers 10:2) or transliterate. No translator encountering the generic Greek 'trumpet' would choose the specifically Israelite shophar — a ram's horn with Sinai covenant associations.

Uses שֶׁנִּפְתַּח פֶּתַח — the verb נִפְתַּח (niftach, niphal of פתח, 'was opened') immediately followed by the noun פֶּתַח (petach, 'opening/doorway'). This is a Hebrew wordplay on the root פ.ת.ח — 'an opening was opened.' Greek θύρα ἠνεῳγμένη ('a door having been opened') uses two unrelated roots (θύρα = door; ἀνοίγω = open), missing the Hebrew's internal sound play entirely. A back-translator from Greek would not reproduce this.

Uses רוֹצֶה לְהַרְאוֹת ('I desire to show you') — expressing personal will and desire (from רצה, H7521). Greek δείξω σοι is simply 'I will show you' — a neutral future. The Hebrew reveals the speaker's inner desire; the Greek merely states intention. A back-translator would write אַרְאֶה אוֹתְךָ ('I will show you'), not 'I desire to show you.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: בֹּא לְכָאן ('come here'). Greek: Ἀνάβα ὧδε ('come UP here'). Greek specifies upward ascent (ἀναβαίνω); Hebrew uses the neutral בוא (come) without directional ascent.
Hebrew: 'I desire to show you' (personal will). Greek: 'I will show you' (simple future). Different modality.
Hebrew has a textual gap marked by brackets [ ] after רָאִיתִי, suggesting a lacuna in the manuscript. The Greek text has no corresponding gap.
translation_notes: 'Shophar' is transliterated rather than translated as 'trumpet' to preserve the specific instrument — a curved ram's horn, not a metal trumpet. The shophar's sound accompanied the giving of Torah at Sinai.
'Opening' for petach rather than 'door' — the Hebrew uses petach (an opening/entrance, H6607), not דֶּלֶת (delet — a physical door). The heavens have an opening, not a door with hinges.

הַמְדַבֶּרֶת (hamedabberet) uses the feminine participle form, agreeing with קוֹל (voice), which can take feminine agreement in Hebrew. This grammatical feature is native Hebrew and would not arise from translation.
textual_notes: The shophar at heaven's opening echoes Exodus 19:16,19 where the shophar sounds at Sinai as YHWH descends. The seer is summoned by the same instrument that accompanied the original theophany.
Brackets [ ] in the source text after רָאִיתִי indicate a gap in the manuscript — possibly a word or phrase lost in transmission.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שׁוֹרֶה עָלַי רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ ('the Holy Spirit rested upon me') — the Spirit descends UPON the prophet, the classic OT prophetic formula (cf. Num 11:25-26, Isa 11:2, 61:1). Greek ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι ('I became in the spirit') reverses the direction — the prophet enters a spiritual state. These are opposite perspectives: Hebrew = the Spirit comes TO the person; Greek = the person enters THE spirit. A back-translator from Greek would write הָיִיתִי בָּרוּחַ ('I was in the spirit'), not 'the Spirit rested upon me.'

Uses תֵיכֶף וּמִיָּד — a doubled-emphasis phrase meaning 'immediately and at once,' a distinctly Hebraic intensification pattern (cf. Mishnaic Hebrew). The Greek has only εὐθέως ('immediately') — one word. No back-translator would spontaneously generate the Hebrew double-adverb construction from a single Greek word.

Uses יֹשֵׁב (yoshev, H3427) for BOTH the throne ('set/placed') AND the occupant ('sitting'). The same word describes the throne's establishment and the ruler's enthronement — a wordplay on the root י.שׁ.ב. Greek uses ἔκειτο ('was placed') for the throne and καθήμενος ('sitting') for the occupant — two different verbs. A back-translator would use two different Hebrew verbs too.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Holy Spirit rested upon me' (Spirit acts on prophet). Greek: 'I became in the spirit' (prophet enters state). Opposite directional metaphor.

Hebrew: רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ ('the Spirit of Holiness' — explicitly 'the Holy Spirit'). Greek: ἐν πνεύματι ('in spirit' — ambiguous, could mean 'in a spirit/ecstatic state'). The Hebrew is theologically explicit; the Greek is ambiguous.
translation_notes: תֵיכֶף (tekhef) is post-biblical Hebrew, common in Mishnaic literature. Its presence in this text reflects a Hebrew composition milieu, not a translation from Greek.

'Set' for the first יֹשֵׁב and 'sitting' for the second — both translate the same Hebrew word but capture the dual sense: the throne is 'seated' (established) in the heavens, and one is 'seated' (enthroned) upon it.
textual_notes: The phrase רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ (ruach ha-qodesh — 'Spirit of Holiness') appears in Psalm 51:13 and Isaiah 63:10-11. It is also the standard rabbinic Hebrew term for the Holy Spirit, used throughout Mishnah and Talmud.

one_way_hebrew: NEAR-VERBATIM from Ezekiel 1:26 — כְּמַרְאֵה אֶבֶן סַפִּיר ('like the appearance of a sapphire stone'). Ezekiel uses this exact phrase to describe the throne vision: כְּמַרְאֵה אֶבֶן סַפִּיר דְּמוּת כִּסֵּא (Ezek 1:26). The Hebrew Revelation preserves Ezekiel's distinctive vocabulary מַרְאֵה (mar'eh, H4758 — 'appearance/vision'). Greek ὅμοιος ὁράσει ('similar in appearance') is generic. A back-translator from Greek might use דוֹמֶה (domeh — 'resembling') or כְּעֵין (ke'ein — 'like the look of'), not the specific Ezekiel term.

Uses סַפִּיר וְיָשְׁפֵה ('sapphire and jasper'). Greek has ἰάσπιδι καὶ σαρδίῳ ('jasper and sardius/carnelian'). The Hebrew has DIFFERENT STONES in a DIFFERENT ORDER. Sapphire (סַפִּיר, H5601) appears in the Hebrew but NOT in the Greek; sardius (σάρδιον) appears in the Greek but NOT in the Hebrew. These are independent gem traditions — one cannot derive from the other.

Uses נֹפֶךְ (nofech, H5306) for the bow's color — one of the High Priest's breastplate stones (Ex 28:18, 39:11). Greek has σμαραγδίνῳ ('emerald'). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate σμαραγδ- or use בָּרֶקֶת (bareqet) or some other stone name, not the Torah breastplate vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sapphire and jasper' (סַפִּיר וְיָשְׁפֵה). Greek: 'jasper and sardius' (ἰάσπιδι καὶ σαρδίῳ). Different stones in different order.
Hebrew: bow 'like turquoise' (כמו נפך). Greek: bow 'like an emerald in appearance' (ὁμοία ὁράσει σμαραγδίνῳ). Different stone identifications.
translation_notes: 'Bow' for qeshet (H7198) — the same word means both 'rainbow' and 'war bow.' The Hebrew preserves this ambiguity; the word carries both the covenant sign (Gen 9:13-16, where God sets his qeshet in the clouds) and military imagery.
מַרְאֵיהוּ (mar'eihu) uses the archaic long possessive suffix -הוּ rather than the standard -וֹ. This is a feature of elevated/archaic Hebrew prose.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:26-28 provides the template: sapphire throne, a figure upon it, and a bow (qeshet) surrounding it. Ezekiel 1:28: כְּמַרְאֵה הַקֶּשֶׁת ('like the appearance of the bow'). The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this entire visual composition.

The breastplate stones (sapphire, jasper, nofech) connect the throne vision to the priestly garments — the divine throne is described in the same vocabulary as the High Priest's vestments (Exodus 28:17-20).

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'crown') — the royal crown of the Persian court (Esther 1:11, 2:17, 6:8). Greek has στεφάνους (stephanous — 'wreaths/victory garlands') — the athlete's or victor's wreath, not a royal crown. A back-translator from Greek would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — the standard Hebrew for stephanos) or would transliterate. No translator encountering the Greek victor's wreath would choose keter, the Persian royal diadem of Esther.

Uses לָבוּשׁ בְּמַלְבּוּשִׁים — 'clothed in garments,' an internal cognate construction where the verb (lavush, H3847 — 'clothed') and noun (malbushim, H4403 — 'garments') share the same root ל.ב.שׁ. This is a native Hebrew intensification pattern. Greek περιβεβλημένους ἐν ἱματίοις ('wrapped in garments') uses unrelated roots (περιβάλλω / ἱμάτιον). A back-translator would not spontaneously generate the Hebrew cognate pattern.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: כֶּתֶר (keter — royal crown). Greek: στεφάνους (stephanous — victor's wreath). Different types of headgear with different connotations.
Greek adds εἶδον ('I saw') — absent from the Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Crowns' for keter — preserving the royal crown meaning rather than the victor's wreath implied by the Greek. These are not garlands of victory but royal diadems.

'Elders' for zekeinim (H2205) — the standard OT word for tribal elders, city elders, and the elders of Israel who stood before YHWH (Ex 24:9-11). The heavenly council of elders mirrors Israel's earthly governance structure.
textual_notes: The twenty-four elders may correspond to the twenty-four priestly divisions (mishmarot) established by David in 1 Chronicles 24:1-19 for Temple service. Each division served in rotation; all twenty-four are represented before the heavenly throne.
The white garments echo the priestly linen garments (בִּגְדֵי בָד — Lev 16:4) worn for service in the Holy Place.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נֵרוֹת (nerot, H5216 — 'lamps') — the specific word for the lamps of the Menorah (Ex 25:37: וְעָשִׂיתָ אֶת נֵרֹתֶיהָ שִׁבְעָה — 'and you shall make its LAMPS seven'). The Hebrew sees seven MENORAH LAMPS before the throne — the heavenly Tabernacle's menorah. Greek has λαμπάδες πυρὸς καιόμεναι ('torches of fire burning'). A back-translator from Greek would write לַפִּידֵי אֵשׁ בּוֹעֲרִים ('burning torches of fire', cf. Gen 15:17), not the menorah-specific nerot. The Hebrew author identifies the seven lights as the menorah; the Greek translator rendered this as generic fiery torches.

Hebrew order: קוֹלוֹת וּרְעָמִים וּבְרָקִים ('sounds, thunders, lightnings'). Greek order: ἀστραπαὶ καὶ βρονταὶ καὶ φωναί ('lightnings, thunders, voices'). The orders are REVERSED. The Hebrew places 'sounds' first, matching the Sinai account where קֹלֹת (kolot — 'sounds/thunderclaps') comes first (Ex 19:16: קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים — 'sounds and lightnings'). The Hebrew follows OT Sinai word-order; the Greek does not.

Uses שִׁבְעָה רוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה ('seven spirits of YHWH', H3068) — with the divine name. Greek has ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ ('seven spirits of God'). The Hebrew preserves the Tetragrammaton; the Greek substitutes the generic 'God.' A back-translator from Greek would write שבע רוחות אלהים ('seven spirits of God'), not YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew order: sounds, thunders, lightnings. Greek order: lightnings, thunders, sounds. Completely reversed sequence.

Hebrew: נֵרוֹת ('lamps'). Greek: λαμπάδες πυρὸς καιόμεναι ('torches of fire burning'). Different objects — menorah lamps vs. burning torches. Greek adds 'of fire' and 'burning,' both absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'spirits of YHWH.' Greek: 'spirits of God.' Different divine name.
translation_notes: 'Lamps' for nerot — preserving the menorah connection. These are the seven-branched lampstand's lamps, not generic torches.

'Sounds' for kolot rather than 'voices' — the word קוֹל means both 'voice' and 'sound/thunder.' In the context of thunder and lightning, 'sounds' captures the Sinai theophany meaning (Ex 19:16 uses kolot for thunderclaps).
textual_notes: Exodus 19:16 at Sinai: וַיְהִי קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים וְעָנָן כָּבֵד עַל הָהָר וְקֹל שֹׁפָר חָזָק מְאֹד — 'And there were sounds and lightnings and a heavy cloud upon the mountain, and a very strong shophar sound.' The throne room vision recreates Sinai: sounds, lightning, and shophar (v1).

Zechariah 4:2-6 describes a golden menorah with seven lamps (שִׁבְעָה נֵרוֹתֶיהָ) and identifies them: 'Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit, says YHWH of Hosts.' The seven lamps = the Spirit of YHWH is already an OT equation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יָם (yam, H3220 — 'sea') — the word carries massive OT theological weight: the primordial chaos sea (Gen 1:10), the sea YHWH split (Ex 14-15), and the molten sea in Solomon's Temple (יָם מוּצָק, 1 Kings 7:23-26). The 'sea before the throne' directly parallels the bronze sea before the Temple. Greek θάλασσα ('sea') is neutral. While both say 'sea,' the Hebrew yam activates the entire Temple-cosmological complex.

Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut, H1823 — 'like the likeness of') — the EXACT word from Ezekiel's merkavah vision, used repeatedly (Ezek 1:5, 1:10, 1:13, 1:16, 1:22, 1:26, 1:28, 10:1). This is Ezekiel's signature visionary vocabulary. Greek ὁμοία ('resembling') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּמוֹ (kemo — 'like') or כְּעֵין (ke'ein — 'like the appearance of'), not the Ezekiel-specific demut.

Uses אַחְלָמָה (achlamah, H306) — one of the twelve High Priest's breastplate stones (Ex 28:19, 39:12). Greek has κρυστάλλῳ ('crystal'). A back-translator from Greek would write גָּבִישׁ or קֶרַח (ice/crystal), not the priestly breastplate gem. The Hebrew author consistently describes heavenly reality in breastplate vocabulary.

CRITICAL: Uses חַיּוֹת (chayyot, H2416 — 'living creatures') — the EXACT word from Ezekiel 1:5 for the four living creatures of the merkavah (chariot-throne): וּמִתּוֹכָהּ דְּמוּת אַרְבַּע חַיּוֹת ('and from its midst the likeness of four living creatures'). Greek ζῷα ('living beings') is a reasonable equivalent, but the Hebrew word directly invokes Ezekiel's specific vision. A back-translator might use בְּרִיּוֹת (briyot — 'creatures') or other terms, but the Ezekiel-trained Hebrew author naturally reaches for chayyot.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: צְלוֹחִית ('glass/flask' — a vessel word). Greek: ὑαλίνη ('glassy/of glass' — a material adjective). Same difference as in Rev 21:21.
Hebrew: כִּדְמוּת אַחְלָמָה ('like the likeness of crystal/amethyst'). Greek: ὁμοία κρυστάλλῳ ('resembling crystal'). Different comparison word and different material.
Brackets [ ] appear in the Hebrew text between וּבְתוֹךְ and הַכִּסֵּא, indicating a lacuna in the manuscript.
translation_notes: צְלוֹחִית (tselochit) is post-biblical Hebrew for a glass flask or vial. No standard Strong's number. It appears again in Rev 21:21.
'Living creatures' for chayyot — this is the standard translation of Ezekiel's chayyot. NOT 'beasts' or 'animals' — these are the angelic throne-bearers of the merkavah.
textual_notes: 1 Kings 7:23-26 — Solomon's Temple had a 'molten sea' (יָם מוּצָק) before the Temple entrance. The heavenly sea before the heavenly throne mirrors the earthly Temple's architecture. The Temple was built as a copy of the heavenly pattern (Ex 25:9,40).

Ezekiel 1:5,22 — the living creatures and something 'like the likeness of a firmament' (כְּעֵין הָרָקִיעַ) above them, 'like crystal' (כְּעֵין הַקֶּרַח). The sea of glass parallels Ezekiel's crystal firmament above the chayyot.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut, H1823) for the lion — again the Ezekiel merkavah word — then switches to the simple כְּ (ke — 'like') prefix for the remaining three creatures. This MATCHES Ezekiel's pattern in Ezek 1:5,10 where דְּמוּת introduces the creatures and then specific faces are listed with shorter comparisons. A back-translator from Greek would use the same comparison word for all four (ὅμοιον appears for each in Greek).

Uses שׁוֹר (shor, H7794 — 'ox/bull') — a mature working animal. Greek has μόσχῳ (moscho — 'calf/young bull'). This MATCHES Ezekiel 1:10 which has פְּנֵי שׁוֹר ('face of an ox'), not a calf. The Hebrew preserves Ezekiel's specific animal; the Greek substitutes a younger animal. A back-translator from Greek μόσχος would use עֵגֶל (egel — 'calf'), not shor.

Uses כְּאָדָם (ke-adam — 'like a man', H120) — matching Ezekiel 1:5 where the living creatures have דְּמוּת אָדָם ('the likeness of a man'). Greek has ἔχον τὸ πρόσωπον ὡς ἄνθρωπος ('having a face like a man') — it adds 'face' (πρόσωπον) which the Hebrew omits. The Hebrew is closer to Ezekiel's phrasing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: כְּשׁוֹר ('like an ox'). Greek: ὅμοιον μόσχῳ ('resembling a calf'). Different age of the animal — mature ox vs. young calf.
Hebrew: כְּאָדָם ('like a man'). Greek: ἔχον τὸ πρόσωπον ὡς ἄνθρωπος ('having a face like a man'). Greek adds 'face' — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: כְּנֶשֶׁר ('like an eagle'). Greek: ἀετῷ πετωμένῳ ('a flying eagle'). Greek adds 'flying' — absent from Hebrew.
Brackets [ ] appear in the Hebrew text before אַרְיֵה, indicating a gap in the manuscript — possibly a word like פני (face of) was lost.
translation_notes: 'Ox' for shor — NOT 'calf.' The Hebrew specifies a mature bovine, consistent with Ezekiel's vision.
'Man' for adam (H120) — the generic human/mankind term, connecting to the first adam of Genesis. Not אִישׁ (ish — 'a man/male individual') but the broader category of humanity.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:10 — וּדְמוּת פְּנֵיהֶם פְּנֵי אָדָם וּפְנֵי אַרְיֵה אֶל הַיָּמִין... וּפְנֵי שׁוֹר מֵהַשְּׂמֹאול... וּפְנֵי נֶשֶׁר ('the likeness of their faces: a face of a man, and a face of a lion on the right... a face of an ox on the left... and a face of an eagle'). The Hebrew Revelation preserves Ezekiel's EXACT animals: lion, ox, man, eagle — in the same creatures that Ezekiel saw.
The order lion-ox-man-eagle differs from Ezekiel's man-lion-ox-eagle but preserves the same four creatures. This reordering may reflect theological prioritization.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 6:3: קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת — 'Holy, holy, holy, YHWH of Hosts!' Isaiah's seraphim cry this before the throne. The Hebrew Revelation preserves the Isaiah quotation EXACTLY, including the compound divine name יהוה צבאות (YHWH Tsevaot). Greek has Ἅγιος ἅγιος ἅγιος Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('Holy holy holy Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי הָאֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי ('Lord God Almighty'), NOT the Isaiah quote. No translator encountering 'Lord God Almighty' would independently reconstruct the exact Isaiah 6:3 formula with YHWH Tsevaot.

CRITICAL — Uses הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה ('who was, and is, and shall be') — THREE FORMS of the root ה.ו.ה / ה.י.ה, from which the divine name YHWH derives. This is an ETYMOLOGICAL EXPANSION of the name YHWH itself: past (הָיָה), present (הֹוֶה), future (יִהְיֶה). The Hebrew author explicates what the name YHWH means — 'He who was, is, and shall be.' Greek changes the third element to ὁ ἐρχόμενος ('the coming one'), breaking the etymological connection to the divine name. A back-translator from Greek would write הַבָּא ('the coming one'), not יִהְיֶה ('shall be'). Only a Hebrew author thinking in Hebrew about the divine name would produce this tripartite formula.

Uses הָאַדִּיר (ha-addir, H117 — 'the Mighty/Majestic') — an OT divine epithet (Ps 8:2,10; 93:4; Ex 15:10-11; Isa 33:21). Greek has ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('the All-Ruler/Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek Pantokrator would use שַׁדַּי (Shaddai — 'Almighty'), the traditional Hebrew equivalent. No translator would choose the distinctive OT epithet addir from the Greek compound word.

Uses מְנוּחָה (menuchah, H4496 — 'rest') — the theologically weighted 'rest' of the Promised Land (Deut 12:9: כִּי לֹא בָאתֶם עַד עַתָּה אֶל הַמְּנוּחָה — 'for you have not yet come to the rest'), of the Sabbath (Ex 23:12), and of God's own dwelling place (Ps 132:14: זֹאת מְנוּחָתִי — 'this is my rest'). Greek ἀνάπαυσιν ('respite/pause') is generic. A back-translator might use מרגוע or הפוגה, not the Land/Sabbath/Temple rest word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת הָאַדִּיר ('YHWH of Hosts, the Mighty'). Greek: Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). Entirely different divine title construction.
Hebrew: וְיִהְיֶה ('and shall be' — future of 'to be'). Greek: ὁ ἐρχόμενος ('the coming one'). Different concept — ongoing existence vs. coming/arrival.
Hebrew: 'within filled with eyes.' Greek: κυκλόθεν καὶ ἔσωθεν γέμουσιν ὀφθαλμῶν ('around and within full of eyes'). Greek adds 'around' (κυκλόθεν); Hebrew has only 'within.'
translation_notes: הֹוֶה (hoveh) — the present participle from the root ה.ו.ה. The consonants הוה are the core of the divine name יהוה. The author is spelling out what YHWH means through its verbal forms.

'Hosts' for Tsevaot (H6635) — meaning heavenly armies/organized forces. YHWH Tsevaot = 'YHWH of Armies,' the God who commands the angelic hosts. NOT 'Lord Almighty' — the Hebrew is specifically military/organizational.
textual_notes: Isaiah 6:1-3 provides the direct source: 'I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up... Above it stood the seraphim: each one had six wings... And one cried unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, YHWH of Hosts.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces: (1) the throne, (2) the creatures with six wings, (3) the exact trisagion formula.

The six wings connect to Isaiah's seraphim (Isa 6:2) rather than Ezekiel's chayyot which have four wings (Ezek 1:6). The Hebrew Revelation MERGES Ezekiel's four living creatures (chayyot with four faces) with Isaiah's seraphim (six-winged singers of the trisagion). This synthesis is native to Hebrew theological thinking.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting unto everlasting') — the classic OT eternity formula appearing in Psalms 90:2 (מִן הָעוֹלָם עַד הָעוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל — 'from everlasting to everlasting you are God'), 103:17, 106:48, and 1 Chronicles 16:36. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). A back-translator from Greek would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים ('for ages of ages'), not the Psalmic formula. The Hebrew preserves the Psalter's exact phrasing.

WORDPLAY: The חַיּוֹת (chayyot — 'living creatures') give praise to הַחַי (hachai — 'the Living One'). Both derive from the root ח.י.ה (to live). The LIVING creatures worship the LIVING God. Greek ζῷα... τῷ ζῶντι preserves some connection but the Hebrew wordplay is phonetically sharper (chayyot/chai).

Uses שֶׁבַח וְהוֹדָאָה ('praise and thanksgiving'). Greek has δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν καὶ εὐχαριστίαν ('glory and honor and thanksgiving'). Hebrew has two items; Greek has three. Hebrew lacks 'glory' and 'honor'; Greek adds them. A back-translator from Greek would include כבוד ויקר ('glory and honor'), not omit them.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: שֶׁבַח וְהוֹדָאָה ('praise and thanksgiving' — two items). Greek: δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν καὶ εὐχαριστίαν ('glory and honor and thanksgiving' — three items). Different lists.
Hebrew: מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting unto everlasting' — Psalmic formula). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages' — Hellenistic formula).
translation_notes: שֶׁבַח (shevach) as a noun is more common in post-biblical and Aramaic usage (cf. Dan 2:23, 4:31). Its use here reflects the linguistic milieu of the Hebrew text.

הוֹדָאָה (hoda'ah — 'thanksgiving/confession') derives from the root ידה (yadah, H3034 — 'to give thanks/confess'). This root is used in Judah's name (Gen 29:35) and throughout the Psalms for thanksgiving.
textual_notes: Psalm 106:48 — בָּרוּךְ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִן הָעוֹלָם וְעַד הָעוֹלָם ('Blessed be YHWH, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting'). This is the doxology closing Book IV of the Psalter, using the identical eternity formula.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses וּמִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpalelim, hitpael of פלל, H6419 — 'praying'). This is the specific Hebrew verb for PRAYER — the hitpael reflexive form used throughout the OT for addressing God (1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:28, Dan 9:4). Greek has προσκυνήσουσιν ('they will worship/prostrate'). A back-translator from Greek proskuneo would use וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ (vayishtachavu — 'and they bowed down/worshipped'), the standard Hebrew equivalent of proskuneo. No translator would render 'prostrate' as 'pray' (hitpalel). The Hebrew author sees the elders engaged in Jewish prayer, not merely physical prostration.

CRITICAL: Uses וְזוֹרְקִים (zorekim, H2236 — 'casting/dashing') — the specific PRIESTLY verb for dashing sacrificial blood against the altar (Lev 1:5,11; 3:2; 7:2; 8:19,24; 9:12; Num 18:17; 2 Kings 16:13; 2 Chron 29:22). The elders DASH their crowns before YHWH as a priest dashes blood. Greek βαλοῦσιν (balousin — 'they will throw/cast') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use הִשְׁלִיכוּ (hishlichu — 'they threw') or הֵנִיחוּ (henichu — 'they laid down'), NOT the sacrificial zaraq. This verb transforms the scene into a priestly offering — the crowns become a sacrifice.

Uses לְפָנָיו ('before HIM') for where the crowns are cast. Greek has ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου ('before the THRONE'). The Hebrew directs the offering to the PERSON; the Greek directs it to the FURNITURE. A back-translator from Greek would write לפני הכסא ('before the throne'), not לפניו ('before him').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: וּמִתְפַּלְּלִים ('and praying'). Greek: προσκυνήσουσιν ('and they will worship/prostrate'). Different actions — Jewish prayer vs. physical prostration.
Hebrew: 'casting (zaraq) their crowns before HIM.' Greek: 'casting (ballo) their crowns before the THRONE.' Different verb and different recipient.
Hebrew: כִּתְרֵיהֶם ('their crowns' — keter, royal diadems). Greek: στεφάνους ('their wreaths' — stephanos, victory garlands). Same distinction as verse 4.
translation_notes: 'Praying' for mitpalelim — preserving the specifically Jewish prayer-verb rather than generic 'worshipping.' The hitpael of פלל carries the reflexive sense of self-examination before God.

'Casting' for zorekim — though it may seem an unusual translation for what the elders do with their crowns, the priestly-sacrificial connotation of zaraq is essential. They do not merely 'throw' or 'lay down' their crowns; they OFFER them as a priest offers blood.
textual_notes: Leviticus 1:5 — וְזָרְקוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִם אֶת הַדָּם עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ סָבִיב ('and the sons of Aaron the priests shall dash the blood against the altar around'). The same verb zaraq is used for the elders' crown-offering, making them priestly figures performing a sacrifice before YHWH.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בֹּרֵא (boré, H1254 — 'Creator') — the active participle of the verb used EXCLUSIVELY for divine creation in the OT (Gen 1:1: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים — 'In the beginning Elohim created'). ברא is NEVER used of human making — only God בורא. Greek ἔκτισας ('you created') is a generic creation verb (κτίζω can be used of human founding of cities). A back-translator from Greek would use בָּרָאתָ (barata — past tense 'you created') as a verb, not the participial title-form בֹּרֵא ('you are Creator'). The Hebrew presents creation as God's ongoing identity — 'you ARE Creator' — not merely a past act.

CRITICAL: Uses עַל יַד רְצוֹנְךָ ('by the hand of your will', H3027 + H7522) — the Hebrew idiom עַל יַד (al yad — 'by the hand of/through the agency of') makes the divine will PHYSICAL and CONCRETE. The 'hand' (yad) of God's desire fashioned all things. Greek has only διὰ τὸ θέλημά σου ('through your will') — abstract, no hand. A back-translator from Greek would write בִּגְלַל רְצוֹנְךָ ('because of your will') or עַל פִּי רְצוֹנְךָ ('according to your will'), not the 'hand' idiom. The hand of God is a distinctive Hebrew theological motif (Ex 15:6, Deut 2:15, Josh 4:24, Isa 41:20, 48:13).

Uses אָדוֹן (Adon, H136 — 'Lord/Master'). Greek has ὁ Κύριος καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ('the Lord and our God'). The Hebrew uses the single OT title Adon; the Greek expands to 'Lord AND our God.' A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי וֵאלֹהֵינוּ ('our Lord and our God'), not the singular Adon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: אָדוֹן ('Lord'). Greek: ὁ Κύριος καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ('the Lord and our God'). Greek expands to a double title with possessive 'our.'

Hebrew: כָּבוֹד וְתִפְאֶרֶת ('glory and splendor' — two items). Greek: τὴν δόξαν καὶ τὴν τιμὴν καὶ τὴν δύναμιν ('glory and honor and power' — three items). Greek adds δύναμιν ('power'), absent from Hebrew. Hebrew has תפארת ('splendor'); Greek has τιμήν ('honor') — different concepts.
Hebrew: נַעֲשָׂה הַכֹּל ('all was made' — one verb, passive). Greek: εἰσὶν καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν ('they exist and were created' — two verbs). Greek adds 'they exist' (εἰσίν), absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: רְאוּיָה (re'uyah — 'worthy') is a post-biblical Hebrew form from the root ראה (to see), meaning 'fit/fitting/worthy.' No standard Strong's number. Its feminine form here may agree with an implied subject or reflect late Hebrew gender flexibility.

'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) — a word encompassing beauty, glory, and ornamental majesty. It is used of the priestly garments (Ex 28:2: לְכָבוֹד וּלְתִפְאָרֶת — 'for glory and for splendor') and of YHWH himself (Isa 60:19, 1 Chron 29:11).
'Creator' for boré (active participle) rather than 'you created' (past tense) — the Hebrew makes creation a defining title, not merely a historical event.
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 29:11 (David's prayer) — לְךָ יְהוָה הַגְּדֻלָּה וְהַגְּבוּרָה וְהַתִּפְאֶרֶת ('Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the power and the splendor'). The same תִּפְאֶרֶת (tiferet) appears in this heavenly doxology as in David's earthly doxology.

Genesis 1:1 uses בָּרָא (bara) for divine creation. The participial form בֹּרֵא ('Creator') makes this a present-tense identity: the one on the throne IS and REMAINS the Creator. Isaiah 40:28 uses this form: בּוֹרֵא קְצוֹת הָאָרֶץ ('Creator of the ends of the earth').
Isaiah 48:13 — אַף יָדִי יָסְדָה אֶרֶץ ('indeed my HAND founded the earth'). The 'hand' of God as the agent of creation is a recurring Hebrew motif that the Greek text loses.

5.summary: Revelation 5 in Hebrew is saturated with Temple/Tabernacle liturgical vocabulary and Psalm doxology patterns that could not plausibly derive from back-translation of the Greek text. The strongest one-way markers are: (1) מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans/censers', v8) vs. Greek φιάλας ('bowls') — the Levitical Yom Kippur implement has no connection to the Greek word; (2) מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת ('from the clan', v5) vs. Greek φυλῆς ('tribe') — a more specific kinship term no back-translator would choose; (3) רוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה ('spirits of YHWH', v6) quoting Zechariah 4:10, where Greek substitutes the generic θεός; (4) the Psalm doxology formula מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם (vv. 13-14) vs. Greek εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων; (5) כֹהֲנִים before מְלָכִים ('priests before kings', v10), following Exodus 19:6 priority against the Greek order; (6) the sealed-deed language of verse 1 echoing Jeremiah 32:10-14; (7) לִשְׁבֹּר ('to break', vv. 2,5) vs. Greek λῦσαι ('to loose') for the seals; (8) קָנִיתָ ('you acquired/created', v9) vs. commercial Greek ἠγόρασας ('you bought'). The chapter also contains multiple distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew forms — רְאוּיָה (worthy, feminine invariable), כֵּיוָן שֶׁ (since), בְשָׁעָה שֶׁ (in the moment that), שׁוּם (any) — that fingerprint authentic Hebrew composition in the Second Temple period, not back-translation. The attribute lists consistently differ between Hebrew and Greek (4 vs. 7 in v12; 3 vs. 4 in v13), ruling out translation in either direction. The Hebrew text presents a coherent Yom Kippur-in-heaven scene: the Passover lamb (שה) stands before the throne as High Priest, the fire-pans (מחתות) carry incense (קטורת) = prayer (תפלה), the lyre (כנור) of David accompanies the new song (שיר חדש) of the Psalms, and the elders answer Amen (עונים אמן) in the pattern of 1 Chronicles 16:36 and Nehemiah 8:6.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The scroll is described as חָתוּם בַּחֲתִימוֹת מִבִּפְנִים וּמִבַּחוּץ — 'sealed with seals from within and from without.' This matches the ancient Israelite double-sealed deed described in Jeremiah 32:10-14, where Jeremiah's deed of purchase (ספר המקנה) had a sealed copy and an open copy. Seven seals parallel the practice of witnesses sealing a legal document. Greek says γεγραμμένον ἔσωθεν καὶ ὄπισθεν κατεσφραγισμένον ('written within and on the back, sealed') — describing WRITING on both sides, not SEALING on both sides. The Hebrew sees a legal deed; the Greek sees a manuscript. No back-translator from Greek would describe sealing on both sides when the Greek describes writing on both sides.

Uses סֵפֶר (sefer, H5612 — 'scroll/document') — the word for a legal document in Jeremiah 32:10-14 (ספר המקנה — 'deed of purchase'). Greek βιβλίον is generic 'book/scroll.' The Hebrew implies a legal deed requiring witnessed seals.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sealed with seals from within and from without' — describes double-sealing. Greek: 'written within and on the back, sealed' — describes writing on both sides with sealing mentioned separately.
Hebrew: 'in his right hand' (ביד ימינו — explicitly 'hand'). Greek: ἐπὶ τὴν δεξιάν ('upon the right') — no explicit 'hand.'
translation_notes: חֲתִימוֹת (chatimot — 'seals') is from the root חתם (chatam, H2856 — 'to seal'). This is a later Hebrew noun form, not the biblical חוֹתָם (chotam, H2368 — 'signet ring/seal'). The form chatimot suggests the act of sealing, not the seal-object itself — the seals as legal attestations, not as physical stamp-rings.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 32:10-14 describes the sealed deed: 'I signed the deed (ספר), sealed it (ואחתם), got witnesses... I took the deed of purchase, both that which was sealed (החתום) and that which was open (הגלוי).' The same vocabulary of sefer + chatam appears here in Revelation 5. The scroll before the throne is a legal deed — a title deed to creation that requires an authorized heir to open.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִשְׁבֹּר (lishbor — 'to break', H7665) for the seals. Greek has λῦσαι ('to loose/untie'). The Hebrew verb שָׁבַר implies violent, irreversible rupture — breaking a vessel (Jer 19:11), breaking a yoke (Jer 28:2,10), breaking bones (Ex 12:46). A back-translator from Greek λῦσαι ('loose') would use התיר (hitir — 'to untie/release'), NOT the forceful destruction verb שבר. The breaking of seals echoes the breaking of the covenant tablets — an act of sovereign authority.

Uses צֹעֵק (tso'eq — 'crying out', H6817) — the specific Hebrew verb for cries of distress or urgent proclamation (Gen 4:10 — Abel's blood 'cries out'; Ex 2:23 — Israel 'cried out' under slavery; Judg 3:9,15). Greek κηρύσσοντα means 'proclaiming/heralding' — an official announcement. A back-translator from Greek would use מכריז (machriz — 'proclaiming'), not the raw, urgent tso'eq.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἰσχυρόν ('strong/mighty') to describe the messenger — absent in Hebrew. Hebrew just says 'one messenger.'
Hebrew: 'to break' (לשבר) the seals. Greek: 'to loose' (λῦσαι) the seals. Different physical action.
translation_notes: רְאוּיָה (re'uyah — 'worthy') is in the FEMININE form, even though it describes a masculine subject. This is characteristic of Mishnaic Hebrew, where ראויה became an invariable predicate adjective. No back-translator from Greek ἄξιος (masculine 'worthy') would produce this distinctly later Hebrew feminine form. This word appears repeatedly in the chapter (vv. 2, 4, 9, 12) and has no standard Strong's number — it is a post-biblical Hebrew adjective from the root ראה.
