greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'praying to YHWH' (prayer verb + Tetragrammaton). Greek: 'worshipped God' (prostration verb + generic divine title).
translation_notes: 'Praying' for mitpallelim — the hitpael of פלל is the standard Hebrew prayer verb, covering petition, intercession, and worship-through-speech. It implies verbal communion, not mere prostration.
'Living-creatures' for chayyot preserves the Ezekiel throne-vision connection without misleadingly rendering it as 'animals' or 'beasts.'

one_way_hebrew: The sevenfold doxology uses distinctly Hebrew liturgical vocabulary: שֶׁבַח (shebach — 'praise'), הוֹדָאָה (hoda'ah — 'thanksgiving'), תְּהִילּוֹת (tehillot — 'praises', the word that titles the Book of Psalms). Greek's sevenfold list differs significantly: εὐλογία (blessing), δόξα (glory), σοφία (WISDOM), εὐχαριστία (thanksgiving), τιμή (honor), δύναμις (power), ἰσχύς (strength). Where Hebrew has תְּהִילּוֹת ('praises'), Greek has σοφία ('wisdom') — completely unrelated concepts. A back-translator could not independently produce this Hebrew liturgical vocabulary from the Greek list.

Hebrew: [מֵעוֹלָם] וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from eternity and unto eternity') — a BIDIRECTIONAL eternal formula encompassing both past and future. Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages') — future-directed only. The Hebrew echoes Psalm 90:2: מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל ('From eternity to eternity, you are El'). A back-translator from the Greek future-only formula would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים, not the bidirectional Psalm formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew sevenfold list: praise (שֶׁבַח), thanksgiving (הוֹדָאָה), praises (תְּהִילּוֹת), glory (כָּבוֹד), splendor (תִּפְאֶרֶת), power (כֹּחַ), might (גְבוּרָה). Greek sevenfold list: blessing (εὐλογία), glory (δόξα), wisdom (σοφία), thanksgiving (εὐχαριστία), honor (τιμή), power (δύναμις), strength (ἰσχύς). Only partial overlap; 'praises' vs. 'wisdom' is an irreconcilable difference.
Greek places Amen both before and after the doxology. Hebrew has Amen only at the end.
translation_notes: The bracketed [מֵעוֹלָם] indicates an editorial restoration of a damaged or missing word in the manuscript — a textual-critical feature characteristic of Hebrew manuscript tradition, not back-translation.
תְּהִילּוֹת (tehillot) is the plural of תְּהִלָּה (tehillah, H8416), the word that names the Book of Psalms (סֵפֶר תְּהִלִּים). Its appearance in a doxology is natural Hebrew worship language.
textual_notes: Psalm 90:2: מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל — 'From eternity to eternity, you are El.' The Hebrew doxology formula echoes this.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מֵאֵיזֶה מָקוֹם (me-eizeh maqom — 'from which place', H4725) where Greek has simply πόθεν ('whence'). The Hebrew asks about the specific place of origin; the Greek asks a generic directional question. The phrase מֵאֵיזֶה מָקוֹם is a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew construction that a back-translator from Greek's simple πόθεν would never produce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from which place did they come?' (מֵאֵיזֶה מָקוֹם — asks about specific place). Greek: 'whence did they come?' (πόθεν — generic direction).
translation_notes: מֵאֵיזֶה (me-eizeh — 'from which') is a post-biblical Hebrew interrogative, characteristic of Mishnaic syntax.
וַיַּעַן (vayya'an — 'and he answered', H6030) uses the wayyiqtol narrative form, natural for Hebrew storytelling.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses וְזִקְּקוּ (v'ziqqu — 'and they refined', H2212, piel of זקק) — a METALLURGICAL term meaning to purify metals by smelting (Mal 3:3, Ps 12:7 [6], Job 28:1). Greek: ἐλεύκαναν (eleukanan — 'they whitened/bleached') from λευκαίνω. A back-translator from Greek would use הִלְבִּינוּ (hilbinu — 'they whitened') from the root לבן. The Hebrew says the garments were REFINED as silver in a crucible; the Greek says they were BLEACHED white. These are entirely different metaphors — refiner's fire vs. laundry. The Hebrew connects to Malachi 3:2-3 where the coming messenger will 'sit as a refiner and purifier (מְזַקֵּק) of silver.'

Hebrew: מִתּוֹךְ הַרְבֵּה צַעַר ('from the midst of much distress'). Greek: ἐκ τῆς θλίψεως τῆς μεγάλης ('out of the great tribulation'). Hebrew מִתּוֹךְ (mitoch — 'from the midst/through the center of') implies passing THROUGH the heart of distress, not merely coming out of it. And הַרְבֵּה (harbeh — 'much') is quantitative while Greek μεγάλης ('great') is qualitative. The Hebrew צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress') is a less technical term than Greek θλῖψις ('tribulation'). A back-translator from the technical Greek would use הַצָּרָה הַגְּדוֹלָה (ha-tsarah ha-gedolah — 'the great tribulation') from צרה (H6869).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'refined' (וְזִקְּקוּ — metallurgical purification). Greek: 'whitened' (ἐλεύκαναν — bleaching). Different conceptual world.
Hebrew: 'from the midst of much distress' (quantitative, non-technical). Greek: 'out of the great tribulation' (qualitative, with definite article suggesting a specific event).
translation_notes: 'Refined' for ziqqu — the root זקק means to purify metals by smelting. The garments are purified not by bleaching but through the refiner's fire of the lamb's blood.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/trouble') is a post-biblical Hebrew form without a standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Malachi 3:2-3: 'For he is like a refiner's fire and like launderers' soap. He shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (מְזַקֵּק וּמְטַהֵר כֶּסֶף), and he shall purify the sons of Levi.' The same root זקק links the purification of the saints' garments to the Malachi refining prophecy.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses וְשֵׁרְתוּ (v'shertu — 'and they minister', H8334, from שרת) — the specific verb for priestly/Levitical SERVICE before YHWH: Aaron's priestly garments worn 'when he ministers' (בְּשָׁרְתוֹ, Ex 28:35,43); the Levites 'minister before the tabernacle' (Num 1:50, 3:6); 'YHWH set apart Levi to minister before him' (Deut 10:8); Samuel 'ministered before YHWH' (1 Sam 2:11). Greek λατρεύουσιν ('they serve/worship') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use עָבְדוּ (avdu — 'they served'), the standard equivalent of λατρεύω in the LXX. The Hebrew sees this innumerable company performing PRIESTLY ministry.

The feminine verb תָּדוּר ('she shall dwell', from root דור — 'to dwell', cf. Ps 84:11, Isa 38:12) appears with the masculine subject 'the one who sits on the throne' (וְזֶה שֶׁיֹּשֵׁב). This gender mismatch implies an unstated feminine entity as the actual dwelling agent — almost certainly the שְׁכִינָה (Shekhinah, the divine indwelling presence), which is grammatically feminine in Hebrew. Greek σκηνώσει ('shall tabernacle') has no gender marking, so this theological depth is invisible in the Greek. No back-translator would introduce a feminine verb where a masculine subject is clear.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the throne of YHWH' (הַכִּסֵּא יַהְוֶה — with Tetragrammaton). Greek: 'the throne of God' (τοῦ θρόνου τοῦ θεοῦ).
Hebrew: תָּדוּר (feminine — 'she shall dwell', hinting at Shekhinah). Greek: σκηνώσει ('shall tabernacle/tent') — genderless, with tabernacle connotation absent from Hebrew דור.
Hebrew uses 'in his temple' (ἐν τῷ ναῷ αὐτοῦ) is absent — the phrase appears only in Greek, not in this Hebrew text.
translation_notes: 'Minister' for shertu preserves the priestly-service connotation. This is the verb of Levitical service before YHWH, not generic worship.
בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'because of/for the sake of') is a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew preposition, absent from biblical Hebrew.

תָּדוּר from root דור ('to dwell', cf. Ps 84:11 מִדּוּר 'from dwelling') rather than the expected שכן ('to dwell/tabernacle') which would directly match the Greek σκηνόω. The choice of דור over שכן may be deliberate — avoiding the tabernacle-specific terminology.
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 29:23: 'Solomon sat on the throne of YHWH (כִּסֵּא יְהוָה) as king.' The phrase 'throne of YHWH' is a specific OT construction.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: This is a VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 49:10: לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ וְלֹא יַכֵּם שָׁרָב וָשָׁמֶשׁ — 'They shall not hunger and not thirst, and scorching heat and sun shall not strike them.' The Hebrew matches Isaiah WORD FOR WORD. Greek changes the order: ὁ ἥλιος (sun) first, then καῦμα (heat) — the reverse of Isaiah's and Hebrew Revelation's שָׁרָב (scorching heat) THEN שָׁמֶשׁ (sun). Greek also adds ἔτι ('anymore') twice, absent from both Isaiah and this Hebrew text. A back-translator from Greek would follow the Greek order and include ἔτι. The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact sequence.

Uses שָׁרָב (sharav, H8273 — 'scorching heat/mirage') — an extremely rare word occurring only in Isaiah 35:7 and 49:10 in the entire OT. Greek καῦμα ('heat') is a common, generic word. A back-translator would use the common חֹם (chom — 'heat', H2527), not the rare Isaiah-specific sharav. The presence of this rare vocabulary IS the Isaiah quotation — it could not arise independently.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'scorching heat and sun' (שָׁרָב וָשָׁמֶשׁ — Isaiah 49:10 order). Greek: 'the sun... any heat' (ὁ ἥλιος... πᾶν καῦμα — reversed order).
Greek adds ἔτι ('anymore') twice — absent from both the Hebrew and from Isaiah's original.
translation_notes: The pronoun וְהִיא (v'hi — feminine singular) preceding masculine plural verbs is notable. It likely functions as a collective pronoun referring back to the חַבְרוּתָה (fellowship, feminine noun) of v9, or as a discourse marker. The feminine reference preserves grammatical agreement with the feminine noun introduced four verses earlier.
textual_notes: Isaiah 49:10 (source text): לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ וְלֹא יַכֵּם שָׁרָב וָשָׁמֶשׁ כִּי מְרַחֲמָם יְנַהֲגֵם וְעַל מַבּוּעֵי מַיִם יְנַהֲלֵם ('They shall not hunger nor thirst, scorching heat and sun shall not strike them, for he who has compassion on them shall lead them, and by springs of water shall guide them.'). The first half is quoted verbatim in v16; the second half's theme (leading to waters) is taken up in v17.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּאֵר מַיִם (be'er mayim — 'a well of waters', H875). Greek: ζωσὰς πηγὰς ὑδάτων ('living springs of waters'). A back-translator from Greek πηγή ('spring/fountain') would write מַעְיָן (ma'yan — 'spring') or מָקוֹר (maqor — 'source/fountain'), NEVER בְּאֵר (be'er — 'well'). A well is DUG; a spring flows naturally. The Hebrew evokes the patriarchal wells of Genesis: Hagar's well (Gen 16:14), Be'er-sheva (Gen 21:31), Isaac's wells (Gen 26:18-25), the well where Jacob meets Rachel (Gen 29:2). Greek adds ζωσάς ('living') which is absent from Hebrew — the Hebrew's 'well of waters' is sufficient without the qualifier.

CRITICAL: The second half is a NEAR-VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 25:8: וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים ('And the Lord YHWH will wipe a tear from upon all faces'). This Hebrew text has יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים instead of אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה, but the construction is identical: 'shall wipe... a tear... from upon all faces' (מָחָה...דִּמְעָה...מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים). Greek: ἐξαλείψει ὁ θεὸς πᾶν δάκρυον ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν ('God shall wipe every tear from their eyes'). The Greek changes 'from upon all FACES' to 'from their EYES,' and 'a tear' to 'every tear.' A back-translator from Greek would write כָּל דִּמְעָה מֵעֵינֵיהֶם, not the Isaiah quotation.

Uses יְנַהֲגֵם (yenahaagem — 'shall lead them', H5090) — continuing the Isaiah 49:10 allusion where the second half reads כִּי מְרַחֲמָם יְנַהֲגֵם ('for he who has compassion on them shall LEAD them'). The SAME verb נהג in the SAME conjugation. The lamb takes the role of Isaiah's 'compassionate one.' Greek uses TWO verbs: ποιμανεῖ ('shall shepherd') AND ὁδηγήσει ('shall guide'). A back-translator from Greek would produce both verbs, not the single נהג that directly quotes Isaiah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a well of waters' (בְּאֵר מַיִם — dug well, no modifier). Greek: 'living springs of waters' (ζωσὰς πηγὰς ὑδάτων — natural springs, with 'living' modifier). Different water source entirely.

Hebrew: 'a tear from upon all faces' (דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים — Isaiah 25:8 quotation). Greek: 'every tear from their eyes' (πᾶν δάκρυον ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν). Different body part (faces vs. eyes), different quantity (a tear vs. every tear).
Hebrew: one verb 'shall lead them' (יְנַהֲגֵם — from Isaiah 49:10). Greek: two verbs 'shall shepherd... and shall guide' (ποιμανεῖ... ὁδηγήσει). Greek adds the shepherding verb.
Greek adds 'that which is in the midst of the throne' (τὸ ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ θρόνου) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Well of waters' for be'er mayim — preserving the dug-well imagery that evokes the patriarchal narrative. A well requires labor and intention; it is sought and found.
'Shall lead' for yenahaagem — the verb נהג (H5090) means to drive/lead, used for driving flocks (Gen 31:18, Ex 3:1) and leading people (Isa 49:10, 2 Chr 25:11).
textual_notes: Isaiah 49:10b: כִּי מְרַחֲמָם יְנַהֲגֵם וְעַל מַבּוּעֵי מַיִם יְנַהֲלֵם ('for he who has compassion on them shall lead them, and by springs of water shall guide them'). The Revelation Hebrew substitutes בְּאֵר (well) for מַבּוּעֵי (springs) but preserves the verb נהג and the leading-to-waters theme. The lamb takes the role of Isaiah's 'compassionate one' (מְרַחֲמָם).

Isaiah 25:8: וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים — the identical construction appears here with a different divine name form (YHWH Elohim instead of Adonai YHVH). This is the same Isaiah 25:8 quotation found in Revelation 21:4.

8.summary:
Revelation 8 in Hebrew is structured as a three-part liturgical drama: (1) the Yom Kippur ceremony (vv.3-5), (2) the Exodus plague sequence (vv.7-12), and (3) the Jericho shofar pattern (throughout). The Hebrew vocabulary consistently uses Torah/Temple terminology that the Greek cannot capture.

The chapter contains at least 15 strong one-way translation markers:

1. שׁוֹפָרוֹת (shopharot — 'ram's horns') vs Greek σάλπιγγες ('trumpets') — used three times (vv.2,6,13), connecting to Jericho (Josh 6), Sinai (Ex 19), and Yom Kippur (Lev 25:9).
2. מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans') — Levitical fire-pan vocabulary (Lev 16:12, Num 16:6) vs Greek λιβανωτόν ('censer').
3. תְּקִיעָה vocabulary: לִתְקוֹעַ/תּוֹקֵעַ (to blast) — the shofar-specific verb vs generic Greek σαλπίζω.
4. דָּרַךְ (darakh — 'trod') vs Greek ἐστάθη ('stood') — dynamic priestly approach vs static posture.
5. יָצַק (yatsaq — 'poured') vs Greek ἔβαλεν ('threw') — liturgical pouring vs violent casting.
6. בָּלוּל (balul — 'mixed') — Torah offering/Babel vocabulary vs generic Greek μεμιγμένα.
7. יֶרֶק הַשָּׂדֶה ('green herbage of the field') — Exodus plague vegetation vs Greek χόρτος ('grass').
8. הָלַךְ (halakh — 'went') for the burning mountain vs Greek ἐβλήθη ('was thrown') — active vs passive agency.
9. נִטְבְּעוּ (nitbe'u — 'were sunk') — Red Sea verb (Ex 15:4) vs Greek διεφθάρη ('destroyed').
10. בְּאֵרוֹת (be'erot — 'wells') — patriarchal vocabulary vs Greek ποταμοί ('rivers').
11. תּוֹלַעַת (tola'at — 'Worm') vs Greek Ἄψινθος ('Wormwood') — entirely different names.
12. נִלְקָה (nilqah — 'was eclipsed') — technical astronomical Hebrew vs Greek ἐπλήγη ('struck').
13. רֹחֵף (rochef — 'hovering') — Genesis 1:2 creation verb vs Greek πετωμένου ('flying').
14. Aramaic חֲדָא (chada — 'one') — bilingual code-switching impossible in back-translation.
15. קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'thunderings') — Exodus plague vocabulary (Ex 9:23) setting up the plague sequence.

EXODUS PLAGUE PARALLELS: The four shofar judgments replay the Exodus plagues in sequence: (1) hail and fire (7th plague, Ex 9:23-24), (2) water→blood (1st plague, Ex 7:20), (3) bitter water (Marah, Ex 15:23), (4) darkness (9th plague, Ex 10:21-23). The Hebrew vocabulary in each case uses the Exodus terminology directly.

YOM KIPPUR CEREMONY: Verses 3-5 reproduce the Day of Atonement ritual with exact Levitical vocabulary: the fire-pan (machtah, Lev 16:12), incense (qetoret), the sanctuary (heikhal), smoke ascending before YHWH. The priestly intercession precedes the judgments — the prayers of the holy ones are offered before the plagues are poured out.

JERICHO PATTERN: Seven shopharot, seven messengers, sequential blasting — directly mirroring Joshua 6:4 (seven priests with seven shopharot of jubilee). The walls of the old world are breached as Jericho's walls fell.

CREATION UNDONE: The chapter systematically reverses Genesis 1 — earth struck (v7), sea struck (vv.8-9), fresh water struck (vv.10-11), luminaries struck (v12) — moving backwards through the days of creation. The messenger who witnesses this uses the Genesis 1:2 hovering verb (rachaf), closing the circle. What began with the Spirit hovering over the deep ends with a messenger hovering over the ruins.

one_way_hebrew: Uses Aramaic חֲדָא (chada — 'one') instead of Hebrew אֶחָד/אַחַת (echad/achat). This is a bilingual marker — a Hebrew author naturally code-switching into Aramaic, as first-century Jews did daily. A back-translator from Greek ἡμιώριον ('half an hour') would use the standard Hebrew אחת, not an Aramaic numeral. The casual mixing of Hebrew and Aramaic is a hallmark of authentic first-century Jewish composition.

Uses כֵּיוָן (keivan — 'when/as soon as') — a post-biblical Hebrew conjunction from Aramaic. Biblical Hebrew would use כַּאֲשֶׁר (ka'asher). No back-translator from Greek ὅτε ('when') would produce this distinctively later Hebrew/Aramaic form.

Uses שׁוֹתְקִים (shotkím — active participle, 'were being silent', H8367) — all of them actively silenced themselves. Greek σιγή (sige) is a noun ('silence') — a passive state. The Hebrew depicts persons choosing to be silent; the Greek merely reports that silence existed. A back-translator from the Greek noun would use a nominal construction like דממה (demamah — 'stillness'), not the active participle of שתק.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'about one hour' (כְּשָׁעָה חֲדָא). Greek: 'about half an hour' (ὡς ἡμιώριον). The Hebrew has a full hour; the Greek has half.
Hebrew: 'the seventh' — no object specified, relying on context. Greek: 'the seventh seal' (τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν ἑβδόμην) — makes the referent explicit.
translation_notes: The Hebrew omits 'seal' (חותם) after 'the seventh,' relying on the reader to follow from the preceding chapter. This economy of expression is characteristic of Hebrew narrative style.
textual_notes: The mixing of Hebrew and Aramaic (כיון, חדא) alongside standard Hebrew forms places this text in the linguistic world of first-century Jewish Palestine, where both languages were in daily use. This is natural for a native author but implausible for a back-translator working from a single-language Greek source.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שׁוֹפָרוֹת (shopharot — 'ram's horns', H7782) — the specific curved horn of a ram, blown in Torah ceremonies (Lev 25:9), at Sinai (Ex 19:16,19), and at Jericho (Josh 6:4-20). Greek uses σάλπιγγες (salpinges — 'trumpets'), a generic term for metal instruments. A back-translator from Greek would use חֲצוֹצְרוֹת (chatsotsrot — 'trumpets', Num 10:2) — the Hebrew word for the silver trumpets. No one translating σάλπιγξ would choose שׁוֹפָר, the ram's horn of the covenant. This single word choice connects the seven blasts to Jericho, to Sinai, and to Yom Kippur. The Hebrew author writes shopharot throughout this chapter (vv.2,6,13) — never trumpets.

Uses בָּאִים (ba'im — 'coming', active participle of H935) — the messengers are arriving in procession before YHWH. Greek has ἑστήκασι ('have stood/stand' — perfect of ἵστημι), depicting them already stationed. The Hebrew presents a dynamic scene of approach; the Greek presents a static tableau. A back-translator from Greek would use עוֹמְדִים (omdim — 'standing'), not באים.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: לִפְנֵי יַהְוֶה ('before YHWH'). Greek: ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ ('before God'). The Hebrew uses the personal covenant name; the Greek uses the generic title. This pattern recurs throughout the chapter (vv.2,4).
Hebrew: 'coming before' (באים). Greek: 'standing before' (ἑστήκασι). Different postures — procession vs. station.
translation_notes: 'Ram's horns' for shopharot — the shofar is specifically the curved horn of a ram (or ibex), not a manufactured metal instrument. The seven shopharot echo the seven ram's horns of Jericho (Josh 6:4: שִׁבְעָה שׁוֹפְרוֹת הַיּוֹבְלִים — 'seven ram's horns of jubilee').
textual_notes: The seven-shofar pattern is established in Joshua 6:4 — seven priests with seven shopharot circle Jericho for seven days. In Revelation 8, seven messengers with seven shopharot unleash judgment. The Hebrew connects these events through identical vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans', PLURAL, H4289) — the specific vessels for carrying live coals in the Tabernacle/Temple service. This is the exact word for the fire-pan in Leviticus 16:12 (Yom Kippur: 'he shall take a fire-pan full of coals of fire'), Numbers 16:6,17,37-39 (Korah's rebellion), and Exodus 27:3. Greek has λιβανωτόν (libanōton — 'censer', SINGULAR). A back-translator from Greek would use מַקְטֶרֶת (maqteret — 'incense burner') or transliterate, not reach for the Levitical fire-pan word. The PLURAL also matters — in v5 the text switches to singular הַמַּחְתָּה ('THE fire-pan'), suggesting the messenger selects one from a set, mirroring Temple ritual procedure.

Uses דָּרַךְ (darakh — 'trod/marched', H1869) — a verb meaning to step purposefully, used for treading a winepress (Isa 63:3), drawing a bow (Ps 7:13), and marching in military procession. Greek has ἐστάθη ('stood'). A back-translator from Greek would use עָמַד (amad — 'stood'), not the dynamic דרך. The Hebrew presents the messenger treading with purpose toward the sanctuary — a priestly/military approach, not a static posture.

Uses הֵיכָל (heikhal — 'sanctuary/temple', H1964) — the specific word for the Temple's inner hall, Solomon's sanctuary (1 Ki 6:3,5,17), and the heavenly sanctuary (Ps 11:4, 18:7). Greek has θυσιαστήριον ('altar'). The Hebrew locates the messenger at the sanctuary building; the Greek locates him at the altar. A back-translator from Greek 'altar' would use מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach), not heikhal.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'trod beside the sanctuary' (דרך אצל ההיכל). Greek: 'stood upon the altar' (ἐστάθη ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον). Different verb, different preposition, different location.
Hebrew: מחתות (PLURAL, 'fire-pans'). Greek: λιβανωτόν (SINGULAR, 'censer'). Different number and different vessel type.
Hebrew: 'before the sanctuary and before the throne' — two locations. Greek: 'upon the golden altar before the throne' — one location (the altar).
Greek adds 'all' (πάντων) to 'the prayers of ALL the saints' — absent from the more concise Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Fire-pans' for machtot — preserving the Levitical vessel type. These are the flat, shovel-like pans used to carry live coals, not enclosed censers.
'Trod' for darakh — capturing the purposeful, weighty step of priestly approach. The messenger doesn't merely 'stand' — he treads with authority.

The entire scene mirrors the Yom Kippur service of Leviticus 16:12-13 — the High Priest takes the fire-pan of coals, adds incense, and brings the cloud of incense before the mercy seat. The Hebrew vocabulary (machtah, qetoret, heikhal) is identical to the Torah's Yom Kippur instructions.
textual_notes: Leviticus 16:12-13: 'He shall take a fire-pan (מַחְתָּה) full of coals of fire from upon the altar before YHWH, and two handfuls of finely ground incense (קְטֹרֶת), and bring it inside the curtain.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this Yom Kippur scene — fire-pan, incense, and approach to the divine presence.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָלַךְ (halakh — 'went/walked', H1980) for the smoke's movement. Greek has ἀνέβη (anebe — 'ascended'). A back-translator from Greek 'ascended' would use עָלָה (alah — 'went up'), not the general movement verb הלך. The Hebrew doesn't impose upward direction — the smoke simply 'went' before YHWH. The Greek assumes vertical ascent; the Hebrew describes horizontal/general movement toward the divine presence.

The phrase קְטֹרֶת הַקְּדוֹשִׁים ('incense OF the holy ones') treats the incense as BELONGING TO the holy ones — it is their incense, their offering. Greek has θυμιαμάτων ταῖς προσευχαῖς τῶν ἁγίων ('incense WITH the prayers of the saints') — incense and prayers as two separate things traveling together. The Hebrew IDENTIFIES incense with the holy ones' offering; the Greek ACCOMPANIES prayer with incense. This echoes Psalm 141:2: 'Let my prayer be set before you as incense' (תִּכּוֹן תְּפִלָּתִי קְטֹרֶת לְפָנֶיךָ).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: הלך ('went'). Greek: ἀνέβη ('ascended'). Different directional concepts.
Hebrew: 'incense of the holy ones' (genitive possession). Greek: 'incense with/to the prayers of the saints' (dative association). Different grammatical relationship between incense and the saints.
translation_notes: 'Went' for halakh — preserving the Hebrew's non-directional description. The smoke 'went' before YHWH without specifying upward motion.
textual_notes: Psalm 141:2 provides the conceptual key: prayer IS incense before YHWH. The Hebrew construction 'incense of the holy ones' embodies this identification — the incense represents them directly.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יָצַק (yatsaq — 'poured out', H3332) — the specific verb for pouring molten metal (Ex 25:12, 1 Ki 7:24), pouring oil (2 Ki 4:4), and pouring libations. This is a deliberate, controlled, priestly/liturgical action. Greek has ἔβαλεν (ebalen — 'cast/threw'). A back-translator from Greek 'threw' would use הִשְׁלִיךְ (hishlich — 'cast/threw'), not the liturgical pouring verb. The Hebrew presents the fire-casting as a sacred ritual act — a priestly pouring; the Greek presents it as a violent throw.

Uses קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'thunderings/voices', H6963) — the SAME word used in Exodus 9:23,28,29,33,34 for the 'thunderings' that accompanied the seventh plague of hail and fire. The next verse (v7) describes hail and fire falling on earth. The Hebrew author uses the Exodus plague vocabulary as a deliberate setup for the plague sequence that follows. Greek φωναί ('voices') is generic.

Note the switch from PLURAL מַחְתּוֹת ('fire-pans', v3) to SINGULAR הַמַּחְתָּה ('THE fire-pan', v5). The messenger arrived carrying multiple fire-pans but selects THE specific one for the ritual — mirroring Temple procedure where multiple vessels existed but specific ones were designated for specific rites.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: יצק ('poured' — controlled, ritual). Greek: ἔβαλεν ('threw/cast' — abrupt, forceful). Different types of action.
Hebrew: 'filled it with fire' (no source specified). Greek: 'filled it from the fire of the altar' (ἐκ τοῦ πυρὸς τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου). Greek adds 'of the altar' as the fire's source.
Greek adds σεισμός ('earthquake') after thunders and lightnings — entirely absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew has only three phenomena (thunderings, thunders, lightnings); the Greek has four.
translation_notes: 'Poured out' for yatsaq captures the liturgical precision — not a violent throw but a deliberate ritual pouring of sacred fire upon the earth.

'Thunderings' for qolot — this word means both 'voices' and 'thunderclaps.' In the Exodus plague context, it specifically denotes thunder (Ex 9:23). The translation 'thunderings' preserves the Exodus connection.
textual_notes: Exodus 9:23 — 'YHWH sent thunderings (קֹלֹת) and hail, and fire ran down to the earth.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this sequence: qolot first, then (in v7) hail and fire upon the earth. The Exodus plague framework is unmistakable.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִתְקוֹעַ (litqoa — 'to blast', infinitive of H8628) — the specific verb for blowing the shofar throughout the OT. תקע is the technical term in Joshua 6:4,9,13,16,20 for the shofar blasts at Jericho, in Numbers 10:3-10 for the shofar signals of the camp, and in Joel 2:1,15 for the alarm shofar. Greek σαλπίσωσι (salpisōsi) is a generic verb for any instrument. A back-translator from the generic Greek verb would not produce this shofar-specific Hebrew term. The verb תקע and the noun שׁוֹפָר form a fixed Hebrew pair — they belong together in a way that no Greek vocabulary can replicate.

Uses מוּכָנִים (muchanim — 'prepared/readied', from kun H3559 — 'to be established/prepared'). This is the same root used in Exodus 19:11,15 when Israel was told to be 'prepared' (נְכֹנִים) for the Sinai theophany. The messengers are 'prepared' for the shofar blasts using the same vocabulary Israel was 'prepared' for the revelation at Sinai — the first time God spoke amid shofar blasts (Ex 19:16,19). A back-translator from Greek ἡτοίμασαν ('prepared themselves') could use הכינו (hechinu) but would miss the Sinai-theophany resonance that a Hebrew author naturally produces.
translation_notes: 'Blast' for תקע — this is a sharp, penetrating sound produced by the ram's horn, not a melodic trumpet call. The Hebrew תקיעה (teqi'ah) remains the technical term for the shofar blast in Jewish liturgy to this day.
'Prepared' for muchanim echoes the Sinai preparation — Israel readied itself for divine encounter, and now the messengers ready themselves for divine judgment.
textual_notes: Joshua 6:4 — 'seven priests shall carry seven ram's horns of jubilee (שִׁבְעָה שׁוֹפְרוֹת הַיּוֹבְלִים) before the ark.' Seven shopharot, seven priests, seven days. Revelation 8 mirrors this: seven shopharot, seven messengers, seven judgments.

one_way_hebrew: EXODUS 7TH PLAGUE: The entire verse reproduces the seventh plague of Egypt — hail and fire (Exodus 9:23-24: 'YHWH sent thunderings and hail, and fire ran down to the earth'). The Hebrew vocabulary directly parallels the Exodus account: ברד (hail), אשׁ (fire), ארץ (earth). The preceding verse's קולות ('thunderings') completes the Exodus 9:23 tableau.

Uses בָּלֻל (balul — 'mixed', pual passive of H1101) — the specific verb for MIXING grain offerings with oil in Torah sacrifices (Lev 2:4-5, 7:10,12; Ex 29:2: חַלֹּת מַצּוֹת בְּלוּלֹת בַּשֶּׁמֶן — 'unleavened cakes mixed with oil'). The hail and fire are described as 'mixed' (balul) using OFFERING vocabulary — as if the judgment is itself a sacrifice. Greek μεμιγμένα (memigmena) is generic 'mixed.' This same root בלל (balal) gives Babel its name (Gen 11:9 — 'he confused/mixed'). A back-translator from Greek would use מעורב (me'orav — 'mixed'), not the sacrificial/Babel-laden בלול.

Uses יֶרֶק הַשָּׂדֶה ('green herbage of the field', H3418 + H7704) — echoing Exodus 10:15 where the locusts ate 'every green thing' (כָּל יֶרֶק), and Genesis 1:30 ('every green herb'). Greek has πᾶς χόρτος χλωρός ('all green grass'). The Hebrew adds הַשָּׂדֶה ('of the field') which is absent from Greek. A back-translator from Greek would write כל עשב ירוק ('all green grass'), not the OT-rooted ירק השדה. The phrase connects this destruction to the creation and plague narratives.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: ירק השדה ('green herbage of the field'). Greek: πᾶς χόρτος χλωρός ('all green grass'). Different botanical terms; Hebrew adds 'of the field.'
Hebrew uses בלול ('mixed' — sacrificial/Babel vocabulary). Greek uses μεμιγμένα ('mixed' — generic).
translation_notes: 'Mixed' for balul preserves the sacrificial offering resonance. The hail-fire-blood mixture is described using the same verb as grain offerings mixed with oil.
'Green herbage of the field' for yereq hasadeh — this is broader than 'grass'; yereq encompasses all green vegetation, connecting to Genesis 1's creation of plant life.
textual_notes: Exodus 9:23-25: 'YHWH sent thunderings (קלת) and hail (ברד), and fire (אשׁ) ran down to the earth (ארצה)... and the hail struck every herb of the field (כל עשב השדה) and broke every tree of the field (כל עץ השדה).' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this plague with its Torah vocabulary intact: hail, fire, trees, green herbage of the field.

one_way_hebrew: EXODUS 1ST PLAGUE: Water turned to blood (Ex 7:20-21: 'all the water in the river was turned to blood'). The Hebrew naturally connects sea-to-blood with the Nile-to-blood plague. The Hebrew language of 'became blood' (היה דם) echoes the Exodus phrasing.

Uses הָלַךְ (halakh — 'went', H1980) — the burning mountain WENT into the sea under its own power or by divine propulsion. Greek has ἐβλήθη (eblethe — 'was thrown/cast'), a passive verb implying an external agent threw it. A back-translator from Greek 'was thrown' would use הֻשְׁלַךְ (hushlakh — 'was cast'), not the active movement verb הלך. The Hebrew presents the mountain as moving with agency — walking, going — while the Greek presents it as passively thrown. This is a fundamental difference in how the event is conceived.

The consonantal text שרף (soref — 'burning') resonates with שרפים (seraphim — 'burning ones', Isa 6:2,6). While the pointed text reads as a participle meaning 'burning,' the consonantal ambiguity with 'seraph' may be intentional — a great mountain, a fiery being, going into the sea.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: הלך ('went' — active, self-directed motion). Greek: ἐβλήθη ('was thrown' — passive). Fundamentally different agency.
Greek adds ὡς λαμπάς ('like a torch') — absent from the Hebrew's simpler description.
translation_notes: 'Went' for halakh — preserving the Hebrew's depiction of active movement, not passive casting.

Jeremiah 51:25 provides an OT precedent: 'Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain (הר המשחית)... I will make you a burned mountain (הר שרפה).' The image of a burning mountain cast into judgment has prophetic roots.
textual_notes: The sea turning to blood combines two Exodus motifs: the first plague (Nile→blood, Ex 7:20) and the Red Sea judgment. The Hebrew author layers these plague memories.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נִטְבְּעוּ (nitbe'u — 'were sunk', nifal of tava H2883) — the EXACT verb used for the Egyptians sinking in the Red Sea. Exodus 15:4: טֻבְּעוּ בְיַם סוּף ('they were sunk in the Sea of Reeds'). The ships are described as 'sinking' using the Red Sea victory vocabulary. Greek has διεφθάρη (diephthare — 'were destroyed/corrupted'). A back-translator from Greek 'destroyed' would use נִשְׁחֲתוּ (nishchatu — 'were corrupted/destroyed'), NOT the Red Sea sinking verb. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter — the Hebrew author instinctively uses Exodus vocabulary for maritime catastrophe.

Uses בְּרִיאוֹת (bri'ot — 'creations', from bara H1254 — 'to create') — the sea creatures are called 'creations,' using the root exclusively reserved for divine creation in the OT (Gen 1:1,21,27; 2:3,4; 5:1,2). Greek has κτισμάτων (ktismaton — 'created things'), which is conceptually parallel but uses a different root. The Hebrew connects the sea creatures directly to Genesis 1:21 where God 'created (ברא) the great sea creatures.' The destruction undoes the creation.

Uses סְפִינוֹת (sefinot — 'ships', H5600) — the authentic Hebrew word for sea-going vessels, used in Jonah 1:5 (the prophet descending into the hold of the סְפִינָה). Greek uses πλοίων (ploiōn — 'boats'). The Hebrew word is rarer and more literary than the common אֳנִיָּה (oniyyah — 'ship').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: ניטבעים ('were sunk' — Red Sea vocabulary). Greek: διεφθάρη ('were destroyed'). Entirely different verbs with different echoes.
Hebrew: בריאות ('creations'). Greek adds τὰ ἔχοντα ψυχάς ('having souls/lives') — a qualifier absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Creations' for bri'ot — preserving the Genesis creation verb ברא. These are not merely 'creatures' but divine creations being destroyed.
'Sunk' for nitba'im — the Red Sea echo is essential. The ships sink as Pharaoh's army sank.
textual_notes: Exodus 15:4-5 (Song of the Sea): 'Pharaoh's chariots and his army he cast into the sea... they sank (טֻבְּעוּ) in the Sea of Reeds. The depths covered them; they went down (ירדו) into the depths like a stone.' The Hebrew Revelation uses this exact verb for the ships' fate, linking the second shofar judgment to the Red Sea.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּאֵרוֹת (be'erot — 'wells/springs', plural of be'er H875). Greek has ποταμῶν ('rivers') and πηγάς ('springs'). A back-translator from Greek 'rivers' would use נְהָרוֹת (neharot — 'rivers'), NOT the patriarchal well vocabulary. Wells (be'erot) are foundational to Hebrew identity — Beer-sheba (Gen 21:31), Beer-lahai-roi (Gen 16:14), the well disputes of Isaac (Gen 26:15-22), the well where Jacob met Rachel (Gen 29:2-10). The Hebrew author sees water sources as 'wells' — the communal gathering places of Israel's ancestors. The Greek author sees them as 'rivers.' These are different cultural frames that a back-translator would never interchange.

Hebrew describes the star as כוכב אחד ('one star' — H259). Greek has ἀστὴρ μέγας ('a great star'). The Hebrew emphasizes its singularity ('one'); the Greek emphasizes its size ('great'). A back-translator from Greek would write כוכב גדול ('a great star'), not כוכב אחד ('one star').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: בארות ('wells'). Greek: ποταμῶν καὶ πηγάς ('rivers and springs'). Different water sources — Hebrew has ONE type (wells); Greek has TWO types (rivers and springs).
Hebrew: כוכב אחד ('one star'). Greek: ἀστὴρ μέγας ('a great star'). Different attribute — singularity vs. magnitude.
Greek adds ὡς λαμπάς ('like a torch') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Wells' for be'erot — NOT 'rivers.' The Hebrew locates the contamination at the communal water sources central to Israelite life. Wells are where communities gather, where marriages are arranged, where covenants are made.
textual_notes: The poisoning of wells connects to Exodus 15:23 (the bitter waters of Marah) which the next verse will develop. It also evokes the well-poisoning motif — the destruction of what sustains communal life.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תּוֹלַעַת (tola'at — 'worm', H8438) as the star's name. Greek uses Ἄψινθος (Apsinthos — 'Wormwood,' the bitter plant). If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would write לַעֲנָה (la'anah — 'wormwood', H3939), the standard Hebrew word for the bitter plant (Deut 29:17, Jer 9:14, 23:15, Amos 5:7). No back-translator would render 'Wormwood' as 'Worm.' The Hebrew תולעת carries completely different associations: the scarlet worm (תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי) used for Tabernacle dye (Ex 25:4, 26:1, 28:5), the worm of decay (Isa 14:11, 41:14, 66:24 — 'their worm shall not die'), and Psalm 22:7 — 'I am a worm (תולעת) and not a man.' The star is named 'Worm' — decay, corruption, mortality — not after a plant.

Uses בְּנֵי אָדָם (bene adam — 'sons of adam/man', H1121 + H120) — the Genesis creation term, emphasizing humanity as descendants of the original adam formed from adamah. Greek has ἀνθρώπων (anthrōpōn — 'men', generic). A back-translator from Greek would write אנשׁים (anashim — 'men') or simply אדם ('men'), not the compound form בני אדם which carries the Genesis genealogical weight.

Uses עַל יַד הַמַּיִם ('by the hand of the waters') — the idiom על יד (al yad, 'upon the hand of') personifies the waters as having agency, as if they acted with hands. This idiom is used in the OT for acting through agents: 'by the hand of Moses' (ביד משה), 'by the hand of YHWH' (ביד יהוה). Greek simply says ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων ('from the waters') — no personification. A back-translator would use מן המים ('from the waters'), not the personifying idiom.

MARAH PARALLEL: The waters 'became bitter' (היה מר) — directly echoing Exodus 15:23: 'they could not drink the waters of Marah, for they were bitter (מָרִים); therefore its name was called Marah (מָרָה).' The third Exodus plague-echo in sequence.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: תולעת ('Worm'). Greek: Ἄψινθος ('Wormwood' — a plant). Entirely different names with different semantic fields: worm (decay/mortality) vs. wormwood (bitterness).
Hebrew: בני אדם ('sons of adam'). Greek: ἀνθρώπων ('men'). Different anthropological framing.
Hebrew: על יד המים ('by the hand of the waters'). Greek: ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων ('from the waters'). Hebrew personifies; Greek does not.

Hebrew: מפני מורריהם ('because of their embitterers'). Greek: ὅτι ἐπικράνθησαν ('because they were embittered'). Hebrew uses an active agentive noun ('embitterers'); Greek uses a passive verb ('were embittered').
translation_notes: 'Worm' for tola'at — NOT 'wormwood.' The Hebrew name invokes decay and mortality, not merely bitterness. The worm that devours in the grave (Isa 14:11) and the scarlet-worm of the Tabernacle (Ex 25:4) share this word.
'Sons of adam' — preserving the creation genealogy. Humanity dies 'by the hand of the waters' as descendants of the adam who was formed from the ground.
'Embitterers' for morrereihem — a rare agentive form from the root מרר (to be bitter), suggesting active agents of bitterness within the waters.
textual_notes: Exodus 15:23-25: 'When they came to Marah, they could not drink the waters... for they were bitter (מרים)... and YHWH showed him a tree, and he cast it into the waters, and the waters became sweet.' At Marah, a tree made bitter water sweet; in Revelation, a falling star (Worm) makes sweet water bitter — an inverted Exodus. The Hebrew vocabulary (מר, מים) is identical.
Isaiah 14:11 — 'the worm (תולעת) is spread under you' — spoken to the king of Babylon cast down from heaven. A star named 'Worm' falling from heaven echoes this Isaiah imagery of a fallen ruler.

one_way_hebrew: EXODUS 9TH PLAGUE: Darkness (Exodus 10:21-23 — 'there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days'). The fourth plague-echo in sequence: hail/fire (7th plague), blood (1st plague), bitter water (Marah), now darkness (9th plague). The Hebrew author follows the Exodus plague framework.

Uses נִלְקָה (nilqah — 'was eclipsed') — a technical astronomical term in Hebrew. The root לקה in later Hebrew specifically means 'to be eclipsed' (ליקוי חמה = 'solar eclipse'; ליקוי לבנה = 'lunar eclipse'). This is specialist vocabulary that a Hebrew astronomer/author would naturally use. Greek has ἐπλήγη ('was struck') — a generic verb. A back-translator from Greek would use הֻכָּה (hukah — 'was struck'), not the technical astronomical term for eclipse. This word choice reveals an author thinking in Hebrew astronomical categories.

Uses זֹרֵחַ (zoreach — 'shining/rising', qal participle of zarach H2224) — the specific Hebrew verb for the rising/shining of the sun (Gen 32:32, Judg 9:33, 2 Sam 23:4). Malachi 3:20 [4:2]: 'the sun of righteousness shall rise (זרח) with healing in its wings.' Greek has φαίνω ('shine/appear') — generic. A back-translator would use מאיר (me'ir — 'giving light') or simply אור ('light'), not the sunrise-specific verb zarach.

MANUSCRIPT LACUNA: The text contains [   ] — a gap between נלקה and השלישׁ, indicating a word was illegible or missing in the source manuscript. This physical manuscript artifact would not exist in a back-translation from Greek, which would flow without gaps. This is evidence of copying from an actual Hebrew manuscript.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: נלקה ('was eclipsed' — technical astronomical term). Greek: ἐπλήγη ('was struck' — generic).
Hebrew: לא זורח ('not shining/rising'). Greek: μὴ φαίνῃ ('not appearing/shining'). Different verbs — Hebrew uses the sunrise verb.
Hebrew has a manuscript lacuna [   ] — absent from Greek, which flows continuously.
translation_notes: 'Eclipsed' for nilqah — this is the precise Hebrew astronomical term, not merely 'struck' or 'smitten.' The luminaries undergo eclipse, not assault.
'Shine' for zoreach — this verb specifically denotes the rising/radiating of the sun. The day 'does not zarach' — the sunrise itself fails.
textual_notes: Exodus 10:21-22: 'YHWH said to Moses, Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt... and there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.' The fourth shofar judgment echoes this ninth plague. Note: in Exodus, darkness is the plague before the final devastating plague (death of firstborn). In Revelation, darkness (v12) precedes the three 'woes' announced in v13.
Joel 2:31 [3:4]: 'The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and terrible day of YHWH comes.' The eclipse of luminaries is a standard Hebrew prophetic sign.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רֹחֵף (rochef — 'hovering', H7363) — the EXACT verb from Genesis 1:2 where the Spirit of God 'hovered' (מְרַחֶפֶת) over the face of the waters. This verb occurs only TWICE in the entire OT: Genesis 1:2 (the Spirit hovering over creation) and Deuteronomy 32:11 (an eagle hovering over its young). Greek has πετωμένου (petōmenou — 'flying'). A back-translator from Greek would use עָף (af — 'flying', H5774), the common Hebrew word for flight. No one translating 'flying' would reach for the exceedingly rare creation-verb רחף. The messenger 'hovers' in the heavens using the same verb as the Spirit at creation — the undoing of creation (plagues on earth, sea, water, sky) is witnessed by one who hovers as the Spirit once hovered over the primordial deep.

Uses צָעַק (tsa'aq — 'cried out', H6817) — a verb of distress, urgent outcry, and prophetic alarm (Ex 14:10, Judg 3:9, 1 Sam 7:9, Isa 19:20). This is the cry of Israel in Egypt (Ex 14:10), the cry of the oppressed seeking deliverance. Greek has λέγοντος ('saying') — neutral speech. A back-translator from Greek 'saying' would use אמר (amar — 'said'), not the anguished outcry verb צעק.

Uses הַשּׁוֹפָרֹת (hashopharot — 'the ram's horns', H7782) a final time, maintaining the shofar vocabulary throughout the chapter. Greek σάλπιγγος ('trumpet') never captures the shofar's covenantal significance. The Hebrew 'sound of the shopharot' (קול השופרות) is a fixed biblical phrase (Josh 6:5,20; 2 Sam 6:15; Ps 47:6).

NOTE: Some Greek manuscripts read ἀετοῦ ('eagle') instead of ἀγγέλου ('angel'). If the original Greek had 'eagle,' then the Hebrew verb רחף is even more striking — Deuteronomy 32:11 uses רחף SPECIFICALLY for an eagle hovering over its young. The Hebrew verb choice perfectly matches the eagle tradition that some Greek manuscripts preserve, suggesting the Hebrew is closer to the original reading.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: רחף ('hovering' — Genesis 1:2 creation verb). Greek: πετωμένου ('flying' — generic). Fundamentally different verbs.
Hebrew: בשמים ('in the heavens'). Greek: ἐν μεσουρανήματι ('in mid-heaven'). Different spatial descriptions.
Hebrew: צעק ('cried out' — distress cry). Greek: λέγοντος ('saying' — neutral speech).
Hebrew: שצריכים ('that must' — later Hebrew necessity word). Greek: τῶν μελλόντων ('who are about to'). Different modality — Hebrew expresses obligation; Greek expresses imminence.
translation_notes: 'Hovering' for rochef — this is the Genesis 1:2 creation verb, NOT mere 'flying.' The messenger hovers over the earth as the Spirit once hovered over the waters.
'Cried out' for tsa'aq — capturing the prophetic distress. This is not calm speech but an anguished warning cry.
אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') and צְרִיכִים (tsrikhim — 'must/need') are later Hebrew forms without standard Strong's numbers, characteristic of the text's first-century linguistic layer.
הַדָּרִים (hadarim — 'the dwellers') is from a later Hebrew form meaning 'residents/inhabitants.'
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2: וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם — 'and the Spirit of Elohim was hovering over the face of the waters.' Deuteronomy 32:11: כְּנֶשֶׁר יָעִיר קִנּוֹ עַל גּוֹזָלָיו יְרַחֵף — 'like an eagle stirs up its nest, over its young it hovers.' These are the ONLY two OT occurrences of רחף. A messenger using this verb in the heavens invokes both the Spirit at creation and the protective eagle of Deuteronomy's Song of Moses.

The three woes (אוי אוי אוי) correspond to the three remaining shofar blasts. The structure parallels Ezekiel 16:23 (וַיְהִי אַחֲרֵי כָּל רָעָתֵךְ אוֹי אוֹי לָךְ — 'woe, woe to you') and Isaiah 6:3's triple-holy (קדושׁ קדושׁ קדושׁ) — three-fold repetition for emphasis and completeness.

9.summary: Revelation 9 in Hebrew draws massively on Genesis cosmology (tehom/the Deep, used 5 times), the Exodus plague tradition (arbeh/locusts, tannur/furnace), Joel's locust-army imagery (Joel 1:6 verbatim, Joel 2:4 echo), and Torah-specific vocabulary (toqea for shofar-blowing, lehashchit for Flood-destruction, noshech for serpent-biting, rechev for chariotry). The chapter contains at least 12 clear one-way translation markers: (1) תהום ('the Deep') for the abyss — the Genesis 1:2 primordial chaos, not ἄβυσσος; (2) 'the great SEA called Euphrates' (ים not נהר) vs. Greek 'the great RIVER'; (3) 'corners of the Temple' vs. 'horns of the golden altar'; (4) 'garments of PITCH' vs. 'breastplates of JACINTH'; (5) 'chariotry' (rechev) vs. 'cavalry armies'; (6) the Hebrew→Greek direction of explanation in v10 ('his name in the Hebrew tongue is Avadon, and in the tongue of Yavan, Apollyon'); (7) the Joel 1:6 verbatim singular שניו ('its teeth') within a plural context; (8) 'tails like a LOCUST' vs. 'tails like SCORPIONS'; (9) כח (koach — raw power) vs. ἐξουσία (exousia — delegated authority). The most critical marker is the theological divergence in v19: the Hebrew says survivors were spared BECAUSE they repented (עשו תשובה), while Greek says they did NOT repent (οὐ μετενόησαν) — directly contradictory claims. Further one-way markers include (10) 'the Satan' (singular with article) vs. 'demons' (plural); (11) עבודה זרה ('foreign worship,' the Rabbinic technical term) vs. 'idols'; and (12) חרס ('clay' — Mesopotamian idol material) vs. χαλκᾶ ('bronze'). The Hebrew text is consistently more concise than the Greek, and several brackets indicate lacunae where the source may be damaged.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תּוֹקֵעַ (toqea, H8628) — the specific Torah word for ritual blowing of the shofar (Num 10:3-7, Josh 6:4,9,13, Judg 3:27, 7:18). Greek ἐσάλπισεν simply means 'trumpeted.' The Hebrew naturally reaches for the Torah's ritual-blowing term; a back-translator would use a generic verb.

Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom, H8415 — 'the Deep') — the primordial deep of Genesis 1:2 (וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל פְּנֵי תְהוֹם). Greek has τῆς ἀβύσσου ('the abyss'). The Hebrew word evokes the pre-creation chaos waters. A back-translator from ἄβυσσος would likely transliterate or use a different term, not reach for the Genesis cosmological word. The brackets [   ] in the source suggest a lacuna where Greek has 'the pit of the abyss' (τοῦ φρέατος τῆς ἀβύσσου) — the Hebrew is more concise, simply 'of the Deep.'
greek_deviations: Greek: 'the key of the pit of the abyss' (κλεὶς τοῦ φρέατος τῆς ἀβύσσου). Hebrew: 'the key of the Deep' (המפתח מתהום). Greek adds 'pit' (φρέαρ); the Hebrew has only 'the Deep.'
translation_notes: 'The Deep' for tehom preserves the Genesis 1:2 cosmological connection — the same primordial waters that existed before creation.
Brackets in the source text indicate missing text likely corresponding to Greek 'pit of.'
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל פְּנֵי תְהוֹם ('and darkness was upon the face of the Deep'). The tehom is the primordial chaos that precedes ordered creation. The Hebrew author sees the abyss not as a Greek mythological underworld but as the Genesis pre-creation void.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom) THREE times in a single verse — a concentrated repetition emphasizing the Genesis cosmological dimension. Greek varies between φρέαρ ('pit') and ἄβυσσος ('abyss'). The Hebrew hammers the single primordial term.

Uses תַּנּוּר (tannur, H8574 — 'furnace/oven') — the word from Abraham's covenant vision in Genesis 15:17 (תַּנּוּר עָשָׁן — 'a smoking furnace') and the prophetic judgment imagery of Malachi 4:1. Greek uses κάμινος (generic furnace). A back-translator would not specifically choose the Abraham-covenant furnace word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew opens 'the Deep' directly (פתח התהום); Greek opens 'the pit of the abyss' (τὸ φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσου) — again adding 'pit' as a distinct structure.
Hebrew repeats 'the Deep' (תהום) three times for rhetorical emphasis. Greek varies its terminology.
translation_notes: 'Furnace' for tannur — the covenant/judgment furnace of Genesis 15:17 and Malachi 4:1.
אֲוִיר (avir — 'air') is a post-biblical Hebrew term without a standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Genesis 15:17 — 'And behold, a smoking furnace (תנור עשן) and a flaming torch that passed between those pieces.' The covenant-furnace imagery links this judgment to the Abrahamic covenant.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַרְבָּהִים (arbahim) — an unusual plural of אַרְבֶּה (arbeh, H697 — 'locust'). The locust is the eighth plague of Egypt (Ex 10:4-19) and Joel's apocalyptic army (Joel 1:4, 2:25). Greek ἀκρίδες is generic 'locusts.' The Hebrew connects these creatures directly to the Exodus plague tradition.

Uses לְהַשְׁחִית (lehashchit — 'to destroy', Hiphil of שׁחת H7843) — the specific verb God uses for the Flood: 'I am about to destroy them' (Gen 6:13 — מַשְׁחִיתָם), and for the destruction of Sodom (Gen 13:10, 19:13). Greek has ἐξουσίαν ὡς ἔχουσιν ἐξουσίαν οἱ σκορπίοι ('authority as the scorpions have authority') — an entirely different statement. The Hebrew says 'authority to destroy'; the Greek compares authority to scorpions. A back-translator from Greek would not use the Flood/Sodom verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'authority to destroy' (רשות להשחית). Greek: 'authority as the scorpions of the earth have authority' (ἐξουσίαν ὡς ἔχουσιν ἐξουσίαν οἱ σκορπίοι τῆς γῆς). Entirely different construction — one states purpose, the other makes a comparison.
Brackets in the Hebrew source around both 'locusts' and near 'authority' suggest editorial restorations or lacunae.
translation_notes: רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority/permission') is a post-biblical Hebrew term common in Mishnaic Hebrew. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Joel 1:4 — 'What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust (ארבה) ate.' Joel 2:25 — 'I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust (ארבה) has eaten.' The Hebrew author draws from the Joel tradition of locusts as instruments of divine judgment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יֶרֶק (yereq, H3419 — 'greenery') and עֵשֶׂב הַשָּׂדֶה ('herb of the field', H6212+H7704) — Genesis creation vocabulary. Gen 1:30: 'every green herb' (כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב). Gen 2:5: 'every herb of the field' (כָּל עֵשֶׂב הַשָּׂדֶה). The Hebrew author draws on the creation narrative's specific botanical terminology. Greek uses χόρτον ('grass') and χλωρόν ('green thing') — more generic terms. A back-translator from Greek would use דֶּשֶׁא (deshe — 'grass'), not the Genesis pair yereq/esev.

Uses חֲתִימֹת מִיַּהְוֶה ('seals from YHWH') — from the root חתם (chatam, H2856 — 'to seal'), used for sealing documents and covenants (1 Kings 21:8, Neh 9:38, Dan 12:4). Greek says 'the seal of God' (σφραγῖδα τοῦ θεοῦ) — singular where Hebrew has plural, and generic θεός where Hebrew has the specific covenant name YHWH. A back-translator from Greek would never independently choose the Tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'greenery and herb of the field' (ירק ועשב השדה). Greek: 'the grass of the earth nor any green thing' (χόρτον τῆς γῆς οὐδὲ πᾶν χλωρόν). Different vegetation terms and 'field' vs. 'earth.'
Hebrew: 'seals from YHWH' (חתימות מיהוה — plural, with YHWH). Greek: 'the seal of God' (σφραγῖδα τοῦ θεοῦ — singular, with θεός). Different number and divine name.
translation_notes: תַּזִּיקוּ (tazziku — 'you shall harm') is from the root נזק, common in Mishnaic Hebrew but not standard in the OT. No Strong's number.
חֲתִימֹת (chatimot — 'seals') is a post-biblical plural noun form from חתם. No standard Strong's for this nominal form.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 9:4 — 'Go through the midst of the city... and set a mark (תָו) upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations.' The Hebrew concept of a divine mark/seal on foreheads protecting the righteous from judgment is rooted in Ezekiel.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נוֹשֵׁךְ (noshech — 'bites', H5391) for the scorpion's sting. This is the same root used for the serpent's bite in Genesis 49:17 (נֹשֵׁךְ עִקְּבֵי סוּס — 'biting the horse's heels') and the fiery serpents of Numbers 21:6-9. The word also means 'to charge interest' (Deut 23:20) — literally 'biting' someone financially. Greek παίσῃ simply means 'strikes.' The Hebrew connects the scorpion-plague to the serpent imagery of Torah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'when one bites' (באם שנושך — serpent-bite language). Greek: 'when it strikes a man' (ὅταν παίσῃ ἄνθρωπον — generic striking).
translation_notes: צַעֵר/צַעַר (tsa'er/tsa'ar — 'afflict/affliction') is post-biblical Hebrew. No standard Strong's number. Greek uses βασανίζω ('torment/torture').

greek_deviations: Hebrew is much shorter — only 'they shall seek death and not find it.' Greek adds an entire second clause: 'and shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them' (καὶ ἐπιθυμήσουσιν ἀποθανεῖν, καὶ φεύξεται ὁ θάνατος ἀπ' αὐτῶν). The personification of death fleeing is absent from the Hebrew.
translation_notes: תַּחְכִּימוּ — morphologically unusual. Possibly an intensive form from the root חכה (chakhah, H2442 — 'to wait/long for'), or a textual variant. The contextual meaning 'to seek/long for' is clear and matches Greek ζητήσουσιν ('they shall seek').

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut — 'in the likeness of', H1823) — the creation term from Genesis 1:26 (נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ — 'Let us make man in our image, in our likeness'). The Hebrew naturally reaches for this theologically loaded word. Greek uses ὡς στέφανοι ὅμοιοι ('like crowns similar to'). A back-translator from Greek would not choose the Genesis creation term.

DIRECT ECHO of Joel 2:4: כְּמַרְאֵה סוּסִים מַרְאֵהוּ ('like the appearance of horses is their appearance'). The Hebrew Revelation's locust-horse comparison and the precise phrasing מראיהם כמראות reproduce Joel's apocalyptic locust army imagery. A back-translator from Greek would have no reason to reproduce the Joel phrasing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the locusts were like horses' (ארבהים כמו הסוסים). Greek: 'the likenesses of the locusts were like horses' (τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν ἀκρίδων ὅμοια ἵπποις). Greek adds an extra layer of abstraction with 'likenesses.'
translation_notes: כִּתְרֵי (kitrei — 'crowns of') is the construct plural of כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804), appearing in the OT only in Esther (1:11, 2:17, 6:8). A Persian-period word for royal crown.
textual_notes: Joel 2:4-5 — 'Their appearance is like the appearance of horses; like horsemen, so they run. Like the noise of chariots on the tops of mountains they leap.' The Joel parallel extends beyond appearance to the full military imagery.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT ECHO of Joel 1:6: שִׁנָּיו שִׁנֵּי אַרְיֵה ('its teeth are the teeth of a lion'). The Hebrew switches from plural 'their hair' (שַׂעֲרוֹתֵיהֶם) to singular 'its teeth' (שִׁנָּיו) — exactly as Joel does, treating the locust swarm collectively as a single entity. Greek maintains plural throughout (οἱ ὀδόντες αὐτῶν — 'their teeth'). A back-translator from Greek, seeing plural 'their teeth,' would never switch to Joel's singular.
greek_deviations: Hebrew switches from plural 'their hair' to singular 'its teeth' (echoing Joel 1:6). Greek maintains plural consistently.
translation_notes: 'Its teeth' (singular suffix) preserved in translation to show the Joel 1:6 verbatim echo.
textual_notes: Joel 1:6 — 'For a nation has come up against my land, powerful and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion (שִׁנָּיו שִׁנֵּי אַרְיֵה), and it has the fangs of a lioness.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Joel's exact phrase.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'tails like a locust' (כְּזַנְבֵי אַרְבֶּה). Greek (v10): 'tails like scorpions' (οὐρὰς ὁμοίας σκορπίοις). The Hebrew compares the tails to LOCUST tails, maintaining the arbeh identity throughout the passage. The Greek switches to SCORPION tails. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּזַנְבוֹת עַקְרַבִּים ('like scorpion tails'), not 'locust tails.' The Hebrew author consistently identifies these creatures as locusts — the Exodus/Joel plague creature.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tails like a locust' (כזנבי ארבה). Greek (v10): 'tails like scorpions, and stings were in their tails' (οὐρὰς ὁμοίας σκορπίοις καὶ κέντρα). Different creature reference, and Greek adds 'stings' which is absent from Hebrew.

The entire content of Greek v9 — breastplates of iron, the sound of wings like many chariots rushing to battle (θώρακας ὡς θώρακας σιδηροῦς, καὶ ἡ φωνὴ τῶν πτερύγων αὐτῶν ὡς φωνὴ ἁρμάτων) — is ABSENT from the Hebrew text.
translation_notes: The Hebrew maintains locust imagery (ארבה) consistently, while the Greek alternates between locusts and scorpions. This suggests independent traditions rather than translation.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The direction of explanation flows Hebrew→Greek. The author FIRST gives the Hebrew name אֲבַדּוֹן (Avadon, H11) — a NATIVE Hebrew word for the realm of destruction/death appearing six times in the OT (Job 26:6, 28:22, 31:12; Ps 88:12; Prov 15:11, 27:20) — and THEN provides the Greek equivalent for non-Hebrew readers. If this were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would give the Greek name first and the Hebrew as an explanation. The direction of explanation is the direction of composition.

Uses יָוָן (Yavan, H3120) for 'Greece' — the biblical Hebrew geographic name from the Table of Nations (Gen 10:2, son of Yefet) and Daniel's prophecy (Dan 8:21, 10:20, 11:2). A back-translator from Greek would say בְּיוּנִית ('in Greek') or Ἑλληνικῇ transliterated, not use the Torah's genealogical name for the Greek people.
Uses מִתְּהוֹם ('from the Deep') again — consistently tehom rather than any other underworld term. Greek has τῆς ἀβύσσου ('of the abyss').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the Hebrew tongue... in the tongue of Yavan' (בלשון עברי... בלשון יון). Greek: 'in Hebrew... in Greek' (Ἑβραϊστί... ἐν τῇ Ἑλληνικῇ). The Hebrew uses native geographic terminology; the Greek uses Greek adverbs.
translation_notes: 'Avadon' transliterated rather than translated to preserve the proper name. The Hebrew root אבד (avad) means 'to perish/be destroyed.'
'Yavan' for Greece follows biblical Hebrew convention (Gen 10:2, Dan 8:21).
textual_notes: Job 26:6 — 'Sheol is naked before him, and Avadon (אֲבַדּוֹן) has no covering.' Job 28:22 — 'Avadon and Death say, We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.' In the OT, Avadon is personified as a realm parallel to Sheol and Death.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כְּאֵב (ke'ev — 'pain/grief', related to H3511) for 'woe.' This Hebrew word carries a physical-pain connotation — the anguish of bodily suffering (Job 2:13, Jer 15:18). Greek οὐαί is an abstract interjection ('alas!'). The Hebrew turns the woe into a concrete experience of pain. A back-translator from Greek would use הוֹי (hoy — 'woe!', the prophetic interjection) or אוֹי (oy), not the physical-pain word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'one woe has gone' (אחד כעב הלך). Greek: 'the first woe has passed; behold, the two woes come after these things' (Ἡ οὐαὶ ἡ μία ἀπῆλθεν· ἰδού, ἔρχονται ἔτι δύο οὐαὶ μετὰ ταῦτα). Greek adds 'after these things.'
translation_notes: כְּעֵב/כְּאֵב — variant spelling of the noun from root כאב (ka'av, H3510 — 'to be in pain'). The interchange of א and ע is common in late Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses פִּינּוֹת הַהֵיכָל ('corners of the Temple', H6438+H1964). Greek has τῶν τεσσάρων κεράτων τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου τοῦ χρυσοῦ ('the four horns of the golden altar'). These are entirely different structures — the Hebrew envisions the architectural corners of the Temple building; the Greek envisions the horn-projections of the golden incense altar. A back-translator from Greek would write קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ הַזָּהָב ('horns of the golden altar'), not 'corners of the Temple.'

Uses הֵיכָל (heikhal, H1964) — the OT's word for the main Temple hall (1 Kings 6:3,5,17; Ps 5:8, 11:4, 18:7). This is the architectural term for the building itself, not furniture within it. The Greek specifies altar furniture; the Hebrew specifies the sacred building.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ). The Hebrew uses the specific covenant name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'four corners of the Temple' (ארבע פינות ההיכל). Greek: 'four horns of the golden altar' (τεσσάρων κεράτων τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου τοῦ χρυσοῦ). Entirely different sacred structure.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ). Different divine designation.
translation_notes: פִּנָּה (pinnah, H6438 — 'corner') is used for the corners of buildings, the cornerstone (Ps 118:22, Isa 28:16), and the 'four corners' of the earth (Isa 11:12). The voice emanates from the very structure of the Temple.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַיָּם הַגָּדוֹל ('the great sea', H3220+H1419) for what Greek calls ποταμῷ τῷ μεγάλῳ Εὐφράτῃ ('the great RIVER Euphrates'). The Hebrew calls the Euphrates a יָם (yam — 'sea'), not a נָהָר (nahar — 'river'). In OT usage, 'the great sea' (הַיָּם הַגָּדוֹל) is the standard designation for the Mediterranean (Num 34:6-7, Josh 1:4, 9:1, 15:12). A back-translator from Greek 'river' (ποταμός) would write nahar, not yam. The Hebrew author's use of 'sea' for the Euphrates reflects ancient Near Eastern cosmological language where great waters carry chaos associations.

Uses לֵךְ וְחַפֵּשׁ ('go and search for', H1980+H2664). Greek says Λῦσον ('loose/release'). The Hebrew commands a SEARCH mission; the Greek commands a RELEASE. A back-translator from Greek would write הַתֵּר ('loose') or שַׁחְרֵר ('release'), not 'go and search.' The Hebrew implies the bound angels must first be located before they can be released.

Uses אֲסוּרִים (asurim — 'bound/imprisoned', from אסר H631) — the standard OT word for prisoners (Gen 39:20, 40:3,5; Isa 42:7, 49:9, 61:1). The same root appears in Isaiah's liberation prophecy: 'to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out prisoners (אסורים) from the dungeon.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the great sea called Euphrates' (הים הגדול הנקרא פרת). Greek: 'the great river Euphrates' (ποταμῷ τῷ μεγάλῳ Εὐφράτῃ). Sea vs. river — fundamentally different geographic conception.
Hebrew: 'go and search for' (לך וחפש). Greek: 'loose' (Λῦσον). Search mission vs. release command.
translation_notes: The qualifying phrase הַנִּקְרָא פְּרָת ('which is called Euphrates') suggests the author is clarifying which 'great sea' is meant — as if the designation might not be immediately obvious. This is consistent with the unusual identification of the Euphrates as a 'sea.'
textual_notes: Genesis 15:18 — 'To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates (עַד הַנָּהָר הַגָּדֹל נְהַר פְּרָת).' In the Torah, the Euphrates is called a נָהָר (nahar — 'river'), never a יָם (yam — 'sea'). The Hebrew Revelation's deliberate use of 'sea' is a theological choice connecting the Euphrates to cosmic-chaos waters.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּנֵי אָדָם ('sons of Adam', H1121+H120) consistently throughout the chapter rather than a generic word for 'people.' This perpetually links humanity back to Genesis — we are always Adam's children. Greek uses τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('mankind') without the genealogical connection.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in one hour and day and month and year' (using the preposition ב on each time word, with אחד at the end). Greek: 'for THE hour and day and month and year' (εἰς τὴν ὥραν καὶ ἡμέραν καὶ μῆνα καὶ ἐνιαυτόν — using the article). The Hebrew implies a measured duration; the Greek implies a specific appointed time.
translation_notes: שָׁעָה (sha'ah — 'hour/moment', H8160) in this sense is Aramaic-influenced, as in Daniel 3:6, 4:16.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רִכְבֵיהֶם (richveihem — 'their chariotry', from rechev H7393) — the standard OT word for war chariots (Ex 14:7, Josh 11:4, Judg 4:3, 1 Kings 10:26, 2 Kings 6:17 — Elisha's chariots of fire). Greek uses στρατευμάτων τοῦ ἱππικοῦ ('armies of cavalry/horsemen'). A back-translator from Greek would use פָּרָשִׁים (parashim — 'horsemen/cavalry'), not the chariot-specific rechev. The Hebrew envisions chariot warfare in the OT tradition; the Greek envisions mounted cavalry.

The number is רִבֹּתַיִם אַלְפֵי ('two myriads of thousands'). Greek has δύο μυριάδες μυριάδων ('two myriads of myriads' = 200 million). The Hebrew number (two ten-thousands of thousands) is vastly different from the Greek 200 million. These cannot be translation variants — they represent independent numerical traditions.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'chariotry' (רכב — war chariots). Greek: 'cavalry armies' (στρατευμάτων τοῦ ἱππικοῦ — mounted troops). Different military units.
Hebrew: 'two myriads of thousands' (רבתים אלפי). Greek: 'two myriads of myriads' (δύο μυριάδες μυριάδων). Different numbers entirely.
translation_notes: רִבֹּתַיִם (ribbotayim) is the dual form of רְבָבָה (revavah, H7233 — 'myriad/ten thousand'). The dual = 20,000. With אַלְפֵי ('thousands'), the total could be 'twenty thousands' = 20,000 or 'twenty-thousand-fold thousands.'
textual_notes: 2 Kings 6:17 — 'And YHWH opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots (רכב) of fire.' The Hebrew author's use of rechev connects this supernatural army to Elisha's vision of YHWH's heavenly chariot force.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses זֶפֶת (zefet, H2203 — 'pitch/tar') where Greek has ὑακινθίνους ('jacinth/hyacinth-blue'). Pitch is black tar — the substance used to coat Moses' basket (Ex 2:3 — וַתַּחְמְרָה בַחֵמָר וּבַזָּפֶת) and the judgment substance of Edom (Isa 34:9 — 'her streams shall be turned into pitch'). These are entirely different substances. The Hebrew author clothes the riders in Sodom/Edom judgment materials. A back-translator from Greek 'jacinth' would never write 'pitch.'

Uses מַלְבּוּשִׁים (malbushim — 'garments/clothing', H4403) where Greek has θώρακας ('breastplates/armor'). A back-translator from Greek would use שִׁרְיוֹן (shiryon — 'armor/breastplate'), not the general word for clothing. The Hebrew envisions riders CLOTHED in pitch, sulfur, and fire — dressed in the instruments of divine judgment, like the consuming fire of Sodom (Gen 19:24).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'garments of pitch and sulfur and fire' (מלבושים של זפת וגפרית ואש). Greek: 'breastplates of fire and jacinth and sulfur' (θώρακας πυρίνους καὶ ὑακινθίνους καὶ θειώδεις). Garments vs. breastplates, and pitch vs. jacinth.
Hebrew brackets [  ] between 'lion heads' and 'from their mouths' suggest missing text.
translation_notes: The combination of pitch (זפת), sulfur (גפרית), and fire (אש) echoes the destruction of Sodom — Gen 19:24: 'Then YHWH rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah sulfur (גפרית) and fire (אש).' Isaiah 34:9 adds pitch (זפת) to the judgment materials. The Hebrew author clothes the riders in the full arsenal of divine judgment.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:9 — 'And her streams shall be turned into pitch (זפת), and her dust into sulfur (גפרית), and her land shall become burning pitch.' The Hebrew triad of pitch-sulfur-fire is an Isaiah/Genesis judgment motif.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from these three was killed' (concise, six words). Greek adds an expanded explanation: 'by the fire and the smoke and the sulfur going out of their mouths' (ἐκ τοῦ πυρὸς καὶ τοῦ καπνοῦ καὶ τοῦ θείου τοῦ ἐκπορευομένου ἐκ τῶν στομάτων αὐτῶν). The Hebrew is characteristically terse; the Greek is characteristically explanatory.
Hebrew: 'from these three' (מאילו השלושה — the three substances). Greek: 'by these three plagues' (ὑπὸ τῶν τριῶν πληγῶν τούτων). Greek adds the word 'plagues.'
translation_notes: נֶהֱרַג (neherag — 'was killed', Niphal of הרג H2026) — the strong verb for killing/slaying used from Cain onward (Gen 4:8, 34:25, Ex 2:14).

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֹּחַ (koach — 'power/strength', H3581) where Greek has ἐξουσία ('authority'). These are fundamentally different concepts: koach is raw power/might (Gen 4:12 — the ground's power; Ex 9:16 — God's power; Deut 8:17 — 'my power made me this wealth'). Exousia is delegated authority/permission. A back-translator from Greek exousia would use רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority') or שִׁלְטוֹן (shilton — 'dominion'), not the raw-might word koach.

Uses נְחָשִׁים (nechashim — 'serpents', H5175) — THE word for the serpent of Eden (Gen 3:1), the fiery serpents in the wilderness (Num 21:6-9), and prophetic serpent imagery (Isa 27:1). The Eden/serpent theology permeates this imagery. Greek uses ὄφεσιν ('snakes'). Both mean serpent, but the Hebrew form carries the full weight of Torah serpent theology — from Eden's nachash to the bronze nachash of healing.

Hebrew: 'with these they KILL them' (הורגים אותם — using הרג, the strong killing verb). Greek: 'with them they do HARM' (ἐν αὐταῖς ἀδικοῦσιν — using ἀδικέω, 'to wrong/harm'). The Hebrew is more severe — these serpent-tails kill, they don't merely injure.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'their power' (כחם — koach, raw might). Greek: 'their authority' (ἐξουσία — delegated authority). Different concept.
Hebrew: 'with these they kill them' (ובאילו הורגים אותם). Greek: 'with them they do harm' (ἐν αὐταῖς ἀδικοῦσιν). Kill vs. harm.
translation_notes: The serpent-tail imagery connects to Genesis 3:15 — the serpent strikes at the heel. Here the serpent-tails attack from behind, an image of treacherous assault consistent with the nachash of Eden.
textual_notes: Numbers 21:6 — 'And YHWH sent fiery serpents (נחשים שרפים) among the people, and they bit the people, and many people of Israel died.' The combination of serpents and death from divine judgment echoes this Revelation passage.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL THEOLOGICAL DIVERGENCE: The Hebrew says survivors were NOT killed BECAUSE (בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁ) they REPENTED (עָשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה). Greek (v20) says the survivors DID NOT repent (οὐ μετενόησαν). These are OPPOSITE theological messages. The Hebrew presents EFFECTIVE judgment — the plagues achieved their purpose of producing repentance, and the repentant were spared. The Greek presents HARDENED HEARTS — the plagues failed to produce repentance. These cannot be translation variants in either direction.

Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return') — the quintessential Hebrew concept of turning back to God, from the root שׁוּב (shuv, H7725 — 'to return'). This is directional — a physical turning back. Greek μετάνοια ('change of mind') is a cognitive concept. The Hebrew teshuvah carries the full weight of prophetic call-to-return theology (Hos 14:2, Joel 2:12-13, Jer 3:12,14).

Uses הַשָּׂטָן (ha-Satan — 'the Satan/Adversary', H7854) with the definite article — a TITLE meaning 'the Adversary/Accuser' (Job 1:6-12, 2:1-7; Zech 3:1-2; 1 Chr 21:1). Greek has τὰ δαιμόνια ('demons' — plural). The Hebrew mentions the singular Adversary; the Greek mentions plural spirits. These are entirely different theological categories. A back-translator from Greek 'demons' would never write 'the Satan' with the definite article.

Uses עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ('foreign worship', H5656+H2114) — the standard Rabbinic technical term for idol worship (see Mishnah tractate Avodah Zarah). Greek uses τὰ εἴδωλα ('idols'). A back-translator from Greek would use אֱלִילִים (elilim — 'worthless things') or פְּסִילִים (pesilim — 'graven images'), not the Rabbinic legal term.

Uses חֶרֶס (cheres, H2789 — 'clay/earthenware') in the idol materials list. Greek has τὰ χαλκᾶ ('bronze things'). The Hebrew says CLAY; the Greek says BRONZE. A back-translator from Greek would write נְחֹשֶׁת (nechoshet — 'bronze'), not cheres. The Hebrew lists clay idols — a specifically Mesopotamian type of idol (clay figurines are the most common archaeological finds in Babylon and Assyria).
contradictions: Hebrew: survivors were spared BECAUSE they repented. Greek: survivors did NOT repent. These are directly contradictory theological claims about the efficacy of divine judgment.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'because they repented' (בשביל שעשו תשובה). Greek: 'they did not repent' (οὐ μετενόησαν). Opposite meanings — the most significant textual divergence in this chapter.
Hebrew: 'the Satan' (השטן — singular adversary with article). Greek: 'demons' (δαιμόνια — plural spirits). Singular vs. plural, title vs. class.
Hebrew: 'foreign worship' (עבודה זרה). Greek: 'idols' (εἴδωλα). Different terminology.
Hebrew materials: clay (חרס), stone, wood, silver, gold. Greek: gold, silver, bronze (χαλκᾶ), stone, wood. Different order and clay vs. bronze.
Hebrew disabilities: walk, speak, hear (הלך, דבר, שמע). Greek: see, hear, walk (βλέπειν, ἀκούειν, περιπατεῖν). Hebrew includes 'speak' but not 'see'; Greek includes 'see' but not 'speak.'
translation_notes: 'Because they repented' — the Hebrew בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁ is unambiguous: it means 'because/on account of the fact that.' The survivors lived because of their repentance.
עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (avodah zarah — 'foreign worship/service') is THE standard Rabbinic term for idolatry. It literally means 'strange/alien service' — worship that is foreign to YHWH.
The Hebrew distinguishes two groups: v19 — those spared because they repented; v20 — those who did NOT repent. The Greek lumps all survivors into one category of impenitence.
textual_notes: The idol polemic echoes Psalm 115:4-7: 'They have mouths but do not speak; eyes but do not see; ears but do not hear.' Also Psalm 135:15-17. The Hebrew version lists 'walk, speak, hear' — closer to Daniel 5:23 ('gods of silver and gold, bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know') but with 'speak' substituted for 'see.'

Joel 2:12-14 — 'Return to me with all your heart... rend your hearts and not your garments. Return to YHWH your God, for he is gracious and merciful... Who knows whether he will turn and relent?' The Hebrew Revelation's theology of effective repentance aligns with Joel's call to return.

one_way_hebrew: The Hebrew distinguishes TWO groups of survivors: v19 — those spared because they repented and abandoned the Satan and idolatry; v20 — those who did NOT repent of sorcery, fornication, and theft. Greek lumps ALL survivors as one group of unrepentant people. The Hebrew presents a more nuanced moral framework that recognizes both repentance and impenitence among the survivors.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'their sorceries and their fornications or their thefts' (3 sins). Greek (v21): 'their murders, their sorceries, their fornication, their thefts' (4 sins — adds φόνων, 'murders'). Hebrew omits 'murders.'
Brackets [  ] in the Hebrew source between 'sorceries' and 'fornications' suggest missing text, possibly corresponding to Greek's additional 'murders.'
translation_notes: כִּשְׁפֵיהֶם (kishfeihem — 'their sorceries', from כשף H3785) — the OT term for witchcraft/sorcery (Ex 22:17, Deut 18:10, 2 Kings 9:22, Mic 5:11, Nah 3:4). Greek φαρμακειῶν ('drug-sorceries') emphasizes the pharmaceutical/potion aspect; the Hebrew kishuf encompasses broader occult practice.
גְּנֵבוֹת (genevot — 'thefts', from גנב H1589/H1591) echoes the Decalogue commandment (Ex 20:15 — לֹא תִּגְנֹב, 'you shall not steal').

10.summary: Revelation 10 in Hebrew centers on the bat kol (heavenly voice), the scroll-swallowing prophetic commission, and the completion of YHWH's counsels. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers.
