The most striking are: (1) בַּת קוֹל (bat kol) — the uniquely rabbinic term for a heavenly voice, appearing twice (vv. 4, 8) with no Greek equivalent and no possibility of back-translation; (2) יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah — 'dry-land') — the Genesis 1:9-10 creation term, used three times (vv. 2, 5, 8) where Greek has generic 'earth'; (3) שׁוֹפָרוֹת with תּוֹקְעִים — the Sinai/Jericho/Jubilee vocabulary (v. 7) vs. Greek 'trumpets'; (4) הַסּוֹדוֹת יַהְוֶה... לַעֲבָדָיו וְלִנְבִיאָיו — the near-quote of Amos 3:7 using סוֹד/YHWH/servants/prophets (v. 7), where the Greek has none of these four Hebrew terms; (5) the Daniel 12:7 oath formula בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם with BOTH hands raised (vv. 5-6) vs. Greek's single hand and expanded phrasing; (6) הַבֹּרֵא as a participial divine title vs. the Greek descriptive clause (v. 6); (7) הַשִּׁבְעָה מַלְאָכִים ('the seven messengers,' cardinal) vs. Greek τοῦ ἑβδόμου ἀγγέλου ('the seventh angel,' ordinal) (v. 7); (8) the plural honorific תְּנוּ addressing a single angel (v. 9); (9) בוֹלֵעַ ('swallow,' the Jonah/Korah verb) vs. Greek 'eat up' (vv. 9-10); (10) צַעַר ('pain') vs. Greek 'bitterness' (vv. 9-10); and (11) the gender oscillation of the scroll pronoun (fem. v9, masc. v10). The chapter's sustained use of yabashah marks the angel as standing on the CREATION domain (sea + dry-land from Genesis 1), while the Amos 3 connection (lion cry in v3 echoing Amos 3:8, divine counsels in v7 quoting Amos 3:7) provides a unified prophetic framework. The Hebrew draws on Daniel 12 for the oath scene and Ezekiel 3 for the scroll-eating, weaving these OT threads into a tapestry that no back-translator from Greek could independently reconstruct.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַרְאֵיהוּ (mar'ehu — 'his appearance/vision', H4758) — the specific Ezekiel vision word (Ezek 1:5,13,16,26,27,28, 8:2, 40:3, 43:3). Greek has τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ('his face'). A back-translator from Greek would use פָּנָיו (panav — 'his face'), not the Ezekiel-specific mar'eh. The Hebrew describes the angel's total visual impression, not just his face.

Uses כְּלַהֶבֶת אֵשׁ ('like a flame of fire', H3852) — lahevet is the word for the flame of the burning bush (Exodus 3:2 — לַהַבַּת אֵשׁ). Greek has ὡς στύλοι πυρός ('as pillars of fire'), echoing the Exodus wilderness pillar instead. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּעַמּוּדֵי אֵשׁ ('like pillars of fire'), not the burning-bush term. The Hebrew connects the angel's feet to the theophany at the bush; the Greek translator substituted the pillar of cloud and fire — different Exodus imagery entirely.

Uses קֶשֶׁת (qeshet — 'bow', H7198) — the same word for God's covenant bow set in the clouds after the Flood (Gen 9:13-16: אֶת קַשְׁתִּי נָתַתִּי בֶּעָנָן — 'I have set my bow in the cloud'). Greek has ἶρις ('rainbow/iris'). The Hebrew word is loaded with Noahic covenant theology — this is THE bow of the covenant, not merely a rainbow. A back-translator from Greek ἶρις would not naturally reach for the Genesis covenant term.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἰσχυρόν ('mighty/strong') to describe the angel — absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'his appearance like the sun' (total visual impression). Greek: 'his face as the sun' (only the face).
Hebrew: 'like a flame of fire' (burning bush imagery). Greek: 'as pillars of fire' (wilderness pillar imagery). Different Exodus echoes.
translation_notes: 'Appearance' for mar'ehu rather than 'face' — preserving the broader visual sense and the Ezekiel vision-vocabulary connection.
'Bow' for qeshet rather than 'rainbow' — preserving the Genesis 9 covenant terminology. The angel bears the covenant sign in the cloud.

'One cloud' — the Hebrew specifies אֶחָד (echad), which may function as an intensifier or indefinite article in later Hebrew, but may also emphasize the singularity/unity of the cloud wrapping the angel.
textual_notes: The angel's description combines creation and covenant imagery: clothed in a cloud (Exodus theophany, Ex 13:21, 19:9), bearing the covenant bow (Genesis 9), with burning-bush flame feet (Exodus 3:2). This is a composite OT divine-presence portrait that no back-translator would independently assemble.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סֵפֶר (sefer — 'scroll/document', H5612) — the standard OT word for a written document (Deut 24:1; Isa 29:11-12; Jer 32:10-12). Greek has βιβλαρίδιον (biblaridion — 'little book'), a Greek diminutive. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate or use סֵפֶר קָטָן ('small scroll'), not the unmodified sefer. The Hebrew never uses a diminutive — this is simply a scroll, the same word used for the Torah scroll, the scroll of the covenant, and Jeremiah's scroll.

CRITICAL: Uses יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah — 'the dry-land', H3004) — the specific creation word from Genesis 1:9-10 (וַיִּקְרָא אֱלֹהִים לַיַּבָּשָׁה אֶרֶץ — 'and God called the dry-land earth'). Greek uses γῆ (ge — 'earth/land'). A back-translator from Greek would use אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth/land'), not the Genesis creation term. The angel stands on the sea and the dry-land — the two domains separated at creation. This creation vocabulary appears three times in this chapter (vv. 2, 5, 8).

Uses דָּרַךְ (darakh — 'trod/stepped', H1869) — the verb for treading on high places (Deut 33:29), treading the winepress (Isa 63:3, Mic 1:3), and bending the bow in conquest (Jer 51:3). Greek has ἔθηκε (etheke — 'placed/set'). The Hebrew verb implies authority and dominion — one treads upon what one rules over. A back-translator from Greek 'placed' would use שָׂם (sam — 'put') or הִנִּיחַ (hiniach — 'set down'), not the dominion verb darakh.
greek_deviations: Greek: βιβλαρίδιον ('little book' — diminutive). Hebrew: סֵפֶר ('scroll'). Greek uses a diminutive absent from Hebrew.
Greek: ἔθηκε ('placed/set'). Hebrew: דָּרַךְ ('trod'). Different verbs with different connotations — neutral placement vs. authoritative treading.
translation_notes: 'Trod' for darakh captures the Hebrew verb's connotation of dominion and authority — the angel exercises rule over sea and land.
'Dry-land' for yabashah preserves the Genesis 1 creation distinction from erets ('earth'). The sea-and-dry-land pairing is creation vocabulary.
textual_notes: The sea-and-dry-land pairing recalls Genesis 1:9-10 and Jonah 1:9 where Jonah declares: 'I fear YHWH, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry-land (הַיַּבָּשָׁה).' The angel stands as lord over the two creation domains.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צָעַק (tsa'aq — 'cried out', H6817) for the angel's voice, not שָׁאַג (sha'ag — 'roared') which is THE standard Hebrew word for a lion's roar (Amos 3:4,8; Hos 11:10; Joel 4:16). Greek has ἔκραξε ('cried out'). A back-translator could choose either verb, but the author's deliberate choice of tsa'aq — the verb of the Exodus cry for deliverance (Ex 2:23, 14:10; Judg 3:9,15, 4:3, 6:6) — reframes the angel's lion-cry as a cry that initiates deliverance, not a roar of dominance.

Uses קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'voices', H6963) where Greek has βρονταί ('thunders'). The Hebrew word is the same as the 'thunderings' at Sinai (Ex 19:16 — קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים, 'thunderings and lightnings'; Ex 20:18 — the people saw the קוֹלֹת). At Sinai, divine voice and thunder were indistinguishable — the qolot were simultaneously God's speech and heaven's thunder. A back-translator from Greek βρονταί ('thunders') would use רְעָמִים (re'amim — 'thunders'), not the theologically loaded, Sinai-specific qolot.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'seven thunders uttered their voices' (ἑπτὰ βρονταί). Hebrew: 'seven voices speaking in their voices' (שבעה קולות). The Hebrew maintains the Sinai ambiguity between divine speech and thunder.
Greek: ἐλάλησαν ('uttered/spoke'). Hebrew: מְדַבְּרִים ('speaking' — pi'el participle of דבר). The Hebrew uses a continuous participle (ongoing speech), not a completed action.
translation_notes: 'Voices' for qolot preserves the Hebrew ambiguity: at Sinai, God's 'voices' WERE the 'thunders' (Ex 19:16, 20:18; Ps 29). The seven voices both speak and thunder simultaneously.

שָׁעָה (sha'ah) as 'hour' is a later Hebrew/Aramaic temporal word (cf. Dan 3:6, 4:16), indicating the text's linguistic register. In biblical Hebrew the root שעה (H8159) means 'to gaze/look' — the 'hour' meaning reflects Second Temple usage.
textual_notes: The lion comparison echoes Amos 3:8 — 'The lion has roared (שָׁאַג), who will not fear? The Lord YHWH has spoken, who can but prophesy?' — which directly precedes the Amos 3:7 quotation appearing in verse 7 of this chapter. The Hebrew author draws on Amos 3 as a sequential source unit: lion cry (v3), divine counsels revealed to prophets (v7).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בַּת קוֹל (bat qol — literally 'daughter of a voice') — the uniquely Jewish/rabbinic term for a heavenly voice, a diminished echo of divine speech. This is a technical Hebrew idiom with no Greek equivalent. Greek has φωνὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ('a voice from heaven'). A back-translator from Greek would NEVER produce bat qol — they would write קוֹל מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם ('a voice from heaven'). Bat qol is a concept embedded in Hebrew/Aramaic thought: a 'daughter' (echo/derivative) of the original divine voice that ceased with the last prophets. This appears twice in this chapter (vv. 4, 8) and is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire Hebrew Revelation.

Uses רָצִיתִי (ratsiti — 'I desired/wanted', H7521) — a verb of inner will and desire. Greek has ἔμελλον γράφειν ('I was about to write'). The Hebrew describes Yochanan's psychological state (desire to write); the Greek describes his impending action (about to write). A back-translator from Greek would use עָמַדְתִּי ל... ('I was about to...') or הָיִיתִי עָתִיד ('I was going to'), not the desire verb ratsah.

הָאוֹמֶרֶת (ha'omeret) — feminine participle, grammatically agreeing with the feminine bat qol. This natural gender agreement demonstrates the author thinks in Hebrew. A back-translator would not need to produce this specifically feminine participial form to match the technical bat qol idiom.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I desired to write' (רציתי — psychological state). Greek: 'I was about to write' (ἔμελλον — impending action).
Hebrew: bat qol (technical rabbinic concept). Greek: generic 'voice from heaven.'
translation_notes: 'Heavenly-voice' for bat qol captures the technical meaning without the literal 'daughter of a voice.' The bat qol in Jewish tradition is a diminished form of prophecy — an echo of the divine voice.
'Desired' for ratsiti — the Hebrew emphasizes that Yochanan WANTED to write, not merely that he was about to. His will was overridden by divine command.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:26 and 12:4,9 use סָתַם (satam — 'seal up', H5640) for concealing prophetic content until the appointed time. The command to 'seal' rather than 'write' connects directly to Daniel's sealed visions — same verb, same concept of restricted revelation.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has 'raised his right AND his left to the heavens' — BOTH hands raised. Greek has τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ('his hand' — SINGULAR). A back-translator from Greek would write יָרֶם יָדוֹ ('raised his hand,' singular). The Hebrew's two-hands posture follows Daniel 12:7 EXACTLY: וַיָּרֶם יְמִינוֹ וּשְׂמֹאלוֹ אֶל הַשָּׁמַיִם ('and he raised his right hand and his left hand to the heavens'). The Hebrew copies Daniel's angel gesture with precision; the Greek reduces it to a standard one-hand oath. No back-translator from Greek would independently recover the Daniel 12:7 two-hand detail.

Second occurrence of יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah, H3004 — 'dry-land'). The sustained use of the Genesis 1 creation term throughout the chapter (vv. 2, 5, 8) is a deliberate literary pattern, not a coincidence a back-translator would reproduce three times.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: both hands raised (יְמִינוֹ וּשְׂמֹאלוֹ — 'his right and his left'). Greek: one hand raised (τὴν χεῖρα — 'the hand,' singular).
translation_notes: The brackets [ ] in the source text indicate a lacuna — a gap where text was lost or illegible. The surrounding syntax flows coherently without the missing material.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:7 — 'And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river: he raised his right hand and his left hand to the heavens and swore by the Living-One of eternity.' The Hebrew Revelation follows Daniel's angel with precision: both hands raised (v5), same oath formula (v6). The Greek Revelation follows Daniel less closely by reducing to a single hand.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT PARALLEL to Daniel 12:7: וַיִּשָּׁבַע בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם ('and he swore by the Living-One of eternity'). The Hebrew oath formula is identical to Daniel's. Greek has ὤμοσεν ἐν τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('swore by the one living unto the ages of the ages'). The Hebrew is a compact oath formula used as a divine title; the Greek is an expanded descriptive phrase. A back-translator from Greek would write בְּחֵי לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים ('by the living one forever and ever'), not the compact Danielic formula בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם.

Uses הַבֹּרֵא (habore — 'THE Creator', H1254) — a participial divine TITLE with the definite article, from the Genesis 1:1 creation verb בָּרָא (bara). Greek has ὃς ἔκτισε ('who created') — a descriptive relative clause. A back-translator from Greek would write שֶׁבָּרָא ('who created'), not the title form 'the Creator.' The Hebrew treats creation as a divine NAME; the Greek treats it as a divine ACT.

Uses בָּהּ (bah — 'in it,' feminine singular) for the heavens, then בָּהֶם (bahem — 'in them,' masculine plural) for earth and sea. This mixed-gender reference pattern — treating שָׁמַיִם as a feminine collective, then switching to masculine plural — is natural Hebrew. A back-translator from the consistent Greek ἐν αὐτοῖς would use a uniform pronoun throughout.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Creator' (הַבֹּרֵא — participial title). Greek: 'who created' (ὃς ἔκτισε — relative clause). Title vs. description.
Hebrew: 'by the Living-One of eternity' (compact formula). Greek: 'by the one living unto the ages of the ages' (expanded description).
translation_notes: 'The Living-One of eternity' for bechey ha'olam — preserving this as a title/name rather than a description. This is how YHWH is named in Daniel's oath formula.
'The Creator' for habore — preserving the participial title form that makes creation itself a divine name.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:7 full context: 'And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he raised his right hand and his left hand to the heavens and swore by the Living-One of eternity (בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם), that it would be for a time, times, and half a time.' Both angels raise both hands and use the same oath formula, but declare different things about time — Daniel's angel sets a duration; this angel declares time's end.
The creation formula (heavens + what's in them, earth, sea + all in them) echoes Exodus 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:6 — liturgical creation confessions used in OT worship.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שׁוֹפָרוֹת (shofarot — 'shofars/rams' horns', H7782) with תּוֹקְעִים (toq'im — 'blow', H8628). These are the specific Sinai/Jericho/Jubilee terms. At Sinai: 'the voice of the shofar' (Ex 19:16,19, 20:18). At Jericho: 'blow (תָּקַע) on the shofars' (Josh 6:4,8,9,13,16,20). On Yom Kippur: 'you shall blow (תָּקַע) the shofar' (Lev 25:9). Greek uses σαλπίζω/σάλπιγξ ('sound a trumpet'). A back-translator from Greek would use חֲצוֹצְרָה (chatsotsrah — 'metal trumpet') not שׁוֹפָר (ram's horn), and might use a generic verb rather than the technical תָּקַע.

CRITICAL: Uses הַסּוֹדוֹת (hasodot — 'the counsels/secrets', H5475 — PLURAL) of YHWH. Greek has τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ θεοῦ ('the mystery of God' — SINGULAR). Multiple differences: (1) Hebrew plural vs. Greek singular; (2) Hebrew סוֹד (sod — 'counsel/council') vs. Greek μυστήριον ('mystery'); (3) Hebrew YHWH vs. Greek θεός ('God'). The Hebrew סוֹד is the word for YHWH's intimate divine council (Jer 23:18,22; Ps 25:14, 89:8; Job 15:8; Prov 3:32) — the inner circle of divine deliberation. A back-translator from Greek would use רָז (raz — Daniel's Aramaic 'mystery', Dan 2:18-19,27-30,47) or render μυστήριον in some other way, not the OT-specific סוֹד.

NEAR-QUOTE of Amos 3:7: כִּי לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דָּבָר כִּי אִם גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ אֶל עֲבָדָיו הַנְּבִיאִים — 'For the Lord YHWH does nothing unless he reveals his counsel (sodo) to his servants the prophets.' The Hebrew has: הסודות יהוה כמו שמודיע לעבדיו ולנביאיו — same key vocabulary: סוד + יהוה + עבדים + נביאים. A back-translator from Greek, which lacks all four of these specific Hebrew terms, would not independently reconstruct this Amos quotation.

Hebrew: הַשִּׁבְעָה מַלְאָכִים ('the SEVEN messengers' — cardinal number, all seven). Greek: τοῦ ἑβδόμου ἀγγέλου ('the SEVENTH angel' — ordinal number, one specific angel). A back-translator from Greek would write הַמַּלְאָךְ הַשְּׁבִיעִי ('the seventh messenger'), not הַשִּׁבְעָה מַלְאָכִים ('the seven messengers'). The Hebrew envisions the completion of all seven shofar blasts as a unified event; the Greek isolates the seventh.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the seven messengers' (all seven, cardinal). Greek: 'the seventh angel' (one, ordinal).
Hebrew: 'the counsels' (plural, סוֹדוֹת). Greek: 'the mystery' (singular, μυστήριον).
Hebrew: 'YHWH' (the divine name). Greek: 'God' (θεοῦ).
Hebrew: 'he made known' (neutral הוֹדִיעַ). Greek: 'he declared good news' (εὐηγγέλισεν, from εὐαγγελίζω). The Greek adds a 'good news/gospel' connotation absent from the neutral Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Counsels' for sodot rather than 'mysteries' — preserving the Hebrew concept of divine council deliberation (sod) as distinct from Greek μυστήριον.
'Shofars' rather than 'trumpets' — the shofar is a ram's horn, not a metal trumpet (חֲצוֹצְרָה). The instruments carry entirely different theological weight: Sinai, Jericho, Jubilee, Rosh HaShanah.
textual_notes: Amos 3:7 is the direct OT source for this verse's language. In Amos, the declaration that YHWH reveals his sod to his servants the prophets comes immediately after the lion metaphor (Amos 3:4,8) — the same lion that appears in v3 of this chapter. The Hebrew author works through Amos 3 as a sequential source: lion cry (v3) → divine counsels revealed to prophets (v7).

The feminine plural תִּכְלֶינָה ('shall be completed') agrees with the implied feminine referent — the counsels/events. The messengers are masculine, but the things to be completed are treated as feminine, a natural Hebrew construction.

one_way_hebrew: Second occurrence of בַּת קוֹל (bat qol). Here the participle is masculine אֹמֵר (omer) rather than feminine אוֹמֶרֶת (omeret) as in v4. The shift from feminine (agreeing with the grammatically feminine bat qol) to masculine (reflecting the male speaker behind the voice) is a natural Hebrew phenomenon — the author shifts between grammatical agreement and notional agreement. A back-translator from Greek, which has no such gender alternation in the source, would not produce this shift.

Third occurrence of יַבָּשָׁה (yabashah — 'dry-land', H3004). The threefold repetition of the Genesis 1 creation vocabulary throughout the chapter (vv. 2, 5, 8) is a sustained literary pattern that stamps the entire vision with creation theology.
greek_deviations: Greek: βιβλαρίδιον ('little book' — diminutive). Hebrew: סֵפֶר ('scroll'). As in v2, the Hebrew never diminishes the scroll.
The gap marked [ ] in the source text between הספר and הפתוח suggests a word was lost. Greek has no corresponding gap.
translation_notes: The masculine אֹמֵר (omer) after bat qol may indicate the bat kol here serves as the vehicle for a male speaker — possibly YHWH himself speaking through the heavenly voice-echo.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּנוּ (tenu — 'give!', PLURAL imperative of natan, H5414) when addressing a single angel. This is the Hebrew honorific plural — using plural address for a being of superior rank, analogous to the majestic plural. Greek has δός μοι (dos moi — 'give me,' singular imperative). A back-translator from the Greek singular imperative would write תֵּן (ten — singular), not the respectful plural. This reveals a Hebrew-speaking author's instinct for polite address to an angelic being.

Uses בוֹלֵעַ (bole'a — 'swallow', H1104) — the verb for swallowing whole, used of the great fish swallowing Jonah (Jonah 2:1) and the earth swallowing Korah (Num 16:30,32,34; Deut 11:6). Greek has κατάφαγε (kataphage — 'eat up/devour'). A back-translator from Greek would use אָכַל (akhal — 'eat') not בָּלַע (bala — 'swallow'). Eating involves chewing and processing; swallowing is whole absorption. The scroll is not to be analyzed (chewed) but internalized whole.

Uses צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'pain/distress') where Greek has πικρανεῖ ('shall make bitter'). A back-translator from Greek would use מַר (mar — 'bitter') or יְמָרֵר (yemarer — 'make bitter'). The Hebrew describes physical pain in the innards; the Greek describes a taste sensation (bitterness). Different bodily experiences entirely.

Uses feminine אוֹתָהּ (otah — 'it,' fem.) for the scroll, though סֵפֶר (sefer) is grammatically masculine. This may reflect the author thinking of the content as תּוֹרָה (torah — feminine) or מְגִלָּה (megillah — 'scroll,' feminine). In v10, the pronoun switches to masculine אוֹתוֹ. This gender oscillation is a natural Hebrew phenomenon that a back-translator from Greek (which uses consistent neuter throughout) would not produce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'swallow it' (בוֹלֵעַ — swallow whole). Greek: 'eat it up' (κατάφαγε — devour). Different physical actions.
Hebrew: 'it shall make for you pain' (צער — physical suffering). Greek: 'it shall make your belly bitter' (πικρανεῖ — bitterness). Different sensory experience.
Hebrew: 'Give me' (תנו — plural/honorific address to a single angel). Greek: 'Give me' (δός — singular, no honorific).
translation_notes: 'Swallow' for bole'a rather than 'eat' — preserving the Hebrew verb's meaning of whole ingestion without chewing. The prophetic word enters whole.
'Pain' for tsa'ar — later Hebrew for distress/suffering, distinct from the Greek concept of bitterness. Prophecy causes internal pain, not merely a bitter taste.
כִּדְבַשׁ (kidvash — 'like honey') echoes Ezekiel 3:3 where the scroll tastes מָתוֹק כִּדְבַשׁ ('sweet like honey'). Both prophets consume a divine scroll with the same result.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 3:1-3 is the direct OT parallel: 'Son of man, eat this scroll... So I ate it, and it was in my mouth like honey for sweetness.' The Hebrew Revelation follows the Ezekiel scroll-eating pattern closely but adds the element of internal pain — prophecy is sweet to receive but painful to carry.

one_way_hebrew: Now uses masculine אוֹתוֹ (oto — 'it,' masc.) for the scroll, matching the masculine סֵפֶר, after the feminine אוֹתָהּ in v9. This gender oscillation within two consecutive verses is a natural Hebrew phenomenon — the author shifts between thinking of the physical scroll (masc. sefer) and its content (fem. torah/megillah). A back-translator from Greek, which uses consistent neuter τὸ βιβλαρίδιον throughout, would maintain uniform grammatical reference.

Uses two distinct verbs in sequence: בוֹלֵעַ (bole'a — 'swallowed,' H1104) for the initial act, then אָכַלְתִּי (akhalti — 'I ate,' H398) for the completed process. The Hebrew distinguishes swallowing (whole ingestion) from eating (full digestion). Greek uses only κατέφαγον (katephagon — 'ate up') for the action. This lexical distinction is a natural Hebrew feature.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'it made for me pain in my innards' (צער — physical suffering). Greek: 'my belly was made bitter' (ἐπικράνθη — embittered). Same divergence as v9 — pain vs. bitterness.
translation_notes: The two-verb distinction (swallowed → ate) mirrors the prophetic process: the scroll enters whole (swallowing) then is processed through experience (eating). Prophecy is received as complete revelation, then digested through living it out.

one_way_hebrew: Uses TWO distinct Hebrew words for 'peoples': לְאֻמִּים (le'umim, H3816 — 'nations') AND עַמִּים (amim, H5971 — 'peoples'). These carry different nuances: le'umim emphasizes ethnic/national identity (Gen 25:23, Ps 2:1, Isa 34:1); amim emphasizes communal/social grouping. Greek has λαοῖς ('peoples') and ἔθνεσιν ('nations') PLUS γλώσσαις ('tongues') and βασιλεῦσι ('kings') — a FOUR-fold list vs. the Hebrew THREE-fold list. A back-translator from Greek would include לְשׁוֹנוֹת (leshonot — 'tongues'), which the Hebrew entirely lacks.

Uses צָרִיךְ (tsarikh — 'must/need') — a Mishnaic Hebrew word absent from the biblical corpus. This reveals the author's linguistic register: a Hebrew speaker of the Second Temple period using living vernacular Hebrew, not a translator artificially reconstructing biblical idiom from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three categories (nations, peoples, kings). Greek: four categories (peoples, nations, tongues, kings). Greek adds 'tongues/languages' absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: לְאֻמִּים then עַמִּים (two distinct Hebrew words for 'peoples'). Greek: λαοῖς then ἔθνεσιν — different order and different semantic range.
translation_notes: 'Nations' for le'umim and 'peoples' for amim — preserving the distinction between the two Hebrew terms. Le'umim has a more ethnic/political sense; amim has a more communal/social sense.
צָרִיךְ (tsarikh) as 'must' — characteristic Mishnaic Hebrew indicating obligation/necessity, further evidence of the text's living Hebrew register rather than artificial back-translation.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 1:10 — 'I have appointed you this day over nations (גּוֹיִם) and over kingdoms (מַמְלָכוֹת).' The prophetic commission to address nations and kings echoes the classical prophetic calling. The Hebrew Revelation recommissions Yochanan in the pattern of Jeremiah.

11.summary: Revelation 11 in Hebrew presents the two witnesses passage with multiple layers of Torah, prophetic, and later Hebrew vocabulary that cannot derive from the Greek Textus Receptus. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers. The STRONGEST are: (1) 'torches' (אבוקות) vs. 'lampstands' (λυχνίαι) in v4 — completely different objects; (2) 'the INNER sanctuary' vs. 'the OUTER court' in v2 — opposite spatial references that no translator would reverse; (3) 'the HOLY city' vs. 'the GREAT city' in v8 — opposite characterizations of Jerusalem; (4) 'OUR lord' vs. 'THEIR Lord' in v8 — a person switch no translator would introduce; (5) the Exodus 15:16 dread-and-terror word-pair (פחד ואימה) in v11 — a specific OT quotation collapsed to 'great fear' in Greek; (6) the textual lacuna in v10 — a manuscript gap that only an original text tradition would preserve. The chapter is saturated with later Hebrew forms (אילו, רשות, כיון, צער, שעה, דרס) that indicate natural post-Temple Hebrew composition rather than translation. The witnesses combine the powers of Moses (blood, plagues) and Elijah (fire, drought, ascension), and the narrative is structured around Torah legal vocabulary: עדים (covenantal witnesses), עדות (covenantal testimony), תהום (the primordial Deep), and נגעים (Levitical plagues). The Hebrew and Greek diverge most dramatically on spatial theology (inner vs. outer sanctuary), the characterization of Jerusalem (holy vs. great), and the witnesses' instruments (torches vs. lampstands).

one_way_hebrew: Uses הֵיכַל (heykal, H1964 — 'sanctuary/temple hall') paired with the Tetragrammaton: הַהֵיכַל יַהְוֶה ('the sanctuary of YHWH'). Greek has τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ('the temple of God'). The Hebrew preserves the specific divine name YHWH where the Greek generically says 'God' (Θεός). A back-translator from Greek would write היכל אלהים ('sanctuary of God'), not 'sanctuary of YHWH.' The Tetragrammaton is untranslatable from a Greek source that lacks it.

Uses הַמִּתְפַּלְּלִים (hamitpalelim — 'those praying', Hithpael of פלל H6419). Greek has τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας ('those bowing/worshipping'). These are different religious activities. A back-translator from Greek would write המשתחוים (hamishtachavim — 'those bowing down/worshipping'), the standard Hebrew for proskyneō. The Hebrew author uses the rabbinic technical term for verbal prayer/intercession (hitpalel), not physical prostration.

Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut — 'in the likeness of', H1823). This is the prophetic vision formula from Ezekiel (Ezek 1:5, 1:10, 1:22, 1:26, 8:2, 10:1, 10:21-22). Greek has ὅμοιος ('similar to'). A translator from Greek could use כמו (kemo) or דומה (domeh). The Hebrew author naturally uses the Ezekielian vision vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὁ ἄγγελος εἱστήκει λέγων ('the angel stood saying') — specifying an angel as the speaker. Hebrew has simply ואמר ('and he said') without identifying the speaker.
Greek: 'the temple of God' (τοῦ Θεοῦ). Hebrew: 'the sanctuary of YHWH' (יהוה). Different divine designation.
Greek: 'those worshipping' (προσκυνοῦντας — physical prostration). Hebrew: 'those praying' (מתפללים — verbal intercession).
translation_notes: 'Sanctuary' for heykal — the specific inner hall of the Temple (1 Kings 6:3,5,17), distinguishing it from the broader temple complex (bayit).
כִּדְמוּת (kidmut) is the same word used in Genesis 1:26 (בדמותנו — 'in our likeness') and throughout Ezekiel's visions. It carries stronger theological weight than a simple simile.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 40:3-5 — Ezekiel is given a measuring reed to measure the temple. The pattern of receiving a reed to measure sacred space is an Ezekiel motif. Both the Hebrew Revelation and Ezekiel use קנה (qaneh — 'reed') as the measuring instrument.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew says הַהֵיכָל הַפְּנִימִי ('the INNER sanctuary', H6442). Greek says τὴν αὐλὴν τὴν ἔξωθεν τοῦ ναοῦ ('the court which is OUTSIDE the temple'). These are OPPOSITE spatial references — inner vs. outer. No translator working from the Greek 'outer court' would write 'inner sanctuary.' The Hebrew author envisions the innermost sanctum itself being given over to the nations — a far more radical profanation than merely ceding the outer court. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.

Uses זְרוֹק (zeroq — 'cast/throw', imperative of zaraq H2236). In priestly Torah texts, zaraq is the technical verb for sprinkling sacrificial blood on the altar (Lev 1:5,11; Num 18:17; 2 Kings 16:13). Using the priestly sprinkling verb for an act of EXCLUSION from sacred space creates a profound irony that only a Hebrew author immersed in priestly vocabulary would produce.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'the inner sanctuary' (ההיכל הפנימי). Greek: 'the court outside the temple' (τὴν αὐλὴν τὴν ἔξωθεν τοῦ ναοῦ). Opposite spaces excluded from measurement.
Hebrew: ἔκβαλε ἔξω ('cast out') in Greek is a general verb. Hebrew uses zaraq — a priestly technical term.
contradictions: The inner/outer reversal between Hebrew and Greek represents a genuine theological divergence, not a translation variant. In the Hebrew vision, YHWH's withdrawn presence renders even the innermost sanctum available for profanation. In the Greek, only the outer (Gentile) court is given over. These are irreconcilable spatial theologies.
translation_notes: דָרְסוּ (darsu — 'they shall trample') is a later Hebrew/Aramaic verb not attested in the OT. No standard Strong's number. Greek πατήσουσι likewise means 'trample/tread.'
חֳדָשִׁים (chodashim, H2320) means both 'months' and 'new moons.' The root חדש carries the meaning 'new/renewal' — the liturgical calendar term.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:13-14 — 'How long shall the vision be... to give both the sanctuary and the host to be trampled underfoot?' The trampling of the holy city echoes Daniel's vision of the sanctuary's profanation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵדִים (edim — 'witnesses', H5707) — the specific Torah legal term. Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15 establish that 'at the mouth of TWO witnesses or THREE witnesses' a matter is confirmed. The phrase 'two witnesses' (שני עדים) directly invokes the Torah's evidentiary standard. Greek μάρτυσι ('witnesses/martyrs') is broader and later acquired the meaning 'martyr.' The Hebrew stays within Torah legal vocabulary.

Hebrew has present-tense נוֹתֵן (noten — 'I give/am giving'). Greek has future δώσω ('I will give'). The Hebrew participle presents the act as ongoing — God is continuously giving his witnesses. Greek places it in the future. These are different temporal perspectives a translator would not interchange.
greek_deviations: Greek adds an implied 'power/authority' (some MSS have ἐξουσίαν) — 'I will give [power] to my two witnesses.' Hebrew simply says 'I give my two witnesses' without the addition of power/authority.
Hebrew: present participle נוֹתֵן ('I give'). Greek: future indicative δώσω ('I will give'). Different tense.
translation_notes: 'Witnesses' for edim preserves the Torah legal-covenantal sense. These are not mere observers but covenant witnesses with legal standing under Torah.
1,260 days = 42 months = 3½ years — matching the 42 months of trampling in verse 2. The prophesying and the trampling are concurrent.
textual_notes: The two-witness requirement (Deut 19:15) governs all of Torah jurisprudence. God sends the minimum required number of covenant witnesses to render a legal verdict against the nations.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲבוּקוֹת (avukot — 'torches'). Greek has λυχνίαι ('lampstands'). These are entirely different objects. A back-translator from Greek 'lampstands' would write מְנוֹרוֹת (menorot — 'menorahs/lampstands'), the standard Hebrew for Temple lampstands (Ex 25:31ff). The Hebrew author writes 'torches' — portable, outdoor flames evoking Gideon's torches (Judg 7:16,20) and night watchmen. The Greek translator converted the unfamiliar image to Temple furniture. This is one of the clearest one-way markers in the chapter: no translator from λυχνίαι would produce אבוקות.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'torches' (אבוקות). Greek: 'lampstands' (λυχνίαι). Completely different objects — portable outdoor flames vs. Temple furniture.

Hebrew: 'Elohim of the earth' (אלהי הארץ). Some Greek MSS have κυρίου ('Lord') while others have θεοῦ ('God'). The Zechariah 4:14 source has אֲדוֹן כָּל הָאָרֶץ ('the Lord of ALL the earth'). Neither Greek nor Hebrew Revelation preserves 'all' (כל), but the Hebrew uses a different divine title than the source.
translation_notes: אֲבוּקוֹת (avukot — 'torches') is a later Hebrew word not attested in the OT. No standard Strong's number. Its use here is natural Hebrew vocabulary, not a translation artifact.
'Olives' for zeitim — olive trees in Zechariah's vision supply oil for the lampstand. The Hebrew Revelation pairs olives with torches (oil-fed flames) rather than olives with lampstands.
textual_notes: Direct allusion to Zechariah 4:3,11-14 — the two olive trees standing beside 'the Lord of all the earth.' Zechariah's vision concerned Zerubbabel (royal) and Joshua (priestly) — the two anointed offices. The witnesses embody both royal and priestly authority.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says simply 'fire shall come and burn them' (תבוא אש ושרף אותם) — fire arrives as divine judgment without specifying its source. Greek has πῦρ ἐκπορεύεται ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτῶν ('fire proceeds out of their mouth'). The Greek adds the dramatic detail of fire issuing from the witnesses' mouths. The Hebrew presents fire as an external divine act — God sends fire, as with Elijah (2 Kings 1:10-12). A back-translator from Greek would include 'from their mouth' (מפיהם); its absence from the Hebrew is a one-way marker.

The Hebrew verse is a single concise statement. The Greek repeats the entire conditional clause and adds 'he must be killed in this way' (οὕτω δεῖ αὐτὸν ἀποκτανθῆναι). The Hebrew's brevity is characteristic of Hebrew prophetic style, not a condensation of Greek.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'fire comes out of their mouth and devours their enemies' (πῦρ ἐκπορεύεται ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτῶν). Hebrew: 'fire shall come and burn them.' No mention of fire from mouths in the Hebrew.
Greek repeats the entire clause and adds a consequence: 'if anyone wants to harm them, he must be killed in this way.' Hebrew gives only one clause — far more concise.
translation_notes: רוֹצֶה (rotseh — 'desires/wants') is from the root רצה, which in the OT (H7521) carries connotations of delight, will, and acceptance (Ps 40:13, 51:16). Later Hebrew uses it as a general verb for 'want.'
'Burn' for saraf (H8313) — the same verb used for the burning of Sodom (Gen 19:24-25 uses a different verb, but saraf is used for divine burning throughout Leviticus).
textual_notes: 2 Kings 1:10-12 — Elijah called down fire from heaven on the captains who came against him. The fire imagery connects the witnesses to Elijah's prophetic authority.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues', H5061) — the specific Levitical term for divine afflictions: the plagues of Egypt (Ex 11:1) and priestly skin inspections (Lev 13-14). Greek πᾶσαν πληγήν ('every plague/blow') is more generic. A back-translator from Greek would likely use מַכּוֹת (makot — 'blows/strikes') or מגפה (magefah — 'plague'). The Hebrew author reaches for the Torah's technical Levitical term.

Uses לַהֲפֹךְ (lahafokh — 'to turn/overturn', H2015) for the water-to-blood transformation. This is the specific verb used for God's overturning of Sodom (Gen 19:21,25,29; Deut 29:23; Isa 13:19) and for the first Egyptian plague (Ex 7:17 — 'the water shall be turned to blood'). Greek στρέφειν is more neutral. The Hebrew verb carries overtones of catastrophic divine judgment beyond mere transformation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: רשות ('permission/authority') — a characteristically Mishnaic Hebrew word with no OT Strong's number. Greek: ἐξουσίαν ἔχουσιν ('they have authority'). The later Hebrew vocabulary is natural composition, not translation.
Hebrew: 'in the days of their prophesying' (בימי נבאיהם). Greek: 'in the days of their prophecy' (ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς προφητείας αὐτῶν). Hebrew uses a verbal noun form; Greek uses the abstract noun.
translation_notes: 'Authority' for reshut — this Mishnaic Hebrew word carries the nuance of 'permission granted by a higher authority,' distinct from the more forceful Greek ἐξουσία. The witnesses act under divine license.
The threefold power structure — shutting heavens, turning water to blood, striking with plagues — combines the powers of Elijah (rain) and Moses (blood and plagues).
textual_notes: 1 Kings 17:1 — Elijah declared 'there shall be neither dew nor rain these years.' Exodus 7:17-20 — Moses turned water to blood. The witnesses exercise the combined authority of Israel's two greatest prophets.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom — 'the Deep', H8415) — the primordial chaos waters from Genesis 1:2 (וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵי תְהוֹם — 'and darkness upon the face of the Deep'). Greek has ἄβυσσος ('abyss'). While ἄβυσσος can correspond to tehom, the Hebrew word carries creation theology — the beast emerges from the pre-creation chaos, the unformed void that preceded God's ordering of the world. The OT resonances are far richer: Gen 1:2, 7:11, 8:2; Ps 42:7, 104:6; Isa 51:10. A back-translator might coincidentally use tehom, but the creation-theology dimension is uniquely Hebrew.

Uses עֵדוּתָם (edutam — 'their testimony', H5715). The root עדות (edut) is the specific Torah word for covenantal witness — the Ark is called אֲרוֹן הָעֵדוּת ('Ark of the Testimony', Ex 25:22), the Tabernacle is called מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדוּת ('Dwelling-place of the Testimony', Ex 38:21). Greek μαρτυρία is broader. The Hebrew connects the witnesses' mission to Torah covenantal testimony.

Uses הַחַיָּה (ha-chayyah — 'the beast/living creature', H2416). This word means both 'living thing' (Gen 1:24, 2:19) and 'wild beast' (Gen 3:1, 37:20). It shares the root with חַיִּים ('life'). Greek θηρίον ('wild beast') is unambiguous. The Hebrew creates an ironic tension: the 'living thing' from the Deep brings death. A back-translator from Greek's unambiguous θηρίον would not stumble into this semantic layering.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: שֶׁהָלַךְ ('that went/goes', from הלך — 'walk'). Greek: τὸ ἀναβαῖνον ('the one ascending'). Hebrew uses the common motion verb; Greek uses the more dramatic 'ascending.' A back-translator from Greek would use עולה (oleh — 'ascending'), not הלך ('walking').
Hebrew: masculine verb הלך with feminine noun חיה — a gender mismatch characteristic of later Hebrew, not calqued from Greek where neuter θηρίον takes neuter participle.
translation_notes: Consonantal כלא (kala, H3607) means 'to shut up, restrain, withhold.' In context — 'after they shut up their testimony' — the sense is 'completed/concluded,' i.e., when their testimony reaches its appointed end. The consonantal root is כלא (with aleph), not כלה (H3615 — 'to finish'), though both converge in meaning here.
'The Deep' for tehom — preserving the Genesis creation connection. Not 'abyss' (a Greek loanword) or 'pit.'
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — the Deep (tehom) is the primordial chaos that preceded creation. The beast's origin in tehom marks it as an anti-creation force, emerging from the very chaos that God subdued at the beginning.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew calls Jerusalem הָעִיר הַקְּדוֹשָׁה ('the HOLY city', H6918). Greek calls it τῆς πόλεως τῆς μεγάλης ('the GREAT city'). Opposite characterizations. A back-translator from Greek 'great city' would write העיר הגדולה ('the great city'), not 'the holy city.' The Hebrew author maintains Jerusalem's sacred status even while comparing it to Sodom and Egypt — a profound theological tension that the Greek resolves by stripping the holiness designation. This is a major one-way marker.

Uses אֲדוֹנֵינוּ (adoneinu — 'OUR lord', H113, 1st person plural suffix). Greek has ὁ κύριος αὐτῶν ('THEIR Lord', 3rd person). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדוֹנֵיהֶם (adoneihem — 'their lord'), not אֲדוֹנֵינוּ ('our lord'). The Hebrew author includes himself among those who belong to the crucified lord — a first-person confession absent from the Greek.

Uses רְחוֹבוֹת (rechovot — 'plazas/broad places', H7339, PLURAL). Greek has τῆς πλατείας (singular 'street/plaza'). The Hebrew naturally pluralizes — a city has multiple public spaces. Same plural pattern appears in Rev 21:21.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the holy city' (העיר הקדושה). Greek: 'the great city' (τῆς πόλεως τῆς μεγάλης). Opposite characterization of Jerusalem.
Greek adds πνευματικῶς ('spiritually') — 'which is SPIRITUALLY called Sodom and Egypt.' Hebrew has simply 'which is called' (הנקרא) — no qualifier.
Hebrew: 'our lord' (אדונינו — 1st person). Greek: 'their Lord' (αὐτῶν — 3rd person). Different perspective.
Greek has singular πλατείας ('street'). Hebrew has plural רחובות ('plazas').
translation_notes: נִצְלַב (nitslav — 'was crucified') is from the root צלב, a native Hebrew/Aramaic verb attested in rabbinic literature. The Niphal conjugation is natural Hebrew grammar. No standard OT Strong's number since crucifixion was not an Israelite practice.
כֵּיוָן (keivan — 'because/since') is a later Hebrew conjunction not found in the OT. Its natural use here is characteristic of an author writing in post-Temple Hebrew, not translating from Greek.
textual_notes: Isaiah 1:10 — 'Hear the word of YHWH, you rulers of Sodom; give ear to the Torah of our God, you people of Gomorrah.' The prophet addresses Jerusalem's leaders as 'rulers of Sodom' while the city retains its identity as the place of YHWH's Torah. The Hebrew Revelation preserves this same tension — the city is simultaneously 'holy' and 'Sodom.'

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew has TWO groups: 'peoples and tribes' (עמים ושבטים). Greek has FOUR: 'peoples and tribes and tongues and nations' (λαῶν καὶ φυλῶν καὶ γλωσσῶν καὶ ἐθνῶν). The four-part formula is a characteristic Revelation pattern in Greek (5:9, 7:9, 10:11, 13:7, 14:6). A back-translator working from Greek's standard four-part formula would include all four terms. The Hebrew author uses a simpler, more natural Hebrew pair.

Uses אֵיזֶה (eizeh — 'some/which ones'). This is a distinctly post-biblical Hebrew indefinite pronoun common in Mishnaic Hebrew. It has no Greek equivalent being translated — Greek uses βλέπουσιν ἐκ τῶν λαῶν ('they look from among the peoples'). The colloquial Hebrew eizeh is natural authorial vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Greek has four groups: peoples, tribes, tongues, nations. Hebrew has two: peoples, tribes.

Greek: 'shall not allow their dead bodies to be put into tombs' (οὐκ ἀφήσουσι τὰ πτώματα αὐτῶν τεθῆναι εἰς μνήματα). Hebrew: 'shall not bury them' (ולא תקברו אותם). Hebrew is far more concise; Greek specifies 'placed into tombs.'
translation_notes: The denial of burial is among the gravest dishonors in Israelite culture (1 Kings 14:11, Jer 7:33, 16:4, 22:19). The Hebrew reader understands the full weight of this horror.
textual_notes: Psalm 79:2-3 — 'They have given the dead bodies of your servants as food for the birds of the heavens, the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them.' The unburied corpses echo the Psalm 79 lament over Jerusalem's desecration.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אִישׁ לְרֵעֵיהוּ (ish le-re'ehu — 'each man to his neighbor', H376+H7453). This is a fixed OT idiom appearing throughout the Tanakh (Ex 11:2, 32:27; Jer 31:34; Zech 3:10; Est 9:19,22). Greek has πέμψουσιν ἀλλήλοις ('they shall send to one another'). A back-translator from Greek's generic reciprocal would not produce this specific idiomatic pair. The Hebrew formulaic expression is too distinctive to derive from the Greek.

The text preserves a LACUNA: [  ] appears between כי and הנביאים. A manuscript gap exists in the source. This kind of scribal awareness — marking gaps rather than filling them — is characteristic of an original textual tradition, not a translation. A translator working from Greek would produce a seamless text; only a scribe copying from a damaged Hebrew original would preserve the gap.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'these two prophets tormented (ἐβασάνισαν) those dwelling on the earth.' Hebrew: 'these prophets made much distress (צער).' Greek implies active torture; Hebrew implies causing grief. Different severity.
Greek specifies 'two prophets' (δύο προφῆται). Hebrew says only 'these prophets' (הנביאים הללו) without the number.

Greek: 'they shall make merry and send gifts' (εὐφρανθήσονται... καὶ δῶρα πέμψουσιν). Hebrew: 'they shall rejoice and send gifts' (ישמחו... וישלחו מתנות). Similar but Hebrew שמח and Greek εὐφραίνω have different ranges of meaning.
translation_notes: אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') is a distinctly later Hebrew demonstrative pronoun, common in Mishnaic Hebrew. Its repeated use (vv. 10, 11) shows the author writes naturally in post-biblical idiom.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/sorrow') is a later Hebrew word without a standard OT Strong's number. The root appears in Genesis 34:7 (עָצַב/עצר) but the noun form צער is Mishnaic.
'[...]' preserves the textual lacuna present in the Hebrew source.
textual_notes: The gift-sending echoes Esther 9:19,22 — the celebration of Purim, where Jews sent 'portions each man to his neighbor' (אִישׁ לְרֵעֵהוּ). The earth-dwellers' celebration over the prophets' deaths is a dark inversion of Purim — a festival of deliverance turned into a festival of murder.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פַּחַד וְאֵימָה (pachad ve-eimah — 'dread and terror', H6343+H367) with the verb נפל ('fell'). This EXACT combination echoes Exodus 15:16: תִּפֹּל עֲלֵיהֶם אֵימָתָה וָפַחַד — 'Terror and dread FALL upon them' — from the Song of the Sea describing the nations' fear at the Exodus. Greek has simply φόβος μέγας ('great fear' — one word). A back-translator from Greek's single word 'great fear' would write פחד גדול ('great fear') or יראה גדולה ('great fear'), NOT the specific Exodus 15:16 word-pair. The Hebrew author quotes the Song of the Sea; the Greek translator summarized it.

Hebrew says 'they arose and stood upon their feet' (קמים המה ודורסים על רגליהם) without explaining HOW they came back to life. Greek adds πνεῦμα ζωῆς ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς αὐτούς ('a spirit of life from God entered into them') — a theological explanation absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew lets the miracle speak for itself; the Greek adds mechanism. A back-translator from Greek would include the 'spirit of life' detail.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'a spirit of life from God entered into them' (πνεῦμα ζωῆς ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ). Absent from Hebrew — the Hebrew simply says 'they arose.'
Greek: φόβος μέγας ('great fear' — single concept). Hebrew: פחד ואימה ('dread AND terror' — paired nouns from Exodus 15:16). The Hebrew is more specific and OT-rooted.
translation_notes: דוֹרְסִים (dorsim — 'treading/standing') is the same later Hebrew verb as in verse 2 (דרס). Here it means 'standing firmly' — treading on their own feet, i.e., standing upright.
'Dread and terror' preserves the Hebrew word-pair rather than collapsing it to 'great fear.'
textual_notes: Exodus 15:16 — 'Terror and dread fall upon them; by the greatness of your arm they are still as stone.' The nations' fear at the Exodus is re-enacted at the witnesses' resurrection.

Ezekiel 37:10 — 'And the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood upon their feet' (ויעמדו על רגליהם). The dry bones vision parallels the witnesses' resurrection. Note: the Greek Revelation may be drawing on Ezekiel's 'spirit/breath' language where the Hebrew Revelation does not.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שׂוֹנְאֵיהֶם (son'eihem — 'their enemies/haters', from sane' H8130 — 'to hate'). Greek has ἐχθροὶ αὐτῶν ('their enemies'). A back-translator from Greek could use אוֹיְבֵיהֶם (oyveihem, from oyev — 'enemy') or צָרֵיהֶם (tsareihem, from tsar — 'adversary'). The choice of the 'hate' root (שנא) implies visceral personal hatred. This is the same root used of Esau's hatred (Gen 27:41) and the enemies in the Psalms (Ps 21:8, 34:21, 69:4). The vocabulary carries emotional, not political, enmity.

Uses בְּעָנָן אֶחָד ('in ONE cloud', H6051+H259 — numeral). Greek has ἐν τῇ νεφέλῃ ('in THE cloud' — definite article). Hebrew specifies 'one cloud' with the numeral; Greek uses the article. The Hebrew 'one cloud' connects to Daniel 7:13 (עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא — 'with the clouds of heaven') and the pillar of cloud in the wilderness (Ex 13:21). A back-translator from Greek 'the cloud' would write בֶּעָנָן ('in the cloud') without the numeral.
greek_deviations: Greek: φωνὴ μεγάλη ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ('a great voice from heaven'). Hebrew: קול אחד ('one voice'). Hebrew has 'one' where Greek has 'great,' and 'from heaven' is absent from the Hebrew.
Greek: Ἀνάβατε ὧδε ('Come up HERE'). Hebrew: simply עלו ('Ascend!'). Hebrew is more concise — no destination specified.
translation_notes: 'Ascend' for alu — the verbal root עלה (alah, H5927) is the pilgrimage word: Israel 'goes up' to Jerusalem (Ps 122:4), offerings 'go up' on the altar. The witnesses' ascent is the ultimate aliyah.
'Enemies' for son'eihem — literally 'their haters,' preserving the emotional dimension.
textual_notes: 2 Kings 2:11 — Elijah ascended to heaven in a whirlwind. The witnesses' ascension in a cloud echoes both Elijah's departure and Yeshua's ascension (Acts 1:9 — 'a cloud received him out of their sight').

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּנֵי אָדָם (benei adam — 'sons of Adam/mankind', H1121+H120). Greek has ὀνόματα ἀνθρώπων ('NAMES of men'). Hebrew counts 'sons of Adam' (living people); Greek counts 'names of men' (identities). A back-translator from Greek would write שְׁמוֹת אֲנָשִׁים ('names of men'), not the Hebrew collective expression בני אדם. The Hebrew phrase echoes the creation account — these are children of Adam who perish.

Uses שֶׁבַח (shebach — 'praise'). This is the specific Hebrew/Aramaic praise word from Daniel (Dan 2:23, 4:34). Greek has δόξαν ('glory'). A back-translator from Greek would use כָּבוֹד (kavod — 'glory'), not the Daniel-specific shebach. The Hebrew connects the survivors' response to Daniel's Babylonian-context praise.

Uses נִבְהֲלוּ (nivhalu — 'were terrified', Niphal of bahal H926). This is the exact verb used for Belshazzar's terror at the writing on the wall (Dan 5:9 — 'then King Belshazzar was greatly terrified/נִבְהַל'). Greek has ἔμφοβοι ἐγένοντο ('became fearful'). The Hebrew verb implies panicked, paralyzing terror — stronger than the Greek.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'seven thousand names of men' (ὀνόματα ἀνθρώπων). Hebrew: 'seven thousand of the sons of Adam' (מבני אדם). Different counting objects — names vs. people.
Greek: 'gave glory' (ἔδωκαν δόξαν). Hebrew: 'gave praise' (נתנו שבח). Different response — glory vs. praise.
Greek: ἔμφοβοι ('fearful'). Hebrew: נבהלו ('terrified'). Different intensity.
translation_notes: רַעֲדוֹת (ra'adot — 'tremblings') from the root רעד (H7460 — 'to tremble'). The plural form suggests repeated or rolling tremors, not a single cataclysmic quake. No exact OT Strong's for the plural noun form.
שָׁעָה (sha'ah — 'hour') is a later Hebrew word for a time unit, not the OT word. Its use here reflects natural post-biblical Hebrew.
textual_notes: 1 Kings 19:18 — YHWH reserved seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal. The seven thousand who die here may be a deliberate inverse echo: where Elijah's seven thousand were faithful survivors, these seven thousand perish. Both numbers are connected to the Elijah narrative that underlies the entire two-witnesses passage.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/sorrow'). Greek has οὐαί ('woe' — an exclamation/interjection). A back-translator from Greek 'woe' would write הוֹי (hoy) — the standard OT prophetic interjection (Isa 5:8,11,18,20,21,22; Amos 5:18, 6:1). The Hebrew author chose a NOUN of suffering (distress), not a prophetic exclamation. These are different word classes entirely: a Greek exclamation cannot produce a Hebrew abstract noun.
greek_deviations: Greek: Ἡ οὐαὶ ἡ δευτέρα ('the second woe' — an exclamation). Hebrew: הצער השני ('the second distress' — a noun). Different word class and concept.
Greek adds ταχύ ('quickly') — 'the third woe comes QUICKLY.' Absent from the Hebrew. Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/sorrow') is a later Hebrew word without a standard OT Strong's number. It conveys inner grief and suffering, distinct from the externalized prophetic 'woe.'

12.summary: Revelation 12 in the Hebrew (spanning Greek 11:15–12:17) is structured as a sustained Exodus replay. The vocabulary is drawn from Torah and Prophets with remarkable specificity: נס (sign/banner, not the standard אות), תנין (the primordial chaos sea-serpent of Isaiah 27:1 and Ezekiel 29:3), משבר (birth-stool from 2 Kings 19:3), חרון אף (the fixed OT burning-anger formula), eagle wings (Exodus 19:4, Deuteronomy 32:11), and the adamah that opens its mouth and swallows (Numbers 16:30-33). The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek: (1) ארון לוחות הברית ('ark of the TABLETS of the covenant') vs. Greek's bare 'ark of the covenant'; (2) בית תפלה ('house of prayer,' Isaiah 56:7) vs. Greek 'temple'; (3) the tripartite divine-name play ההיה והוה ויהיה unpacking YHWH into was/is/shall-be — impossible to generate from the Greek ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν; (4) אדמה ('ground') echoing Numbers 16 vs. Greek generic γῆ; (5) ישועה ('deliverance') vs. Greek 'helped'; (6) כים גדול ('like a great SEA') vs. Greek 'like a river'; (7) the dragon TREADS (דרך) toward the woman vs. Greek 'stood'; (8) two titles — המשחית ('the destroyer') and המסית (the Deuteronomy 13 idolatry-incitement term) — vs. Greek's single 'deceiver'; (9) 'they reckoned their lives as nothing' vs. Greek 'they did not love their lives unto death'; (10) מעולם ועד עולם (the psalm formula) vs. Greek 'unto the ages of ages'; (11) ימשל ('shall rule,' governance) vs. Greek βασιλεύσει ('shall reign as king'); (12) YHWH throughout vs. Greek 'God'; (13) משיחו ('his anointed') vs. Greek 'Jesus Christ'; (14) Hebrew omits 'ancient serpent' which Greek adds; (15) Hebrew adds לדור שם ('to dwell there') absent from Greek; (16) מובא ('was brought,' reverent presentation) vs. Greek ἡρπάσθη ('was snatched up,' urgent rescue); (17) מפניך ('your face') vs. Greek 'your name'; (18) להשקיט ('to silence') vs. Greek 'to sweep away by flood'; (19) מתפללים ('praying') vs. Greek 'worshipping'; (20) העשירים ('the rich') vs. Greek 'the kingdoms.' The chapter also features consistent post-biblical Hebrew forms (פרנס, עכשיו, כיון ש, זמן, בשביל, כלום, אילו) that a back-translator would never produce. The Exodus typology runs through every section: the tannin/Pharaoh pursues the woman/Israel with sea-waters into the wilderness where YHWH sustains her on eagle's wings, and the adamah that once swallowed Korah now swallows the enemy's weapon to deliver her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting unto everlasting') — the exact psalm formula from Psalm 90:2, 103:17, 1 Chronicles 16:36. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages'). A back-translator from Greek would write לעולמי עולמים ('to ages of ages'), not the psalm formula.

Uses יִמְשֹׁל (yimshol — 'shall rule/have dominion', H4910) — the governance verb from Genesis 1:16-18, 3:16, 37:8. Greek βασιλεύσει means specifically 'shall reign as king.' A back-translator from Greek would use יִמְלוֹךְ (yimloch — 'shall reign,' from מלך H4427), the exact cognate of βασιλεύω. The Hebrew ימשל implies dominion; the Greek βασιλεύω implies royal enthronement.

Uses תֹּקֵעַ (toqea — 'blasts,' H8628) — the specific verb for shofar blowing in the Torah's warfare and festival contexts (Num 10:3-10, Josh 6:4-20, Judg 3:27, 7:18-22). A natural Hebrew author reaches for this deeply rooted OT term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the rich (עשירים) of this world go, all of them, after our lord Yeshua.' Greek: 'the kingdoms (βασιλεῖαι) of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ' (τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ). Completely different — individual wealthy people following vs. political entities transferring sovereignty.
Hebrew names ישוע (Yeshua) explicitly as a single figure. Greek says 'our Lord AND his Christ' (κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ) — two distinct referents.
Hebrew: 'from everlasting to everlasting' (psalm formula). Greek: 'unto the ages of ages' (Hellenistic formula).
translation_notes: The consonantal עשירים (with shin) can only be 'rich ones' (H6223). There is no consonantal ambiguity. The Hebrew text genuinely presents a different scene from the Greek — the wealthy submitting, rather than kingdoms transferring.
textual_notes: Psalm 90:2 — מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל ('from everlasting to everlasting, you are God'). The Hebrew formula attributes to the anointed one a phrase reserved for YHWH in the Psalms.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying,' H6419, hitpael reflexive of פלל) — the distinctly Hebrew prayer verb, carrying connotations of intercession and self-judgment (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10,12,26-27, 1 Kings 8:28-54, Dan 9:4). Greek has προσεκύνησαν ('worshipped/prostrated'). A back-translator from Greek would use מִשְׁתַּחֲוִים (mishtachavim — 'bowing/worshipping'), not the prayer verb. The Hebrew says they PRAY; the Greek says they WORSHIP.
Uses יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) twice. Greek has τῷ θεῷ ('God'). A back-translator from Greek would use אֱלֹהִים (Elohim), not the personal Name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'pray to YHWH' (מתפללים ליהוה). Greek: 'worshipped God' (προσεκύνησαν τῷ θεῷ). Different verb and different divine designation.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ). Same pattern throughout this chapter — Hebrew consistently uses the personal Name.
translation_notes: The hitpael form מתפללים implies reflexive engagement — they 'pray themselves' before YHWH, not merely perform an external act of worship.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲדוֹן צְבָאוֹת ('Lord of Hosts,' H113+H6635) — a variant of the standard OT divine title (cf. Isa 1:24, 3:1, 10:16,33, 19:4). Greek has κύριε ὁ θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek 'Almighty' (παντοκράτωρ) would use שַׁדַּי (Shaddai) or כָּל־יָכוֹל ('all-powerful'), NOT צבאות ('Hosts/armies').

CRITICAL: The tripartite formula הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה ('the one who was, and is, and shall be') derives ALL THREE tenses from the root היה/הוה — the very root from which the divine Name YHWH is understood to derive (Ex 3:14). This name-play is ONLY possible in Hebrew. Greek has ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν ('the one who is and who was') — using unrelated Greek verbs with no connection to a divine Name. The Hebrew author is UNPACKING the Tetragrammaton. A Greek author could never produce this play on the Hebrew divine Name.

Hebrew: 'we give praise' (נותנים שבח). Greek: εὐχαριστοῦμέν σοι ('we give thanks to you'). Different — praise (שבח) vs. thanks (εὐχαριστέω). A back-translator from Greek would use מוֹדִים (modim — 'we give thanks'), not שבח.
greek_deviations: Greek 11:17 continues: ὅτι εἴληφας τὴν δύναμίν σου τὴν μεγάλην καὶ ἐβασίλευσας ('because you have taken your great power and have reigned'). This entire clause is ABSENT from the Hebrew.

Many Greek TR manuscripts omit 'and who is to come' (καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος) in 11:17. The Hebrew preserves all three temporal aspects (was, is, shall be). Where Greek does include the third aspect, it uses ἐρχόμενος ('coming') — a DIFFERENT concept from 'shall be' (יהיה).
translation_notes: וְהֹוֶה (vehove) — the present participle of the archaic root הוה (H1933), meaning 'existing/being.' This root is virtually absent from standard biblical prose but appears in Ecclesiastes (2:22, 11:3) and is the backbone of the Tetragrammaton.
textual_notes: Exodus 3:14 — אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה ('I will be what I will be'). The tripartite formula in this verse expands this same root across all three temporal dimensions — past (הָיָה), present (הֹוֶה), and future (יִהְיֶה).

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַף וְחֵימָה ('anger and wrath,' H639+H2534) — a stock OT word-pair occurring as a formulaic doublet (Deut 29:27, Jer 21:5, 32:37, Ezek 5:15). Greek ὠργίσθησαν ('were angry') is a single verb. A back-translator from one Greek verb would produce a single Hebrew noun, not the OT's fixed two-word formula.

Uses מִפָּנֶיךָ ('your face/before you,' H6440) — 'those who fear your FACE/PRESENCE.' Greek has τὸ ὄνομά σου ('your NAME'). A back-translator from Greek 'your name' would write שִׁמְךָ (shimcha), not מִפָּנֶיךָ. The Hebrew expression ירא מפני ('fear from before') is a standard OT construction (Deut 28:10, Isa 41:5, Jer 5:22).

Uses הַשְׁחִית (H7843) for BOTH God's judgment and the destroyers' crime — the same root creating a measure-for-measure (מידה כנגד מידה) justice pattern: they 'destroyed' → God will 'destroy' them. The Hebrew reader hears the wordplay immediately.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'those who fear your FACE' (מפניך). Greek: 'those who fear your NAME' (τὸ ὄνομά σου). Different object of reverence.
Hebrew: 'anger and wrath' (two nouns). Greek: 'were angry' (one verb). Different expression.
translation_notes: אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') is a post-biblical Hebrew demonstrative pronoun, absent from the OT. Its appearance here marks the author as writing in later Hebrew, not translating from Greek.
'Wages' for שָׂכָר (sachar) — framing prophetic service as labor earning recompense (Gen 30:28, 31:8).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲרוֹן לוּחוֹת הַבְּרִית ('the ark of the TABLETS of the covenant,' H727+H3871+H1285). Greek has ἡ κιβωτὸς τῆς διαθήκης αὐτοῦ ('the ark of his covenant'). The Hebrew adds לוּחוֹת ('tablets') — the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments stored inside the ark (Deut 9:9,11,15, 10:1-5, 1 Kings 8:9). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית ('ark of the covenant') without adding 'tablets.' The Hebrew author knows what the ark CONTAINED.

Uses בֵּית תְּפִילָּה ('house of prayer,' H1004+H8605) TWICE — an echo of Isaiah 56:7 (כִּי בֵיתִי בֵּית תְּפִלָּה יִקָּרֵא לְכָל הָעַמִּים — 'for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples'). Greek has ναός ('temple/sanctuary'). A back-translator from Greek ναός would use הֵיכָל (heichal — 'temple') or מִקְדָּשׁ (miqdash — 'sanctuary'), NOT the Isaiah-specific phrase 'house of prayer.' This is the SAME term used in Rev 21:22.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'ark of the TABLETS of the covenant.' Greek: 'ark of his covenant.' Hebrew specifies the tablets.
Hebrew: 'house of prayer' (בית תפלה). Greek: 'temple' (ναός). Different term with different connotations.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' — this is the phrase Yeshua himself used when cleansing the Temple (Matt 21:13, quoting Isaiah 56:7). The Hebrew author naturally uses Isaiah's own term.
textual_notes: The Sinai theophany parallel is unmistakable: voices, thunders, lightnings, and quaking (cf. Ex 19:16-18, 20:18). The opening of the heavenly house of prayer reveals the same covenant objects and phenomena that accompanied the original covenant.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נֵס (nes, H5251 — 'sign/banner/standard') — the word for Moses' bronze serpent on a pole (Num 21:8-9) and for prophetic banners visible from afar (Isa 11:10, 13:2, 18:3, 49:22, 62:10). Greek has σημεῖον μέγα ('great sign'). A back-translator from Greek σημεῖον would use אוֹת (ot — 'sign'), the standard word for signs and wonders (Ex 4:8-9, Deut 4:34, Isa 7:14). The Hebrew נס carries connotations of a military standard RAISED HIGH for all to see — fundamentally different from אות.

Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'royal crown/diadem') — the specific crown from Esther (1:11, 2:17, 6:8) and Proverbs (4:9, 12:4, 17:6). Greek has στέφανος ('victor's wreath/garland'). A back-translator from Greek στέφανος would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — 'wreath/garland,' H5850), which is the direct Hebrew equivalent of στέφανος. The Hebrew כתר is the ROYAL crown, not the athletic or victory wreath.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: נֵס ('sign/banner'). Greek: σημεῖον ('sign'). The Hebrew nuance of a raised standard is absent from Greek.
Hebrew: כֶּתֶר ('royal crown'). Greek: στέφανος ('victor's wreath'). Different type of crown.
translation_notes: אֶחָד used twice ('one woman,' 'one crown') — functioning as an indefinite article, a common later Hebrew usage.
textual_notes: The imagery of sun, moon, and twelve stars echoes Joseph's dream (Gen 37:9 — 'the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me'). The woman wears Israel's patriarchal symbols.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַמַּשְׁבֵּר (hamashber, H4866 — 'birth-stool/the breaking-place') — the specific term for the birthing seat where women sat during delivery (2 Kings 19:3 / Isa 37:3 — 'children have come to the mashber but there is no strength to bring forth'; Hos 13:13). Greek has βασανιζομένη τεκεῖν ('tormented to give birth'). The Hebrew gives the CONCRETE IMAGE of a woman on the birth-stool; the Greek gives an abstract description of torment. A back-translator from Greek would write מְעוּנָּה לָלֶדֶת ('tormented to deliver'), not invoke the birth-stool imagery.

Uses צוֹעֶקֶת (tso'eqet — 'crying out,' H6817) — the specific verb for crying out in distress under oppression. This is the EXODUS CRY VERB — Israel's cry under Egypt (Ex 2:23, Judg 3:9,15, 4:3, 6:7, 10:10). The woman's cry echoes Israel's cry in Egypt. Greek κράζουσα ('crying') is generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sitting upon the birth-stool' (concrete physical image). Greek: 'tormented to give birth' (abstract description). Entirely different imagery.
Hebrew has a lacuna marked with brackets [ ] between the two clauses. The text may have originally contained additional material.
translation_notes: צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'anguish/pain') lacks a standard OT Strong's number; it is a post-biblical Hebrew form.
בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'on account of') is post-biblical Hebrew, absent from the OT. A back-translator working from Greek would use biblical מִפְּנֵי (mipnei) or בַּעֲבוּר (ba'avur).
textual_notes: 2 Kings 19:3 / Isaiah 37:3 — כִּי בָאוּ בָנִים עַד מַשְׁבֵּר וְכֹחַ אַיִן לְלֵדָה ('children have come to the birth-stool but there is no strength to deliver'). Hezekiah's crisis metaphor of a nation in labor. The same image applied to the woman of Revelation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תַּנִּין (tannin, H8577 — 'dragon/sea-serpent') — the primordial chaos-creature of the OT: created by God (Gen 1:21), Egypt's serpent (Ex 7:9-12), the chaos-monster slain by YHWH (Isa 27:1 — 'Leviathan the fleeing serpent, the tannin in the sea'; Isa 51:9 — 'was it not you who cut Rahab, who pierced the tannin?'), and Pharaoh himself (Ezek 29:3, 32:2). Greek δράκων ('dragon') is generic. The Hebrew word carries an entire OT mythology of YHWH's primordial victory over chaos.

Uses כְּתָרִים (ketarim — 'royal crowns,' H3804) — the same royal crown word as verse 6. Greek has διαδήματα ('diadems'). While both indicate royalty, the Hebrew keter specifically links the dragon's false kingship to the Esther/Proverbs crown vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Greek adds πυρρός ('fiery red') to describe the dragon — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew dragon has no color.
Greek calls it μέγας δράκων ('great dragon'). The Hebrew does not say 'great' here (it reserves גדול for the sign, not the dragon itself).
translation_notes: The tannin is consistently associated with the sea and with Egypt in the OT. Identifying it here sets up the Exodus typology that runs through the chapter — the dragon/Pharaoh pursuing the woman/Israel.
textual_notes: Isaiah 27:1 — 'In that day YHWH with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the TANNIN that is in the sea.' The eschatological defeat of the tannin is an Isaiah prophecy being fulfilled.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דָּרַךְ (darach, H1869 — 'to tread/march') — the verb for treading grapes in a winepress (Isa 63:3, Lam 1:15), bending the war bow (Ps 7:13, 11:2, 37:14), and military advance (Num 24:17, Judg 5:21). Greek ἕστηκεν means simply 'stood.' A back-translator from Greek would use עָמַד (amad — 'stood,' H5975). The Hebrew verb implies aggressive, predatory ADVANCE — the dragon MARCHES toward the woman, not merely stands before her.

Uses זָרַק (zaraq, H2236 — 'cast/hurled/threw') — a verb whose primary OT context is the priestly sprinkling/casting of blood on the altar (Lev 1:5,11, 3:2,8,13, 7:2). Greek βάλλω ('throw/cast') is generic. A back-translator would use הִשְׁלִיךְ (hishlich — 'cast/threw,' H7993), the common throwing verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tread before' (דרך — aggressive march). Greek: 'stood before' (ἕστηκεν — stationary). Fundamentally different postures.
Hebrew: בְּאִם שֶׁנּוֹלָד ('when/if it was born') — using the conditional particle אם. Greek: ὅταν τέκῃ ('whenever she gives birth') — temporal conjunction. The Hebrew carries a shade of uncertainty.
translation_notes: 'Tread' for דרך preserves the Hebrew verb's aggressive, military-advance connotation — this is not a dragon waiting but a dragon advancing.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:10 — 'It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it cast down to the ground.' The dragon's tail sweeping stars echoes Daniel's vision of the horn casting down the heavenly host.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמְנַהֵג (hamnaheg — 'the one who leads/drives,' from H5090 נהג) — the verb for leading flocks (Gen 31:18, Ex 3:1), driving chariots (2 Kings 9:20), and guiding nations (Isa 11:6). Greek μέλλει ποιμαίνειν means 'is about to SHEPHERD.' A back-translator from Greek ποιμαίνω would use רוֹעֶה (ro'eh — 'shepherding,' H7462), NOT מנהג. The Hebrew uses a leading/driving verb; the Greek uses a shepherding verb.

Uses מוּבָא (muva — 'was brought,' passive of H935 בוא) — implying reverent PRESENTATION before the throne. Greek ἡρπάσθη means 'was SNATCHED UP/seized' (from ἁρπάζω). These are radically different: Hebrew describes liturgical presentation; Greek describes urgent rescue. A back-translator from Greek would use נֶחְטַף (nechtaf — 'was snatched').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the one who LEADS' (present participle — ongoing quality). Greek: 'who is ABOUT TO shepherd' (μέλλει — future/imminent). Different temporal aspect and different verb.
Hebrew: 'was brought before YHWH' (reverent presentation). Greek: 'was caught up to God' (ἡρπάσθη — urgent rescue). Different action and different divine name.
Hebrew: 'the peoples' (העמים). Greek: 'all the nations' (πάντα τὰ ἔθνη). Greek adds 'all.'
translation_notes: שֵׁבֶט (shevet, H7626) means both 'rod/staff' and 'tribe' in Hebrew. The Psalm 2:9 allusion (תְּרֹעֵם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל — 'you shall break them with a rod of iron') is clear in both Hebrew and Greek traditions.
textual_notes: Psalm 2:9 — the messianic psalm of the son who inherits the nations. Both Hebrew and Greek Revelation quote it, but the Hebrew uses the original Hebrew of the psalm.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָלְכָה (halchah — 'she went,' H1980) — neutral movement. Greek ἔφυγεν means 'she FLED' (from φεύγω). A back-translator from Greek would use בָּרְחָה (barchah — 'she fled,' H1272). The Hebrew says she WENT; the Greek says she FLED. The Hebrew presents a purposeful journey; the Greek presents an escape.

Uses כֵּיוָן שׁ (keivan she — 'since/because') — a post-biblical Hebrew conjunction ABSENT from the OT entirely. Greek has ὅπου ('where' — locative). The Hebrew constructs a CAUSAL clause ('since there was prepared'); the Greek constructs a LOCATIVE clause ('where she has a place'). A back-translator from Greek 'where' would write אֲשֶׁר שָׁם or בַּמָּקוֹם שׁ ('in the place where'), not the causal כיון ש.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she went' (הלכה — purposeful journey). Greek: 'she fled' (ἔφυγεν — escape). Different posture.
Hebrew: 'since there was prepared for her a place from YHWH' (causal clause naming YHWH). Greek: 'where she has a place prepared by God' (locative clause naming 'God').
Hebrew: 'to sustain her' (one actor implied — YHWH). Greek: 'that they may nourish her' (τρέφωσιν — third person plural, unspecified agents).
translation_notes: לְפַרְנֵס (lefarnes — 'to sustain/provide for') is a post-biblical Hebrew/Aramaic verb extensively used in Rabbinic literature. No OT Strong's number. A back-translator from Greek τρέφω would use כִּלְכֵּל (kilkel — 'to sustain,' Gen 45:11, 47:12) or זוּן (zun — 'to feed'). The natural use of פרנס marks a Hebrew author writing in contemporary vocabulary.
textual_notes: The Exodus typology: the woman goes to the wilderness (מדבר) where YHWH sustains her — exactly as Israel went into the wilderness where YHWH sustained them with manna (Ex 16). The 1,260 days = 3.5 years, half of 7.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נַעֲשָׂה מִלְחָמָה ('war was made,' from עשה H6213 + מלחמה H4421) — the OT military formula for conducting war (Josh 11:18, Judg 3:10, 1 Sam 28:15, 2 Sam 11:7). Greek ἐγένετο πόλεμος ('war arose/happened,' from γίνομαι). A back-translator from γίνομαι would use הָיָה (hayah — 'was'), not the active formula נעשה ('was made').

The Hebrew makes the war explicitly BILATERAL: 'Mikhael with his messengers fought... and its messengers fought against them' (ומלאכיו לחמו עימם). Both sides actively engage. Greek is more compressed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the messenger Mikhael' (המלאך מיכאל — singular title, then with his messengers). Greek: 'Michael and his angels' (Μιχαὴλ καὶ οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτοῦ). Minor structural difference — Hebrew emphasizes Mikhael's role as THE messenger.
translation_notes: מִיכָאֵל (Mikhael, H4317) — meaning 'Who is like El?' — the only named archangel in the OT (Dan 10:13,21, 12:1). His name is itself a theological question.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:1 — 'At that time shall arise Mikhael, the great prince who stands over the sons of your people.' The Hebrew Revelation fulfills Daniel's prophecy of Mikhael's eschatological war.

greek_deviations: Very close correspondence between Hebrew and Greek here. Both say the dragon's forces did not prevail and their place was no longer found in heaven.
translation_notes: נִצְּחוּ (nitschu — from H5329 נצח) — the same root as 'eternity/enduring' (נֶצַח). The verb implies lasting, decisive victory — or here, the lack of it.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has TWO functional titles — הַמַּשְׁחִית ('the destroyer,' from H7843 שחת) AND הַמַּסִּית ('the inciter/seducer,' from H5496 סות). Greek has only ὁ πλανῶν ('the one deceiving') — one function. Moreover, מַסִּית (masit) is the specific TORAH LEGAL TERM for one who incites others to idolatry (Deut 13:7[6]) — a capital crime. A back-translator from Greek πλανάω would use מַתְעֶה (mat'eh — 'deceiver'), not the Deuteronomy 13 legal terminology.

CRITICAL: Greek adds ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος ('the ancient serpent') — a title ENTIRELY ABSENT from the Hebrew. The Hebrew does NOT connect the dragon to the Genesis serpent (נחש). Greek also adds Διάβολος ('Devil') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew has one title (שטן — Adversary) plus two functions (destroyer, inciter); the Greek has four titles (serpent, devil, dragon, Satan) plus one function (deceiver). These are fundamentally different naming schemes.

Uses לָדוּר שָׁם ('to dwell there') — a clause ABSENT from Greek, which simply says ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν γῆν ('was cast to the earth'). The Hebrew adds PURPOSE — the casting is a sentence of EXILE, not mere removal. The dragon is sentenced to dwell on earth.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'the ancient serpent' (ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος) and 'the Devil' (Διάβολος) — both absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'the destroyer and the inciter' (two functional titles). Greek: 'the deceiver' (one function).
Hebrew: 'all the world' (כל העולם — olam, 'world/age'). Greek: 'the whole inhabited earth' (τὴν οἰκουμένην ὅλην — oikoumene).
Hebrew adds 'to dwell there' (לדור שם) — absent from Greek.
translation_notes: שָׂטָן (satan, H7854) means 'adversary/accuser/opposer' (Job 1-2, Zech 3:1, 1 Chr 21:1). The Greek Σατανᾶς is a transliteration of the Hebrew — the Greek BORROWED the Hebrew term. Hebrew is the source language for this title.
textual_notes: The verb שחת (H7843 — 'destroy') connects this verse to verse 4 where the same root appears twice: 'to destroy those who destroyed the earth.' The dragon IS the destroyer — this title links him to the destroyers of v4.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲרוֹן אַף ('burning anger/fierce wrath,' H2740+H639) — a fixed OT compound expression occurring 39 times (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, 32:14, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, Judg 2:14, 2 Kings 23:26, etc.). This is formulaic Hebrew — a set phrase that a native speaker reproduces automatically. Greek θυμὸν μέγαν ('great wrath') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would write חֵמָה גְּדוֹלָה ('great wrath') or כַּעַס גָּדוֹל ('great anger'), NOT the fixed OT formula חרון אף.

Uses זְמָן (zman, H2165 — 'time/season') — an Aramaic-influenced word rare in the OT (only Neh 2:6, Esth 9:27,31, Eccl 3:1, Dan 2:16,21). This is NOT the standard biblical Hebrew עֵת (et — 'time'). A back-translator from Greek καιρός would choose the standard biblical עת, not the Aramaic-tinged זמן. Its use marks a Hebrew author writing in later Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'burning anger' (חרון אף — stock OT compound). Greek: 'great wrath' (θυμὸν μέγαν). Different expression.
Hebrew: 'because of this' (ובשביל זה — post-biblical). Greek: 'therefore' (διὰ τοῦτο).
translation_notes: בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'because of') and הַדָּרִים (hadarim — 'those who dwell') are both post-biblical Hebrew forms. A back-translator would not produce these.
אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') appears again — the same post-biblical demonstrative as in verse 4.
