one_way_hebrew: Uses רָדַף (radaf, H7291 — 'to pursue/chase/persecute') — a word saturated with Exodus resonance: the Egyptians PURSUING Israel (Ex 14:4,8,9,23, 15:9), Laban pursuing Jacob (Gen 31:23,36), enemies pursuing the righteous (Deut 28:22,45, Lev 26:17,36). The dragon/tannin PURSUING the woman through the wilderness replays the Exodus — Pharaoh pursuing Israel. Greek ἐδίωξεν ('pursued/persecuted') corresponds, but lacks the Exodus-specific weight.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the woman who had given birth' (שילדה — without specifying what). Greek: 'the woman who had given birth to the MALE CHILD' (τὴν γυναῖκα ἥτις ἔτεκεν τὸν ἄρρενα). Greek specifies; Hebrew is concise.
translation_notes: כֵּיוָן שׁ (keivan she — 'when/since') appears for the third time in this chapter (vv. 11, 15a, 17) — a consistent post-biblical Hebrew conjunction throughout.
textual_notes: The Exodus pattern is now explicit: the tannin (= Pharaoh, Ezek 29:3) pursues (רדף — the Exodus verb) the woman (= Israel) into the wilderness (מדבר) where YHWH sustains her. Every element has a Torah parallel.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah, H127 — 'ground/soil') where Greek has γῆ (ge — 'earth'). This is the SAME distinction noted in Rev 21:1. A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth'), not אדמה. The use of adamah here DIRECTLY echoes Numbers 16:30-33 where the ADAMAH opened its mouth and swallowed Korah: וּפָצְתָה הָאֲדָמָה אֶת פִּיהָ וּבָלְעָה אֹתָם ('and the GROUND opened its mouth and swallowed them'). The verbal parallel is unmistakable.

CRITICAL: The phrase פָּתְחָה אֶת פִּיהָ וּבָלַע ('opened its mouth and swallowed') nearly quotes Numbers 16:32 verbatim: וַתִּפְתַּח הָאָרֶץ אֶת פִּיהָ וַתִּבְלַע אֹתָם ('and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them'). The Hebrew Revelation deliberately echoes the Korah rebellion narrative — the same ground that swallowed YHWH's enemies now swallows the dragon's weapon. A back-translator from Greek would reproduce this pattern only by coincidence.

Uses יְשׁוּעָה (yeshu'ah, H3444 — 'salvation/deliverance') — the grand OT word for divine rescue (Ex 14:13, 15:2, Judg 15:18, 1 Sam 11:13, Ps 3:8). Greek ἐβοήθησεν means merely 'helped' (from βοηθέω). A back-translator from Greek 'helped' would use עָזַר (azar — 'helped,' H5826), not the theologically loaded ישועה. The Hebrew frames this as a divine DELIVERANCE act.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the woman had DELIVERANCE from the ground' (ישועה — grand salvation). Greek: 'the earth HELPED the woman' (ἐβοήθησεν — simply helped). Different scale of imagery.
Hebrew: 'the GROUND' (אדמה, H127). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ). Different Hebrew term, carrying the Numbers 16 resonance.
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') preserves the critical distinction from erets and the Numbers 16 allusion — the adamah that swallowed Korah now swallows the dragon's flood.
textual_notes: Numbers 16:30-33 — The ground (אדמה) opening its mouth (פצתה את פיה) and swallowing (ובלעה) Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. In Numbers, the ground swallows rebels; in Revelation, the ground swallows the dragon's weapon to SAVE the woman. Same mechanism, inverted purpose — judgment becomes salvation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַנּוֹתָרִים (hanotarim — 'the remnant/survivors,' from H3498 יתר) — carrying the weight of Isaiah's remnant theology (Isa 1:9, 10:20-22, 11:11,16, 37:4,31-32, Mic 5:7[6]). Greek τῶν λοιπῶν ('the rest/remaining') is neutral. The Hebrew 'remnant of her seed' echoes Isaiah's 'remnant of Israel.' This is a theologically loaded term in Hebrew; a flat word in Greek.

Uses הָעוֹשִׂים ('those who DO/KEEP,' from H6213 עשה) the commandments — the TORAH'S OWN VERB for observing commandments (Ex 20:6 — עוֹשֵׂי מִצְוֹתָי 'those who do my commandments'; Deut 5:10, 6:25, 7:11, 26:16). Greek τηρούντων ('keeping/guarding') uses τηρέω. A back-translator from Greek would use שׁוֹמְרִים (shomrim — 'keeping/guarding,' from שמר H8104), the natural Hebrew equivalent of τηρέω. But the Hebrew author uses עשה — the Torah's specific verb.

Uses עֵדוּת שֶׁל מְשִׁיחוֹ ('testimony of his ANOINTED,' H5715+H4899) — no personal name, only the messianic TITLE. Greek has μαρτυρίαν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ('the testimony of Jesus Christ') — with the personal name. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate ישוע or use both name and title. The Hebrew uses only the generic title משיחו ('his anointed'), which any Jewish reader would understand as the expected messianic figure.

Uses מִצְוֹת יַהְוֶה ('commandments of YHWH,' H4687+H3068) — a standard Torah expression (Deut 8:6, 11:1, 26:17, 28:9, 30:16). Greek has τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ θεοῦ ('the commandments of God'). The Hebrew uses the personal Name; the Greek uses the generic 'God.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'testimony of his anointed' (משיחו — title only, no personal name). Greek: 'testimony of Jesus Christ' (named).
Hebrew: 'those who DO the commandments of YHWH' (עושים — Torah verb, YHWH — personal Name). Greek: 'those who KEEP the commandments of God' (τηρούντων — different verb, θεοῦ — generic).
Hebrew: נתמלא באף ('was filled with anger'). Greek: ὠργίσθη ('was wroth'). Hebrew is more vivid — filled to capacity with anger.
translation_notes: עֵדוּת (edut, H5715 — 'testimony') is the specific word for the covenant tablets stored in the ark (Ex 25:16,21, 31:18, 32:15, 40:20 — לוּחוֹת הָעֵדוּת 'the tablets of the testimony'). This creates a link back to verse 5 where the ark of the TABLETS of the covenant was seen.
textual_notes: The chapter ends by defining the remnant with TWO markers: (1) keeping YHWH's commandments (Torah observance) and (2) believing in the testimony of his anointed (messianic faith). The Hebrew presents these as complementary, not competing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גְּבוּרוֹת (gevurot — 'mighty deeds/power,' H1369 plural) — a specifically Hebrew concept of God's power-acts (Deut 3:24, Ps 20:6, 71:16, 106:2, 145:4,12, 150:2). Greek has THREE separate nouns: σωτηρία ('salvation'), δύναμις ('power'), and βασιλεία ('kingdom'). A back-translator from three Greek nouns would not collapse them into the single Hebrew gevurot. The Hebrew carries a richer concept — all God's mighty acts — in one word.

Uses עַכְשָׁיו (achshav — 'now') — a post-biblical Hebrew word absent from the OT (biblical Hebrew uses עַתָּה — attah). A Hebrew author writing naturally uses achshav; a back-translator working from Greek ἄρτι would choose the biblical עתה.

Uses כָּל עֵת ('at all times') for the adversary's activity. Greek has ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός ('day and night'). A back-translator from Greek would write יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה ('day and night'), not the abstract כל עת.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the might of our Elohim and his anointed' (one attribute shared by two). Greek: 'the salvation, and power, and kingdom of our God, AND the authority of his Christ' (four attributes split across two). Massively expanded in Greek.
Hebrew: 'now is SEEN' (נתראה — made visible). Greek: 'now has COME' (ἄρτι ἐγένετο — came about). Different — visibility vs. arrival.

Hebrew: 'at all times an adversary against them.' Greek: 'who accused them before our God day and night.' Greek specifies the venue ('before God'), the time pattern ('day and night'), and the action ('accused'). Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: Hebrew uses the verbal noun לשטן (lesatan — 'as adversary') rather than the title השטן ('the Adversary'). He functioned as an adversary; it was his role.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עַל יַד ('by the hand of,' H5921+H3027) — a standard Hebrew idiom meaning 'by means of / through the agency of' (2 Sam 14:30, 2 Kings 14:27). Literally 'upon the hand of.' Greek uses the simple preposition διά ('through'). A Hebrew author naturally reaches for this concrete body-part idiom; a back-translator from Greek would use the preposition בְּ (be — 'by/through').

CRITICAL: Uses וְחִשְּׁבוּ אֶת חַיֵּיהֶם לִכְלוּם ('and they RECKONED their lives as NOTHING,' from H2803 חשב — 'to reckon/account'). Greek has οὐκ ἠγάπησαν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτῶν ἄχρι θανάτου ('they did NOT LOVE their SOULS unto DEATH'). These are ENTIRELY different expressions — one about valuation (reckoning as nothing), the other about affection (not loving unto death). A back-translator from Greek would write לֹא אָהֲבוּ אֶת נַפְשׁוֹתָם עַד מָוֶת ('they did not love their souls unto death'). The Hebrew concept is economic — they assessed the VALUE of their lives at zero.

Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716) — the Passover lamb of Exodus 12:3-5, consistent with its use throughout this Hebrew Revelation (cf. Rev 21:9). Greek ἀρνίον ('little lamb') is a diminutive form that does not carry the Passover specificity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'they reckoned their lives as nothing.' Greek: 'they did not love their lives unto death.' Completely different expression — valuation vs. affection.
Hebrew: חַיֵּיהֶם ('their lives,' H2416 — the state of being alive). Greek: τὴν ψυχήν ('their soul/life,' ψυχή). Different word — concrete 'lives' vs. 'soul.'
translation_notes: כְּלוּם (klum — 'nothing') is a post-biblical Hebrew word, absent from the OT. Common in Rabbinic literature. No standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כְּנֶשֶׁר גָּדוֹל ('like a great eagle,' H5404) — directly echoing Exodus 19:4: 'You have seen what I did to Egypt, and I bore you on EAGLES' WINGS (כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים) and brought you to myself.' And Deuteronomy 32:11: 'As an EAGLE (נשר) stirs up its nest, hovers over its young, spreads its WINGS (כנפיו), takes them, bears them on its pinions.' The woman-Israel receives eagle wings for wilderness flight — EXACTLY the Exodus imagery. Greek τοῦ ἀετοῦ τοῦ μεγάλου ('the great eagle') corresponds, but the Hebrew naturally integrates with the Torah's eagle-wing theology.

Uses לֵילֵךְ ('to GO,' H1980) — even though the woman has wings, she GOES (walks) into the wilderness. Greek ἵνα πέτηται means 'that she might FLY' (from πέτομαι). A back-translator from 'fly' would use לָעוּף (la'uf — 'to fly'). The Hebrew uses ordinary travel language — like Israel GOING through the wilderness on foot, even under divine wings.

Uses עֵת... עִיתִּים (et... ittim — 'a time... times') — echoing Daniel 7:25, 12:7 in the Hebrew original. The plural עיתים is natural Hebrew for the plural of עת. Greek καιρὸν καὶ καιρούς also echoes Daniel's LXX. Both traditions quote Daniel, but the Hebrew preserves the original Hebrew form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to GO' (הלך) into the wilderness. Greek: 'to FLY' (πέτομαι). Different — walking vs. flying.
Hebrew: 'to the place which YHWH gave her' (naming YHWH as source). Greek: 'to her place' (no divine attribution).
Hebrew: לפרנס ('to sustain') — same post-biblical verb as v11. Greek: τρέφεται ('she is nourished').
textual_notes: Exodus 19:4 — וָאֶשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם עַל כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים וָאָבִא אֶתְכֶם אֵלָי ('I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself'). The woman's eagle wings are a deliberate replay of the Exodus deliverance.
Daniel 7:25 / 12:7 — 'a time, times, and half a time.' The same duration as the 1,260 days of v11 (3.5 years), connecting both wilderness periods.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כְּיָם גָּדוֹל ('like a great SEA,' H3220). Greek has ὕδωρ ὡς ποταμόν ('water like a RIVER'). The Hebrew compares the flood to a SEA (יָם) — the cosmological chaos-waters, the sea YHWH split at the Exodus (Ex 14), the sea where the tannin dwells (Isa 27:1). A back-translator from Greek ποταμός ('river') would use נָהָר (nahar — 'river,' H5104), NOT ים. The tannin/sea-serpent attacking with sea-waters is a coherent mythological image in Hebrew; 'river' breaks the connection.

Uses לְהַשְׁקִיט (lehashqit — 'to silence/make still,' from H8252 שקט). Greek has ποταμοφόρητον ποιήσῃ ('to make her flood-carried'). The Hebrew euphemistically describes drowning as 'silencing' or 'making still' — the woman would be made quiet (dead). A back-translator from Greek would use לִשְׁטוֹף (lishtof — 'to flood/wash away'), not the 'silencing' verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like a great SEA.' Greek: 'like a RIVER.' Sea vs. river — fundamentally different cosmological imagery.
Hebrew: 'to silence her' (euphemism for destroy). Greek: 'to make her flood-carried' (mechanism of destruction).
[מפיו] ('from its mouth') appears in brackets in the Hebrew text, suggesting textual uncertainty or editorial restoration. Greek has ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ ('from his mouth') without ambiguity.
translation_notes: Brackets around [מפיו] preserved from the source text, indicating this phrase may be a later restoration or is textually uncertain.
textual_notes: The tannin/sea-serpent casting SEA-waters against the woman continues the Exodus cosmic-battle imagery: YHWH defeated the tannin and the sea at the Exodus (Isa 51:9-10 — 'Was it not you who cut Rahab, who pierced the tannin? Was it not you who dried up the sea?'). Now the tannin retaliates with the sea.

13.summary: Revelation 13 in Hebrew is saturated with Torah legal vocabulary and OT prophetic echoes that cannot derive from the Greek text. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers: (1) פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'carved-image') — the Second Commandment word, used three times for the idol (vv. 15-16), where Greek has neutral εἰκών; (2) הִסִּית + אוֹתוֹת וּמוֹפְתִים — the full Deuteronomy 13 false-prophet formula (enticement + signs and wonders) assembled in v15; (3) מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying') used four times for idol-worship (vv. 5, 9, 13, 16) where Greek has προσκυνέω ('bow down'); (4) חַבּוּרָה (chaburah — Isaiah 53:5 'wound/stripe') for the animal's wound; (5) תִּקְוָה (tiqvah — 'hope') vs. Greek ὑπομονή ('patience') in v11; (6) אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground') vs. γῆ ('earth') for the second animal's origin in v12; (7) רוּחַ וְנֶפֶשׁ ('spirit AND soul') vs. Greek's single πνεῦμα in v16; (8) triple wisdom vocabulary in v19 (chokhmah + tevunah + sekhel) vs. Greek's two terms; (9) מְשׁוּחְרָרִים (meshuchrarim — legal manumission term) vs. generic 'free' in v17; (10) סוּס (sus — 'horse') vs. πάρδαλις ('leopard') in v3; (11) 'Who is like this animal?' parody of Exodus 15:11; (12) the textual lacuna in v13 showing authentic manuscript transmission. The Deuteronomy 13 pattern is the most compelling: the ground-animal is constructed as the Torah's false prophet who performs signs and wonders (אותות ומופתים), incites (מסית) the people, and commands them to make a carved-image (פסל) — the full legal framework of enticement to idolatry. No back-translator from Greek could independently reconstruct this coherent Torah-law pattern using precisely the Deuteronomy 13 vocabulary for all three elements.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דָּרַכְתִּי (darakhti — 'I trod/marched', H1869) — the verb for treading a winepress (Isa 63:3), marching upon high places (Mic 1:3), and bending a bow (Jer 9:2). Greek TR has ἐστάθη ('he stood' — 3rd person, from ἵστημι). A back-translator from Greek 'stood' would write עָמַדְתִּי (amadti — 'I stood') from עמד, not the active martial verb דרך. The Hebrew implies purposeful treading, not static standing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 1st person 'I trod' (דרכתי). Greek TR: 3rd person ἐστάθη ('he/it stood') — the dragon is the subject. Some Greek manuscripts read ἐστάθην ('I stood' — 1st person), but even those use 'stood,' not 'trod.'
This verse is Greek 12:18. The Hebrew places it as 13:1, suggesting a different chapter-division tradition that ties the sand-of-the-sea vision to the sea-animal's emergence.
translation_notes: 'Trod' for darakh preserves the active, purposeful quality of the Hebrew verb — stepping/marching, not merely standing.
textual_notes: The Hebrew chapter division places the 'sand of the sea' as the opening of the sea-animal chapter, creating a narrative bridge: the visionary treads to the shore and watches the animal emerge. Greek attaches it to the end of chapter 12 as the dragon's action.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַיָּה (chayyah — 'living creature/animal', H2416) — the generic OT word for wild animals (Gen 1:24-25, 7:14, 9:10). Greek θηρίον ('wild beast') carries inherent negativity. The Hebrew word is neutral — the same word describes the living creatures of creation. A back-translator from θηρίον would choose a negative term like חַיַּת רָעָה ('evil beast').

Uses TWO distinct blasphemy words: חֵירוּפִים (cherupim — 'reproaches/revilings', from חרף H2778) AND גִדּוּפִים (giddupim — 'blasphemies', from גדף H1442). Greek has only singular βλασφημίας ('blasphemy'). The Hebrew distinguishes between taunting reproach (cheruf — the Goliath-type taunt, 1 Sam 17:26) and outright blasphemy (gidduf). A back-translator from Greek's single word would use one Hebrew word, not two.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'names of revilings AND blasphemies' (two categories). Greek: 'names of blasphemy' (one category, singular βλασφημίας).
translation_notes: 'Animal' for chayyah rather than 'beast' — preserving the Hebrew word's neutrality. The word simply means 'living creature.'

חֵירוּפִים (cherupim) is a later Hebrew abstract-noun plural from חרף (H2778). The closest Strong's nominal form is H2781 (cherpah — 'reproach'). גִדּוּפִים (giddupim) is similarly a later plural from גדף (H1442).
textual_notes: Daniel 7:3-7 describes four animals (חֵיוָן in Aramaic, cognate of חַיָּה) rising from the sea with composite features. The Hebrew Revelation uses the same root vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דְּמוּת (demut, H1823 — 'likeness/form'), the word from Genesis 1:26 ('Let us make man in our likeness') and Ezekiel's throne visions (Ezek 1:5, 1:16, 1:26, 8:2, 10:1). Greek ὅμοιον means simply 'similar to.' A back-translator would use דּוֹמֶה (domeh — 'resembling'), not the theologically loaded demut.

Uses תַּנִּין (tannin, H8577 — 'dragon/sea-serpent'), the OT chaos-monster (Gen 1:21, Ex 7:9-12, Isa 27:1, 51:9, Ezek 29:3, 32:2). Greek δράκων ('dragon') is a generic mythological term. The Hebrew tannin carries deep creation theology — it is the primordial sea-creature that YHWH created (Gen 1:21) and subdues (Isa 51:9, Ps 74:13).

Uses גְּבוּרָה (gevurah, H1369 — 'might/valor') where Greek has ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην ('great authority'). These are fundamentally different: Hebrew gevurah = raw power, martial strength, valor; Greek exousia = delegated authority, jurisdiction. A back-translator from Greek would use רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority'), not the warrior-word gevurah.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew has סוּס (sus — 'horse', H5483). Greek has παρδάλει ('leopard'). Daniel 7 has נָמֵר (namer — 'leopard'). The Hebrew substitutes 'horse' for 'leopard' — these are entirely different animals. The consonants ס-ו-ס bear no resemblance to נ-מ-ר; this cannot be a scribal or translation error. The Hebrew represents either a different textual tradition or a deliberate substitution, possibly connecting to the horse imagery elsewhere in Revelation (ch. 6, 9, 19).
Hebrew: 'great might' (גבורת גדולה). Greek: 'great authority' (ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην). Power vs. authority.
translation_notes: 'Likeness' for demut preserves the Genesis/Ezekiel creation-vision language.
'Dragon' for tannin — while tannin literally means 'sea-serpent/great reptile,' 'dragon' is used for consistency with its role as the supernatural adversary.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:4-6 lists lion, bear, and leopard as three of the four beasts. The Hebrew Revelation combines bear-feet and lion-mouth (matching Daniel) but substitutes horse for leopard. The horse may connect to the horse-riders of Revelation 6 and 9, or reflect a distinct Hebrew apocalyptic tradition.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַבּוּרָה (chaburah — 'wound/stripe/bruise', H2250), the word from Isaiah 53:5: וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא לָנוּ ('and by his stripe we are healed'). Greek πληγή ('blow/plague') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use מַכָּה (makkah — 'blow/strike'), not the Isaiah 53 word. The Hebrew creates a dark parody: the animal's wound-healing mimics the Suffering Servant's healing.

Uses הָעוֹלָם (ha-olam — 'the world/age', H5769) where Greek has ὅλη ἡ γῆ ('the whole earth'). Hebrew olam has a temporal/eternal dimension ('age/eternity') absent from erets ('earth'). A back-translator from Greek would write כָּל הָאָרֶץ ('all the earth'), not ha-olam.

Uses מִשְׁתּוֹמֵם (mishtomem — 'was astonished/appalled', from שׁמם H8074). This verb also means 'to be devastated/desolated' — the same root as שְׁמָמָה (shemamah — 'desolation'). Greek ἐθαύμασεν ('marveled') is neutral or positive. The Hebrew carries horror and devastation; the Greek carries wonder and admiration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'resembling a wound of death' (describes appearance). Greek: 'as though slain to death' (ὡς ἐσφαγμένην εἰς θάνατον — describes the act of slaughter). Different perspective.
Hebrew: 'was astonished on account of' (בשביל — causal). Greek: 'followed after' (ὀπίσω — directional). The Hebrew describes emotional response; the Greek describes physical following.
translation_notes: 'Wound' for chaburah preserves the Isaiah 53 echo. The same root appears in Isaiah 1:6 for Israel's unhealed wounds.
textual_notes: Isaiah 53:5 — 'he was wounded for our transgressions... and by his wound/stripe (chaburah) we are healed (nirpa).' The same chaburah+healing combination appears here applied to the animal — a counterfeit of the Servant's suffering.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying', hitpael of פלל H6419). This is THE standard Hebrew verb for prayer to God (1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:28-30, Dan 6:10). Greek προσεκύνησαν means 'bowed down/worshipped' — a physical act. A back-translator from Greek would use הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ (hishtachavu — 'prostrated themselves'), not the prayer-specific hitpallel. The Hebrew makes the idolatry explicitly a form of PRAYER — people address the dragon and animal as one addresses God. This verb recurs throughout the chapter (vv. 5, 9, 13, 16) as a deliberate thematic marker.

'Who is like this animal?' (מי דומה לזאת החיה) echoes the most iconic Hebrew praise formula: מִי כָמוֹכָה בָּאֵלִם יְהוָה ('Who is like you among the gods, O YHWH?' — Ex 15:11). Also Psalm 35:10, 71:19, 89:6, 113:5. The Hebrew reader immediately recognizes this as a blasphemous parody of the Exodus victory song. Greek τίς ὅμοιος τῷ θηρίῳ carries no such literary echo.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'power and dominion' (כח וממשלה — two concepts). Greek: 'authority' (ἐξουσίαν — one concept). Hebrew has two words where Greek has one, and the Hebrew concepts (raw power + ruling dominion) differ from delegated 'authority.'
translation_notes: 'Prayed' for mitpallelim — this is not merely 'worshipped' but specifically prayer-worship, the verbal-spiritual act of directing prayer to a deity.
'Dominion' for memshalah (H4475) — from the root משל ('to rule'), used in Genesis 1:16 for the sun and moon's dominion over day and night.
textual_notes: The parody structure: In Exodus 15:11, Israel sings 'Who is like YHWH?' after the sea victory. Here, humanity asks 'Who is like the animal?' after the sea-animal emerges. The Hebrew inverts the Exodus narrative — from the sea comes not salvation but a counterfeit object of worship.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נִפְלָאוֹת (nifla'ot — 'wonders/marvels', H6381) — the same word for God's miraculous deeds (Ex 3:20, 15:11, Ps 77:14, 78:12). Greek μεγάλα means merely 'great things.' A back-translator from Greek would use גְּדוֹלוֹת (gedolot — 'great things'), not the theologically loaded nifla'ot. The Hebrew implies the animal speaks words that counterfeit divine wonders.

Uses חֵירוּף (cheruf — 'reproach/reviling', from חרף H2778). This is the same noun family used for Goliath's taunting of Israel's armies (1 Sam 17:26) and Rabshakeh's taunting of YHWH (2 Kings 19:4). Greek βλασφημία is generic. The Hebrew specifies the TYPE of blasphemy: military-style taunting reproach.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'words of wonders and reproach' (miraculous claims + insults). Greek: 'great things and blasphemies' (μεγάλα καὶ βλασφημίας — generic greatness + blasphemy).

Hebrew: 'until the time was finished' (עד שכלא הזמן — temporal boundary). Greek: 'authority was given to it to act for forty-two months' (ἐξουσία ποιῆσαι μῆνας — mandate granted). Different framing: Hebrew gives a time limit; Greek gives a commission.
translation_notes: הַזְּמָן (ha-zeman — 'the time') is a post-biblical Hebrew word for 'appointed time,' common in Mishnaic Hebrew. No standard Strong's number. Its use here (rather than biblical עֵת or מוֹעֵד) reflects the text's late Second Temple linguistic stratum.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:25 — the little horn speaks 'great things' against the Most High for 'a time, times, and half a time' (= 42 months). The Hebrew Revelation follows Daniel's time frame while adding the specifically Hebrew nifla'ot vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חָרֵף (charef, H2778 — 'to revile/taunt/reproach'), the verb for Goliath's defiance of Israel (1 Sam 17:10,25,26,36,45), Rabshakeh's taunting of YHWH (2 Kings 19:4,16,22; Isa 37:4,17,23), and Sennacherib's blasphemy (2 Kings 19:22 — 'Whom have you reviled and blasphemed?'). Greek βλασφημέω is generic. The Hebrew connects the animal's speech to Israel's most infamous blasphemers.

Uses the divine name יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) where Greek has τὸν θεόν ('God'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֱלֹהִים (Elohim — 'God'), not the covenant name YHWH. The Hebrew text consistently uses the Tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two targets — YHWH and those dwelling in the heavens. Greek: three targets — God's name (τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ), his tabernacle (τὴν σκηνὴν αὐτοῦ), and those tabernacling in heaven. The Hebrew is more concise, omitting 'his name' and 'his tabernacle' as separate objects.
translation_notes: 'Revile' for charef — stronger than 'blaspheme,' carrying the specific sense of taunting, mocking, and verbally assaulting, as in a military challenge.

הַדָּרִים (ha-darim — 'those dwelling') uses a later Hebrew/Aramaic root for dwelling rather than the biblical יֹשְׁבִים (yoshvim, from ישב H3427). This form recurs throughout the Hebrew text (vv. 9, 13, 15).

one_way_hebrew: Uses נִצֵּחַ (nitseyach, H5329 — 'to overcome/conquer'), the same root as מְנַצֵּחַ (menatseach) in the Psalm superscriptions ('for the choirmaster/conductor'). The root carries dual meaning: to lead/conduct AND to be victorious. Greek νικῆσαι ('to conquer') has only the victory sense. The Hebrew verb has a richer semantic range rooted in the Psalter.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all the peoples and nations' (עמים ואומים — 2 categories). Greek: 'every tribe and tongue and nation' (πᾶσαν φυλὴν καὶ γλῶσσαν καὶ ἔθνος — 3 categories). Greek adds 'tongue' (γλῶσσαν); Hebrew uses עמים ('peoples') rather than φυλή ('tribe').
translation_notes: 'Holy ones' for kedoshim — the standard OT term for those set apart for YHWH (Ps 34:9, Dan 7:18,21,25).
אוּמִים (ummim — 'nations') is a post-biblical Hebrew plural from אוּמָּה ('nation'), common in rabbinic literature. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:21 — 'this horn made war with the holy ones and prevailed against them.' The Hebrew Revelation follows Daniel's language directly.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּרִיאַת (beri'at — 'creation of', from ברא H1254) where Greek has καταβολῆς ('foundation/laying down'). Hebrew ברא is THE Genesis 1:1 verb — 'In the beginning God CREATED.' Greek 'foundation' implies construction; Hebrew 'creation' implies divine ex nihilo act. A back-translator from Greek would use יְסוֹד (yesod — 'foundation'), not ברא.

Uses הַנֶּהֱרָג (neherag — 'the slain one', from הרג H2026), the common verb for killing (Gen 4:8 — Cain killed Abel). Greek ἐσφαγμένου (from σφάζω) specifically means ritual slaughter. The Hebrew uses the general killing verb rather than a sacrifice-specific term like שָׁחַט (shachat — 'to slaughter ritually'). A back-translator from Greek σφάζω would choose שׁחט, not הרג.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'creation of the world' (בריאת העולם). Greek: 'foundation of the world' (καταβολῆς κόσμου). Different metaphors for the world's origin.
translation_notes: Again uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים ('pray') — maintaining the chapter's consistent prayer vocabulary where Greek has 'worship/bow down.'
'Scroll' for sefer (H5612) — scrolls were the standard writing format of the Hebrew period.
מִכִּתְחִילַּת (mikitchillat — 'from the beginning of') is a later Hebrew compound form. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Psalm 69:28 — 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living' (ספר חיים). Daniel 12:1 — 'everyone found written in the book.' The 'scroll of life' concept has deep OT roots.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Whoever has ears hears' (מי שיש לו אזנים שומע — declarative present). Greek: 'If anyone has an ear, let him hear' (εἴ τις ἔχει οὖς ἀκουσάτω — conditional + imperative). The Hebrew states a fact; the Greek issues a command.
Hebrew: אָזְנַיִם (oznayim — 'ears', dual form for paired organs). Greek: singular οὖς ('ear').
translation_notes: The Hebrew literally says 'whoever has ears — he hears' (present tense, indicative). 'Let him hear' captures the exhortative force implied by context, though the Hebrew grammar is declarative.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תִּקְוָה (tiqvah — 'hope', H8615). Greek has ὑπομονή ('patience/endurance'). These are fundamentally different. Hebrew tiqvah is the great OT hope word (Jer 29:11 — 'plans to give you a tiqvah and a future'; 31:17 — 'there is tiqvah for your future'; Lam 3:29 — 'perhaps there is tiqvah'; Job 14:7 — 'there is tiqvah for a tree'). A back-translator from Greek ὑπομονή would use סַבְלָנוּת (savlanut — 'patience'), NOT the prophetic hope word. The Hebrew says retributive justice gives HOPE; the Greek says it requires PATIENCE. Entirely different theological orientations.

Uses מִשְׁמָר (mishmar — 'custody/guard-post', H4929) where Greek has αἰχμαλωσίαν ('captivity'). Hebrew mishmar is judicial/legal confinement (Gen 40:3-4 — Joseph in mishmar; 42:17 — brothers in mishmar; Lev 24:12; Num 15:34). Greek 'captivity' implies war-capture; Hebrew 'custody' implies legal detention. A back-translator from Greek would use שְׁבִי (shevi — 'captivity'), not the judicial term mishmar.

Adds נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh — 'soul/life', H5315): 'kills another soul by the sword.' Greek has no equivalent — simply 'kills by sword.' The Hebrew makes it explicitly about taking a person's life-breath, echoing Torah murder language: 'whoever strikes a nefesh' (Num 35:11,15,30).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'hope' (תקוה). Greek: 'patience' (ὑπομονή). Completely different concepts.
Hebrew: 'custody' (משמר). Greek: 'captivity' (αἰχμαλωσία). Different type of confinement.
Hebrew adds 'another soul' (נפש אחר) to the sword clause — absent in Greek.
translation_notes: 'Hope' for tiqvah is critical — the word Rachel named her son's city for (1 Chr 4:12), the word Jeremiah used to sustain exiles, the word Job clung to in suffering. It reframes the entire verse from endurance to expectation.
'Faithfulness' for emunah (H530) — from Habakkuk 2:4 ('the righteous shall live by his emunah'). Not merely 'faith/belief' but active fidelity and trustworthiness.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 15:2 — 'Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; those destined for captivity, to captivity.' The Hebrew Revelation echoes this retributive justice pattern.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground/soil', H127) where Greek has γῆ ('earth/land'). As in Revelation 21:1, the Hebrew distinguishes between adamah (the soil from which Adam was formed, Gen 2:7; the soil cursed for Adam's sake, Gen 3:17) and erets (earth/land). The first animal rises from the sea (יָם); the second rises from the adamah. Greek uses γῆ for both concepts. A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use אֶרֶץ (erets), not the Genesis creation-word adamah. The adamah connects the second animal to the dust of human origin — it is an earth-born, human-derived creature, a counterfeit 'adam' rising from the 'adamah.'
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') preserves the Genesis creation distinction. The adamah/erets contrast carries the same theological weight as in Rev 21:1.
'Like the lamb' (כמו להשה) — the same word שֶׂה (seh H7716), the Passover lamb from Exodus 12:3-5, is used here. The second animal mimics the Lamb with counterfeit horns — a false Passover lamb.
textual_notes: The two animals form a counterfeit trinity: the dragon (counterfeit God), the sea-animal (counterfeit messianic ruler), and the ground-animal (counterfeit prophet who performs signs). The ground-animal's emergence from adamah — man's source material — makes it the most human of the three.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses נִפְלָאוֹת (nifla'ot — 'wonders', H6381) — the divine miracle vocabulary. Combined with אותות ומופתים in v15, this creates the full Deuteronomy 13 false-prophet pattern: a prophet performs wonders and signs to entice to idolatry.

The personification of הָאֲדָמָה (adamah — 'the ground') as praying is striking. The Hebrew says the ground ITSELF and its inhabitants pray. In Greek, only the inhabitants worship (τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ κατοικοῦντας). The Hebrew echoes the OT theme of creation's participation in both sin and redemption.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence' (τὴν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ πρώτου θηρίου πᾶσαν ποιεῖ) — this clause is absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew goes directly to the wonders.
Hebrew: 'whose wounds were healed' (חבורותיה — PLURAL 'wounds'). Greek: 'whose plague of death was healed' (ἡ πληγὴ τοῦ θανάτου — SINGULAR 'plague of death'). Different number and terminology.
translation_notes: The raw manuscript has a lacuna [    ] (empty brackets) before חבורותיה — a gap in the text, likely a missing preposition (מן — 'from'). This scribal gap is evidence of authentic manuscript transmission, not a polished back-translation.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 13:1-3 — 'If a prophet arises among you and gives you a sign or wonder (אות או מופת), and the sign or wonder comes to pass, and he says, Let us go after other gods... you shall not listen.' The ground-animal fulfills this false-prophet pattern exactly.

one_way_hebrew: Uses singular הָאָדָם (ha-adam — 'the man/mankind', H120 with the definite article), echoing Genesis where God walks with 'the adam.' Greek has plural τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('men'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲנָשִׁים (anashim — 'men') or בְּנֵי אָדָם (benei adam — 'sons of man'), not the Genesis-laden ha-adam. Same pattern as Rev 21:3.
greek_deviations: Hebrew omits 'great signs' (σημεῖα μεγάλα) and 'down to the earth' (εἰς τὴν γῆν) present in Greek. The Hebrew is notably more concise: fire falls from heavens before the man.
translation_notes: The fire from heaven echoes 1 Kings 18:38 (YHWH sends fire on Elijah's altar) and 2 Kings 1:10-12 (Elijah calls fire from heaven). The ground-animal counterfeits Elijah's prophetic power.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'carved-image', H6459) — the EXACT word from the Second Commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶּסֶל ('you shall not make for yourself a carved-image', Ex 20:4, Deut 5:8). Greek εἰκόνα ('image') is neutral. A back-translator from Greek would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image') or דְּמוּת (demut — 'likeness'), not the Decalogue's specific prohibition word. The Hebrew author deliberately uses pesel, making the act an explicit violation of the Second Commandment.

CRITICAL: Uses הִסִּית (hissit — 'incited/enticed', hiphil of סות H5496) — the specific verb from Deuteronomy 13:6: 'If your brother... entices you (יְסִיתְךָ) secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods.' This is the Torah's technical legal term for enticement to idolatry. Greek πλανᾷ ('deceives/leads astray') is different — deception vs. active incitement. A back-translator from Greek would use הִתְעָה (hit'ah — 'led astray'), not the Deuteronomy 13 legal term.

CRITICAL: Uses the phrase אוֹתוֹת וּמוֹפְתִים (otot u-moftim — 'signs and wonders', H226+H4159) — the EXACT pair from Deuteronomy 13:1-2 where a false prophet gives 'a sign or a wonder' (אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵת) to entice to idolatry, and from the Exodus plagues (Deut 4:34, 6:22, 7:19, 26:8). Greek has only σημεῖα ('signs') — no 'wonders.' The Hebrew preserves the full Deuteronomy false-prophet formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'incited' (הסית). Greek: 'deceives' (πλανᾷ). Different verbs with different legal implications.
Hebrew: 'signs and wonders' (אותות ומופתים — full paired formula). Greek: only 'signs' (σημεῖα). Hebrew preserves the complete OT formula.
Hebrew: 'wounds of the sword' (חבורות חרב — plural). Greek: 'wound of the sword' (τὴν πληγὴν τῆς μαχαίρας — singular).
Hebrew: 'and was healed' (נתרפאה). Greek: 'and lived' (ἔζησεν — 'came back to life'). Healing vs. resurrection — different concepts.
translation_notes: 'Carved-image' for pesel captures the specific meaning: an idol carved from wood or stone, as prohibited in the Decalogue. Not merely an 'image' or 'representation.'
'Incited' for hissit carries the legal force of Deuteronomy 13 — criminal enticement to apostasy, punishable by death under Torah law.
textual_notes: The convergence of THREE Deuteronomy 13 elements — הסית (enticed), אותות ומופתים (signs and wonders), and פסל (carved-image) — shows the Hebrew author constructing the ground-animal as the ultimate Deuteronomy 13 false prophet. This cannot be reconstructed from the Greek text, which uses different vocabulary for all three.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has BOTH רוּחַ (ruach — 'spirit/breath', H7307) AND נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh — 'life-breath/soul', H5315). Greek has only πνεῦμα ('spirit/breath'). This is the Hebrew two-part anthropology from Genesis 2:7 where God breathes into Adam and he becomes a נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה ('living soul'). The carved-image receives both spirit and soul — a grotesque parody of the Genesis creation of man. A back-translator from Greek πνεῦμα would use only רוּחַ, not add נֶפֶשׁ. The distinction between ruach and nefesh is a fundamentally Hebrew concept.

Uses יִרְצֶה (yirtseh — 'would be willing/desire', from רצה H7521), the verb for God's acceptance of sacrifices (Lev 1:3-4 — 'he shall offer it of his own will', לִרְצֹנוֹ). Greek has simply ἐὰν μή ('whoever does not'). The Hebrew adds the element of WILLINGNESS — the test is not whether one worships but whether one is WILLING to pray. רצה carries the sense of delight and willing acceptance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spirit and life-breath' (ruach ve-nefesh — two terms). Greek: 'spirit' (πνεῦμα — one term). The Hebrew has the fuller anthropological framework.
Hebrew: 'whoever was not willing to pray' (tests inner willingness). Greek: 'whoever does not worship' (tests outward action). Different standard: heart vs. act.
translation_notes: 'Spirit and life-breath' — ruach is the animating wind/breath from God; nefesh is the resulting life-being/soul. Together they constitute full animate existence.

The giving of ruach and nefesh to a pesel inverts Genesis 2:7 — God breathed into man; now a false prophet breathes into a carved idol. It also recalls Psalm 115:4-7 and 135:15-17 where idols have mouths but cannot speak. Here, the pesel is given what OT idols lack.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סִימָן (siman — 'sign/mark'), a later Hebrew word for a distinguishing mark or token. Greek χάραγμα (charagma — 'engraving/stamp') specifically means an engraved/branded mark (from χαράσσω — 'to engrave'). The Hebrew siman is a general sign or token; the Greek implies physical branding. Different types of marking.

CRITICAL: Uses עֲבָדִים וּמְשׁוּחְרָרִים ('servants and freed-ones'). Greek has ἐλευθέρους καὶ δούλους ('free and slaves'). Two major differences: (1) The ORDER is reversed — Hebrew puts servants first, then freed; Greek puts free first, then slaves. (2) The Hebrew term מְשׁוּחְרָרִים (meshuchrarim) is the specific legal term for manumitted slaves — those formally released from servitude (from the root שחרר). A back-translator from Greek ἐλεύθερος ('free man') would use בֶּן חוֹרִין (ben chorin — 'free-born'), not the legal manumission term. The Hebrew reflects Torah slave-law vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Pair order reversed throughout: Hebrew 'great and small, wealthy and poor, servants and freed.' Greek: 'small and great, rich and poor, free and slave.'
Hebrew: singular 'his right hand' (יד ימינו) but plural 'their foreheads' (מצחיהם). This grammatical number inconsistency is preserved from the source text.
translation_notes: 'Sign' for siman rather than 'mark' — preserving the Hebrew word's broader meaning as a distinguishing token.
'Freed' for meshuchrarim — not free-born people but formerly enslaved people who have been emancipated. A precise legal distinction.
textual_notes: The forehead-and-hand placement echoes Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18 — 'bind them as a sign (אות) on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.' The animal's sign parodies the Torah's tefillin commandment.

greek_deviations: Hebrew repeats 'on his hand or on his forehead' from the previous verse. This repetition suggests the Hebrew verse division includes detail that Greek distributes across two verses.
translation_notes: קָנָה (qanah, H7069 — 'to buy/acquire') and מָכַר (makhar, H4376 — 'to sell') are standard OT commercial vocabulary (Gen 25:10, 47:20; Ruth 4:5; Prov 23:23).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has THREE wisdom/intelligence words: חָכְמָה (chokhmah — 'wisdom', H2451) + תְּבוּנָה (tevunah — 'understanding', H8394) + שֶׂכֶל (sekhel — 'intelligence', H7922). Greek has only TWO: σοφία ('wisdom') + νοῦν ('mind'). The triple wisdom vocabulary is a distinctly Hebrew literary pattern: Proverbs 1:2 — 'to know wisdom and instruction, to discern words of understanding (tevunah)'; Daniel 1:17 — 'knowledge and intelligence (sekhel) in all literature and wisdom (chokhmah).' A back-translator from Greek's two terms would use two Hebrew terms, not three.

Uses בַּעַל שֶׂכֶל (ba'al sekhel — 'master of intelligence', H1167+H7922). The ba'al X idiom is a characteristically Hebrew construction: בַּעַל חֲלוֹמוֹת (ba'al chalomot — 'master of dreams', Gen 37:19). Greek ὁ ἔχων νοῦν ('the one having a mind') is flat by comparison.

Uses הַסַּךְ (ha-sakh — 'the sum/total'), a bookkeeping/accounting term for a calculated total. Greek has only ὁ ἀριθμός ('the number'). The Hebrew specifies the result is a computed sum — the product of gematria calculation.

Uses וְתִמָּצֵא (vetimmatse — 'and you shall find', niphal of מצא H4672). This is direct address to the reader: 'YOU will discover.' Greek states declaratively 'and his number IS...' The Hebrew makes it an interactive puzzle to be solved by the reader.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three wisdom terms (chokhmah + tevunah + sekhel). Greek: two (sophia + nous).
Hebrew: 'the number of one man' (אדם אחד — one specific individual). Greek: 'a number of a man' (ἀριθμὸς ἀνθρώπου — generic). The Hebrew specifies one particular person.
Hebrew: 'you shall find the sum' (interactive, addressed to reader). Greek: 'his number is' (declarative statement).
translation_notes: הַסַּךְ (ha-sakh) is a post-biblical accounting term (Mishnaic Hebrew) for 'the total/sum.' No standard Strong's number.
צָרִיךְ (tsarikh — 'must/needs to') is also post-biblical, common in Mishnaic Hebrew. These forms reinforce the text's late Second Temple linguistic stratum.
textual_notes: The number 666 in Hebrew gematria could correspond to various names. The Hebrew text's emphasis on 'one man' (adam echad) and its interactive 'you shall find' suggests the original audience knew which person was meant. Hebrew gematria and Greek isopsephia yield different name-candidates from the same number.

14.summary: Revelation 14 in Hebrew contains an extraordinary density of one-way translation markers — linguistic features that can only originate in Hebrew and could not arise from back-translation of the Greek. The chapter draws on a remarkably wide range of Hebrew sources: Genesis creation language (רחף/hovering v6, דמות/likeness v14), Exodus/Sinai vocabulary (קולות/thunders v2, פסל/graven-image vv9,11, חרמש/sickle v14), Levitical priestly terminology (זרק/cast-as-sacrifice v18, קברות השדה/field-plots v19), Psalm language (מזמרים/singing v3, רמיה/deceit v5, כנור/harp v2), and prophetic texts (Isaiah 21:9 quoted verbatim in v8, Joel 4:13 echoed in vv15-18). Most striking are: (1) The consonantal proof in v8 that השקיט derives from שקט ('silence') not שקה ('give drink') — Bavel SILENCED the nations, a reading impossible to derive from the Greek. (2) The rabbinic technical term בת קול (bat qol — 'heavenly voice', v13), which embeds the text within a post-biblical Jewish linguistic world. (3) The martyrdom concept קידוש יהוה (qiddush YHWH — 'sanctification of the Name', v13), a specifically rabbinic theological category absent from the Greek. (4) The אֵוַן גֵּילִיוֹן compound (v6), which phonetically resembles εὐαγγέλιον but parses as a Hebrew 'proclamation-tablet.' (5) The consistent use of תפילה ('prayer') where Greek has 'worship/glory' — the Hebrew author frames all divine encounter as prayer. (6) The use of קברות השדה ('field-plots') as a measurement unit in BOTH chapters 14 and 21, confirming a consistent Hebrew measurement system with no Greek equivalent. (7) The distinction between רוח ('spirit', v5) and Greek στόμα ('mouth') — the Hebrew locates integrity in the inner spirit rather than outward speech. The chapter uses the Tetragrammaton (יהוה) consistently where Greek has θεός, and the Passover-lamb term שֶׂה where Greek has the generic ἀρνίον.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716) — the specific Passover lamb from Exodus 12:3-5 (שֶׂה לְבֵית אָבוֹת — 'a lamb per household'). Greek uses ἀρνίον, a generic diminutive 'little lamb.' A back-translator from Greek would more likely use כֶּבֶשׂ (keves) or טָלֶה (taleh). The consistent use of seh throughout this Hebrew text ties the messianic figure directly to the Passover.

Uses הַר צִיּוֹן (Har Tsiyon, H2022+H6726) — the specific mountain of YHWH's dwelling in the Psalms (Ps 2:6, 48:2, 125:1) and prophets (Isa 2:3, 4:5, 24:23, Joel 3:5). This is natural Hebrew usage; the Greek Σιών is a transliteration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the name of his Father' (only the Father's name). Greek: τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ — 'HIS name AND his Father's name.' Greek adds the Lamb's name. A back-translator from Greek would not omit the Lamb's name.
Hebrew: 'upon them' (עליהם) — unspecified location. Greek: 'on their foreheads' (ἐπὶ τῶν μετώπων αὐτῶν). The Hebrew is less specific.
translation_notes: Tsiyon is transliterated from the Hebrew צִיּוֹן rather than anglicized as 'Zion.'
textual_notes: Psalm 2:6 — 'I have set my king upon Tsiyon, my holy mountain.' The lamb standing on Har Tsiyon directly fulfills the messianic-king enthronement psalm.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רַעַשׁ (ra'ash, H7494 — 'earthquake/roaring/tumult') for the sound of waters. Greek has φωνήν ('voice/sound'). Ra'ash is used in Ezekiel 3:12-13 for the sound of YHWH's glory departing (קוֹל רַעַשׁ גָּדוֹל — 'a sound of great tumult'). A back-translator from Greek's generic 'sound' would not reach for the Ezekiel glory-departure verb.

Uses קוֹלוֹת (kolot, H6963 — 'thunders') — the specific word for the thunders at Sinai (Ex 19:16: וַיְהִי קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים — 'and there were thunders and lightnings'). Greek uses βροντῆς ('thunder'). A back-translator would use רעם (ra'am — 'thunder'), not the Sinai-specific kolot.

Uses כִּינּוֹר (kinnor, H3658) — David's specific instrument (1 Sam 16:16,23; 2 Sam 6:5; Ps 33:2, 71:22, 150:3). Greek has κιθαρῳδῶν κιθαριζόντων ἐν ταῖς κιθάραις αὐτῶν ('harpers harping on their harps') — a triple expansion. The Hebrew uses a single word with deep Davidic associations.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like the sound of a harp' (single concise phrase). Greek: 'like harpers harping on their harps' (triple expansion). The Hebrew is characteristically terse.
Greek adds 'from heaven' (ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) and uses 'many waters' (ὑδάτων πολλῶν) where Hebrew has 'great waters' (מים גדולים).
translation_notes: 'Roaring' for ra'ash captures the seismic/overwhelming quality — this is not a gentle sound but an earthquake-like rumble.
'Thunders' for kolot: this word means both 'voices' and 'thunders' in Hebrew. Context and the Sinai echo demand 'thunders.'
textual_notes: Ezekiel 43:2 — 'And behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the east. And his voice was like the sound of many waters (כְּקוֹל מַיִם רַבִּים).' The Hebrew Revelation draws on this Ezekiel theophany imagery.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְזַמְּרִים (mezammerim, H2167 — 'singing/making music') — the specific word for musical worship in the Psalms (Ps 27:6, 57:8, 66:2, 68:5, 105:2). Greek ᾄδουσιν is generic 'they sing.' The Hebrew word connotes instrumental worship, not mere singing.

Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah, H127 — 'ground/soil') NOT אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth/land'). Greek uses γῆ (ge — 'earth'). Same distinction as Revelation 21:1 — adamah echoes Genesis 2:7 where man was formed from the adamah. A back-translator from Greek would use ארץ, not the Genesis-laden adamah.

Uses שֶׁקָּנָה (she-qanah — 'who acquired,' ACTIVE voice, 3ms perfect of קנה H7069). Greek uses ἠγοράσθησαν ('were purchased' — PASSIVE voice). The Hebrew says the Lamb/YHWH actively acquired them; the Greek says they were passively bought. A back-translator from Greek passive would write שֶׁנִּקְנוּ (she-niqnu — passive), not the active form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'as a new song' (כשיר חדש — with comparative כ, 'like/as a song'). Greek: ᾠδὴν καινήν ('a new song' — with ὡς 'as if'). Both use the simile but the Hebrew prefix כ is more terse.
Hebrew: 'acquired from the ground' (active, from adamah). Greek: 'redeemed from the earth' (passive, from ge). Different voice, different word for earth.
translation_notes: 'Sang' for mezammerim — the root zamar encompasses both singing and instrumental music-making. The Psalms use this word for accompanied worship.
'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') preserves the Genesis 2:7 theological connection — they were acquired from the very soil from which Adam was formed.
textual_notes: Psalm 40:3 — 'He put a new song (שִׁיר חָדָשׁ) in my mouth.' The Hebrew 'new song' is a recurrent OT motif (Ps 33:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9, 149:1, Isa 42:10).

one_way_hebrew: Uses חָטְאוּ (chat'u — 'sinned', from חטא H2398). Greek says οὐκ ἐμολύνθησαν ('were not defiled'). The Hebrew frames it as SIN; the Greek frames it as ritual DEFILEMENT. A back-translator from Greek would use לֹא נִטְמְאוּ (lo nitme'u — 'were not defiled', from טמא H2930), not the sin-verb חטא.

CRITICAL: Uses כִּבְתוּלוֹת (ki-vtulot — 'LIKE virgins', H1330) with the comparative prefix כ ('like/as'). This is a SIMILE. Greek says παρθένοι γάρ εἰσιν ('for they ARE virgins') — a statement of identity. The Hebrew says they are LIKE virgins; the Greek says they ARE virgins. A back-translator from Greek would write בתולות הם ('they are virgins'), not the simile כבתולות.

Uses בִּכּוּרוֹת (bikkurot — 'firstfruits', H1061) — the specific Temple harvest-offering term (Ex 23:16,19; 34:22,26; Num 18:13; Deut 26:10). This is the Shavuot/Weeks offering. Greek ἀπαρχή also means 'firstfruit' but the Hebrew form specifically evokes the Temple festival offering.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sinned with women' (moral transgression). Greek: 'not defiled with women' (ritual impurity). Different categories — sin vs. defilement.
Hebrew: 'LIKE virgins' (simile with כ). Greek: 'ARE virgins' (identity claim). Fundamentally different assertion.
Hebrew: 'firstfruits for YHWH and the lamb.' Greek: 'firstfruit to God and to the Lamb' (τῷ θεῷ). Hebrew uses the Tetragrammaton; Greek uses θεός.
translation_notes: The bracket [וְהֵם] in the source suggests editorial restoration of a damaged passage.
'Firstfruits' for bikkurot — the Shavuot/Pentecost offering of the first harvest yield, presented at the Temple. The 144,000 are the harvest offering to YHWH.
textual_notes: Leviticus 23:17 — 'You shall bring from your dwellings two loaves of bread for a wave offering... they are firstfruits (בִּכּוּרִים) to YHWH.' The 144,000 as bikkurot connects them to the Shavuot offering.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּרוּחָם (be-rucham — 'in their spirit', H7307). Greek says ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτῶν ('in their MOUTH'). The Hebrew locates truthfulness in the inner spirit; the Greek locates it in outward speech. A back-translator from Greek would write בְּפִיהֶם (be-fihem — 'in their mouth'), not ברוחם ('in their spirit'). This is a massive difference — inner integrity vs. verbal accuracy.

Uses נְקִיִּים (neqiyyim — 'innocent/clean', H5355) — the specific word for those innocent of bloodguilt (Ex 23:7; Deut 19:10, 21:8-9; 2 Kings 21:16, 24:4). Greek says ἄμωμοι ('without blemish' — a sacrificial term). A back-translator from Greek would use תְּמִימִים (temimim — 'unblemished'), the standard sacrificial-quality word. The Hebrew author frames them as judicially innocent, not sacrificially perfect.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in their spirit' (רוחם). Greek: 'in their mouth' (στόματι). Different seat of truthfulness — internal vs. external.
Hebrew: 'innocent' (נקיים — judicial acquittal). Greek: 'without blemish' (ἄμωμοι — sacrificial quality). Different conceptual frame.
translation_notes: רְמִיָּה (remiyyah, H7423 — 'deceit/treachery') — used in the Psalms for inner duplicity (Ps 32:2, 34:14, 52:4, 101:7, 120:2). The Hebrew specifically targets inward deceit, consistent with 'in their spirit.'
'Innocent' for neqiyyim captures the judicial/legal sense — declared not guilty, free of blood.
textual_notes: Psalm 32:2 — 'Blessed is the man to whom YHWH imputes no iniquity, and in whose spirit (רוח) there is no deceit (רמיה).' The Hebrew Revelation quotes this psalm nearly verbatim.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רֹחֵף (rochef, H7363 — 'hovering') — one of the rarest verbs in the entire OT, appearing only in Genesis 1:2 (the Spirit of God 'hovering' over the waters — מְרַחֶפֶת) and Deuteronomy 32:11 (an eagle 'hovering' over its young). Greek uses πετόμενον ('flying'). A back-translator from Greek 'flying' would use עָף (uf — 'fly', H5774), the common word. NO translator would independently reach for the ultra-rare Genesis creation verb. The messenger hovers like the Spirit at creation.

CRITICAL: Uses אֵוַן גֵּילִיוֹן as the object the messenger carries. Greek has εὐαγγέλιον αἰώνιον ('eternal gospel'). The Hebrew compound phonetically resembles 'euangelion' but parses as two Hebrew words: אֵוַן (possibly a variant of אֶבֶן — 'stone') and גֵּילִיוֹן (from גלה H1540 — 'to reveal'; cf. Isaiah 8:1 where גִּלָּיוֹן means 'tablet'). The Hebrew author either (a) hears the Greek-sounding word and parses it through Hebrew morphology as a 'stone tablet of revelation,' or (b) the original Hebrew 'even gilyon' was heard by Greek speakers as 'euangelion.' Either way, this is a uniquely Hebrew phenomenon — a back-translator from Greek would simply transliterate εὐαγγέλιον, not construct a Hebrew compound.

Uses עַמִּים וּלְאוּמִּים ('peoples and nations', H5971+H3816) — a standard OT poetic word pair (Gen 25:23, Ps 2:1, Isa 34:1, 51:4). Greek has the four-fold πᾶν ἔθνος καὶ φυλὴν καὶ γλῶσσαν καὶ λαόν ('every nation and tribe and tongue and people'). A back-translator from Greek would reproduce four terms, not the classic Hebrew two-term parallelism.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'hovering' (רחף — Genesis creation verb). Greek: 'flying' (πετόμενον). Different verbs with vastly different theological weight.
Hebrew: 'even gilyon' (a Hebrew compound — stone tablet / proclamation-tablet). Greek: εὐαγγέλιον αἰώνιον ('eternal gospel'). Greek adds 'eternal' (αἰώνιον) which is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'peoples and nations' (two categories). Greek: 'every nation, tribe, tongue, and people' (four categories).
translation_notes: 'Hovering' for rochef preserves the Genesis 1:2 creation connection — the same Spirit-hovering verb.
'Proclamation-tablet' for even gilyon: the second element (gilyon) means 'tablet/scroll of revelation' (cf. Isa 8:1). The compound suggests a written decree being carried through the heavens.
הַדָּרִים (ha-darim — 'those dwelling') uses a post-biblical Hebrew participial form from דור, rather than the standard biblical הַיֹּשְׁבִים from ישב (H3427).
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם ('and the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters'). The same rare verb now describes a messenger hovering in mid-heaven with a proclamation.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַבְּאֵרוֹת (ha-be'erot — 'the wells', H875). Greek says πηγὰς ὑδάτων ('springs/fountains of waters'). A back-translator from Greek would use מַעְיְנוֹת מַיִם ('springs of water'), not בְּאֵרוֹת ('wells'). Be'erot are DUG wells — the patriarchal wells of Abraham and Isaac (Gen 21:25-30, 26:15-22), covenant landmarks that were the subject of disputes and oaths (Beer-sheva = 'well of the oath'). The Hebrew creation list — heavens, earth, sea, wells — includes human-accessed subterranean water as part of the created order. This is a uniquely Hebraic perspective.

Uses תְּפִילָּה (tefillah — 'prayer', H8605) TWICE where Greek uses δότε αὐτῷ δόξαν ('give him glory') and προσκυνήσατε ('worship/bow down'). These are entirely different actions: prayer vs. glory-giving, prayer vs. prostration. A back-translator from Greek would use הָבוּ לוֹ כָּבוֹד ('give him glory') and הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ ('bow down'), not the tefillah idiom.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'wells' (בארות — dug wells). Greek: 'springs of waters' (πηγὰς ὑδάτων). Different water source — patriarchal wells vs. natural springs.

Hebrew: 'the day of judgment' (היום הדין). Greek: 'the hour of his judgment' (ἡ ὥρα τῆς κρίσεως αὐτοῦ). Hebrew uses 'day' (broader); Greek uses 'hour' (more specific). Greek adds 'his' which Hebrew lacks.
Hebrew: 'make prayer to him' (twice). Greek: 'give him glory' + 'worship him who made.' Different concepts — prayer vs. giving glory and bowing down.
translation_notes: 'Wells' for be'erot — these are dug wells, distinct from springs (ma'ayanot) or fountains (maqorot). The patriarchal association is inescapable.
'Prayer' for tefillah — this word encompasses petition, intercession, and communion with God. It is the standard word for Jewish liturgical prayer.
textual_notes: The creation list (heavens, earth, sea, wells) echoes Exodus 20:11 — 'For in six days YHWH made the heavens and the earth, the sea and all that is in them.' But the Hebrew substitutes 'wells' for 'all that is in them,' grounding the cosmic creation in the tangible, patriarchal landscape.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 21:9: נָפְלָה נָפְלָה בָּבֶל — 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon.' The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact wording with the doubled verb for emphasis.

CRITICAL — CONSONANTAL TEXT: The consonants ה-ש-ק-י-ט can ONLY derive from the root ש-ק-ט (shaqqat — 'to be quiet/still', H8252). The hifil הִשְׁקִיט means 'she silenced/quieted.' Greek says πεπότικεν ('she has made to drink', from ποτίζω). If the root were שקה (to give drink, H8248), the hifil 3fs would end in ת-ה (tav-he): הִשְׁקְתָה — but the consonantal text ends in ט (tet), proving the root is שקט. The Hebrew says Bavel SILENCED the nations with her wine; the Greek says she made them DRINK. A back-translator from Greek 'made drink' would use הִשְׁקְתָה (from שקה), which has completely different consonants. This is among the strongest consonantal one-way markers in the chapter.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she silenced' (השקיט from שקט — 'to silence/quiet'). Greek: 'she made to drink' (πεπότικεν from ποτίζω). Entirely different verbs. The Hebrew image is drugging nations into passivity/silence; the Greek image is forcing them to drink.
Greek adds θυμός ('wrath/passion'): 'the wine of the wrath (θυμοῦ) of her fornication.' Hebrew has only 'the wine of her harlotry' — no wrath.
translation_notes: 'Silenced' for hishqit (hifil of שקט) — Bavel drugged the nations into stupor and silence with the wine of her harlotry. This is a more sinister image than merely 'making them drink' — she rendered them mute and passive.
Uses בָּבֶל (Bavel, H894) — the Hebrew name for Babylon, used throughout the OT from Genesis 11:9 onward.
textual_notes: Isaiah 21:9 — 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon (נָפְלָה נָפְלָה בָּבֶל), and all the graven images (פסילי) of her gods are shattered to the ground.' The Hebrew Revelation preserves the Isaiah source text; the Greek paraphrases it.

The wordplay potential: השקיט (silence) sounds close to השקה (give drink). The Hebrew author may have deliberately chosen the 'silence' verb knowing its phonetic proximity to 'drink,' achieving a double meaning — she both drugged them (drink) and silenced them.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel, H6459 — 'graven image') — the exact word from the Second Commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל (Ex 20:4 — 'You shall not make for yourself a graven image'). Greek uses εἰκών ('image'). A back-translator from Greek εἰκών would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image') or דְּמוּת (demut — 'likeness'), NOT the Ten Commandments word pesel. The Hebrew author explicitly frames beast-worship as a violation of the Second Commandment.

Uses חַיָּה (chayyah — 'living-creature', H2416) for the 'beast' — the SAME word used for the living-creatures around the throne in verse 3 (הָאַרְבַּע חַיּוֹת). The beast is ironically called a 'living thing.' Greek uses θηρίον ('wild beast') — a specifically negative term. A back-translator from Greek θηρίον would use a pejorative term, not the neutral chayyah.

Continues using תְּפִילָּה (tefillah — 'prayer') where Greek has προσκυνεῖ ('worships/bows down'). The Hebrew consistently frames false worship as 'prayer' — the same word used for legitimate prayer to YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'graven-image' (פסל — Second Commandment term). Greek: 'image' (εἰκών — neutral term for any image). Different theological framing.
Hebrew: 'beast' (חיה — neutral 'living-creature'). Greek: 'wild beast' (θηρίον). Different connotation — the Hebrew's ironic use of chayyah is lost in Greek.
Hebrew: 'make his prayer to' (תפילתו). Greek: 'worships' (προσκυνεῖ). Prayer vs. prostration.
translation_notes: 'Graven-image' for pesel — this is the specific carved/hewn idol, as opposed to מַסֵּכָה (massechah — 'molten image'). The distinction matters: a pesel is hand-made.
סִימָן (siman — 'sign/mark') is a post-biblical Hebrew term common in rabbinic literature (b. Shabbat 55a, etc.). It has no standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:4-5 — לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל... לֹא תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לָהֶם ('You shall not make a graven image... you shall not bow down to them'). The Hebrew Revelation recasts the beast-worship warning using the exact Torah prohibition language.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲרוֹן (charon, H2740 — 'fierce/burning anger') TWICE — once for the wine and once for the cup. This is the specific OT word for YHWH's burning anger (Ex 32:12; Num 25:4, 32:14; Josh 7:26; 2 Kings 23:26; Isa 13:9,13). Greek uses θυμός ('passion/wrath') for both. Charon specifically denotes HOT anger — a burning rage. A back-translator from the more generic Greek θυμός would not independently select charon both times.

Uses כּוֹס (kos, H3563 — 'cup') — the prophetic judgment cup (Isa 51:17,22; Jer 25:15-28; Ps 75:8: 'In YHWH's hand there is a cup, and the wine is foaming'). Greek ποτήριον ('drinking vessel') is generic. The Hebrew carries the full weight of the prophetic judgment-cup tradition.

Uses וְיֵעָנֵשׁ (ye'anesh — 'shall be punished', from ענש H6064). Greek says βασανισθήσεται ('shall be tormented'). The Hebrew verb means judicial punishment — a fine or penalty. The Greek means torture/torment. A back-translator from 'tormented' would use יְעֻנֶּה (ye'unneh — from ענה, to afflict/torture), not the judicial ענש.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'punished' (ענש — legal penalty). Greek: 'tormented' (βασανίζω — tortured). Different penal concept — judicial sentence vs. active torture.
Hebrew: 'wrath of YHWH' (חרון יהוה). Greek: 'wrath of God' (θυμοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ). Tetragrammaton vs. generic divine title.
translation_notes: 'Wrath' and 'fury' for the two occurrences of charon — the doubled use intensifies YHWH's burning anger. The cup is ITSELF fury, filled with the wine of fury.
'Punished' for ye'anesh is critical — this is a legal penalty, not arbitrary torment. The punishment is judicially determined.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:15 — כִּי כֹה אָמַר יְהוָה... קַח אֶת כּוֹס הַיַּיִן הַחֵמָה הַזֹּאת ('For thus says YHWH... Take this cup of the wine of fury'). The Hebrew Revelation draws on the Jeremiah judgment-cup tradition.
Isaiah 51:17 — 'Rouse yourself, rouse yourself! Stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from YHWH's hand the cup (כּוֹס) of his fury (חֲמָתוֹ).' The same cup imagery.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְנוּחָה (menuchah, H4496 — 'rest') — the specific word for the eschatological promised rest (Deut 12:9; Ruth 1:9; Ps 23:2, 95:11, 132:14). Those who worship the pesel are denied the menuchah — the sabbath rest that YHWH promised Israel. Greek ἀνάπαυσιν is a generic 'rest/cessation.' A back-translator might use menuchah, but the theological weight of the term — its connection to the promised land, the Sabbath, and eschatological rest — would be coincidental.

Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם (me-olam ve-ad olam — 'from age to age') — a standard OT doxological formula (Ps 41:14, 90:2, 103:17, 106:48; 1 Chr 16:36). Greek uses εἰς αἰῶνας αἰώνων ('unto ages of ages'). Both are idiomatic in their respective languages.

Continues using פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'graven image') and מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying') where Greek uses εἰκών ('image') and προσκυνεῖ ('worships'). The Hebrew consistently frames the sin as prayer-to-an-idol, using the Second Commandment vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the smoke of their punishment' (עונש — legal punishment). Greek: 'the smoke of their torment' (βασανισμός — torment). Same distinction as v10.
Hebrew: 'who pray to the graven-image' (מתפללים לפסל). Greek: 'who worship the beast and his image and receive the mark of his name' (expanded list). Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: עוֹנֶשׁ (onesh — 'punishment') is from the root ענש (H6064). It denotes a legally imposed penalty — the same root used in v10.
'From age to age' for me-olam ve-ad olam — this captures the Hebrew temporal concept better than 'forever and ever.' The Hebrew עוֹלָם means a long but bounded age/era.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:10 — 'Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up from age to age (מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם — me-olam ve-ad olam).' The Hebrew Revelation quotes Isaiah 34's judgment oracle against Edom verbatim.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תִּקְוָה (tiqvah, H8615 — 'hope'). Greek uses ὑπομονή ('patience/endurance'). A back-translator from Greek 'patience' would write סַבְלָנוּת (savlanut — 'patience') or קַוָּאי (qavvai — 'enduring'), NOT tiqvah ('hope'). These are fundamentally different concepts — hope (confident expectation of future good) vs. patience (endurance under present trial). The Hebrew says the saints have HOPE; the Greek says they have PATIENCE.

Uses the name יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua, H3442) — the Hebrew name meaning 'he saves' or 'salvation,' the same name as Joshua son of Nun (Neh 8:17). Greek has Ἰησοῦ (Iesou). The Hebrew form is natural; a back-translator from Greek would typically transliterate.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'hope' (תקוה). Greek: 'patience' (ὑπομονή). Entirely different concepts.
Hebrew: 'commandments of YHWH' (מצוות יהוה). Greek: 'commandments of God' (τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ θεοῦ). Tetragrammaton vs. θεός.
Hebrew: 'believe in Yeshua' (מאמינים בישוע). Greek: 'the faith of Jesus' (τὴν πίστιν Ἰησοῦ). Hebrew has active believing; Greek has 'the faith of' — different grammatical construction.
translation_notes: בְּכָאן (b'chan — 'herein') is a post-biblical Hebrew demonstrative adverb, characteristic of later Hebrew linguistic registers.
'Hope' for tiqvah — the word that gives its name to the Israeli national anthem (Hatikvah). The root קוה means 'to wait/expect with confidence.'
textual_notes: Jeremiah 17:13 — מִקְוֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה ('The hope of Israel is YHWH'). The tiqvah of the saints is grounded in the same root as Israel's hope in YHWH.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בַּת קוֹל (bat qol — literally 'daughter of a voice') — the specific RABBINIC technical term for a heavenly/divine voice (b. Berakhot 3a; b. Sotah 48b; b. Sanhedrin 11a; m. Avot 6:2). This is THE standard rabbinic term for post-prophetic divine communication. Greek simply says φωνήν ('a voice'). NO back-translator from Greek would introduce the specifically rabbinic bat qol terminology. This is among the strongest proofs of Hebrew authorship in the entire chapter — it embeds the text within the rabbinic linguistic world.

CRITICAL: Uses קִידּוּשׁ יַהְוֶה (qiddush YHWH — 'sanctification of YHWH') — the concept of קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם (qiddush ha-shem — 'sanctification of the Name'), which in rabbinic tradition means MARTYRDOM — dying to sanctify God's name (b. Sanhedrin 74a-b; Sifra Emor 9:5). Greek says ἐν κυρίῳ ἀποθνῄσκοντες ('dying in the Lord'). 'Dying IN the Lord' (Greek) means dying while belonging to the Lord. 'Dying FOR the sanctification of YHWH' (Hebrew) means dying as an act of martyrdom to sanctify the divine Name. These are ENTIRELY different theological concepts. No back-translator would introduce the qiddush ha-shem concept from the Greek.

Uses שׁוֹכְנִים (shochenim — 'dwelling/finding repose', from שכן H7931) — the root of שְׁכִינָה (Shekinah, God's dwelling presence). Greek uses ἀναπαύσονται ('they shall rest'). A back-translator from Greek would use יָנוּחוּ (yanuchu — 'they shall rest', from נוח H5117), not the theologically loaded שכן. The Hebrew says the martyrs dwell in God's own Shekinah-presence — their rest is a dwelling with God.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: bat qol ('heavenly voice' — rabbinic technical term). Greek: φωνήν ('a voice'). The Hebrew carries a whole theology of divine communication absent from Greek.
Hebrew: 'those who die for the sanctification of YHWH' (martyrdom concept). Greek: 'the dead who die in the Lord' (belonging to the Lord). Different theology of death.
Hebrew: 'they find repose' (שוכנים — Shekinah-dwelling verb). Greek: 'they shall rest' (ἀναπαύσονται — generic rest). Different quality of afterlife experience.
translation_notes: 'Heavenly voice' for bat qol — this translates the rabbinic concept rather than the literal 'daughter of a voice.' The bat qol is how God communicates after the cessation of prophecy.
'Sanctification' for qiddush — preserving the Hebrew martyrdom concept. In rabbinic tradition, dying al qiddush ha-shem ('for the sanctification of the Name') is the highest form of witness.
מֵעַכְשָׁיו (me-achshav — 'from now') is a characteristically post-biblical Hebrew temporal adverb; the biblical equivalent would be מֵעַתָּה (me-attah, H6258).
textual_notes: The bat qol concept appears throughout rabbinic literature as the mode of divine communication after the last prophets. Its presence here places the text within a Hebrew-speaking Jewish milieu that is aware of post-biblical theological developments.

Leviticus 22:32 — וְלֹא תְחַלְּלוּ אֶת שֵׁם קָדְשִׁי וְנִקְדַּשְׁתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ('You shall not profane my holy name, and I will be sanctified among the children of Israel'). This is the Torah root of the qiddush ha-shem concept.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּדְמוּת (ki-demut — 'like the likeness of', H1823) — the word דְּמוּת is from Genesis 1:26: 'Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness (דְּמוּתֵנוּ).' Greek has ὅμοιον υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου ('like a son of man') — a Daniel 7:13 reference. The Hebrew author uses the Genesis creation word (demut) rather than the Aramaic bar enash (son of man) idiom. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ ('like a son of man'), the Daniel phrase, not the Genesis demut.

Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'crown') — the royal/imperial crown of Persian origin (Esth 1:11, 2:17, 6:8). Greek uses στέφανον ('wreath/crown'). The Hebrew keter is the sovereign's diadem; the Greek stephanos is a victor's wreath. A back-translator from Greek stephanos would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — 'wreath-crown'), not keter.

Uses חֶרְמֵשׁ (chermesh, H2770 — 'sickle') — the Israelite harvest sickle (Deut 16:9: 'From when the sickle (חֶרְמֵשׁ) is first put to the standing grain'; Deut 23:26). Greek uses δρέπανον ('sickle'). Both mean sickle, but the Hebrew carries the specific Deuteronomic agricultural-legal association.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like the likeness of a man' (ki-demut adam — Genesis creation language). Greek: 'like a son of man' (ὅμοιον υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου — Daniel 7:13 language). Different OT allusion.
Hebrew: 'crown' (keter — sovereign's diadem). Greek: 'crown' (stephanos — victor's wreath). Different type of crown.
translation_notes: 'Likeness' for demut — preserving the Genesis 1:26 creation connection. The cloud-figure is described using the vocabulary of human creation.
'Crown' for keter — the Persian royal crown, not a laurel wreath. This is the crown of absolute sovereignty.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:13 (Aramaic) — כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ ('like a son of man'). The Hebrew Revelation's choice of דמות over the Danielic phrase suggests the author thinks in Hebrew categories (Genesis) rather than Aramaic ones (Daniel), even when describing the same vision.
Ezekiel 1:26 — כְּמַרְאֵה אָדָם ('like the appearance of a man'). Ezekiel's throne vision uses a similar construction — 'like' + a word for appearance + 'man.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִבֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה (mi-beit ha-tefillah — 'from the house of prayer', H1004+H8605). Greek says ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ ('from the temple'). The Hebrew uses 'house of prayer' — the phrase from Isaiah 56:7 (כִּי בֵיתִי בֵּית תְּפִלָּה יִקָּרֵא לְכָל הָעַמִּים — 'for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples'). A back-translator from Greek ναός ('temple') would use הֵיכָל (heichal) or בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ (beit hamikdash), not the Isaiah-specific 'house of prayer.' Same distinction as Revelation 21:22.

Uses הַךְ (hach — 'strike/smite', imperative of נכה H5221). Greek uses πέμψον ('send/thrust'). The Hebrew is viscerally violent — STRIKE with your sickle. The Greek is mechanical — 'send your sickle.' A back-translator from Greek would use שְׁלַח (shelach — 'send'), not the warrior-verb nakah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the house of prayer' (בית התפילה). Greek: 'from the temple' (ναός). Different designation for the sacred space.
Hebrew: 'strike with your sickle' (הך — smiting verb). Greek: 'send your sickle' (πέμψον — sending verb). Different action.
Hebrew: 'the time of the harvest' (העת הקצירה). Greek: 'the hour to reap has come' (ἦλθεν ἡ ὥρα θερίσαι). Hebrew uses 'time/season' (עת); Greek uses 'hour' (ὥρα).
translation_notes: 'Strike' for hach preserves the martial force of the Hebrew — the harvest is depicted as a battle.
'House of prayer' echoes Isaiah 56:7, which Yeshua quotes in Matthew 21:13 / Mark 11:17. The Hebrew consistently uses this designation instead of 'temple.'
textual_notes: Joel 4:13 (Hebrew; 3:13 English) — שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר ('Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe'). This is the primary OT source for the harvest-judgment imagery in verses 14-19.

one_way_hebrew: Continues הִכָּה (hikkah — 'struck', from נכה H5221) where Greek has ἔβαλεν ('cast/threw'). The Hebrew image is of striking/smiting with the sickle, like a warrior in battle; the Greek is of casting the sickle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew is notably more concise — just 'he struck with his sickle and reaped.' Greek adds ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν ('upon the earth') and ἐθερίσθη ἡ γῆ ('and the earth was reaped'). The Hebrew is characteristically terse.

one_way_hebrew: Uses a DIFFERENT word for sickle: מַעְגָּל (ma'agal — consonants מ-ע-ג-ל), distinct from both חֶרְמֵשׁ (chermesh, vv. 14-16) and מַגָּל (maggal, v. 18). The form ma'agal relates to עגל ('round/circular') — suggesting a curved blade for grape-cutting, distinguished from the straight grain-sickle (chermesh). The Hebrew author uses THREE distinct cutting tools; Greek uses the same word δρέπανον for all. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word throughout, would use one Hebrew word consistently.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'went TO the heavens' (הלך לשמים — ascending direction). Greek: 'came OUT OF the temple which is in heaven' (ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ ἐν οὐρανῷ — exiting direction). Different spatial perspectives.
Greek adds ὀξύ ('sharp') to describe the sickle — absent from Hebrew here (the 'sharpness' appears later in v. 18 via the altar-messenger's command).
translation_notes: מַעְגָּל (ma'agal) — from the root עגל ('round'). Possibly a curved vintner's blade, distinct from the grain-harvest chermesh. The consonantal distinction (מ-ע-ג-ל vs. מ-ג-ל) is deliberate.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַגָּל (maggal, H4038 — 'sickle') — the SAME word from Joel 4:13 (Hebrew; 3:13 English): שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר ('Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe'). The Hebrew Revelation directly echoes Joel's grape-harvest judgment using Joel's exact vocabulary. Greek uses δρέπανον throughout.

CRITICAL: Uses וְזָרַק (ve-zaraq — 'and he cast/threw', H2236) — the specific PRIESTLY verb for throwing/sprinkling sacrificial blood against the altar (Ex 24:6,8; 29:16,20; Lev 1:5,11; 3:2,8,13; 7:2,14; 17:6; Num 18:17; 2 Kings 16:13,15; Ezek 43:18). The grapes are THROWN into the winepress as sacrificial blood is thrown against the altar. Greek uses ἔβαλεν ('cast/threw' — generic). A back-translator from Greek would use הִשְׁלִיךְ (hishlich — 'threw', H7993), the common word for throwing. No translator would choose the priestly sacrificial zaraq unless thinking in priestly-sacrificial categories.

Uses יֶקֶב (yeqev, H3342 — 'winepress') — the lower collection vat where grape juice flows (Num 18:27; Deut 15:14; Isa 5:2; Joel 2:24, 4:13). Greek uses ληνός ('winepress'). Both mean winepress, but the Hebrew yeqev is technically the lower basin, distinct from the upper treading platform (גַּת, gat).

Uses מֶמְשָׁלָה (memshalah, H4474 — 'authority/dominion') for the angel's power over fire. This is the creation-dominion word from Genesis 1:16 (the luminaries given memshalah over day and night). Greek ἐξουσίαν ('authority') is generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew combines Greek verses 18-19 into a single verse (the [19] marker shows where the Greek verse break falls).
Hebrew: 'its fruits are ripened' (נתבשל — from בשל, 'cooked/ripened'). Greek: 'her grapes are fully ripe' (ἤκμασαν). The Hebrew uses a cooking metaphor for ripeness.

Hebrew: 'he cast (zaraq — priestly verb) into the great winepress of the wrath of YHWH.' Greek: 'he cast (ἔβαλεν — generic) into the great winepress of the wrath of God.' Priestly verb + Tetragrammaton vs. generic verb + θεός.
translation_notes: נִתְבַּשֵּׁל (nitbashshel — hitpael of בשל H1310 — 'cooked/ripened') in brackets [נתבשל], suggesting editorial uncertainty about the reading. The verb literally means 'cooked themselves' — a vivid metaphor for fruit ripening in the sun.
'Cast' for zaraq — this priestly blood-sprinkling verb transforms the winepress scene into a cosmic sacrifice. The grapes-as-blood are ritually thrown, not merely tossed.
The Hebrew verse combines Greek 14:18-19, reflecting a different verse division in the Hebrew tradition.
textual_notes: Joel 4:13 (Hebrew) — שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר בֹּאוּ רְדוּ כִּי מָלְאָה גַּת הֵשִׁיקוּ הַיְקָבִים ('Send the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the winepress is full, the vats overflow'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes Joel's vocabulary: מגל (sickle), בשל (ripe), and יקב (winepress-vat).
