Isaiah 63:3 — 'I have trodden the winepress (פּוּרָה) alone... their lifeblood was sprinkled (וְיֵז) on my garments.' The cosmic winepress of divine judgment has deep prophetic roots.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קִבְרוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה (qivrot ha-sadeh — 'field-plots') as the unit of measurement — the SAME uniquely Hebrew measurement that appears in Revelation 21:16 (12,000 field-plots). Greek uses σταδίων ('stadia' — a Greek athletic measurement unit). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as סְטַדְיוֹן or use a standard Hebrew measure like אַמָּה (ammah — 'cubit') or מִיל (mil — 'mile'). No translator from Greek would independently construct a Hebrew land-measurement idiom. The consistent use of qivrot ha-sadeh across BOTH chapters (14 and 21) confirms it is a genuine Hebrew measurement system, not a one-time anomaly.

Uses רֶסֶן (resen, H7448 — 'bridle/halter') — used in Isaiah 30:28 and Psalm 32:9. Greek χαλινός also means 'bridle,' but the Hebrew word carries the prophetic association from Isaiah 30:28 where YHWH puts a resen on the nations to lead them astray.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a thousand and six hundred field-plots' (קברות השדה). Greek: 'a thousand and six hundred stadia' (σταδίων). The numbers match but the measurement units are entirely different — a uniquely Hebrew agrarian unit vs. a Greek athletic unit.
translation_notes: קִבְרוֹת (qivrot) — possibly related to קֶבֶר (qever — 'grave/burial-plot') used as a standardized land-area unit, comparable to how 'acre' originally meant 'the amount of land one yoke of oxen could plow in a day.' The meaning is 'measured field sections.' Compare Kibroth-hattaavah (Num 11:34).
'Field-plots' preserves the agricultural/land-measurement sense without imposing the Greek athletic 'stadia.'
textual_notes: This verse maps to Greek 14:20. The Hebrew chapter has 19 verses where the Greek has 20, because Hebrew verse 18 combines Greek verses 18-19.
The measurement '1,600 field-plots' — the number 1,600 = 4 × 4 × 100, potentially symbolic of completeness (4 = earth's compass points, 100 = fullness).

15.summary: Revelation 15 in Hebrew is structured as a new Exodus. The chapter opens with 'signs and wonders' (ניסים ונפלאות — the Exodus plague formula) and closes with a near-verbatim quotation of Exodus 40:34-35 (the glory of YHWH filling the Tabernacle). Between these Exodus bookends, the overcomers stand beside the sea with lyres — mirroring Israel at the Red Sea — and sing the Song of Moses using the specific feminine form שירה that designates the Exodus triumph genre. The Hebrew uses Torah-specific vocabulary throughout: נגעים (Levitical plagues, not generic Greek πληγαί), פסל (the Decalogue's graven-image term), קערות (Numbers 7 altar-dedication bowls), כנורות (Davidic lyres), חרון אף (the OT compound for YHWH's fierce anger), מלך המלכים (King of kings), ארון הברית (Ark of the Covenant), and משכן (the Sinai Tabernacle). The most striking one-way markers are: (1) ארון הברית ('Ark of the Covenant') where Greek has 'temple of the tabernacle of testimony' — entirely different referents; (2) the Exodus 40:34 verbatim quotation in verse 8, invisible in the Greek; (3) מלך המלכים ('King of kings') against ALL Greek manuscript witnesses which read 'King of saints/nations/ages'; (4) the שירה/שיר distinction for Moses' Exodus song vs. the Lamb's song; (5) the pesel (Decalogue graven-image term) for the beast's image; and (6) the two-sacred-space distinction (בית תפילה vs. משכן) where Greek has one word (ναός) for both. The chapter presents the seven last plagues as the antitype of the Numbers 7 Tabernacle dedication: golden bowls (קערות) once brought to consecrate the altar are now filled with YHWH's חרון אף and poured out to consummate his covenant judgment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the OT pair נִסִּים וְנִפְלָאוֹת ('signs and wonders') — echoing the Exodus plague formula (Deut 6:22, 26:8, 34:11, Jer 32:20-21, Neh 9:10). Greek has singular σημεῖον μέγα καὶ θαυμαστόν ('a sign, great and marvelous'). The Hebrew naturally reaches for the classic two-word pair; the Greek has a single sign with two adjectives. A back-translator from Greek would write אוֹת גְּדוֹלָה וְנִפְלָאָה (singular 'sign'), not the plural pair ניסים ונפלאות.

Uses חֲרוֹן אַף ('burning anger,' H2740 + H639) — the specific OT compound phrase for YHWH's fierce wrath, appearing over 40 times in the Tanakh (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Ps 85:3, Isa 13:9, 13:13, Jer 4:8, 12:13, 25:37, 30:24, Lam 1:12, Nah 1:6, Zeph 2:2). Greek uses the single generic word θυμός ('wrath/fury'). A back-translator from Greek θυμός would use חֵמָה (chemah) or זַעַם (za'am), not the specific two-word compound חרון אף. The compound carries physical imagery: חרון is 'burning heat' and אף is literally 'nostril' — the flushed face of fury.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has plural נִסִּים וְנִפְלָאוֹת ('signs and wonders'). Greek has singular σημεῖον ('one sign').
Greek adds ἄλλο ('another') — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: חרון אף מיהוה ('burning anger from YHWH'). Greek: θυμὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ('wrath of God'). Different divine name and different wrath expression.
translation_notes: 'Signs and wonders' for nisim v'nifla'ot — preserving the classic Exodus pair. The word נס (nes, H5251) in the OT means 'signal/banner/sign'; the 'miracle' sense developed in post-biblical Hebrew, but the pairing with נפלאות anchors it in the Exodus tradition.
'Burning anger' for charon af — a two-word phrase that cannot be reduced to a single English word. The compound is so distinctively Hebraic that its presence alone argues against back-translation.
The consonantal כלא is read as כָּלָה (kalah, H3615 — 'was completed/finished'). The aleph in the source pointing may reflect Aramaic orthographic influence.
textual_notes: The 'signs and wonders' formula (אותות ומופתים / ניסים ונפלאות) is the signature phrase of the Exodus plagues (Deut 6:22, 26:8, 34:11). The seven last plagues of Revelation are presented as a new Exodus — YHWH's final deliverance.
The square brackets [ ] in the source text between השבעה and נגעים indicate an editorial lacuna — a word may be missing from the source manuscript.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צְלוֹחִית (tselochit — 'flask/vial') — a concrete Hebrew vessel word — where Greek has ὑαλίνην (hualinen — 'of glass,' a material adjective). A back-translator from Greek 'glass' would use זְכוּכִית (zechuchit — 'glass'), not צלוחית (flask). The Hebrew sees a sea that resembles a translucent vessel; the Greek sees a sea made of glass as a material. Same distinctive word as in Rev 21:21.

Uses פֶסֶל (pesel — 'graven image,' H6459) — the EXACT word from the Second Commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְּךָ פֶסֶל (Ex 20:4, Deut 5:8 — 'You shall not make for yourself a graven image'). Greek uses εἰκών (eikon — 'image'), a neutral term. A back-translator from εἰκών would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image') or תְּמוּנָה (temunah — 'likeness'), NOT the Decalogue's specific idolatry term פסל. The Hebrew author condemns the beast's image with the Torah's own vocabulary for prohibited idol-making.

Uses כִּנּוֹרוֹת (kinnorot — 'lyres,' H3658) — David's instrument (1 Sam 16:23, 2 Sam 6:5, Ps 33:2, 137:2, 150:3), THE instrument of Israelite worship. Greek κιθάρα is the Greek lyre. More significantly, the Hebrew says כִּנּוֹרוֹת יהוה ('lyres of YHWH') — instruments belonging to YHWH, echoing 2 Chr 7:6 (כְּלֵי שִׁיר יהוה — 'instruments of song of YHWH') and 1 Chr 16:42. A back-translator from κιθάρας τοῦ θεοῦ ('harps of God') would not independently produce the Davidic/Levitical term kinnor paired with the tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Greek adds καὶ ἐκ τοῦ χαράγματος αὐτοῦ ἐκ τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ ('and from his mark, from the number of his name') — two additional elements absent from the more concise Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'its graven-image' (פסל — Decalogue term). Greek: 'his image' (εἰκών — neutral). Different vocabulary with vastly different theological loading.
Hebrew: 'lyres of YHWH.' Greek: 'harps of God' (κιθάρας τοῦ θεοῦ). Different instrument name and different divine name.
translation_notes: 'Flask' for tselochit — a concrete vessel word, not a material description. The sea resembles a translucent vessel, not a sea made of glass as substance.
'Graven-image' for pesel — preserving the Decalogue connection. This is the specific word Moses commanded Israel to smash (Deut 7:5, 12:3).
The square brackets [ ] in the source text before ים suggest an editorial lacuna — a modifier may be missing.
אֵצֶל (etsel, H681 — 'beside/next to') — the same intimate proximity word from Rev 21:3. Expresses physical nearness, not the generic 'upon' (ἐπί) of the Greek.
textual_notes: The overcomers standing beside the sea with lyres echoes Israel standing at the Red Sea after the Exodus (Ex 14:30-15:1). Miriam took a tambourine (Ex 15:20); here they take lyres. The sea of flask mixed with fire is the antitype of the Red Sea.
The phrase 'lyres of YHWH' echoes the Levitical worship context: 2 Chr 7:6, 1 Chr 16:42. The overcomers worship with YHWH's own dedicated instruments.

one_way_hebrew: Uses TWO DIFFERENT Hebrew words for 'song': שִׁירָה (shirah — feminine) for Moses and שִׁיר (shir — masculine) for the Lamb. The feminine שירה is the specific term used for the Song of the Sea — Deuteronomy 31:19,22,30 and 32:44 call it הַשִּׁירָה הַזֹּאת ('this song,' feminine). Greek uses the same word ᾠδή for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word both times, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author deliberately connects Moses' song to the Exodus triumph at the Red Sea through the feminine form.

CRITICAL: Hebrew has מֶלֶךְ הַמְּלָכִים ('King of kings') — a native Hebrew/Aramaic royal title (Dan 2:37, Ezra 7:12). Greek TR has ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν ἁγίων ('King of saints'); other manuscripts read τῶν ἐθνῶν ('of nations') or τῶν αἰώνων ('of ages'). NO Greek manuscript reads τῶν βασιλέων ('of kings') in this verse. A back-translator from ANY Greek variant would not produce מלך המלכים. The Hebrew title independently matches Rev 17:14 and 19:16 where even the Greek has βασιλεὺς βασιλέων. The Hebrew preserves the consistent title throughout; the Greek fractures it into different readings at different points.

Uses מְזַמְּרִים (mezamrim — 'making music,' from zamar H2167) — a Psalms verb specifically meaning 'to sing praises with instruments' (Ps 21:13, 57:7, 98:5, 105:2, 108:1, 147:7, 149:3). Greek ᾄδουσιν (adousin) is generic 'singing.' The Hebrew verb implies instrumental accompaniment — consistent with the kinnorot (lyres) in the previous verse. The Greek loses the connection between instrument and song.

Uses יהוה אֱלֹהֵי הַצְּבָאוֹת ('YHWH Elohei of the Hosts') — the specific OT military-divine name (1 Sam 1:3, 4:4, 17:45, Isa 1:24, 5:16, 6:3, Jer 2:19, Amos 4:13). Greek has Κύριε ὁ θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי or similar — not the specific compound name YHWH Tsevaot which carries the military sense of YHWH commanding heavenly armies.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: מלך המלכים ('King of kings'). Greek TR: 'King of saints' (τῶν ἁγίων). Other Greek witnesses: 'King of nations' (τῶν ἐθνῶν) or 'King of ages' (τῶν αἰώνων). None match the Hebrew.
Greek adds μεγάλα καὶ θαυμαστά ('great AND marvelous'). Hebrew has only גדולה ('great') without 'marvelous.'
Greek adds τοῦ δούλου τοῦ θεοῦ ('the servant of God') after Moses — absent from the Hebrew, which simply says 'of Moshe.'
translation_notes: 'Making music' for mezamrim — capturing the instrumental-plus-vocal nature of zamar, distinct from generic singing. The overcomers play and sing simultaneously.
'Song' translates both shirah and shir in English, but the Hebrew distinction is theologically loaded: shirah (fem.) is the Exodus triumph genre; shir (masc.) is the general song form.
The song shifts from third to second person: 'works of YHWH' then 'your ways' — a typical Psalmic address pattern (enallage), where YHWH is both described and directly addressed.
textual_notes: The Song of Moses (שירת משה) refers to Exodus 15:1-18, the triumph at the Red Sea. By pairing it with the Lamb's song, the Hebrew author presents the final eschatological victory as a new Exodus.

Psalm 111:2 — גְּדֹלִים מַעֲשֵׂי יהוה ('great are the works of YHWH'). Psalm 86:8-10 — 'All nations shall come and worship before you... you are great and do wondrous things.' The song's content is woven from Psalms.
Psalm 145:17 — צַדִּיק יהוה בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו ('Righteous is YHWH in all his ways'). The phrase 'righteous and true are your ways' echoes this Psalm directly.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׁבַח (shebach — 'praise,' from shabach H7623) — a native Hebrew praise verb found in the Psalms (63:4, 117:1, 145:4, 147:12) and Ecclesiastes (4:2, 8:15). Greek has δοξάσει ('glorify'). A back-translator from δοξάζω would use כִּבֵּד (kived — 'glorify/honor') or פֵּאֵר (pe'er — 'glorify'), not the distinctively Hebrew שבח.

Uses נִתְגַּלָּה (nitgalah — 'have been revealed/uncovered,' from galah H1540) — a reflexive form meaning 'became uncovered/disclosed.' The root גלה carries uniquely Hebrew connotations: it is the same root as גָּלוּת (galut — 'exile') and means to 'strip bare/uncover/exile.' Greek has ἐφανερώθησαν ('were made manifest'). A back-translator would use נוֹדְעוּ (nod'u — 'became known'), not galah with its distinctive Hebrew exile/uncovering semantic range.

Echoes Psalm 86:9 nearly verbatim: כָּל גּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתָ יָבוֹאוּ וְיִשְׁתַּחֲווּ לְפָנֶיךָ ('all nations shall come and bow down before you'). The Hebrew preserves the Psalmist's exact construction יָבוֹאוּ וְיִשְׁתַּחֲוֻ לְפָנֶיךָ. Greek has ἥξουσιν καὶ προσκυνήσουσιν ἐνώπιόν σου — a translation, not the source. A back-translator from Greek would not independently reconstruct the Psalm's exact phrasing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'before you' (לְפָנֶיךָ — spatial, 'before your face'). Greek: σε (accusative 'you' — direct object). Different grammatical constructions reflecting different orientations — Hebrew spatial vs. Greek relational.
Hebrew: עַמִּים ('peoples'). Greek: ἔθνη ('nations/gentiles'). Different nuance — amim is more neutral; ethne carries the gentile/pagan connotation.
translation_notes: 'Praise' for shebach — a native Hebrew praise word distinct from 'glorify.' The Hebrew concept of shebach is specifically vocal declaration of praise.
'Revealed' for nitgalah preserves the galah root's primary sense of uncovering what was hidden — YHWH's judgments were concealed and are now laid bare.
textual_notes: Echoes Jeremiah 10:7 — מִי לֹא יִרָאֲךָ מֶלֶךְ הַגּוֹיִם ('Who would not fear you, O King of the nations?'). The Hebrew opening ומי לא יראה לפניך naturally draws on Jeremiah.

Echoes Psalm 86:9-10 — 'All nations shall come and bow down before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name. For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are Elohim.' The Hebrew text weaves together Jeremiah and Psalms — OT intertextuality natural to a Hebrew author.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית ('the Ark of the Covenant,' H727 + H1285) — the most sacred object in the Tabernacle, the gold-covered chest containing the tablets of the Torah (Deut 10:8, 31:9,25-26, Josh 3:3,6, 1 Sam 4:3-4, 1 Kings 8:1,6). Greek has ὁ ναὸς τῆς σκηνῆς τοῦ μαρτυρίου ('the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony'). These are COMPLETELY different things — the ARK (a sacred chest) vs. the TEMPLE of the TABERNACLE (a structure containing it). A back-translator from Greek would write הֵיכַל מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדוּת ('temple of the tabernacle of testimony'), NEVER ארון הברית. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire chapter.

Hebrew uses בְּרִית (berit — 'covenant,' H1285). Greek uses μαρτύριον ('testimony/witness'). The Ark has both associations in the OT: אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית (Ark of the Covenant, Num 10:33, Deut 10:8, Josh 3:3) and אֲרוֹן הָעֵדוּת (Ark of the Testimony, Ex 25:22, 26:33). The Hebrew author chose the COVENANT term, emphasizing YHWH's covenant obligations being enforced through the coming plagues; the Greek reflects the TESTIMONY term. A back-translator would follow the Greek 'testimony,' not independently choose the theologically distinct 'covenant.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Ark of the Covenant' (an object — a gold-covered chest). Greek: 'the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony' (a structure). Entirely different referent — the innermost sacred object vs. the outer sacred building.
Hebrew: בְּרִית ('covenant'). Greek: μαρτύριον ('testimony/witness'). Different theological framing of the Ark's significance.
Greek adds ἰδού ('behold!') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Ark of the Covenant' is the standard English rendering of ארון הברית. The Ark contained the two tablets of the Torah, Aaron's rod that budded, and the jar of manna (Heb 9:4). Its opening signals the enforcement of the covenant through judgment.
textual_notes: The Ark of the Covenant disappeared when Babylon destroyed the First Temple (586 BCE). Jewish tradition holds Jeremiah hid it (2 Macc 2:4-8). The Hebrew Revelation envisions the Ark in its heavenly archetype — now opened, the covenant terms are enforced through the seven plagues.
The seven messengers emerge from the opened Ark (v.6), not from a temple. The plagues originate from the covenant itself — its violation demands its enforcement.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: girdle 'upon their loins' (עַל מָתְנֵיהֶם, H4975). Greek: 'about their chests' (περὶ τὰ στήθη). Different body location. The Hebrew priestly girdle was worn at the waist/loins — matching the priestly garments (Ex 28:4, 29:9, Lev 8:7, 16:4 — the אַבְנֵט worn at the waist). A back-translator from Greek 'chests' would write עַל חֲזֵיהֶם ('upon their chests'), not על מתניהם ('upon their loins'). The Hebrew naturally places the girdle where priestly tradition requires it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'went out to the outside' (from the Ark, v.5). Greek: 'went out from the temple' (ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ). Connected to the v.5 difference — the Hebrew messengers emerge from the Ark of the Covenant; the Greek messengers emerge from a temple.

Hebrew: 'white garments' (מלבושי לבנים — color description). Greek: λίνον καθαρὸν λαμπρόν ('pure bright linen' — material description). Hebrew describes what the garments looked like; Greek describes what they were made of.
Hebrew: girdle 'upon their loins.' Greek: girdle 'about their chests.' Different body placement.
translation_notes: The consonantal text for לבנים reads as לְבָנִים (levanim — 'white,' from lavan H3836). The source vowel pointing (לְבֵינִים) appears irregular and may reflect scribal confusion with לְבֵנִים ('bricks'); the consonantal reading 'white' is clearly correct in context.

'Girdle' for chagor (H2290) — a belt or sash used in both priestly and military contexts (1 Sam 18:4, 2 Sam 20:8). The golden girdle on the loins presents the messengers as priestly figures executing covenant judgment.
textual_notes: The imagery of messengers emerging from the Ark of the Covenant carrying plagues echoes the Ark's fearsome power in the OT: the Ark brought plagues upon the Philistines (1 Sam 5:6-12), struck down Uzzah for unauthorized contact (2 Sam 6:7), and preceded Israel's armies into battle (Num 10:33-35).
White garments with golden girdles are priestly attire — the messengers are presented as priests of the heavenly Tabernacle executing YHWH's covenant judgment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קְעָרוֹת (ke'arot — 'bowls/dishes,' H7086) — the specific Tabernacle dedication bowls from Numbers 7. In Numbers 7:13,19,25,31,37,43,49,55,61,67,73,79,84,85, every tribal leader brought a קַעֲרַת כֶּסֶף ('silver bowl') for the altar dedication — twelve bowls to consecrate the altar. Greek uses φιάλας (phialas — generic 'vials'). A back-translator could use any bowl word; the Hebrew author chose the specific Numbers 7 altar-dedication vessels. The wrath-bowls invert the dedication pattern: what once consecrated the altar now pours out judgment.

Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting and unto everlasting') — the classic OT doxology formula, a direct quote from Psalm 90:2 (מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל — 'from everlasting to everlasting you are God'), and the closing formula of Ps 106:48 and 1 Chr 16:36. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). These are fundamentally different temporal expressions — the Hebrew is a Psalm quotation; the Greek is the standard Greek liturgical formula. A back-translator from Greek would write לעולמי עולמים, not the Psalm 90:2 phrase.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חרון יהוה ('burning anger of YHWH'). Greek: θυμοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ('wrath of God'). Same pattern as v.1 — the specific OT compound phrase vs. generic Greek wrath.
Hebrew: מעולם ועד עולם ('from everlasting and unto everlasting' — Psalm 90:2). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). Different eternal formulas.
translation_notes: 'Bowls' for ke'arot — broad offering dishes used in the Tabernacle service, not narrow vials. The connection to Numbers 7 is essential: these are altar-dedication vessels repurposed for wrath.
'From everlasting and unto everlasting' preserves the Psalm 90:2 echo — YHWH's eternality expressed in the Psalter's own language.
textual_notes: Numbers 7 records twelve tribal leaders bringing silver ke'arot (bowls) to dedicate the Tabernacle altar. The seven golden ke'arot of wrath in this verse invert and intensify the dedication pattern: silver becomes gold, twelve becomes seven (the number of completion), and what was offered for consecration is now poured out for consummation.

Psalm 90:2 — 'Before the mountains were born, or you brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.' The Hebrew formula anchors YHWH's judgment in his eternal nature.

one_way_hebrew: NEAR-VERBATIM QUOTE from Exodus 40:34-35: וּכְבוֹד יהוה מָלֵא אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְלֹא יָכֹל מֹשֶׁה לָבוֹא ('and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle, and Moses was not able to enter'). The Hebrew Revelation has וּכְבוֹד יהוה מָלֵא אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְשׁוּם אֶחָד יוּכַל לֵילֵךְ לְתוֹכָהּ ('and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle, and no one was able to walk into it'). The phrase כבוד יהוה מלא את המשכן is virtually identical to Exodus 40:34. The Greek merely says ἐγεμίσθη ὁ ναὸς καπνοῦ ('the temple was filled with smoke') — losing the entire Exodus quotation. A back-translator from Greek would NEVER independently reconstruct the Exodus 40:34 phrasing.

Uses TWO different terms for sacred space: בֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה ('house of prayer,' H8605) and הַמִּשְׁכָּן ('the tabernacle,' H4908). Greek uses ναός ('temple') as the single referent for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing one word ναός, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes: the prayer-house fills with smoke; the Tabernacle fills with YHWH's glory. Same two-term pattern as Rev 21:22 where the Hebrew distinguishes בית תפילה from בית המקדש while Greek uses one word ναός.

Uses מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan — 'tabernacle/dwelling-place,' H4908) — the specific word for the Tabernacle of Moses (Ex 25:9, 26:1ff), connecting this heavenly vision directly to the Sinai Tabernacle and its construction. Greek ναός is generic 'temple.' The mishkan is YHWH's portable dwelling among his people; the naos is any temple.
greek_deviations: Hebrew distinguishes two sacred spaces: בית התפילה ('house of prayer') filled with smoke, and המשכן ('the tabernacle') filled with YHWH's glory. Greek uses ναός ('temple') as a single referent.

Hebrew: 'the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle' (Exodus 40:34 quote). Greek: 'the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power' (ἐκ τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ). Greek adds 'and from his power' — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: כְבוֹד יהוה ('glory of YHWH'). Greek: δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ ('glory of God'). Different divine name.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' echoes Isaiah 56:7 — 'my house shall be called a house of prayer (בֵּית תְפִלָּה) for all peoples' — which Yeshua quotes in Matt 21:13 / Mark 11:17.
'Tabernacle' for mishkan — the Sinai-specific term, connecting the heavenly scene to the wilderness Tabernacle and its dedication.
'Walk' for leilech — more specific than the Greek εἰσελθεῖν ('enter'). The Hebrew implies physically traversing sacred space.
textual_notes: Exodus 40:34-35 (exact source): וַיְכַס הֶעָנָן אֶת אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד וּכְבוֹד יהוה מָלֵא אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְלֹא יָכֹל מֹשֶׁה לָבוֹא אֶל אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד ('the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle, and Moses was not able to enter'). The Hebrew Revelation replaces 'Moses' with 'no one' — expanding the restriction from one person to all humanity.

1 Kings 8:10-11 records the same pattern at Solomon's Temple dedication: the cloud filled the house, and the priests could not stand to minister because the glory of YHWH filled the house. Both Tabernacle and Temple dedications are echoed — the pattern of glory-filling-so-that-none-can-enter is a signature of YHWH's covenant presence.

The chapter thus ends where it began: with the Tabernacle/Exodus framework. The smoke in the house of prayer and the glory in the tabernacle form a deliberate doublet — judgment (smoke) and presence (glory) simultaneously fill the heavenly sanctuary.

16.summary:
Revelation 16 in Hebrew is structured as a new Exodus plague cycle, with the bowls systematically deploying Torah plague vocabulary: שחין פרח (boils breaking out — plague 6, Ex 9:9), דם (blood — plague 1, Ex 7:20), חשך (darkness — plague 9, Ex 10:21), צפרדעים (frogs — plague 2, Ex 7:27), ברד (hail — plague 7, Ex 9:18). The Greek text uses generic terms (sore, blood, darkness, spirits, hail) that lack these specific Exodus connections.

The chapter contains at least 12 clear one-way translation markers: (1) שחין פרח — the exact Exodus plague phrase (v2), (2) פסל — the Decalogue 'graven image' word (v2), (3) המתפללים — the prayer-verb for idol worship echoing בית התפלה (v2), (4) בארות — 'wells' vs Greek 'rivers and springs' (v4), (5) the ההיה והוה formula playing on the divine name YHWH (v5), (6) Psalm 79:3 verbatim quotation 'poured out blood like water' (v6), (7) שרצים — 'creeping things' vs Greek 'spirits' (v12), (8) תנין — primordial serpent vs Greek 'dragon' (v12), (9) מסלה — Isaiah's prophetic highway (v11), (10) חרון אפו — the specific OT anger compound (v18), (11) הרים וגבעות — the prophetic mountains-and-hills merism vs Greek 'islands and mountains' (v19), (12) תשובה — return-to-God repentance vs Greek mind-change (v9).

Notably, Greek 16:11 is entirely absent from the Hebrew text, which has only 20 verses to the Greek's 21. The Hebrew moves directly from the fifth bowl (darkness, v10) to the sixth bowl (Euphrates, v11). Greek 16:11 repeats the blasphemy-and-non-repentance formula already present in Hebrew v9 — the Hebrew author apparently saw this repetition as unnecessary.

The Hebrew also consistently uses YHWH (יהוה) where Greek has 'God' (Θεός), אלהי הצבאות where Greek has 'God Almighty,' and השטן ('the Adversary') where Greek has 'demons' — maintaining OT divine name theology throughout.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה (beit ha-tefillah — 'house of prayer', H8605). Greek has ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ ('from the temple'). This is the Isaiah 56:7 phrase — 'my house shall be called a house of prayer (בֵּית תְּפִלָּה) for all peoples' — which Yeshua quotes in Matt 21:13. A back-translator from Greek ναός would write הֵיכָל (heikal — 'temple') or מִקְדָּשׁ (mikdash — 'sanctuary'), not the Isaiah-specific 'house of prayer.' Same distinction appears in Rev 21:22.

Uses חֲרוֹן יַהְוֶה (charon YHWH — 'the burning-anger of YHWH', H2740). Greek has τοῦ θυμοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ ('the wrath of God'). The Hebrew חרון is the specific 'burning/fierce anger' of YHWH in the Torah (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26). A back-translator from Greek θυμός would use חֵמָה (chemah — 'wrath/fury'), not the distinctly OT compound חרון.

Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground', H127), not אֶרֶץ (erets). Greek has γῆν (ge — 'earth'). Same word choice seen in Rev 21:1. The author consistently uses the Genesis creation-soil word where Greek has the generic term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the house of prayer' (מבית התפלה). Greek: 'from the temple' (ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ). Different building designation.
Greek adds μεγάλης ('great/loud') to describe the voice — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' preserves the Isaiah 56:7 echo. This same term (beit ha-tefillah) reappears in Rev 21:22.
צָאקוּ appears to be a variant imperative form related to יצק (yatsaq, H3332 — to pour). The aleph insertion is characteristic of later Hebrew phonological development.
textual_notes: The seven bowls of burning-anger parallel the seven plagues of Egypt. The Hebrew author frames the entire sequence using Exodus plague vocabulary, beginning with the Torah's specific anger-term חרון.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שְׁחִין פֹּרֵחַ (shechin poreach — 'boils breaking out'). This is the EXACT phrase from Exodus 9:9-10, the sixth plague of Egypt: שְׁחִין פֹּרֵחַ אֲבַעְבֻּעֹת ('boils breaking out in sores'). Greek has ἕλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρόν ('a bad and evil sore'). A back-translator from the generic Greek 'sore' would NEVER reconstruct the specific Exodus plague phrase. The Hebrew author deliberately frames the first bowl as a repetition of the sixth Egyptian plague.

Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'graven image', H6459) — the specific word from the second commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל ('you shall not make for yourself a graven image', Ex 20:4, Deut 5:8). Greek has εἰκόνα ('image' — generic). A back-translator from Greek would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image'), not the Decalogue-specific pesel.

Uses הַמִּתְפַּלְּלִים (hammitpallelim — 'those praying to', hitpael of palal H6419) for idol worship. Greek has προσκυνοῦντας ('those bowing/worshipping'). The Hebrew uses the PRAYER verb — the same root as תְּפִילָּה (tefillah — prayer) in verse 1. The author creates a deliberate contrast: true prayer (tefillah) belongs in the house of prayer to YHWH; false prayer (hitpallel) goes to the graven image.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: שחין פרח ('boils breaking out' — Exodus plague language). Greek: ἕλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρόν ('a bad and evil sore'). The Hebrew carries the Exodus plague echo; the Greek is generic.
Hebrew: פסל ('graven image' — Decalogue term). Greek: εἰκόνα ('image' — generic term).
translation_notes: 'Boils breaking out' preserves the exact Exodus 9:9-10 phrase.
סִּימָן (siman — 'mark/sign') is a post-biblical Hebrew word. No standard Strong's number. Greek χάραγμα means 'stamp/brand' — a different concept than a sign or marker.
'Graven image' for pesel — the Decalogue word, not a generic 'image.'
textual_notes: Exodus 9:9-10: 'And it shall become fine dust in all the land of Egypt, and shall become boils breaking out (שְׁחִין פֹּרֵחַ) in sores on man and on beast.' The first bowl plague directly replicates the sixth Egyptian plague.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר בַּיָּם תָּמוּת ('and all that was in the sea died'). Greek: πᾶσα ψυχὴ ζῶσα ἀπέθανεν ('every living soul died'). Hebrew uses the general 'all that was' (כל אשר); Greek specifies 'every living soul' (ψυχὴ ζῶσα). The Hebrew echoes the flood narrative style where 'all' perishes without the Greek's added precision.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all that was in the sea died.' Greek: 'every living soul died, the things in the sea.' Greek adds ψυχὴ ζῶσα ('living soul') absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: The sea turning to blood echoes the first Egyptian plague (Ex 7:20-21) where the Nile became blood and all fish died. The Hebrew author extends the Nile plague to the entire sea.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּאֵרוֹת מַיִם (be'erot mayim — 'wells of water', H875). Greek has ποταμούς καὶ πηγὰς τῶν ὑδάτων ('rivers and springs of waters'). The Hebrew has only 'wells' — the specific word for dug wells (Gen 21:30, 26:15-22, Num 21:16-18). A back-translator from Greek, which lists both 'rivers and springs,' would use נהרות ומעינות ('rivers and springs'), NOT the single Hebrew word be'erot. The well (be'er) is a distinctly Patriarchal term — Isaac digs wells, Moses finds his wife at a well. The Hebrew reduction to wells alone points to authorial choice, not translation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'wells of water' (בארות מים — one term). Greek: 'rivers and springs of waters' (ποταμούς καὶ πηγάς — two terms). Hebrew is more concise and uses a different category.
translation_notes: 'Wells' for be'erot preserves the Patriarchal and Exodus resonance — water sources in the wilderness.
textual_notes: Exodus 7:19: 'Stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt — over their rivers, their canals, their pools, and all their reservoirs of water.' The first Egyptian plague struck all water sources. The Hebrew uses wells (be'erot) — perhaps the most vital water source in the land.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The formula הֶהָיָה וְהֹוֶה ('the Was and the Is') uses the root ה-ו-ה (havah, H1933) — the very root behind the divine name YHWH. The participial form הוה shares the consonants of the Tetragrammaton. A Hebrew reader immediately sees the wordplay: YHWH is named because He IS (hoveh) and WAS (hayah). Greek ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν ('the being and the was') cannot replicate this connection to the divine name. A back-translator from Greek would use הַהֹוֶה וְהַהָיָה (reversing the order to match Greek) and would NEVER recreate this pun on the name YHWH.
Hebrew: 'the messenger' (המלאך) — no qualifier. Greek: 'the angel of the waters' (τοῦ ἀγγέλου τῶν ὑδάτων). Greek adds 'of the waters' which is entirely absent from the Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the messenger' (no qualifier). Greek: 'the angel of the waters.' Significant addition in Greek.
Hebrew order: 'Was and Is' (past then present). Greek order: 'being and was' (present then past). Different sequence.
Hebrew: 'holy' (קדוש). Greek: ὅσιος ('holy/devout') — but also Greek TR commonly has 'ὁ ἐσόμενος' ('the one to come') in the fuller formula, here shortened.
translation_notes: 'The Was and the Is' preserves the Hebrew's deliberate use of being-verbs that echo the divine name YHWH (from root הוה — 'to be').

The Hebrew lacks 'and who is to come' which sometimes appears in the Greek formula (Rev 1:4,8, 4:8). Its absence here may be deliberate — judgment is already underway, so the coming is no longer future.
textual_notes: Exodus 3:14: אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה ('I will be what I will be'). The name YHWH itself derives from the root היה/הוה. The Hebrew author's formula plays directly on this etymology.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT OT QUOTATION: שָׁפְכוּ דְּמֵי... כַּמַּיִם ('they poured out blood... like water') is from Psalm 79:3: שָׁפְכוּ דָמָם כַּמַּיִם סְבִיבוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִָם ('they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem'). The Hebrew preserves this Psalm quotation with the root שפך (shafach, H8210) plus the simile כמים ('like water'). Greek simply has αἷμα... ἐξέχεαν ('they poured out blood') WITHOUT the 'like water' simile. A back-translator from the Greek, which lacks this simile, could never produce the Psalm 79 quotation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'poured out the blood... like water' (כמים — Psalm 79:3 quotation). Greek: 'poured out the blood' — no 'like water' simile.
Greek: ἄξιοί εἰσι ('they are worthy'). Hebrew: ראויים ('deserving'). Similar meaning but different words — ראויים is a post-biblical Hebrew term.
translation_notes: רְאוּיִם (re'uyim — 'deserving/worthy') is a post-biblical Hebrew adjective. No standard Strong's number.
'Poured out' for shafach (H8210) — the blood-spilling verb, used for murder (Gen 9:6, 37:22) and sacrifice.
textual_notes: Psalm 79:3 — 'They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them.' The Hebrew author applies this psalm of national lamentation to the end-time judgment — the nations who shed blood like water now drink blood.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַהֵיכָל (ha-heikal — 'the palace/temple', H1964) — the word for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:3,5,17) and for royal palaces. Greek has θυσιαστηρίου ('the altar'). Major divergence — Hebrew says the voice comes from the temple/palace; Greek says from the altar. A back-translator from Greek would write מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach — 'altar'), not heikal.

Uses אֱלֹהֵי הַצְּבָאוֹת (Elohei ha-Tsevaot — 'Elohim of Hosts', H6635) — the compound divine name appearing throughout the prophets (Isa 1:9, Jer 5:14, Amos 3:13). Greek has Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי or אֵל שַׁדַּי, NOT the specific prophetic name 'Elohim of Hosts.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from within the palace' (מתוך ההיכל). Greek: 'from the altar' (ἐκ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου). Different source location.
Greek adds ἀληθιναί ('true') to 'true and righteous are your judgments.' Hebrew has only 'your judgments are righteousness' — no 'true.'
translation_notes: 'Palace' for heikal reflects the dual meaning of the Hebrew word — both temple and royal palace. The heavenly heikal is both God's dwelling and his throne room.
textual_notes: Psalm 19:10 (ET 19:9): מִשְׁפְּטֵי יְהוָה אֱמֶת צָדְקוּ יַחְדָּו — 'The judgments of YHWH are truth, they are righteous altogether.' The messenger's declaration echoes this psalm.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לעשות חם ('to make heat') — the Hebrew verb עשה (asah, H6213 — 'to do/make') with חם (chom — 'heat'). Greek has καυματίσαι ('to scorch/burn'). The Hebrew is indirect — the sun was given permission 'to make heat'; the Greek is violent — 'to scorch men.' The Hebrew framing treats the sun as an instrument given divine permission, consistent with the OT pattern of natural forces acting under God's command (Ps 148:8).

Uses הָאָדָם (ha-adam — 'the man', H120) with the definite article, as in verse 2. Greek has τοὺς ἀνθρώπους (plural 'men'). The Hebrew consistently uses the collective singular ha-adam echoing the Genesis creation account.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἐν πυρί ('with fire') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew has only 'heat,' not 'fire.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return', H8666, from root שוב H7725). Greek has μετενόησαν (metanoeo — 'changed mind'). These are fundamentally different concepts: Hebrew repentance is about RETURNING to God (שוב — the quintessential prophetic call, Hos 14:2, Joel 2:12-13, Mal 3:7); Greek repentance is about CHANGING ONE'S MIND. A back-translator from Greek would use a mind/thought verb, not the return-to-God concept teshuvah.

Uses מְקַלְּלוּ (meqallelu — 'they cursed', H7043) — the OT curse verb (Gen 12:3, Lev 24:11,14). Greek has ἐβλασφήμησαν ('they blasphemed'). Hebrew 'curse' and Greek 'blaspheme' carry different weight — cursing God invokes the Levitical death penalty (Lev 24:15-16); blasphemy is a concept shaped more by Greek thought.

Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues', H5061) — the Levitical term for the Exodus plagues (Ex 11:1) and skin afflictions requiring priestly inspection (Lev 13-14). Greek has πληγάς (plegas — 'blows/strokes'). A back-translator from Greek would more likely use מַכּוֹת (makot — 'blows'), not the Levitical nega'im.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'they cursed YHWH' (direct, using curse verb + divine name). Greek: 'they blasphemed the NAME of God who has authority over these plagues' (expanded, using blasphemy verb + God's name + relative clause). Hebrew is more concise; Greek adds 'the name' and an entire relative clause absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'repentance' (תשובה — return). Greek: μετενόησαν ('changed mind'). Different concept.
translation_notes: 'Repentance' for teshuvah captures the Hebrew concept of returning to God, not merely changing one's mind.
'Plagues' for nega'im preserves the Exodus/Levitical connection.
textual_notes: Joel 2:12-13: 'Return to me (שובו אלי) with all your heart... rend your heart and not your garments, and return (שובו) to YHWH your Elohim.' The Hebrew concept of repentance as teshuvah (return) is central to the prophetic tradition.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נוֹשְׁכִים (noshchim — 'biting', from nashach H5391) — the specific verb for a SERPENT's bite (Gen 49:17, Num 21:6-9, Ecc 10:8,11, Amos 5:19). Greek has ἐμασῶντο ('gnawed/chewed'). The Hebrew serpent-bite verb creates an ironic image: the followers of the beast (serpent/dragon) are now themselves bitten. A back-translator from the Greek 'gnaw/chew' would use לעס (la'as — 'chew') or כסס, not the serpent-specific nashach.

Darkness plague: The fifth bowl brings darkness (חשך, H2821), echoing the ninth Egyptian plague (Ex 10:21-23): וַיְהִי חֹשֶׁךְ אֲפֵלָה ('and there was thick darkness'). The Hebrew author sequences the bowl plagues to mirror Exodus.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'and it darkened it' (והחשך אותו — the throne/realm is darkened). Greek: 'and his kingdom became darkened' (ἡ βασιλεία αὐτοῦ ἐσκοτωμένη). Greek specifies 'his kingdom'; Hebrew darkens 'it' (the throne area).
Hebrew: 'because of distress' (צער). Greek: 'because of the distress' and adds 'because of their sores' (ἐκ τῶν ἑλκῶν αὐτῶν). Greek references the sores from the first bowl; Hebrew does not.
translation_notes: צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/pain') is a post-biblical Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.

Greek 16:11 — 'And they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and sores, and did not repent of their works' — is ENTIRELY ABSENT from the Hebrew text. The Hebrew moves directly from the fifth bowl (v10) to the sixth bowl (v11). This missing verse is significant.
textual_notes: Exodus 10:21-23: The ninth plague of darkness. The Hebrew author places the darkness bowl fifth (not ninth) but uses the same root חשך, maintaining the Exodus plague vocabulary.

The absence of Greek 16:11 from the Hebrew text is noteworthy. The Hebrew has 20 verses for this chapter; the Greek has 21. Greek 16:11 repeats the blasphemy-and-no-repentance formula already present in Hebrew v9 — the Hebrew author may have seen this as redundant.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מְסִלָּה (mesillah — 'highway/raised road', H4546). Greek has ὁδός ('way/road'). The mesillah is the specific Isaiah highway: Isaiah 11:16 — 'And there shall be a highway (מסלה) for the remnant of his people from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.' Isaiah 62:10 — 'Build up, build up the highway (מסלה)!' A back-translator from Greek ὁδός would use דֶּרֶךְ (derekh — 'way/road'), not the Isaianic mesillah. The drying of the Euphrates with a mesillah for eastern kings directly echoes the Exodus crossing and Isaiah's prophesied highway.

Uses ויבש (vayyubash — 'and it dried up', from yavesh H3001). This is the Exodus verb — Joshua 2:10: 'YHWH dried up (הוֹבִישׁ) the waters of the Red Sea before you.' Joshua 4:23: 'YHWH your God dried up (הוֹבִישׁ) the Jordan.' The Euphrates drying is framed as a new Exodus crossing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a highway' (מסלה — Isaiah's specific term). Greek: ἑτοιμασθῇ ἡ ὁδός ('the way might be prepared'). Greek adds 'prepared' and uses a generic word for 'way.'
Greek: 'the great river Euphrates' (τὸν ποταμὸν τὸν μέγαν). Hebrew: 'the river Euphrates' (הנהר פרת) — lacking 'great.'
Hebrew: 'it dried up the river' (ויבש את הנהר). Greek: 'its water was dried up' (ἐξηράνθη τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτοῦ). Hebrew dries the river itself; Greek dries its water.
translation_notes: 'Highway' for mesillah preserves the Isaiah highway prophecy connection.
'From the rising of the sun' (ממזרח השמש) is the Hebrew idiom for 'from the east' — more vivid than the simple directional word.
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:15-16: 'And YHWH will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River (Euphrates) with his scorching wind, and will strike it into seven channels... And there shall be a highway (מסלה) for the remnant of his people.' The drying of the Euphrates for a highway is directly from Isaiah.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שְׁרָצִים (sheratzim — 'creeping/swarming things', H8318). Greek has πνεύματα τρία ἀκάθαρτα ('three unclean SPIRITS'). The Hebrew sheretz is the Torah's specific classification for unclean swarming creatures — Genesis 1:20-21 (creation), Leviticus 11:29-43 (dietary laws). A back-translator from Greek 'spirits' (πνεύματα) would write רוּחוֹת (ruchot — 'spirits'), NEVER the Levitical classification sheratzim. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire chapter: the Hebrew author categorizes these entities using Torah taxonomy, not Greek pneumatology.

Uses תַּנִּין (tannin — 'serpent/sea-creature', H8577) — the primordial creature from Genesis 1:21 (great sea creatures), Isaiah 27:1 (Leviathan the tannin), Isaiah 51:9 (Rahab the tannin), Ezekiel 29:3, 32:2 (Pharaoh as tannin). Greek uses δράκων ('dragon'). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as דרקון, not reach for the OT's primordial creature word tannin.

Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut — 'in the likeness of', H1823) — from the root דמות used in Genesis 1:26 (בִּדְמוּתֵנוּ — 'in our likeness'). This is the creation-theology 'likeness' word. Greek has simple ὡς ('as/like'). A back-translator would write כְּמוֹ (kemo — 'like'), not the theologically loaded kidmut.

Uses צְפַרְדְּעִים (tsefarde'im — 'frogs', H6854) — a word appearing in the OT only in the Exodus plague narrative (Ex 7:27-8:10, Ps 78:45, 105:30). This is exclusively Exodus vocabulary. The frog imagery combined with sheratzim creates a double Exodus plague reference.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: שרצים ('creeping things' — Torah creature classification). Greek: πνεύματα ('spirits'). Entirely different ontological category.
Hebrew: תנין ('serpent/sea-creature'). Greek: δράκων ('dragon'). Different mythological framework.
contradictions: The Hebrew and Greek present fundamentally different entities: the Hebrew has unclean swarming creatures (physical, Torah-classified beings) that RESEMBLE frogs; the Greek has unclean spirits that are LIKE frogs. The Hebrew operates in Levitical purity categories; the Greek in spiritual/pneumatic categories.
translation_notes: 'Creeping things' for sheratzim — the Levitical classification term, not 'spirits.'
'Serpent' for tannin — the primordial sea creature of Hebrew cosmology.
'In the likeness of' for kidmut — the Genesis creation-likeness word.

נביא שקר ('prophet of falsehood') is the standard Hebrew construction for a false prophet (Jer 14:14, 23:25-26, 27:10,14-16). Greek ψευδοπροφήτης is a compound word; Hebrew uses the two-word construct.
textual_notes: Exodus 7:27-8:10 (ET 8:1-14): The second Egyptian plague — frogs (צפרדעים) swarming over the land. The Hebrew author frames these demonic entities using Exodus plague vocabulary: they are creeping-things (sheratzim) in the likeness of frogs (tsefarde'im).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַיּוֹם יַהְוֶה הָאַדִּיר ('the day of YHWH the Mighty'). Greek has τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης τῆς μεγάλης τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ Παντοκράτορος ('that great day of God the Almighty'). The Hebrew uses the OT prophetic formula 'Day of YHWH' (יום יהוה — Joel 1:15, 2:1,11,31; Amos 5:18,20; Isa 13:6,9; Zeph 1:7,14; Mal 3:23) plus the title אַדִּיר (addir — 'mighty/majestic', H117 — Ps 8:2,10, 93:4, Isa 33:21). A back-translator from Greek would write 'the great day of God Almighty' — using גָּדוֹל (gadol — great) not אַדִּיר, and אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי not יהוה.

Uses הַשָּׂטָן (ha-Satan — 'THE Adversary', H7854) with the definite article — the specific figure from Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1-2, where the Satan is a prosecutorial figure in the divine court. Greek has δαιμονίων ('of demons'). Radically different: Hebrew attributes to the singular Adversary; Greek attributes to generic demons.

Uses אוֹתוֹת (otot — 'signs', H226) — the word for the signs of the Exodus (Ex 4:8-9,17,28,30, 7:3, 10:1-2). Greek has σημεῖα ('signs'). While similar in meaning, the Hebrew word carries the specific Exodus-signs resonance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spirits of the Adversary' (רוחות השטן). Greek: 'spirits of demons' (πνεύματα δαιμονίων). Different attribution.
Hebrew: 'the day of YHWH the Mighty.' Greek: 'that great day of God the Almighty.' Different divine title and different adjective.
Hebrew: 'wonders and signs' (ניסים ואותות — two terms). Greek: 'signs' (σημεῖα — one term). Hebrew has an additional category.
translation_notes: נִיסִּים (nissim — 'wonders/miracles') is a post-biblical Hebrew noun. No standard Strong's number.
'The Mighty' for addir preserves the specific Hebrew title — used of YHWH in Psalm 93:4 and Isaiah 33:21.
textual_notes: Joel 2:11,31 (ET 3:4): 'The great and terrible day of YHWH (יוֹם יְהוָה הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא).' The Hebrew author uses the established prophetic formula but substitutes אדיר for the more common גדול ונורא.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֶרְוָה (ervah — 'nakedness/shame', H6172) — the specific Levitical word for sexual nakedness, used 24 times in Leviticus 18 alone ('you shall not uncover the nakedness (ערות) of...'). Greek has ἀσχημοσύνη ('indecency/shame'). A back-translator from Greek would use בּוּשָׁה (bushah — 'shame') or חֶרְפָּה (cherpah — 'reproach'), not the highly specific Levitical ervah.

Uses קָדוֹשׁ (kadosh — 'holy/set-apart', H6918). Greek has μακάριος ('blessed/happy/fortunate'). Fundamentally different: Hebrew says these watchful ones are HOLY (consecrated, set apart for God); Greek says they are BLESSED (happy/fortunate). A back-translator from μακάριος would write אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei — 'happy/blessed'), not kadosh.

Uses יְגֻלֶּה (yegulleh — 'be exposed/uncovered', from galah H1540). This is the verb from Leviticus 18:6ff — 'to uncover nakedness' (לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה). Greek has βλέπωσι ('they see'). The Hebrew uses the Levitical technical term for exposing nakedness; Greek merely says 'they see.' A back-translator from 'see' would write יראו (yir'u), not the Levitical galah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy' (קדוש). Greek: μακάριος ('blessed'). Different attribute.
Hebrew: 'those who do not sleep' (שלא ישנים — negative framing). Greek: ὁ γρηγορῶν ('the one watching/staying awake' — positive framing).
Hebrew has both 'naked' (ערום) AND 'without garments' (בלי מלבושים). Greek has only γυμνός ('naked'). Hebrew is more elaborate.
translation_notes: 'Naked' (arom, H6174) and 'nakedness' (ervah, H6172) use different roots but create a paranomasia in Hebrew. The double emphasis — naked AND without garments — underscores the shame.
'Guard himself' (ושמור את עצמו) — the verb שמר (shamar) is the Torah's watchman word (Gen 2:15 — Adam commanded to 'keep/guard' the garden).
textual_notes: The thief imagery echoes 1 Thess 5:2,4 and Matt 24:43. But the nakedness/garments imagery connects to Genesis 3:7,10,21 — Adam and Eve's nakedness after sin and God's provision of garments. The watchful believer avoids the Edenic shame.

one_way_hebrew: The name הַרְמְגִדֹּן is transparent in Hebrew: הַר (har — 'mountain', H2022) + מְגִדֹּן (Megidon/Megiddo). In Hebrew, this is immediately understood as 'Mountain of Megiddo.' Greek Ἁρμαγεδδών is an opaque transliteration that requires explanation. The self-evident meaning in Hebrew versus the opaque Greek form suggests Hebrew priority — the name originates in the language where it has meaning.

Megiddo (מגדו/מגדון) is the site of decisive OT battles: Judges 5:19 (Deborah's victory), 2 Kings 23:29 (Josiah's death), 2 Chronicles 35:22. The word itself may derive from the root גדד (gadad — 'to cut/gather troops').
translation_notes: The phrase בלשון עברי ('in the tongue of Hebrew') is noteworthy — a Hebrew text explaining that a word is Hebrew. This may indicate the author writes for an audience that reads Hebrew but may also know Greek, or it may be a rhetorical device emphasizing the Hebraic nature of the name.
'Har-Megidon' transliterated rather than translated ('Mountain of Megiddo') to preserve it as a proper noun.
textual_notes: Judges 5:19: 'The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo (מגדו).' Megiddo is the archetypal battlefield of Israel's history.
Zechariah 12:11: 'On that day the mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the valley of Megiddon (מגדון).' The spelling מגדון matches the Hebrew Revelation form.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עָבַר (avar — 'has passed/crossed over', H5674). Greek has γέγονε ('it is done/it has become'). The Hebrew verb avar means to pass through, cross over — the same root as 'Hebrew' (עברי — 'one who crosses over') and the verb used for crossing the Jordan (Josh 3:14-17). This may carry connotations of an ordeal passing through, rather than a mere announcement of completion.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the throne' (מהכסא). Greek: 'from the temple of heaven, from the throne' (ἀπὸ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, ἀπὸ τοῦ θρόνου). Greek adds 'from the temple of heaven.'
Hebrew: 'a voice' (קול). Greek: 'a great voice' (φωνὴ μεγάλη). Greek adds 'great.'
Hebrew: 'this has passed' (זאת עבר). Greek: γέγονε ('it is done'). Different verb with different nuance.
translation_notes: אֲוִיר (avir — 'air') is a later Hebrew/Aramaic word without a standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רַעֲדוֹת (ra'adot — 'tremblings', from ra'ad H7461). Greek has σεισμός ('earthquake' — specifically). Hebrew רעד is a broader term encompassing trembling of the earth AND of people (Ex 15:15 — 'trembling seized the chiefs of Moab'; Ps 2:11 — 'serve YHWH with fear and rejoice with trembling'). A back-translator from the specific Greek σεισμός would use רַעַשׁ (ra'ash — 'earthquake'), not the more general ra'ad.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'that had never been from of old' (שלא היה מעולם — concise). Greek: 'such as had not been since men were on the earth, so great an earthquake' (oἷος οὐκ ἐγένετο ἀφ᾽ οὗ οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐγένοντο ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, τηλικοῦτος σεισμός, οὕτω μέγας — greatly expanded). Greek adds 'since men were on the earth' and 'so great.'
translation_notes: 'From of old' for me'olam (H5769) — the same word as 'eternity/age,' here meaning 'since time immemorial.'
textual_notes: Exodus 19:16,18 — Sinai theophany: 'There were thunders (קולות) and lightnings (ברקים)... and the whole mountain trembled (ויחרד) greatly.' The seventh bowl recapitulates the Sinai theophany with the same vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ (charon appo — 'the burning-anger of his wrath/nose'). This is a distinctly OT compound: חרון (charon, H2740 — 'fierce/burning anger') + אף (af, H639 — 'nose/anger'). It appears as a fixed phrase throughout the OT: Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:18, Josh 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Jer 25:37-38, 30:24, 49:37. Greek has τοῦ θυμοῦ τῆς ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ('of the wrath of his anger'). A back-translator from the two Greek anger-words would use חֵמָה (chemah — wrath) + כַּעַס/אַף (anger), NOT the specific OT compound חרון אפו.
Uses בָּבֶל (Bavel — 'Babel', H894) — the Hebrew name that carries the Genesis 11 etymology of 'confusion' (from root בלל — to confuse). Greek Βαβυλών is a transliteration that loses this wordplay.
Uses עַמִּים (amim — 'peoples', H5971). Greek has ἐθνῶν ('nations/gentiles'). As in Rev 21, Hebrew uses the more neutral 'peoples' while Greek uses the loaded term 'nations/gentiles.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ). Hebrew preserves the divine name.
translation_notes: 'Burning-anger of his wrath' for charon appo — preserving both Hebrew anger-words. חרון is the burning quality; אף is the nose/breath of fury.
'Babel' rather than 'Babylon' to preserve the Hebrew word and its Genesis 11 connection.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:15-16: 'Take this cup of the wine of fury (כוס היין החמה) from my hand, and make all the nations drink it.' The cup of wine imagery is deeply rooted in the prophets (Isa 51:17,22; Jer 25:15-28, 49:12, 51:7; Hab 2:16).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has הָרִים וּגְבָעוֹת ('mountains and hills'). Greek has πᾶσα νῆσος... καὶ ὄρη ('every island... and mountains'). The Hebrew pair 'mountains and hills' is an established OT merism — Isaiah 40:4 ('every mountain and hill shall be made low'), Isaiah 54:10, Ezekiel 6:3, 36:4,6, Hosea 10:8. A back-translator from the Greek 'islands and mountains' would write אִיִּים וְהָרִים ('islands and mountains'), NOT the standard prophetic pair הרים וגבעות. The Hebrew author uses the fixed prophetic formula; the Greek translator substituted 'islands' for 'hills.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'mountains and hills' (הרים וגבעות — OT merism). Greek: 'every island and mountains' (νῆσος... ὄρη). Entirely different pairing.
Hebrew: 'were not seen anymore' (ולא נראו עוד). Greek: 'were not found' (οὐχ εὑρέθησαν). Different verb — 'seen' vs. 'found.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:4: 'Every valley shall be raised up, every mountain and hill (כל הר וגבעה) shall be made low.' The mountains-and-hills pair is Isaiah's eschatological leveling imagery.
Nahum 1:5: 'The mountains quake before him and the hills (גבעות) melt.' Same prophetic pair in judgment context.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בָּרָד (barad — 'hail', H1259) — the seventh Egyptian plague word (Ex 9:18-26): 'YHWH rained hail (בָּרָד) upon the land of Egypt.' The Hebrew author completes the Exodus plague cycle: the bowls began with boils (שחין, plague 6) and end with hail (ברד, plague 7), framing the entire sequence as a new Exodus.

Uses מְחָרְפִים (mecharfim — 'reviling/reproaching', from charaf H2778). This is the verb Goliath used against Israel — 1 Sam 17:26,36: 'who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should defy/reproach (חרף) the armies of the living God?' Greek has ἐβλασφήμησαν ('they blasphemed'). Hebrew 'reproach/defy' and Greek 'blaspheme' carry different nuances: the Hebrew implies taunting or defying God's authority (as a warrior defies an army); the Greek implies sacrilegious speech.
Uses נֶגַע (nega — 'plague', H5061) — again the Levitical/Exodus term, consistent throughout the chapter.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὡς ταλαντιαία ('about a talent in weight') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew does not specify the weight of the hail.
Greek adds ὅτι μεγάλη ἐστὶν ἡ πληγὴ αὐτῆς σφόδρα ('for the plague of it was exceedingly great') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Reviled' for charaf captures the defiance/taunting nuance — not merely 'blasphemed.'
'Plague' for nega — completing the Levitical vocabulary used throughout the chapter.
textual_notes: Exodus 9:18,23-24: 'Behold, about this time tomorrow I will rain very heavy hail (בָּרָד כָּבֵד מְאֹד)... YHWH rained hail upon the land of Egypt.' The seventh bowl hail closes the new-Exodus plague cycle.
Joshua 10:11: 'YHWH threw large stones (אבנים גדלות) from heaven upon them... more died from the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.' Heavenly hail as divine warfare.

17.summary: Revelation 17 in Hebrew contains at least 12 clear one-way translation markers. The most striking are: (1) כמראה שושנים ('like the appearance of roses') for the beast's color — a Hebrew botanical simile where Greek has a simple color word; (2) the היה ולא הוה wordplay using the root of YHWH's name to describe the beast's non-existence; (3) Sheol (שאול) vs. Greek 'destruction' (ἀπώλεια) for the beast's destination — consistently in v8 and v11; (4) סוד (sod — 'divine council secret') vs. Greek μυστήριον; (5) the three-part wisdom formula שכל וחכמה ותבונה; (6) YHWH (twice) vs. Greek Θεός; (7) 'her riches' vs. Greek 'their kingdom' — an irreconcilable divergence; (8) the anti-priestly forehead inscription echoing Exodus 28:38; (9) טומאות (Levitical impurity) vs. Greek βδελύγματα (abominations); and (10) אנשי האדמה ('men of the ground' — Genesis creation language) vs. Greek 'dwellers of the earth.' The chapter also shows consistent use of OT vocabulary: mishpat, qe'arot, midbar, chirufim, machashavah, shemamah, koach/gevurah — all deeply rooted in the Hebrew Bible.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, H4941 — 'judgment') — the standard OT legal/judicial term (Ex 21:1, Deut 1:17, Isa 1:17, Mic 6:8). Greek uses κρίμα (krima — 'verdict/judgment'). While these can map, mishpat carries the full weight of the Torah's covenantal justice system. A back-translator could arrive at mishpat, but the word's Torah resonance is organic here.

Uses קְעָרוֹת (qe'arot, H7086 — 'bowls') — the same word used for the Tabernacle service bowls in Numbers 7:13,19,25 etc. Greek φιάλας ('vials/bowls') is generic. The Hebrew author reaches for the Tabernacle vessel vocabulary.
translation_notes: 'Harlot' for zonah (H2181) — the OT term used for Rahab (Josh 2:1), the harlot metaphor for Israel (Hos 1-3, Ezek 16, 23), and the 'strange woman' of Proverbs.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:13 — 'O you who dwell by many waters (מים רבים), rich in treasures, your end has come.' The harlot on many waters echoes Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמְּשַׁכֶּרֶת (hameshakkeret — 'she who intoxicates', feminine hiphil participle from shakar H7937). Greek ἐμεθύσθησαν ('were made drunk') is a passive verb. The Hebrew casts the harlot as the ACTIVE agent of intoxication — she is 'the intoxicator.' A back-translator from Greek's passive form would write נשתכרו ('they became drunk'), not give the woman an active agentive participle.

Hebrew says simply 'from her wine' (מיינה). Greek expands: 'from the wine of her fornication' (ἐκ τοῦ οἴνου τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς). The Hebrew is more concise. Also Greek adds 'those dwelling on the earth' (οἱ κατοικοῦντες τὴν γῆν) as the subject — absent from the Hebrew, which has only the vague 'those' (אילו).
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'of her fornication' to 'wine' — absent from Hebrew.
Greek identifies 'those dwelling on the earth' as the drunk ones. Hebrew has only 'those' (אילו).
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:7 — 'Babylon was a golden cup in YHWH's hand, making all the earth drunk (משכרת); the nations drank of her wine (מיינה), therefore the nations went mad.' The Hebrew Revelation uses the exact Jeremiah vocabulary: meshakkeret + miyyenah.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כְּמַרְאֵה שׁוֹשַׁנִּים (kemareh shoshannim — 'like the appearance of roses/lilies', H7799). Greek has κόκκινον (kokkinon — 'scarlet'). The Hebrew describes the color through a BOTANICAL SIMILE — the rose-red hue of the shoshannah flower. A back-translator from Greek's 'scarlet' would write שָׁנִי (shani — 'scarlet,' the standard color word) or אָדוֹם (adom — 'red'), NEVER a simile to flowers. The שׁוֹשַׁנָּה appears in Song of Songs 2:1-2 as a symbol of beauty; the beast mimics beauty. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.

Uses מִדְבָּר (midbar, H4057 — 'wilderness') — the loaded OT word for the place of Israel's testing, revelation, and encounter with God (Ex 3:1, 19:1-2, Num 14, Hos 2:14). Greek ἔρημον ('desert') is generic. The woman is found in the midbar — the place where Israel went astray after the golden calf.

Uses חֵירוּפִים (chirufim — 'reproaches/taunts', from charaf H2778). Greek βλασφημίας ('blasphemy') is a Greek religious concept. The Hebrew chirufim is the word for the taunting of enemies against YHWH (2 Ki 19:3, Isa 37:3, Neh 5:9). A back-translator would use גידופים (giddufim) for Greek blasphemy, not the OT taunt-word chirufim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'he brought me' (הביא אותי). Greek adds 'in the spirit' (ἐν πνεύματι) — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'like the appearance of roses' (botanical simile). Greek: 'scarlet' (κόκκινον, direct color). Entirely different mode of description.
translation_notes: 'Roses' for shoshannim — the Hebrew flower (possibly lily or lotus) known for its red color. The simile portrays the beast as beautiful but deceptive.
'Reproaches' for chirufim rather than 'blasphemies' — the Hebrew word means 'taunts/insults hurled at God,' not the Greek religious concept of blasphemy.
textual_notes: Song of Songs 2:1 — 'I am the rose of Sharon, the lily (shoshannah) of the valleys.' The beast is clothed in the beauty of the shoshannah — a parody of the bride.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses טֻמְאוֹת (tum'ot — 'impurities', H2932) — the Levitical ritual impurity concept (Lev 5:3, 7:20-21, 15:3, 22:3, Num 19:13). Greek has βδελυγμάτων ('abominations'). These are FUNDAMENTALLY different concepts: Hebrew tum'ah is ritual/ceremonial defilement requiring purification; Greek bdelygma is moral abomination. A back-translator from Greek would use תועבות (to'evot — 'abominations'), not the Levitical tum'ah. The cup holds priestly impurity, not merely moral corruption.

Uses אֲבָנִים טוֹבוֹת (avanim tovot — 'goodly stones') — the standard OT term for precious gems (Gen 2:12, 1 Ki 10:2, 10:10, 2 Chr 9:10). Greek: λίθῳ τιμίῳ ('precious stone'). The Hebrew preserves the OT gemstone idiom.
Again uses כְּמַרְאֵה שׁוֹשַׁנִּים ('like the appearance of roses') for the color, reinforcing this is a deliberate Hebrew idiom, not a one-off.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'red like the appearance of roses' (one color with simile). Greek: πορφυροῦν καὶ κόκκινον ('purple AND scarlet' — two colors). Different.
Hebrew: 'full of impurities' (concise). Greek: 'full of abominations, and the impurity of her fornication' (γέμον βδελυγμάτων, καὶ ἀκαθάρτητα τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς) — expanded.
translation_notes: 'Impurities' for tum'ot preserves the Levitical ritual concept — this is priestly defilement language, not generic moral language.
כּוֹס (kos, H3563 — 'cup') — the same word used for the cup of YHWH's wrath (Ps 75:8, Isa 51:17,22, Jer 25:15). The harlot's golden cup parodies YHWH's cup of judgment.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:7 — 'Babylon was a golden cup (כוס זהב) in YHWH's hand, making all the earth drunk.' The exact phrase 'cup of gold' (כוס של זהב) appears here, echoing Jeremiah.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סוֹד (sod, H5475 — 'secret/counsel/intimate council'). This is the specific OT word for the divine council (Jer 23:18 — 'who has stood in the sod of YHWH?', Amos 3:7 — 'YHWH does nothing without revealing his sod to his servants the prophets', Ps 25:14 — 'the sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'). Greek μυστήριον ('mystery') is a Greek religious/philosophical term. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as מוסטריון or use the later Hebrew רז (raz — 'mystery,' from Aramaic, Dan 2:18). The author uses the deeply Hebrew sod, rooting this in the prophetic council tradition.

Uses מִצְחָהּ (mitschah — 'her forehead', H4696) — the EXACT word for the High Priest's forehead where the golden plate engraved 'Holy to YHWH' (קדש ליהוה) was placed (Ex 28:38). The harlot bears an inscription on her forehead — an ANTI-PRIESTLY parody. Where the priest bore holiness, she bears the secret of Babylon. No back-translator would create this inversion.

Hebrew says הָעִיר הַגְּדוֹלָה בָּבֶל ('the great CITY Bavel'). Greek says Βαβυλὼν ἡ Μεγάλη ('Babylon the Great') without 'city.' The Hebrew adds 'the city' (העיר), explicitly identifying Babylon as an urban entity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'impurities of the earth' (טומאות). Greek: 'abominations of the earth' (βδελυγμάτων). Again, Levitical vs. moral vocabulary.
Hebrew: 'the great city Bavel.' Greek: 'Babylon the Great.' Hebrew adds 'city.'
translation_notes: 'Secret' for sod rather than 'mystery' — preserving the Hebrew prophetic-council concept rather than importing the Greek μυστήριον.
'Bavel' (not 'Babylon') — the Hebrew name בָּבֶל, which in Genesis 11:9 is connected to בָּלַל (balal — 'to confuse'), a Hebrew wordplay impossible in Greek.
textual_notes: The forehead inscription parodies Exodus 28:36-38 — 'You shall make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it... HOLY TO YHWH. It shall be on Aaron's forehead (מצח).' The harlot wears Babylon's name where the priest wore YHWH's holiness.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֹׁתָה (shotah — 'drinking', active participle from shatah H8354). Greek μεθύουσαν ('being drunk') is a STATE of drunkenness. Hebrew describes the ACT of drinking — she is caught in the act, actively consuming blood. A back-translator from Greek 'drunk' would use שיכורה (shikorah — 'drunk'), not the active participle 'drinking.'

Uses עֵדוּת (edut, H5715 — 'testimony/covenant witness') — the specific OT word for the covenant tablets (Ex 25:16 — 'put the edut in the ark', Ex 31:18 — 'the two tablets of edut'). Greek μαρτύρων ('martyrs/witnesses') shifts to the concept of human witnesses. The Hebrew frames the blood as being from the COVENANT TESTIMONY of Yeshua, not merely from individual witnesses. A back-translator from Greek's 'martyrs' would use עדים (edim — 'witnesses'), not the covenant term edut.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'drinking' (active). Greek: 'drunk' (state). Different imagery.
Hebrew: 'testimony' (edut — covenant concept). Greek: 'martyrs' (μαρτύρων — witnesses). Different concepts.
translation_notes: תְּמִיָּה (temiyyah — 'wonder/astonishment') is a later Hebrew form without a standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אֲנִי רוֹצֶה לֵאמֹר (ani rotseh leimor — 'I want to tell') — a VOLITIONAL expression. Greek ἐγώ σοι ἐρῶ ('I will tell you') is a simple future declaration. The Hebrew angel DESIRES to reveal; the Greek angel simply states what he will do. This personal, volitional tone is natural in Hebrew narrative.

Hebrew: שֶׁיֹּשְׁבָה עָלֶיהָ ('upon which she SITS'). Greek: τοῦ βαστάζοντος αὐτήν ('which CARRIES her'). Different verbs — Hebrew 'sit' (yashav) vs. Greek 'carry/bear' (βαστάζω). A back-translator from Greek would use נושא (noseh — 'carries'), not 'sits.' The Hebrew portrays the woman as enthroned; the Greek portrays the beast as bearing her.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she sits upon it.' Greek: 'it carries her.' Different relationship between woman and beast.
Hebrew: 'I want to tell you.' Greek: 'I will tell you.' Volitional vs. declarative.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הָיָה וְלֹא הֹוֶה (hayah velo hoveh — 'was and is not'). The word הֹוֶה (hoveh — 'existing/present') shares the root הוה with the divine name YHWH (יהוה). The beast's essence is defined by LACKING the root of God's name — it 'was' (hayah) but 'is not hoveh' — it lacks divine Being. This is a profound theological wordplay that exists ONLY in Hebrew. No Greek translator would construct this, and no back-translator could recover it from Greek οὐκ ἔστι ('is not').

CRITICAL: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom, H8415 — 'the deep') — the primordial deep from Genesis 1:2 (תְהוֹם — 'and darkness was upon the face of the deep'). Greek ἀβύσσου ('abyss') is related but tehom carries the specific Genesis creation weight. The beast rises from the pre-creation chaos.

CRITICAL: Uses שְׁאוֹל (Sheol, H7585 — the Hebrew underworld/realm of the dead). Greek has ἀπώλειαν ('destruction/perdition'). These are ENTIRELY different destinations: Sheol is a place of the dead (Gen 37:35, Num 16:30, Ps 16:10); ἀπώλεια is annihilation/ruin. A back-translator from Greek would write אֲבַדּוֹן (Avadon — 'destruction') or כִּלָּיוֹן (killayon — 'annihilation'), NOT Sheol.

Uses אַנְשֵׁי הָאֲדָמָה (anshei ha-adamah — 'men of the ground', H127). Greek: οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ('those dwelling upon the earth'). The Hebrew defines people by their ORIGIN — formed from adamah (Gen 2:7). Greek defines them by their LOCATION — dwelling on the earth. A back-translator from Greek would write יושבי הארץ ('dwellers of the earth'), not the Genesis-laden 'men of the ground.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall go to Sheol' (realm of dead). Greek: 'goes to destruction' (ἀπώλειαν). Different destination entirely.
Hebrew: 'men of the ground.' Greek: 'dwellers of the earth.'

Greek adds an entire clause absent from Hebrew: 'whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world' (ὧν οὐ γέγραπται τὰ ὀνόματα ἐπὶ τὸ βιβλίον τῆς ζωῆς ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου).
translation_notes: 'The deep' for tehom preserves the Genesis 1:2 connection — the beast emerges from primordial chaos.
'Men of the ground' for anshei ha-adamah — humanity defined by its earthly substance, not merely its location.
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — 'and darkness was upon the face of the deep (tehom).' The beast's origin is the primordial chaos that preceded creation.

The hoveh/YHWH wordplay: Exodus 3:14 reveals the divine name through the root היה/הוה — 'I am that which I am' (אהיה אשר אהיה). The beast's defining characteristic is that it is NOT hoveh — it lacks divine existence.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses a THREE-PART wisdom formula: שֵׂכֶל וְחָכְמָה וּתְבוּנָה (sekhel vechokhma utvunah — 'intelligence and wisdom and understanding'). This echoes the OT wisdom triad: Exodus 31:3 (Bezalel filled with חכמה ותבונה ודעת), Proverbs 2:6 ('YHWH gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding'), Daniel 1:17. Greek has ONLY ὁ νοῦς ὁ ἔχων σοφίαν ('the mind having wisdom') — ONE term. A back-translator from Greek would write שכל חכמה or דעת חכמה, not independently reconstruct the full three-part OT formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three wisdom terms (intelligence, wisdom, understanding). Greek: one term (wisdom). The Hebrew preserves the OT triad; the Greek collapses it.
translation_notes: Verses 9 and 10 are partially combined in the Hebrew manuscript, with [10] as a marker in the text. מְלָכִים appears in brackets, suggesting editorial restoration.
textual_notes: The wisdom triad sekhel/chokhmah/tevunah parallels Daniel 1:17,20 and 5:11-14 where Daniel's wisdom is described with multiple terms. The audience needs Daniel-like wisdom to decode the vision.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the second' (השני — ordinal). Greek: 'the other' (ὁ ἄλλος — indefinite). Different identifiers.
Hebrew: 'a short time' (זמן מועט). Greek: 'a little while' (ὀλίγον... μεῖναι — 'he must remain a little'). Greek adds 'remain' (μεῖναι) which is absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: עֲדַיִין (adayin — 'still/yet') is a later Hebrew form, common in Mishnaic Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: Again שְׁאוֹל (Sheol, H7585) vs. Greek ἀπώλειαν ('destruction/perdition'). Consistent with v8 — the Hebrew author consistently uses the Hebrew underworld concept where Greek uses annihilation language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'goes to Sheol.' Greek: 'goes to destruction' (εἰς ἀπώλειαν ὑπάγει). Same divergence as v8.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תִּמְשְׁלוּ (timshleu — 'they shall rule', from mashal H4910 — 'to rule/have dominion'). Greek: ἐξουσίαν... λαμβάνουσι ('receive authority'). The Hebrew says they RULE; the Greek says they RECEIVE AUTHORITY. Different concepts — active governance vs. delegated power. A back-translator from Greek would use יקבלו שלטון ('they will receive authority'), not the active ruling verb mashal.
Hebrew: זְמָן מוּעָט ('a short time'). Greek: μίαν ὥραν ('one hour'). The Hebrew is indefinite; the Greek specifies exactly 'one hour.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'they shall rule as kings' (active verb mashal). Greek: 'they receive authority as kings' (passive reception). Different political concept.
Hebrew: 'a short time.' Greek: 'one hour.' Different specificity.
translation_notes: מְלָכִים (melakhim — 'kings') appears in brackets in the source, suggesting editorial restoration.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:24 — 'the ten horns are ten kings who shall arise.' The imagery directly parallels Daniel's fourth beast vision.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַחֲשָׁבָה (machashavah, H4284 — 'thought/plan/design'). This is the OT word for deliberate intention — used for God's plans (Jer 29:11 — 'thoughts of peace, not of evil'), for evil devices (Gen 6:5 — 'every thought of his heart was only evil'), and for craftsman's design (Ex 31:4). Greek γνώμην ('opinion/purpose') is weaker. The Hebrew carries the weight of deliberate, calculated conspiracy.

Uses כּוֹחָם וּגְבוּרָתָם (kocham ugvuratam — 'their strength and their might') — TWO distinct Hebrew power words. כּוֹחַ (koach, H3581) is raw physical power/ability; גְּבוּרָה (gevurah, H1369) is warrior valor/heroic might (used for Samson's strength, David's warriors, YHWH's mighty acts). Greek: δύναμιν καὶ ἐξουσίαν ('power and authority') — a different pair entirely: Greek power + institutional authority vs. Hebrew strength + warrior valor.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'strength and might' (physical power pair). Greek: 'power and authority' (institutional power pair). Different concepts of power.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716 — 'lamb') — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5. Consistent with ch. 21:9. The Passover connection is maintained throughout.

Uses בְּחִירִים (b'chirim — 'chosen ones', from bachar H972/H977 — 'to choose/elect'). Greek has THREE terms: κλητοὶ καὶ ἐκλεκτοὶ καὶ πιστοί ('called and chosen and faithful'). Hebrew has TWO: 'chosen ones and believers.' Greek adds 'called' (κλητοί) which is absent from Hebrew.

Hebrew order: 'lord of lords AND king of kings.' This is the order found in Deuteronomy 10:17 — 'YHWH your God is the God of gods and the LORD OF LORDS (אדוני האדונים).' The Hebrew preserves the Deuteronomy ordering. Greek uses the same order in TR, but the phrase originates from the Hebrew Bible.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two companion terms — 'chosen ones and believers.' Greek: three terms — 'called, chosen, and faithful.' Greek adds 'called.'
translation_notes: 'Chosen ones' for b'chirim — the OT election term (Isa 42:1 — 'my chosen one'; 65:9 — 'my chosen ones shall inherit it').
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 10:17 — 'For YHWH your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords (אדוני האדנים), the great, the mighty, and the awesome God.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַבְרוּתוֹת (chavrut'ot — 'companies/associations/fellowships') — from the root חבר (chaver — 'companion/friend'). This is a distinctly rabbinic/later Hebrew term (cf. chavruta — 'study partnership' in the Talmud). Greek ὄχλοι ('crowds/mobs') is entirely different — unorganized masses vs. organized associations. A back-translator from Greek 'crowds' would use הֲמוֹנִים (hamonim — 'multitudes') or קהלות (qehalot — 'assemblies'), NEVER the rabbinic chavrut'ot.

Uses אוּמִים (ummim — 'nations') — the later Hebrew form of אומה (ummah). This is NOT the standard biblical גּוֹי (goy — 'nation') or לְאוֹם (le'om — 'people'). The choice of this later Hebrew form is natural for a Hebrew writer but would never be chosen by a back-translator.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: THREE terms — 'peoples, companies, nations.' Greek: FOUR terms — 'peoples, multitudes, nations, tongues' (λαοὶ καὶ ὄχλοι... ἔθνη καὶ γλῶσσαι). Hebrew omits 'tongues' (γλῶσσαι).
Hebrew: 'companies' (organized). Greek: 'multitudes' (unorganized). Different social concept.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שְׁמָמָה (shemamah, H8077 — 'desolation') — the powerful OT word from the Levitical curses (Lev 26:33 — 'your land shall be a desolation'), the prophetic judgments (Isa 1:7, Jer 4:7, 25:11), and Daniel's 'abomination of desolation' (Dan 9:27 — שקוץ שמם). Greek ἠρημωμένην ('desolated') is a standard participle. The Hebrew shemamah carries the covenantal curse weight — this is the Torah's threatened punishment for faithlessness.
greek_deviations: Greek adds γυμνήν ('naked') — 'they shall make her desolate AND naked.' The nakedness element is absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Desolation' for shemamah preserves the Levitical curse and Danielic connections.
The burning of the harlot's flesh echoes the penalty for a priest's daughter who commits fornication (Lev 21:9 — 'she shall be burned with fire').
textual_notes: Leviticus 21:9 — 'And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by playing the harlot (לזנות), she shall be burned with fire (באש תשרף).' The harlot receives the priestly-daughter penalty.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) — the covenant name, TWICE. Greek has ὁ Θεός ('God') — the generic title. A back-translator from Greek Θεός would write אֱלֹהִים (Elohim — 'God'), not the specific Tetragrammaton. The Hebrew author naturally uses YHWH in a context about sovereign control over history.
