Uses רְצוֹנוֹ (retsono — 'his will/desire/pleasure', H7522) — the specific OT word for divine will and favor (Ps 5:12, 30:5, 40:8, 51:18, 103:21, 143:10 — 'teach me to do your ratson'). Greek γνώμην αὐτοῦ ('his purpose/decision') is cognitive/intellectual. Hebrew ratson is volitional/relational — it's about YHWH's desire and pleasure, not merely his decree.

CRITICAL: Hebrew says עָשִׁרוּתֶיהָ (ashiruteha — 'HER riches') — they give the harlot's wealth to the beast. Greek says τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτῶν ('THEIR kingdom') — they give their own kingdom to the beast. FUNDAMENTALLY different: Hebrew — they transfer the harlot's wealth; Greek — they transfer their own sovereignty. A translation from one to the other cannot produce this divergence.
Uses דִּיבּוּרַת (dibburat — 'word of') — a later Hebrew form of דבר, natural in post-biblical Hebrew composition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'YHWH' (covenant name, twice). Greek: 'God' (Θεός, generic title, twice). Major theological difference.
Hebrew: 'her riches' (עשירותיה). Greek: 'their kingdom' (τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτῶν). Different object and different possessor.
Hebrew: 'his will' (ratson — desire). Greek: 'his purpose' (γνώμη — decision).
translation_notes: 'Will' for ratson — this is about YHWH's sovereign pleasure, not merely an intellectual decree.
עָשִׁרוּתֶיהָ (ashiruteha — 'her riches') — later Hebrew form from עשר (osher — 'wealth'). No standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמֹּלֵךְ (hamolekh — 'which reigns', active participle from malakh H4427). Greek: ἡ ἔχουσα βασιλείαν ('the one HAVING a kingdom'). The Hebrew describes ACTIVE REIGNING — she is the one who reigns. The Greek describes POSSESSING a kingdom — she holds sovereignty as a possession. A back-translator from Greek would write שיש לה מלכות ('who has a kingdom'), not use the active reigning participle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'reigns over' (active verb). Greek: 'has a kingdom over' (possession). Different mode of authority.

18.summary: Revelation 18 is saturated with direct OT quotations, most prominently from Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The most striking one-way markers are: (1) The VERBATIM Jeremiah quotation of the four-fold voice formula (קול ששון וקול שמחה קול חתן וקול כלה — Jer 7:34/16:9/25:10); (2) The VERBATIM Jeremiah 51:63-64 sinking formula (ככה תשקע בבל ולא תקום); (3) FIVE specific Ezekiel 27 nautical/trade terms in v17 (mallachim, chovlim, machazikei bedeq, orvei ma'arav, anshei milchamah) that match the Tyre destruction prophecy; (4) Consistent use of אדמה ('ground') instead of ארץ ('earth') throughout the chapter, echoing Genesis creation language and Gen 4:10; (5) שטנים ('adversaries') vs. Greek 'demons'; (6) The cognate accusative נקם את נקמתם ('avenged their vengeance'); (7) YHWH used where Greek has Θεός; (8) מאורות (Genesis creation 'luminaries') vs. Greek 'lamp'; (9) The Isaiah 47:8 queen/widow self-declaration. The chapter reads as an extended midrash on Jeremiah 25, 50-51 and Ezekiel 27, applied to eschatological Babylon.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah, H127 — 'the ground') — NOT אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth'). Greek has ἡ γῆ ('the earth'). The Hebrew consistently uses adamah throughout ch. 18 (vv. 1, 23, 24), tying the imagery to the Genesis creation — the ground that was cursed (Gen 3:17), the ground from which man was formed (Gen 2:7). A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use ארץ, not adamah.

Uses כֹּחַ וּגְבוּרָה (koach ugvurah — 'strength and might') — the physical power pair. Greek: ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην ('great authority'). Hebrew describes raw physical/spiritual power; Greek describes institutional authority. A back-translator would use שלטון (shilton — 'authority'), not the koach/gevurah warrior-power pair.

Uses מֵאוֹרוֹ (me'oro — 'from his light', from or H216). Greek: ἐκ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ ('from his glory'). Hebrew: light radiates; Greek: glory radiates. Different qualities — Hebrew uses the elemental creation light (Gen 1:3); Greek uses a theological concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'strength and might' (physical power). Greek: 'great authority' (institutional power).
Hebrew: 'from his light.' Greek: 'from his glory.'
Hebrew: 'the ground' (adamah). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ).
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') to preserve the Genesis creation connection, as in ch. 21:1.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 43:2 — 'and the earth (הארץ) shone from his glory.' The Hebrew Revelation echoes Ezekiel but substitutes adamah for erets and 'light' for 'glory' — a deliberate variation.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 21:9: נָפְלָה נָפְלָה בָּבֶל ('fallen, fallen is Babylon'). Both Hebrew and Greek preserve the doubled verb, but the Hebrew preserves the exact Isaiah form.

CRITICAL: Uses הַשְּׂטָנִים (hasatanim — 'the adversaries/satans', H7854) — the Hebrew word שׂטן in its original sense of 'adversary/accuser' (Num 22:22, 1 Sam 29:4, 1 Ki 11:14,23, Job 1-2, Zech 3:1). Greek δαιμονίων ('demons') is an entirely different class of being. Hebrew satan = legal adversary/accuser; Greek daimon = spirit being. A back-translator from Greek 'demons' would use שדים (shedim — 'demons,' Deut 32:17, Ps 106:37), NOT satanim.

Uses שְׁרָצִים (sheratzim, H8318 — 'creeping things/swarming creatures') — the specific Levitical creation term from Genesis 1:20-21 and the unclean creatures list (Lev 11:29-31,41-43). Greek has no equivalent term. The Hebrew imports creation/Levitical unclean-animal vocabulary.

Uses לְהַסְתִּיר (lehistir — 'to hide/conceal', from satar H5641). Greek φυλακή means 'prison/guard.' Hebrew: Babylon becomes a HIDING-PLACE (where impure things conceal themselves); Greek: Babylon becomes a PRISON (where things are confined). Different imagery — concealment vs. captivity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'adversaries' (satanim). Greek: 'demons' (δαιμονίων). Different beings.
Hebrew: 'hiding-place.' Greek: 'prison.' Different concept.
Hebrew: 'creeping things' (sheratzim). Greek: no equivalent — adds 'every unclean and hated bird.'
translation_notes: 'Adversaries' for satanim preserves the Hebrew legal/accusatory meaning.
'Creeping things' for sheratzim — the Levitical unclean swarming creatures of Lev 11.
textual_notes: Isaiah 13:21-22 — 'wild beasts shall lie down there... and howling creatures shall fill her houses.' The desolation of Babylon with unclean creatures is an Isaianic image.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תַּאֲוָתֵיהֶם (ta'avateihem — 'THEIR desires/lusts', H8378). Greek: τοῦ στρήνους αὐτῆς ('HER luxury/excess'). Hebrew: the merchants grew rich from THEIR OWN lusts; Greek: they grew rich from HER luxury. Different possessor and different concept — Hebrew internal desire vs. Greek external luxury.

Uses סוֹחֲרִים (socharim — 'merchants', from sachar H5503 — 'to trade/go about'). This is the standard OT merchant word (Gen 23:16, 37:28, Isa 23:2, Ezek 27:21,36). The -im plural is natural Hebrew; the concept of itinerant traders is deeply embedded in the OT.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from their great desires.' Greek: 'from HER luxury.' Different possessor.
Hebrew: 'all drank' (subject unspecified). Greek: 'all the nations drank' — specifies 'nations.'

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT OT QUOTATION: צְאוּ מִמֶּנָּה עַמִּי ('Go out from her, my people') — echoes Jeremiah 51:45 (צְאוּ מִתּוֹכָהּ עַמִּי — 'Go out from her midst, my people') and Isaiah 52:11 (סוּרוּ סוּרוּ צְאוּ מִשָּׁם — 'Depart, depart, go out from there'). The imperative צְאוּ (tse'u — 'go out!') is the Exodus verb — the same command that launched Israel from Egypt. A back-translator from Greek ἐξέλθετε could arrive at tse'u, but the combination tse'u + ammi is the Jeremiah formula.

Uses עֲווֹנוֹתֶיהָ (avonoteiha — 'her iniquities', from avon H5771). Greek: ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις αὐτῆς ('her sins'). Hebrew avon is not merely 'sin' (חטא, chatat) — it is guilt-bearing iniquity, the accumulated weight of wrongdoing and its consequences (Gen 4:13, Ex 34:7, Isa 53:5-6). A back-translator from Greek ἁμαρτία would use חטאת (chatat — 'sin'), not the heavier avon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: one clause — 'so that you not be punished with her.' Greek splits into TWO: 'that you not share in her sins AND that you not receive from her plagues.' Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: תִּתְעַנְּשׁוּ (tit'anshu — 'you be punished') appears in brackets in the source, suggesting editorial restoration. This is a later Hebrew form.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:45 — 'Go out from her midst, my people (צאו מתוכה עמי)! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of YHWH!' The same command, same context — fleeing Babylon before divine judgment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נָגַע (naga, H5060 — 'touched/reached/struck') — the Levitical contact verb used for touching impure things (Lev 5:2-3, 7:19,21, 11:24-39, Num 19:11). Her iniquities have made physical CONTACT with heaven — they have defiled the divine realm. Greek ἠκολούθησαν ('followed/accumulated') means merely that her sins piled up. A back-translator from Greek would use הגיעו (higi'u — 'reached/arrived'), not the Levitical contact verb naga.
Uses YHWH (H3068) — the covenant name. Greek: ὁ Θεός ('God'). Consistent pattern of Hebrew preserving the divine name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'touched the heavens' (physical contact). Greek: 'followed/accumulated up to heaven.' Different metaphor.
Hebrew: YHWH. Greek: God.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:9 — 'for her judgment reaches to the heavens (אל השמים) and is lifted up to the skies.' The same imagery of sin reaching heaven.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּפֶל כִּפְלַיִם (kefel kiflayim — 'double twofold') — an intensified doubling unique to Hebrew, echoing Isaiah 40:2 (כִּי לָקְחָה מִיַּד יהוה כִּפְלַיִם — 'she has received from YHWH's hand double') and Jeremiah 16:18 (וְשִׁלַּמְתִּי... מִשְׁנֶה — 'I will repay double'). The Hebrew uses an emphatic cognate intensification (כפל כפלים) that has no equivalent in Greek's simple διπλώσατε ('double').

Uses שַׁלֵּם (shalem, H7999 — 'repay/complete') — from the root of shalom. This is covenantal restitution language — restoring balance through just recompense (Ex 21:34,36, 22:1-14). Greek ἀπόδοτε ('give back') is simpler.
greek_deviations: Greek adds a whole clause about the cup: 'in the cup which she mixed, mix for her double' (ἐν τῷ ποτηρίῳ ᾧ ἐκέρασε, κεράσατε αὐτῇ διπλοῦν) — absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:2 — 'Speak tenderly to Jerusalem... that she has received from YHWH's hand double (kiflayim) for all her sins.' The same doubling language applied to Jerusalem's punishment is now applied to Babylon.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 47:8: אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד לֹא אֵשֵׁב אַלְמָנָה ('I am, and there is none besides me; I shall not sit as a widow'). The Hebrew preserves the Isaiah 47 prophecy against Babylon — the woman speaks Babylon's own words. Greek κάθημαι βασίλισσα ('I sit as queen') approximates but does not preserve the Isaiah verbal form.

Uses הִתְגָּאָה (hitga'ah — 'was haughty/exalted herself', from ga'ah H1342). This is the verb YHWH uses for his own exaltation (Ex 15:1,21 — 'for he has triumphed gloriously/exalted himself greatly' — גָּאֹה גָּאָה). The harlot commits the sin of usurping divine exaltation. Greek ἐδόξασεν ἑαυτήν ('glorified herself') misses this specific OT echo.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'was haughty' (divine exaltation verb). Greek: 'glorified herself.' Different concept.
Hebrew: 'went after her lusts.' Greek: 'lived luxuriously' (ἐστρηνίασε). Hebrew emphasizes pursuit of desire; Greek emphasizes lifestyle.
translation_notes: עִינּוּיִם (innuyim — 'afflictions') is a post-biblical Hebrew form from the root ענה (anah — 'to afflict'). No standard Strong's number.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress') is a later Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Isaiah 47:7-8 — 'You said, I shall be a lady forever... I shall not sit as a widow (לא אשב אלמנה) nor know the loss of children.' Babylon's self-description is Isaiah's prophecy being fulfilled.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the combined title הָאָדוֹן יַהְוֶה (ha-Adon YHWH — 'the Lord YHWH') — a distinctly OT divine title (Isa 3:1, 10:33, Mic 4:13 etc.). Greek: Κύριος ὁ Θεός ('Lord God'). A back-translator from Greek would write אדני אלהים (Adonai Elohim — 'Lord God'), not the specific Adon + YHWH combination.

Uses עָצוּם (atsum, H6099 — 'mighty/powerful') — used in the OT for overwhelming military power and numerical might (Num 22:6, Deut 4:38, 9:1, 26:5, Joel 2:2, Isa 53:12). Greek ἰσχυρός ('strong') is more generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Lord YHWH.' Greek: 'Lord God.' Different divine title.
Hebrew: 'mighty' (atsum — military/overwhelming). Greek: 'strong' (ischyros — general).
textual_notes: Isaiah 47:9 — 'These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day (ביום אחד): the loss of children and widowhood.' The 'in one day' formula is from Isaiah's Babylon oracle.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שָׁמְמוּ (shamemu — 'shall be desolate/appalled', from shamem H8074). This is the same root as שְׁמָמָה (shemamah — 'desolation') from 17:16. Greek κόψονται ('shall beat their breasts/wail') is a mourning action. Hebrew: they become DESOLATE (they share in the devastation); Greek: they WAIL (they mourn externally). A back-translator from Greek 'wail' would use ספדו (safdu — 'lament') or קוננו (qonenu — 'wail'), not the desolation verb shamem.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall be desolate' (shamem — share in devastation). Greek: 'shall weep and wail' (κλαύσουσι καὶ κόψονται — mourning actions). Different response.
Greek adds 'and wail' (κόψονται) and 'when they see the smoke of her burning (τοῦ πυρώσεως αὐτῆς).' Hebrew is more concise.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אֵימָה (eimah, H367 — 'dread/terror') — the word for paralyzing fear used in the Exodus narrative (Ex 15:16 — 'terror and dread shall fall upon them') and the covenant curses (Deut 32:25). Greek φόβος ('fear') is generic. A back-translator from Greek 'fear' would use יראה (yirah — 'fear'), not the Exodus-terror word eimah.

Uses שְׁבוּרָתַיִךְ (shevuratayikh — 'your breaking') — related to שֶׁבֶר (shever, H7667 — 'breaking/fracture/destruction'). This echoes Jeremiah's constant refrain about שֶׁבֶר (Jer 4:6,20, 6:1,14, 8:21, 14:17, 48:3,5, 50:22,46, 51:54). Greek: ἡ κρίσις σου ('your judgment'). Hebrew: BREAKING (physical/structural destruction); Greek: JUDGMENT (legal verdict). A back-translator from 'judgment' would write משפטך (mishpatekh), not shevurah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your breaking' (structural destruction). Greek: 'your judgment' (legal verdict).
Hebrew: 'because of dread' (eimah). Greek: 'for fear of her torment' (expanded).
Greek: 'in one hour' (ἐν μιᾷ ὥρᾳ). Hebrew: 'suddenly' (פתאם). Different temporal markers.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 50:46 — 'At the cry, The breaking (שבר) of Babylon, the earth trembles.' The exact vocabulary of Babylon's שבר.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שָׁרְקוּ (sharqu — 'hiss/whistle', from sharaq H8319) — the OT gesture of horror and contempt at a destroyed place (1 Ki 9:8, Jer 19:8, 49:17, 50:13, Lam 2:15-16, Mic 6:16, Zeph 2:15). Greek πενθοῦσιν ('mourn'). COMPLETELY different: Hebrew — hissing in horror/contempt (a physical reaction of shock); Greek — mourning in grief. A back-translator from Greek 'mourn' would use ספדו (safdu — 'lament') or התאבלו (hit'ablu — 'mourned'), not the hissing verb sharaq.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'weep and hiss' (grief + horror). Greek: 'weep and mourn' (grief + grief). Hebrew has the OT destruction-hissing gesture.
translation_notes: 'Hiss' for sharaq — the Hebrew gesture of drawing breath sharply through the teeth in shock, used when viewing ruins.
textual_notes: Lamentations 2:15 — 'All who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss (שרקו) and wag their heads.' The identical verb for reaction to Jerusalem's destruction.

one_way_hebrew: The metal list בַּרְזֶל וּבְדִיל וְעוֹפֶרֶת ('iron and tin and lead') echoes Ezekiel 27:12 where Tarshish trades with Tyre in 'silver, iron, tin, and lead' (כסף ברזל בדיל ועופרת). The Hebrew author uses the Ezekiel 27 trade-list vocabulary. Greek lists different items in different order.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list is more condensed. Greek adds: 'purple, scarlet, fine linen,' various types of wood (thyine), 'ivory,' 'marble,' and 'brass' — items absent from the Hebrew list. The lists diverge significantly.
translation_notes: 'Goodly stones' (אבנים טובים) — again the OT standard rather than 'precious stones.'
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:12-25 provides the comprehensive trade list for Tyre that the Hebrew Revelation draws upon for Babylon's merchandise.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נִשְׁמוֹת אָדָם (nishmot adam — 'souls of man') — the EXACT phrase from Ezekiel 27:13 where Tyre trades in נֶפֶשׁ אָדָם (nefesh adam — 'souls of man'). Hebrew uses נשמות (nishmot — 'souls/breaths') from the creation word נשמה (neshamah — Gen 2:7, 'breath of life'). Greek: σωμάτων καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων ('bodies and souls of men'). Greek adds 'bodies' (σωμάτων) which is absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew sees only SOULS being traded; the Greek adds the physical body.
Uses עֲגָלִים (agalim — 'wagons/carts', H5699). Greek ῥεδῶν ('chariots/carriages') is a Latin loanword (rheda). The Hebrew uses the native OT word for carts (Gen 45:19,21,27, Num 7:3-8).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'souls of man.' Greek: 'bodies and souls of men.' Greek adds 'bodies.'
Hebrew: 'white bread.' Greek: σεμίδαλιν ('fine flour'). Different commodity.
Hebrew: 'wagons.' Greek: 'chariots' (ῥεδῶν — Latin loanword).
translation_notes: 'Souls of man' — the trade in human beings, the ultimate moral degradation. The Hebrew uses the creation-breath word (neshamah) to describe the commodity.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:13 — 'Javan, Tubal, and Meshech traded with you; they exchanged souls of man (נפש אדם) and vessels of bronze for your merchandise.' The slave trade vocabulary is drawn from Ezekiel.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נַחַת רוּחַ (nachat ruach — 'satisfaction of spirit') — a distinctly Hebrew/rabbinic phrase meaning inner pleasure or spiritual contentment (Eccl 4:6, 6:5; common in Mishnaic Hebrew). Greek ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῆς ψυχῆς ('the desire of the soul') is different — unfulfilled desire vs. achieved contentment. A back-translator from Greek 'desire' would use תאוה (ta'avah — 'desire'), not the rabbinic nachat ruach.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'satisfaction of spirit' (achieved contentment). Greek: 'desire of the soul' (unfulfilled desire). Opposite orientation.
Hebrew: 'esteemed things' (חשובים). Greek: 'luxurious and splendid things' (τὰ λιπαρὰ καὶ τὰ λαμπρά).
Greek adds mourning details: 'weeping and mourning' (κλαίοντες καὶ πενθοῦντες). Hebrew has only 'weep.'

Hebrew: 'silk and gold and goodly stones and pearls.' Greek: 'fine linen and purple and scarlet (βύσσινον καὶ πορφυροῦν καὶ κόκκινον) and... gold and precious stone and pearls.' Greek has three fabric types; Hebrew has one (silk).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — DIRECT EZEKIEL 27 VOCABULARY: This verse uses FIVE specific nautical/trade terms from Ezekiel 27's prophecy against Tyre: (1) מַלָּחַיִךְ (mallachayikh — 'your sailors', H4419, Ezek 27:9,27,29); (2) חֹבְלָיִךְ (chovlayikh — 'your shipmen/pilots', H2259, Ezek 27:8,27,28,29); (3) מַחֲזִיקֵי בִדְקֵךְ (machazikei bidqekh — 'repairers of your breaches', Ezek 27:9,27 — בדק = breach/crack in a ship); (4) עֹרְבֵי מַעֲרָבֵךְ (orvei ma'aravekh — 'merchants of your wares', Ezek 27:27 — ערב = exchange/guarantee/trade); (5) אַנְשֵׁי מִלְחַמְתֵּךְ (anshei milchamtekh — 'your men of war', Ezek 27:27). This is virtually a quotation of Ezekiel 27:27. Greek uses generic nautical terms (κυβερνήτης, ναῦται etc.). No back-translator from Greek would independently reconstruct the specific Ezekiel 27 terminology.

Uses נֶחֱרַב (necherav — 'was destroyed/laid waste', from charav H2717) — the verb for the destruction of cities and the Temple (Isa 60:12, Jer 26:9, Ezek 26:19). The root חרב also produces חורבן (churban — 'destruction'), the standard term for the Temple's destruction.
greek_deviations: Hebrew preserves five Ezekiel 27 nautical terms. Greek uses standard Greek maritime vocabulary. The lists do not correspond 1:1.
Hebrew: 'repairers of your breaches' (ship repair). Greek: no equivalent — this specialized term is absent.
translation_notes: בֶּדֶק (bedeq, H919) — 'breach/crack' — specifically of ship damage (2 Ki 12:5-12, Ezek 27:9,27). The word is also used for Temple repairs.
The entire verse reads as a list from Ezekiel 27:27, applied to Babylon instead of Tyre — the Hebrew author sees the two prophetic destructions as parallel.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:27 — 'Your riches, your wares, your merchandise (מערבך), your sailors (מלחיך), your shipmen (חבליך), the repairers of your breaches (מחזיקי בדקך), the dealers in your merchandise, and all your men of war (כל אנשי מלחמתך)... shall sink into the heart of the seas.' Nearly verbatim.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נִדְמָה (nidmah — 'is comparable/is like', from damah H1819 — 'to resemble/be like'). This echoes the mockery of Tyre in Ezekiel 27:32 — מִי כְצוֹר כְּדֻמָּה ('who is like Tyre, like the silenced one'). Greek: τίς ὁμοία τῇ πόλει τῇ μεγάλῃ ('who is like the great city'). While similar, the Hebrew nidmah connects to the Ezekiel/Tyre pattern; the Greek approximates but loses the specific verbal form.
greek_deviations: The Hebrew manuscript has a lacuna (gap) at the start of this verse, marked by [      ].
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:32 — 'Who is like Tyre, like the silenced one in the midst of the sea?' The same question of incomparability.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יִזְרְקוּ עָפָר עַל רָאשֵׁיהֶם ('they shall cast dust upon their heads') — the specific OT mourning ritual using the verb זָרַק (zaraq, H2236 — 'to hurl/fling'). This is the priest's verb for hurling blood against the altar (Ex 24:6, Lev 1:5,11, Num 18:17). Using the priestly hurling-verb for the mourning gesture adds ritual gravity. Greek ἔβαλον χοῦν ('threw dust') uses the generic 'throw.'
translation_notes: עַכְשָׁיו (akhshav — 'now') is standard later Hebrew, absent from biblical Hebrew.
textual_notes: Job 2:12 — 'they sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven.' Lamentations 2:10 — 'they have cast dust upon their heads.' The dust-on-heads mourning ritual.

one_way_hebrew: Uses a COGNATE ACCUSATIVE: נִקַּם אֶת נִקְמָתֵיהֶם (niqqam et niqmateihem — 'avenged their vengeance') — a classic Hebrew intensifying construction where the verb and its object share the same root (nqm). This idiomatic Hebrew pattern (cf. Gen 40:8 — חלמנו חלום, 'we dreamed a dream'; Num 11:4 — התאוו תאוה, 'they desired a desire') is natural in Hebrew composition. Greek ἔκρινεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ κρίμα ὑμῶν ('God judged your judgment') uses JUDGMENT vocabulary, not vengeance. Hebrew: VENGEANCE (naqam); Greek: JUDGMENT (krima). Entirely different legal framework — blood vengeance vs. judicial verdict.
YHWH again (H3068) vs. Greek Θεός.

תִּשְׂמְחוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם ('Rejoice, O heavens') echoes Deuteronomy 32:43 (הַרְנִינוּ גוֹיִם עַמּוֹ) and Psalm 96:11 (יִשְׂמְחוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם — 'let the heavens rejoice'). The Hebrew command to the heavens to rejoice is standard OT praise language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'avenged their vengeance' (blood vengeance). Greek: 'judged your judgment' (judicial verdict). Different legal concept.
Hebrew: YHWH. Greek: God.
Hebrew: 'his holy ones and his prophets.' Greek: 'holy apostles and prophets.' Greek adds 'apostles' where Hebrew has 'his holy ones.'
translation_notes: 'Avenged their vengeance' — the cognate accusative construction emphasizes the completeness and appropriateness of the retribution.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:43 — 'Rejoice, O nations, his people, for he will avenge (ינקם) the blood of his servants, and he will render vengeance (נקם) to his adversaries.' The exact vocabulary of divine vengeance.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — DIRECT ALLUSION to Jeremiah 51:63-64: Jeremiah commands Seraiah to bind a stone to the scroll of prophecy against Babylon and cast it into the Euphrates, saying כָּכָה תִּשְׁקַע בָּבֶל ('thus shall Babylon SINK'). The Hebrew Revelation uses the EXACT verb תִּשְׁקַע (tishqa — 'shall sink', from shaqa H8257) and the same formula כָּכָה תשׁקע בבל. Greek uses βληθήσεται ('shall be thrown') — different verb. A back-translator from Greek's 'thrown' would use תושלך (tushlakh — 'shall be thrown'), NOT the specific Jeremiah שקע (sink).
The verb pair תִּשְׁקַע... תָקוּם (tishqa... taqum — 'sink... rise') echoes Jeremiah 51:64 exactly: 'Thus shall Babylon sink and NOT RISE (ולא תקום).' Both verbs match Jeremiah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall sink' (שקע — specific sinking verb from Jeremiah). Greek: 'shall be thrown down' (βληθήσεται — general throwing). Different action.
Greek adds 'with violence' (ὁρμήματι) — absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:63-64 — 'When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates and say: Thus shall Babylon sink (ככה תשקע בבל) and shall not rise (ולא תקום).' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Jeremiah's enacted prophecy.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VERBATIM JEREMIAH QUOTATION: קוֹל שָׂשׂוֹן וְקוֹל שִׂמְחָה קוֹל חָתָן וְקוֹל כַּלָּה ('the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride') is an EXACT quote from Jeremiah 7:34, 16:9, 25:10, and 33:11. This four-fold formula is unique to Jeremiah — it appears NOWHERE else in the OT. The Hebrew Revelation reproduces it verbatim. Greek approximates but rearranges: it adds 'voice of harpers and musicians and pipers and trumpeters' (φωνὴ κιθαρῳδῶν καὶ μουσικῶν καὶ αὐλητῶν καὶ σαλπιστῶν) BEFORE the bridegroom/bride — which breaks the Jeremiah formula. A back-translator from Greek would not independently reconstruct the exact Jeremiah quote.

Also quotes Jeremiah 25:10 which adds קוֹל רֵחַיִם ('sound of millstones'). The Hebrew combines Jeremiah 7:34/16:9 (voice formula) with 25:10 (millstone sound) — a conflation natural for a Hebrew author steeped in Jeremiah.

Uses בַּעֲלֵי מְלָאכוֹת (ba'alei melakhot — 'masters of crafts', H1167 + H4399). בַּעַל (ba'al — 'master/owner/lord') is the OT word for the Canaanite deity, but in its primary sense means 'master/possessor.' The Hebrew compound 'masters of crafts' is an OT construction (1 Chr 4:14, Neh 11:35).
greek_deviations: Greek adds four types of musicians (harpers, musicians, pipers, trumpeters) before the bridegroom/bride — absent from Hebrew, and breaking the Jeremiah formula.
Hebrew switches from 3rd person 'in her' (בה) to 2nd person 'in you' (בך) within the same verse — a jarring but authentic shift that suggests direct prophetic address.
translation_notes: The four-fold 'voice of... voice of...' formula is preserved exactly as it appears in Jeremiah.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:10 — 'I will take from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones (קול רחים) and the light of the lamp.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces the Jeremiah passage with remarkable precision.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְּאוֹרֹת (me'orot, H3974 — 'luminaries') — the Genesis 1:14-16 creation word, consistently used throughout this Hebrew text (ch. 21:11,23). The extinguishing of the luminaries is DE-CREATION — Babylon's fall undoes the creative act. Greek has simply 'light of a lamp' (φῶς λύχνου). The Hebrew scales up the imagery from a household lamp to the cosmic luminaries.
Again uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah, H127 — 'the ground'), not erets. Consistent ch. 18 pattern (vv. 1, 23, 24).

Uses שָׂרִים (sarim, H8269 — 'princes/officials') — the OT governmental term for rulers and commanders (Gen 12:15, Ex 1:11, 1 Sam 8:12, 1 Ki 4:2). Greek: μεγιστᾶνες ('great men'). Hebrew implies governmental authority; Greek implies social status.

Uses הִסִּיתוּ (hissitu — 'they incited/led astray', from sut H5496) — the verb used for inciting someone to evil, especially to idolatry (Deut 13:6 — 'if your brother entices you [יסיתך] to serve other gods'; 1 Ki 21:25 — Jezebel 'incited' Ahab; Job 2:3 — the adversary 'incited' God). Greek ἐπλανήθησαν ('were led astray') is passive. Hebrew: active incitement to evil; Greek: passive deception.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'light of the luminaries' (cosmic). Greek: 'light of a lamp' (domestic). Different scale.
Hebrew: 'princes upon the ground.' Greek: 'great men of the earth.'
Hebrew: 'by your sorceries they led astray' (active). Greek: 'by your sorcery were all nations deceived' (passive).
translation_notes: כִּשּׁוּפַיִךְ (kishufayikh — 'your sorceries', from kashaf H3784) — the Torah sorcery term (Ex 7:11, 22:18 — 'you shall not permit a sorceress to live'). Greek: φαρμακεία ('pharmacy/sorcery') — potion/drug-based magic.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:10 also includes 'and the light of the lamp' (ואור הנר) among the sounds/sights that will cease. The Hebrew continues the Jeremiah 25 series.
Nahum 3:4 — 'Because of the many harlotries of the harlot... who sells nations by her harlotries and peoples by her sorceries (בכשפיה).' Same vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נֶהֶרְגוּ (nehergu — 'were slain', from harag H2026) — the OT violence verb for killing (Gen 4:8 — Cain KILLED Abel; Ex 2:14, 32:27). Greek ἐσφαγμένων ('slaughtered') is from σφάζω, which can imply ritual/sacrificial slaughter. The Hebrew uses the common murder verb, not sacrificial language.

Again הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah — 'the ground', H127) — consistent throughout ch. 18. This echoes Genesis 4:10 — 'the voice of your brother's blood cries to me FROM THE GROUND (מן האדמה).' The blood of the slain cries from the adamah, just as Abel's blood cried from the adamah. A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use ארץ, not create this Genesis 4 echo.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'upon the ground' (adamah — Genesis echo). Greek: 'upon the earth' (γῆ — generic).
textual_notes: Genesis 4:10 — 'The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground (מן האדמה).' The blood-on-the-adamah motif links Babylon's bloodguilt to the primal murder.

19.summary: Revelation 19 in Hebrew is dominated by Hallel liturgy and Isaiah quotations. The most striking one-way markers are: (1) The VERBATIM Psalm 113:1 quotation (הללו עבדי יהוה הללו את שם יהוה) where Greek collapses it to a generic 'praise God'; (2) YHWH גָּבַר ('YHWH has prevailed/conquered') vs. Greek 'the Lord God Almighty reigns' — military victory vs. ongoing sovereignty; (3) מִדּוֹר לְדוֹר ('from generation to generation') vs. Greek 'forever and ever' — OT temporal formula vs. Greek eternal formula, directly from Isaiah 34:10; (4) The priestly blood-SPRINKLING verb זרק (zaraq) vs. Greek 'dipped'; (5) דִּיבּוּר יהוה ('Utterance of YHWH') vs. 'Logos of God'; (6) The Isaiah 11:4 quote הוכיח במישור with the ענבי/ענוי (grapes/meek) consonantal pun; (7) חבר ('companion') vs. Greek 'fellow-slave'; (8) קדושים ('holy') vs. Greek 'blessed' for the wedding-feast guests; (9) Sheol vs. 'lake of fire' (consistent pattern); and (10) חיות השדה ('beasts of the field') vs. Greek 'birds.' The chapter's HalleluYah-saturated worship sections demonstrate organic Hebrew liturgical composition.

one_way_hebrew: HalleluYah (הַלְלוּיָהּ) is organically HEBREW — it means 'Praise Yah!' and embeds the divine name. Greek Ἁλληλούϊα is a transliteration of the Hebrew. The fact that the Greek must BORROW the Hebrew word demonstrates Hebrew priority for this liturgical formula.

Uses כָבוֹד וּגְבוּרָה וְתִפְאֶרֶת (kavod ugvurah vetiferet — 'glory and might and splendor') — THREE praise attributes. Greek has FOUR: σωτηρία καὶ δόξα καὶ τιμὴ καὶ δύναμις ('salvation and glory and honor and power'). The Hebrew triad kavod/gevurah/tiferet parallels 1 Chronicles 29:11 — 'Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the might (הגבורה) and the splendor (התפארת) and the glory (ההוד) and the majesty.' A back-translator from Greek's four terms would not independently arrive at the Chronicles formula.
Uses חַבְרוּתָה (chavrutah — 'company/fellowship') — the same rabbinic term as ch. 17:15. Greek: ὄχλου πολλοῦ ('great multitude').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three praise terms (glory, might, splendor). Greek: four terms (salvation, glory, honor, power). Greek adds 'salvation' and 'honor.'
Hebrew: 'to YHWH our Lord.' Greek: 'to the Lord our God.' Different divine title.
Greek adds 'in heaven' (ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) — the priestly/royal beauty term (Ex 28:2,40 — priestly garments made for 'glory and splendor').
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 29:11 — 'Yours, O YHWH, is the greatness and the might and the splendor and the victory and the majesty.' The same praise vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמַּשְׁחִית (hamashchit — 'who corrupts/destroys', from shachat H7843) — the SAME word as the Destroyer angel in Exodus 12:23 who struck the firstborn. The harlot IS the mashchit — the destroying agent. Greek ἔφθειρε ('corrupted') is generic. The Hebrew word identifies the harlot with the Exodus Destroyer.

Hebrew: דְּמֵי עַבְדּוֹ (demei avdo — 'the blood of his SERVANT', SINGULAR). Greek: τὸ αἷμα τῶν δούλων αὐτοῦ ('the blood of his SERVANTS', PLURAL). Singular vs. plural — Hebrew focuses on each individual servant's blood; Greek generalizes.
Hebrew order: צֶדֶק וֶאֱמֶת (tsedeq ve-emet — 'righteous AND true'). Greek order: ἀληθιναὶ καὶ δίκαιαι ('true AND righteous'). REVERSED. Hebrew puts righteousness first — Torah priority.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the blood of his servant' (singular). Greek: 'the blood of his servants' (plural).
Hebrew order: 'righteous and true.' Greek order: 'true and righteous.'
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:43 — 'He will avenge the blood of his servants (דם עבדיו ינקום).' The Song of Moses provides the vengeance formula.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִדּוֹר לְדוֹר (midor ledor — 'from generation to generation') — the standard OT temporal formula (Ps 33:11, 49:11, 79:13, 85:5, 89:1, 100:5, 102:12, Isa 13:20, 34:10, 51:8). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages'). These are COMPLETELY different temporal expressions: Hebrew uses the OT generational formula; Greek uses the Greek eternal formula. A back-translator from Greek would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים ('forever and ever'), NOT the OT midor ledor. This is a clear one-way marker.

This DIRECTLY quotes Isaiah 34:10 — 'its smoke shall go up from generation to generation (מדור לדור יעלה עשנה); it shall not be quenched night nor day.' Isaiah 34 describes the destruction of Edom; the Hebrew Revelation applies it to Babylon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from generation to generation' (OT formula). Greek: 'unto the ages of ages' (Greek eternal formula). Irreconcilable temporal expressions.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:10 — 'Its smoke shall go up from generation to generation (מדור לדור יעלה עשנה).' Verbatim source.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallalim — 'praying', from palal H6419) — the specific Hebrew verb for formal prayer/intercession (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10, 1 Ki 8:28-30, Dan 9:4). Greek: προσεκύνησαν ('worshipped/bowed down'). Hebrew: they PRAY (verbal communion); Greek: they WORSHIP (physical prostration). A back-translator from Greek would use השתחוו (hishtachavu — 'bowed down'), not the prayer verb.
YHWH (H3068) again vs. Greek Θεός.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'prayed' (verbal communion). Greek: 'worshipped' (physical prostration).
Hebrew: YHWH. Greek: God.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VERBATIM PSALM 113:1 QUOTATION: הַלְלוּיָהּ הַלְלוּ עַבְדֵי יַהְוֶה הַלְלוּ אֶת שֵׁם יַהְוֶה — this is the EXACT opening of Psalm 113, which begins the Egyptian Hallel (Ps 113-118), sung at Passover, Sukkot, and major festivals. Greek collapses this to Αἰνεῖτε τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν ('Praise our God') — a generic command. No back-translator from Greek's simple 'praise God' would independently reconstruct the EXACT opening of Psalm 113:1. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.
Uses YHWH THREE times in this single verse. Greek uses Θεός once. The Hebrew is saturated with the covenant name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: full Psalm 113:1 quotation with YHWH three times. Greek: simple 'Praise our God.' The Hebrew preserves the liturgical source; the Greek reduces it.
Hebrew: 'those who fear before him.' Greek: 'those who fear him.' Hebrew adds 'before his face' (לפניו).
textual_notes: Psalm 113:1 — 'HalleluYah! Praise, servants of YHWH, praise the name of YHWH (הללויה הללו עבדי יהוה הללו את שם יהוה)!' The Egyptian Hallel opening, sung at the Passover seder.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יַהְוֶה גָּבַר (YHWH gavar — 'YHWH has prevailed/conquered'). גָּבַר (gavar, H1396) means to be mighty, to prevail in battle, to overcome (Ex 17:11 — when Moses raised his hand, 'Israel prevailed [וגבר]'; Ps 65:3 — 'iniquities prevail [גברו] against me'; Lam 1:16 — 'the enemy has prevailed [גבר]'). Greek: ἐβασίλευσε Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ ('the Lord God Almighty REIGNS'). COMPLETELY different: Hebrew — YHWH has WON (past tense, military victory); Greek — the Lord REIGNS (present/ongoing sovereignty). A back-translator from Greek 'reigns' would use מָלַךְ (malakh — 'reigns'), not the warrior-victory verb gavar.
Hebrew uses YHWH alone. Greek expands to 'Lord God Almighty' (Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ) — a triple title replacing the simple Tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'YHWH has prevailed' (past tense, military victory). Greek: 'the Lord God Almighty reigns' (ongoing sovereignty). Different tense, different concept.
Hebrew: YHWH (one word). Greek: 'Lord God Almighty' (three titles).
translation_notes: 'Prevailed' for gavar captures the military-victory sense — YHWH has overcome, not merely begun to rule.
textual_notes: Exodus 17:11 — 'When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed (וגבר ישראל); when he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed (וגבר עמלק).' The gavar verb is used for winning in battle.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716 — 'lamb') — the Passover lamb word, consistently throughout.

Uses אִשְׁתּוֹ (ishto — 'his wife', from ishah H802). This is the standard Hebrew word for wife/woman — not 'bride.' The lamb's companion is called his WIFE (already married), not his bride (awaiting marriage). Greek also uses γυνή ('woman/wife'). But cf. ch. 21:2 where the Hebrew uses ishah, not kalah.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'let us rejoice and be glad' (χαίρωμεν καὶ ἀγαλλιώμεθα — two verbs). Hebrew has only 'let us be glad' (one verb).
translation_notes: חֲתֻנָּה (chatunnah — 'wedding') — a post-biblical Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.
מוּכֶנֶת (mukhenet — 'prepared/ready') — later Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: Uses THREE qualities: נָקִי וְטוֹב וְיָפֶה (naqi vetov veyafeh — 'clean and good and beautiful'). Greek has TWO: καθαρὸν καὶ λαμπρόν ('clean and bright'). The Hebrew adds 'good' (tov) — the Genesis creation word ('and God saw that it was good'). The bride's garment has the quality of original creation.

Uses מֶשִׁי (meshi, H4897 — 'silk'). Greek: βύσσινον ('fine linen'). Different fabric. Silk is a luxury import from the East; linen is the priestly fabric (Ex 28:39). The Hebrew dresses the bride in eastern luxury; the Greek dresses her in priestly garments.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'silk' (luxury fabric). Greek: 'fine linen' (priestly fabric).
Hebrew: three qualities (clean, good, beautiful). Greek: two (clean, bright).
Greek adds: 'for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints' — an explanatory gloss absent from Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew says קְדוֹשִׁים (kedoshim — 'HOLY are they'). Greek says Μακάριοι ('BLESSED are they'). These are fundamentally different qualities: 'holy' (set apart for God) vs. 'blessed' (happy/favored). A back-translator from Greek Μακάριοι would write אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei — 'blessed/happy'), not kedoshim ('holy'). This is a clear one-way marker.

Uses אֲכִילַת עֶרֶב (akilat erev — 'the evening meal'). This echoes the PASSOVER meal, which must be eaten in the evening (Ex 12:8 — 'they shall eat the flesh that night'). Greek: τὸ δεῖπνον τοῦ γάμου ('the supper of the marriage'). Hebrew frames the meal as PASSOVER (evening meal with the lamb); Greek frames it as a WEDDING FEAST. A back-translator from Greek would write סעודת החתונה ('the wedding feast'), not 'evening meal.'
דִּבְרֵי יַהְוֶה (divrei YHWH — 'words of YHWH') vs. Greek λόγοι... τοῦ Θεοῦ ('words of God').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy' (kedoshim). Greek: 'blessed' (Μακάριοι). Different quality.
Hebrew: 'evening meal' (Passover context). Greek: 'marriage supper' (wedding context).
Hebrew: 'words of YHWH.' Greek: 'true words of God.'
textual_notes: Exodus 12:8 — 'And they shall eat the flesh that night (בלילה הזה), roasted with fire... with the lamb (שה).' The evening meal with the lamb is the Passover.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֲבֵרֶיךָ (chavereykhа — 'your companion/friend', from chaver H2270). Greek: σύνδουλός σου ('your fellow-servant/co-slave'). FUNDAMENTALLY different relationship: Hebrew — companion/friend (equality, friendship); Greek — fellow-slave (shared servitude). The Hebrew chaver is the rabbinic term for a study partner and friend (b. Berakhot 63b: 'acquire for yourself a chaver'). A back-translator from Greek σύνδουλος would use עבד ('servant/slave'), NEVER the friendship-based chaver.

Uses עֲשֵׂי תְּפִילָּתְךָ לְיַהְוֶה ('make your prayer to YHWH'). Greek: τῷ Θεῷ προσκύνησον ('worship God'). Hebrew: PRAY to YHWH (verbal communication); Greek: WORSHIP God (physical act). And again YHWH vs. God.
Greek adds: 'for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy' (ἡ γὰρ μαρτυρία Ἰησοῦ ἐστι τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς προφητείας) — absent from Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your companion' (friendship). Greek: 'your fellow-servant' (servitude).
Hebrew: 'make your prayer to YHWH.' Greek: 'worship God.'
Greek adds the interpretive gloss about testimony and the spirit of prophecy.
translation_notes: 'Companion' for chaver preserves the Hebrew friendship/study-partner relationship.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: יִשְׁפּוֹט בְּצֶדֶק (yishpot betsedeq — 'judges in righteousness') — echoes Isaiah 11:4 (וְשָׁפַט בְּצֶדֶק — 'and he shall judge in righteousness'). Greek adds: καὶ πολεμεῖ ('and makes war'). The Greek adds a military dimension absent from the Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'and makes war' (καὶ πολεμεῖ) — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'his name WAS' (שמו היה — past tense). Greek: 'called' (καλούμενος — present participle).
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:4-5 — 'He shall judge the poor in righteousness (בצדק)... righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness (אמונה) the belt of his loins.' The Messianic figure judges in righteousness and is characterized by faithfulness — matching the Hebrew name 'Faithful and True.'

greek_deviations: Greek adds 'which no one knew except himself' (ὃ οὐδεὶς οἶδεν εἰ μὴ αὐτός). Hebrew has the same idea but phrases it differently: 'no one knows it except he alone' (שום אחד יודע אותו רק הוא לבדו).
translation_notes: כְּתָרִים (ketarim — 'crowns') — later Hebrew plural from כתר (keter — 'crown'). Greek: διαδήματα ('diadems'). Different type of crown — Hebrew keter is a royal crown; Greek diadema is a royal headband.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses זֹרַק (zoraq — 'sprinkled', from zaraq H2236) — the specific PRIESTLY verb for hurling/sprinkling blood against the altar (Ex 24:6 — Moses 'sprinkled [ויזרק] the blood on the altar'; Lev 1:5,11, 3:2, 7:2, Num 18:17). The garment has blood RITUALLY SPRINKLED on it — this is priestly consecration imagery. Greek: βεβαμμένον ('dipped/dyed'). Hebrew: ritual sprinkling (priestly act); Greek: dipping/dyeing (textile process). A back-translator from Greek 'dipped' would use טָבוּל (tavul — 'dipped'), not the priestly zaraq.

CRITICAL: Uses דִּיבּוּר יַהְוֶה (dibbur YHWH — 'the Utterance/Word of YHWH'). Greek: Ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ('The Word/Logos of God'). Hebrew דִּבּוּר (dibbur) specifically means 'spoken utterance/speech act' — it emphasizes the SPOKEN nature of the divine word (cf. the Ten דִּבְּרוֹת — 'Utterances/Commandments'). Greek λόγος can mean word, reason, account, logic. And again: YHWH vs. God.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sprinkled' (priestly ritual). Greek: 'dipped' (textile dyeing). Different action.
Hebrew: 'Utterance of YHWH.' Greek: 'Word of God.'
Greek: some manuscripts have περιρεραντισμένον ('sprinkled') instead of βεβαμμένον ('dipped'), suggesting awareness of the Hebrew reading.
translation_notes: 'Utterance' for dibbur rather than 'word' — preserving the spoken-speech emphasis of the Hebrew, distinguishing it from Greek logos.
The blood-sprinkled garment echoes Isaiah 63:1-3 — 'Who is this coming from Edom, with garments stained crimson?... I have trodden the winepress alone.'
textual_notes: Exodus 24:6-8 — Moses sprinkled (ויזרק) blood on the altar AND on the people, saying 'Behold the blood of the covenant.' The blood-sprinkled garment connects to the covenant ratification.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צִבְאוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם (tsiv'ot hashamayim — 'the hosts of the heavens', H6635) — the OT angelic-military term from the divine title YHWH Tsevaot ('YHWH of Hosts'). Greek: τὰ στρατεύματα τὰ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ('the armies in heaven'). Hebrew uses the specific Tsevaot vocabulary; Greek uses generic military language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'silk' (מֶשִׁי). Greek: 'fine linen' (βύσσινον). Same fabric divergence as v8.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הוֹכִיחַ בְּמִישׁוֹר (hokhiach bemishor — 'reprove with uprightness') — a DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 11:4 (וְהוֹכִיחַ בְּמִישׁוֹר לְעַנְוֵי אָרֶץ — 'and he shall reprove with uprightness for the meek of the earth'). The Hebrew Revelation substitutes 'grapes of the earth' (ענבי ארץ) for Isaiah's 'meek of the earth' (ענוי ארץ) — a consonantal pun where ענב (grape) and ענו (meek) differ by one letter. This wordplay exists ONLY in Hebrew. Greek πατεῖ τὴν ληνόν ('he treads the winepress') loses the Isaiah quotation entirely and replaces the judicial reproof with physical treading.

Uses חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת (cherev pifiyyot — 'sword of two edges/mouths') — quoting Psalm 149:6 (וְחֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת בְּיָדָם — 'and a two-edged sword in their hand'). Greek: ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα ('sharp sword'). The Hebrew preserves the Psalm citation.

Uses יְנַהֵג (yenaheg — 'shall lead/drive', from nahag H5090). Greek: ποιμανεῖ ('shall shepherd'). Hebrew 'lead/drive' (used for driving flocks and chariots) is different from Greek 'shepherd.' A back-translator would use ירעה (yir'eh — 'shepherd').

Uses בַּחֲרוֹן אַף יַהְוֶה (bacharon af YHWH — 'in the fierce anger of YHWH') — a standard OT expression occurring dozens of times (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, 2 Ki 23:26, Jer 4:8, 30:24). Greek expands to τοῦ θυμοῦ καὶ τῆς ὀργῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ Παντοκράτορος ('the fury and wrath of God Almighty').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'reprove with uprightness the grapes of the earth' (Isaiah 11:4 + grape wordplay). Greek: 'treads the winepress of the fury and wrath of God Almighty.' Completely different imagery.
Hebrew: 'fierce anger of YHWH.' Greek: 'fury and wrath of God Almighty.'
Hebrew: 'lead' (drive). Greek: 'shepherd.'
translation_notes: The ענבי/ענוי (grapes/meek) wordplay: Isaiah 11:4 has 'the meek of the earth' (ענוי ארץ). The Hebrew Revelation changes one consonant to get 'grapes of the earth' (ענבי ארץ), fusing the Messianic judgment of Isaiah 11 with the winepress image of Isaiah 63. This is a characteristically Hebrew exegetical technique.
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:4 — 'He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked. And he shall reprove with uprightness (והוכיח במישור) for the meek of the earth (לענוי ארץ).'
Psalm 2:9 — 'You shall break them with a rod of iron (בשבט ברזל).' The iron rod quotation.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: name written 'upon his garment' (על בגדו). Greek: 'upon his garment AND upon his thigh' (ἐπὶ τὸ ἱμάτιον καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν μηρὸν αὐτοῦ). Greek adds 'and upon his thigh' — absent from Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'upon his thigh' (ἐπὶ τὸν μηρὸν αὐτοῦ) — absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 10:17 — 'For YHWH your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords (אדוני האדנים).' Daniel 2:47 — 'Your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings (מארא מלכין).'

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם ('under the heavens') — standard OT spatial description (Gen 1:9, 6:17, 7:19, Deut 2:25, 4:19, 25:19, 29:20). Greek: ἐν μεσουρανήματι ('in mid-heaven'). Hebrew: below the sky; Greek: in the middle of the sky. Different positions.
Again uses אֲכִילַת עֶרֶב ('evening meal') — the Passover evening meal framing, as in v9.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'under the heavens.' Greek: 'in mid-heaven.'
Hebrew: 'evening meal' (Passover context). Greek: 'supper' (δεῖπνον).
textual_notes: Ezekiel 39:17 — 'Speak to every sort of bird and to every beast of the field: Assemble and come, gather from all sides to my sacrificial feast (זבחי).' The great carrion feast of Ezekiel 39.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גִּבּוֹרִים (gibborim — 'mighty men', H1368) — the OT warrior elite: the gibborim of Genesis 6:4 ('the mighty men of old'), David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:8ff, 1 Chr 11:10ff). Greek: ἰσχυρῶν ('strong men'). The Hebrew carries the weight of the biblical warrior tradition.

Uses מְשׁוּחְרָרִים (meshuchrarim — 'freemen/emancipated ones') — a specifically LEGAL later Hebrew term for manumitted slaves, from the root שחרר. Greek: ἐλευθέρων ('free persons'). The Hebrew implies freed slaves; the Greek implies freeborn citizens.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'princes' (שרים — governmental officials). Greek: 'captains of thousands' (χιλιάρχων — specific military rank).
textual_notes: Ezekiel 39:18-20 — 'You shall eat the flesh of the mighty (גבורים) and drink the blood of the princes (נשיאי) of the earth.' The Ezekiel 39 carrion feast provides the vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַחֲנֵיהֶם (machaneihem — 'their encampments', from machaneh H4264) — the specific OT military camp word (Gen 32:2 — Jacob's 'two camps'; Ex 14:19-20 — the camp of Israel; Num 2 — the arrangement of Israel's camp). Greek: τὰ στρατεύματα ('the armies'). Hebrew uses the OT tribal-military encampment concept; Greek uses a generic army term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has a lacuna [...] before 'the horse,' suggesting a missing word in the manuscript.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נְבִיא הַשֶּׁקֶר (nevi hasheqer — 'the prophet of THE FALSEHOOD', H5030 + H8267). This is the EXACT OT construction from Jeremiah: נְבִיאֵי שֶׁקֶר ('prophets of falsehood' — Jer 23:25-26, 27:15, 29:9). Greek ψευδοπροφήτης ('false prophet') is a Greek compound word. The Hebrew preserves Jeremiah's construction with the definite article (the falsehood — a specific entity); the Greek creates a new compound word.

CRITICAL: Uses בִּשְׁאוֹל הַבּוֹעֵר בְּגָפְרִית ('into the Sheol that burns with sulfur'). Greek: εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός ('into the lake of fire'). AGAIN: Hebrew has SHEOL (the underworld); Greek has 'lake of fire.' This is the SAME consistent pattern seen in ch. 17:8,11, 20:10, and 21:8. The Hebrew ALWAYS uses Sheol where the Greek has 'lake of fire.' This is perhaps the most persistent one-way marker in all of Revelation.

Uses לְהַסִּית (lehasit — 'to lead astray/incite', from sut H5496) — the specific Torah verb for inciting to idolatry (Deut 13:6 — 'if your brother incites you [יסיתך] to serve other gods'). Greek: ἐπλάνησε ('deceived').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Sheol that burns with sulfur.' Greek: 'lake of fire burning with sulfur.' Sheol vs. lake of fire.
Hebrew: 'prophet of the falsehood' (Jeremiah construction). Greek: 'false prophet' (compound word).
Greek adds 'alive' (ζῶντες) and 'the two' (οἱ δύο) — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds 'those who worshipped its image' (τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας τῇ εἰκόνι αὐτοῦ). Hebrew has only 'who prayed to it' — without 'image.'
translation_notes: סִימָן (siman — 'mark/sign') — later Hebrew term. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Genesis 19:24 — 'YHWH rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire (גפרית ואש).' The burning sulfur connects to the paradigmatic divine judgment.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חַיּוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה (chayyot hasadeh — 'beasts of the field', H2416 + H7704) — the standard OT phrase for wild animals (Gen 2:19-20, 3:1,14, 1 Sam 17:44,46, Ezek 34:5,8, 39:4,17). Greek: πάντα τὰ ὄρνεα ('all the birds'). Hebrew: BEASTS OF THE FIELD eat the flesh; Greek: BIRDS eat the flesh. Completely different animals. A back-translator from Greek 'birds' would write עופות (ofot — 'birds'), not chayyot hasadeh. The Hebrew preserves the Ezekiel 39 terminology where both beasts and birds feast on the fallen.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'beasts of the field' (wild animals). Greek: 'all the birds.' Different animals.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 39:4 — 'I will give you to the birds of prey and to the beasts of the field (חית השדה) to be devoured.' Ezekiel 39:17 — 'Speak to every bird and every beast of the field: Assemble and come.' The Hebrew Revelation uses the Ezekiel phrase.

20.summary: Revelation 20 in Hebrew contains several of the most theologically significant one-way markers in the entire book. The most striking are: (1) The SHEOL/GEHINNOM DISTINCTION (v13 uses שאול/Sheol for the generic underworld; v14 switches to גיהנם/Gehinnom for the place of judgment) — a two-tier afterlife geography that exists in Hebrew/Jewish thought but is absent from Greek, which uses Hades for both; (2) The GO'EL VERB (יגאל, v7) for the adversary's release — using the kinsman-redeemer vocabulary rather than generic 'loosing'; (3) The CHUPASH (חפש, v3) slave-emancipation term for the adversary's temporary freedom — Sabbatical/Jubilee release language; (4) The YOM KIPPUR AFFLICTION VERB (יתענו, v10) for eternal punishment — framing eschatological judgment in Day of Atonement language; (5) 'Fire of Sheol' (v10) vs. Greek 'lake of fire' — the persistent pattern; (6) PESEL (פסל, v4) — the Second Commandment idol term; (7) כהנים ליהוה ומשיחו ('priests to YHWH and his anointed one') using the Psalm 2:2 construct form; (8) מעולם ועד עולם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — the OT eternal formula vs. Greek 'ages of ages'; and (9) TANNIN (תנין, v2) — the OT chaos-monster vs. Greek 'dragon.' The chapter demonstrates a Hebrew author thinking in Jewish theological categories (Sheol vs. Gehinnom, go'el redemption, Yom Kippur affliction, Torah idolatry concepts) that are systematically flattened in the Greek translation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom, H8415 — 'the deep') — the Genesis 1:2 primordial deep, consistent with ch. 17:8. Greek ἀβύσσου ('abyss') is related but tehom specifically evokes the pre-creation chaos. The adversary is confined in the primordial deep — pushed back to the pre-creation state.

Uses שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת (shalshelet, H8333 — 'chain') — a Hebrew word that also names one of the rarest Torah cantillation marks, appearing only four times in the entire Torah. The word itself connotes linkage and connection.

Uses הַתַּנִּין (hatannin, H8577 — 'the dragon/sea-monster') — the OT chaos-creature (Gen 1:21 — 'God created the great tanninim'; Isa 27:1 — 'YHWH will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent... and he will slay the tannin that is in the sea'; Isa 51:9 — 'Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the tannin?'; Ezek 29:3, 32:2 — Pharaoh called a tannin). Greek δράκοντα ('dragon') is a Greek mythological creature. The Hebrew tanin is embedded in OT chaos-mythology and creation theology.

Hebrew identifies the dragon with ONE name: הַשָּׂטָן (hasatan — 'THE adversary'). Greek gives FOUR identifiers: τὸν δράκοντα τὸν ὄφιν τὸν ἀρχαῖον ὅς ἐστι Διάβολος καὶ Σατανᾶς ('the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the Devil and Satan'). The Hebrew is more concise — just 'the adversary.' Greek adds 'the ancient serpent,' 'the Devil' — absent from Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: one identifier — 'the adversary.' Greek: four identifiers — 'dragon, ancient serpent, Devil, Satan.' Greek massively expands the identification.
Hebrew uses feminine pronoun שֶׁהִיא (shehi — 'which she is') for the tannin, treating it as feminine.
translation_notes: 'Dragon' for tannin — the OT sea-monster of chaos, not the European dragon.
textual_notes: Isaiah 27:1 — 'In that day YHWH with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon (תנין) that is in the sea.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֻפַּשׁ (chupash — 'freed/released') — from the root related to חָפְשִׁי (chofshi — 'free'), the specific SLAVE-EMANCIPATION term in the Torah (Ex 21:2 — 'in the seventh year he shall go out free [חפשי]'; Deut 15:12-13,18; Jer 34:9-16). Greek λυθῆναι ('to be loosed') is generic. The Hebrew describes the adversary's release using JUBILEE/SABBATICAL liberation vocabulary — the same language used for freeing Hebrew slaves. A back-translator from Greek 'loosed' would use יותר (yutar — 'loosed'), not the Torah emancipation term.
Uses לְהַסִּית (lehasit — 'to lead astray/incite', H5496) — consistently the Deut 13:6 incitement-to-idolatry verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'freed' (chupash — slave emancipation). Greek: 'loosed' (λυθῆναι — generic releasing).
translation_notes: חֻפַּשׁ (chupash) — later Hebrew passive form from the root חפש. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Exodus 21:2 — 'When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free (חפשי).' The sabbatical-release vocabulary applied to the adversary's temporary freedom.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel, H6459 — 'image/idol/carved image') — the specific SECOND COMMANDMENT term (Ex 20:4 — 'You shall not make for yourself a carved image [pesel]'; Deut 4:16,23,25, 5:8, 27:15). Greek: τῇ εἰκόνι ('the image') — a generic term. The Hebrew identifies the beast's image with the Torah's prohibition of idols. A back-translator from Greek εἰκών would use צלם (tselem — 'image'), not the commandment-specific pesel.

Uses מוֹשְׁלִים (moshlim — 'ruling', from mashal H4910 — 'to rule/have dominion'). Greek: ἐβασίλευσαν ('they reigned'). Hebrew mashal emphasizes dominion/governance; Greek basileuo emphasizes royal reign.

Uses מִצְחֵיהֶם (mitscheihem — 'their foreheads', H4696) — the same forehead word connected to the priestly plate in Ex 28:38, as in ch. 17:5. The mark is placed on the forehead — where the priestly holiness plate should be.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'image' (pesel — Torah idol). Greek: 'image' (εἰκών — generic). Different connotation.
Hebrew: 'prayed to it' (מתפללים). Greek: 'worshipped its image' (προσκυνοῦντας). Prayer vs. worship.
Greek adds 'those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God' (τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν πεπελεκισμένων...) — a whole clause absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:9-10,22 — 'Thrones were placed and the Ancient of Days took his seat... the court sat in judgment and the books were opened... judgment was given for the holy ones.' The throne-judgment scene from Daniel.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּקוּמָה (tequmah — 'resurrection/rising') — from the root קום (qum, H6965 — 'to rise/stand up'). This is the Hebrew resurrection concept: the dead STAND UP. Greek ἀνάστασις ('resurrection') is from ἀνά + στάσις ('standing up'). Both languages use the 'rising/standing' metaphor, but the Hebrew form tequmah is distinctly later Hebrew.
translation_notes: תְּקוּמָה (tequmah) — a post-biblical Hebrew form from קום. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Daniel 12:2 — 'And many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground shall awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' The two-stage resurrection concept.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: קָדוֹשׁ הוּא (qadosh hu — 'HOLY is he'). Greek: Μακάριος καὶ ἅγιος ('BLESSED AND holy'). Hebrew has ONE quality (holy); Greek has TWO (blessed and holy). Greek adds 'blessed.' A back-translator from Greek would include both terms.

Uses חֵלֶק (cheleq, H2506 — 'portion/allotment') — the OT inheritance/allotment term. When YHWH is Israel's 'portion' (Ps 16:5, 73:26, 119:57, 142:5; Lam 3:24), the word cheleq is used. The resurrection is an INHERITANCE.
Uses כֹּחַ (koach, H3581 — 'power/strength'). Greek: ἐξουσίαν ('authority'). Hebrew: death has no PHYSICAL POWER; Greek: death has no INSTITUTIONAL AUTHORITY.

CRITICAL: Uses כֹּהֲנִים לְיַהְוֶה וּמְשִׁיחוֹ (kohanim la-YHWH umeshicho — 'priests to YHWH AND HIS ANOINTED ONE'). Greek: ἱερεῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ('priests of God and of Christ'). Hebrew preserves YHWH + מְשִׁיחוֹ (meshicho — 'his anointed one,' with the 3rd person possessive suffix, indicating YHWH's anointed). Greek uses God + Christos. The Hebrew construction 'his anointed' (meshicho) is the form found in Psalm 2:2 (עַל יהוה וְעַל מְשִׁיחוֹ — 'against YHWH and against his anointed one') and 1 Samuel 2:10, 2:35, 24:6,10, 26:9,11,16,23. A back-translator from Greek would write 'priests of God and of Christ,' not use the Psalm 2 construct form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy' (one quality). Greek: 'blessed and holy' (two qualities).
Hebrew: 'YHWH and his anointed one.' Greek: 'God and Christ.'
Hebrew: 'power' (koach). Greek: 'authority' (exousia).
translation_notes: 'His anointed one' for meshicho — preserving the Psalm 2 possessive construct rather than importing the Greek title 'Christ.'
textual_notes: Psalm 2:2 — 'The kings of the earth set themselves... against YHWH and against his anointed one (משיחו).' The exact form used here.
Exodus 19:6 — 'You shall be to me a kingdom of priests (ממלכת כהנים).' The priestly-kingdom concept.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יִגָּאֵל (yigga'el — 'shall be redeemed/released', from ga'al H1350). This is the KINSMAN-REDEEMER verb — the most theologically loaded word in the Hebrew legal system. The go'el (kinsman-redeemer) purchases back a relative's land (Lev 25:25), redeems a relative from slavery (Lev 25:48-49), avenges blood (Num 35:19-27), and — supremely — YHWH is Israel's Go'el (Isa 41:14, 43:1,14, 44:6,22-24, 47:4, 48:17,20, 49:7,26, 54:5,8, 59:20, 60:16, 63:16; Jer 50:34; Job 19:25). Greek λυθήσεται ('shall be loosed') is entirely generic. NO back-translator would EVER choose the go'el/redemption verb to translate Greek 'loosed.' This is perhaps the most theologically charged one-way marker in chapter 20.

Uses מִשִּׁבְיוֹ (mishivyo — 'from his captivity', from shevi H7628) — the standard OT war-captivity term (Num 21:1, Deut 21:10, Judg 5:12, Ps 68:18, 126:1, Jer 30:10, Ezek 39:25). Greek: ἐκ τῆς φυλακῆς αὐτοῦ ('from his prison'). Hebrew: war captivity; Greek: prison confinement.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall be redeemed' (go'el/kinsman-redeemer verb). Greek: 'shall be loosed.' Incompatible vocabulary choices.
Hebrew: 'from his captivity' (war prisoner). Greek: 'from his prison' (criminal confinement).
translation_notes: 'Redeemed' for yigga'el — preserving the astonishing use of the kinsman-redeemer verb for the adversary's release. This may suggest that even the adversary's temporary freedom serves YHWH's redemptive purpose.
textual_notes: Job 19:25 — 'I know that my Redeemer (גואלי, go'ali) lives.' The go'el verb carries the entire weight of divine redemption in the OT.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כְּחוֹל הַיָּם (kechol hayam — 'like the sand of the sea') — the standard OT innumerability simile (Gen 22:17 — 'I will multiply your seed like the sand of the sea'; Gen 32:12, 41:49, Josh 11:4, Judg 7:12, 1 Sam 13:5, 2 Sam 17:11, 1 Ki 4:20). Greek uses the same simile — both traditions share this image from Genesis.
Uses חֵילֹו (cheilo — 'his army/force', from chayil H2428) — the OT military-resource term, same as ch. 21:24.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'to gather them together for war' (συναγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς εἰς πόλεμον). Hebrew has 'to gather his army to come to the war' — the subject gathered differs.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 38:2-9 — the Gog and Magog prophecy. The Hebrew author draws directly from Ezekiel's eschatological battle scenario.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah, H127 — 'the ground') again, not erets. Consistent pattern through these chapters.

Uses הָעִיר הָאֲהוּבָה (ha'ir ha-ahuvah — 'the beloved city', from ahav H157 — 'to love'). This echoes Psalm 87:2 (אֹהֵב יהוה שַׁעֲרֵי צִיּוֹן — 'YHWH loves the gates of Zion') and the prophetic tradition of Jerusalem as God's beloved. Greek: τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἠγαπημένην. Both use 'beloved.'

Uses הַחֵילוֹת הַקְּדוֹשִׁים (hacheilot hakedoshim — 'the holy encampments'). Greek: τὴν παρεμβολὴν τῶν ἁγίων ('the camp of the saints'). Hebrew uses chayil (H2428) in the military camp sense, while Greek uses παρεμβολή.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the ground' (adamah). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ).
Greek adds 'and fire came down from God out of heaven' (ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ). Hebrew has simply 'fire from heavens' — without 'from God.'
textual_notes: 2 Kings 1:10-12 — fire falls from heaven at Elijah's command. The fire-from-heaven motif. Also Genesis 19:24 — fire and sulfur on Sodom.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בָּאֵשׁ שֶׁל הַשְּׁאוֹל ('into the fire of the Sheol'). Greek: εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρὸς καὶ θείου ('into the lake of fire and sulfur'). The MOST persistent one-way marker in Revelation: Hebrew ALWAYS has 'fire of Sheol' where Greek has 'lake of fire.' The Hebrew locates the fiery judgment WITHIN Sheol — the OT underworld that burns (Deut 32:22 — 'a fire is kindled in my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol'). The Greek 'lake of fire' is a different concept entirely.

Uses יִתְעַנּוּ (yit'annu — 'they shall be afflicted', from anah H6031) — the specific YOM KIPPUR verb. Leviticus 16:29,31 and 23:27,29,32 command Israel to 'afflict your souls' (תענו את נפשתיכם) on the Day of Atonement. Greek βασανισθήσονται ('shall be tormented') is torture language. Hebrew: Yom Kippur affliction; Greek: punitive torment. A back-translator from Greek 'tormented' would use יענשו (ye'anshu — 'punished') or ייסרו (yeyassru — 'chastised'), not the Day of Atonement verb.

Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם (me'olam ve'ad olam — 'from everlasting to everlasting') — the standard OT eternal formula (Ps 90:2, 103:17, 106:48, 1 Chr 16:36, 29:10, Neh 9:5). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages'). Different eternal formulas — the Hebrew is OT-rooted; the Greek is Hellenistic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'fire of Sheol.' Greek: 'lake of fire and sulfur.' The most persistent divergence in Revelation.
Hebrew: 'afflicted' (Yom Kippur verb). Greek: 'tormented' (punishment verb).
Hebrew: 'from everlasting to everlasting.' Greek: 'unto the ages of ages.'
translation_notes: 'Afflicted' for yit'annu preserves the Yom Kippur connection — the eternal affliction is framed in Day of Atonement language.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:22 — 'For a fire is kindled in my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol (עד שאול תחתית).' The fire-in-Sheol concept.
Leviticus 16:29 — 'You shall afflict your souls (תענו את נפשתיכם).' The Yom Kippur affliction verb.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נָס (nas — 'fled', from nus H5127 — 'to flee in terror'). This verb is used for fleeing from God's presence (Ex 14:27, Ps 68:1-2 — 'Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him FLEE [ינוסו] before him'; Ps 104:7 — 'at your rebuke the waters FLED'). The heavens and ground flee in terror from the divine presence. Greek ἔφυγεν ('fled') is similar but nus carries the specific OT terror-flight connotation.
Again uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah — 'the ground', H127), not erets. Consistent.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the ground' (adamah). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ).
Hebrew has a lacuna [...] in the text.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:9 — 'Thrones were placed and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow.' The white throne scene from Daniel.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִפְנֵי יַהְוֶה (lifnei YHWH — 'before YHWH', H3068). Greek: ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ ('before God'). The dead stand before the covenant-name God, not merely before 'God.'

Uses סֵפֶר הַחַיִּים (sefer hachayyim — 'the scroll of life') — the OT concept (Ex 32:32-33 — Moses says 'if not, blot me from your scroll [ספרך] which you have written'; Ps 69:28 — 'let them be blotted from the book of the living [ספר חיים]'; Dan 12:1 — 'everyone found written in the book [ספר]'). Greek: τὸ βιβλίον τῆς ζωῆς. Both preserve the concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'before YHWH.' Greek: 'before God.' (Some Greek manuscripts have 'before the throne.')
Greek adds 'according to their works' (κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν) at the end. Hebrew also has 'according to their deeds' (כפי מעשיהם).
textual_notes: Daniel 7:10 — 'The court sat in judgment and the books (ספרין) were opened.' The opened-books judgment scene from Daniel.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וַיָּרֶק (vayyareq — 'and emptied out', from riq H7324 — 'to empty/pour out'). This verb is used for emptying containers (Gen 42:35 — 'as they emptied their sacks'; Jer 48:12 — 'who shall empty [ירקו] his vessels'). The sea DISGORGES its dead as one empties a container. Greek ἔδωκεν ('gave up') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use נתנה (natnah — 'gave'), not the vivid emptying/pouring verb.
Uses הַשְּׁאוֹל (hash'ol — 'the Sheol', H7585). Greek: ὁ ᾅδης ('Hades'). Hebrew Sheol and Greek Hades are related underworld concepts but carry different theological traditions.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'emptied out' (vivid pouring verb). Greek: 'gave up' (generic).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַגֵּיהִנֹּם (haGeihinnom — 'the Gehinnom/Gehenna') — the Valley of (the Son of) Hinnom, the specific GEOGRAPHICAL LOCATION south of Jerusalem where child sacrifice to Molech was performed (2 Ki 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2-6, 32:35, 2 Chr 28:3, 33:6). Greek: ὁ ᾅδης ('Hades' — the Greek underworld). The Hebrew author DISTINGUISHES between Sheol (used in v13 for the generic underworld) and Gehinnom (used here for the place of judgment). Greek uses Hades for BOTH, losing this critical distinction. A back-translator from Greek Hades would use Sheol consistently, not switch to Gehinnom. The Sheol/Gehinnom distinction is native to Hebrew/Jewish theological discourse — Sheol is where all dead go; Gehinnom is the place of judgment. This distinction exists ONLY in Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'cast into the fire' (באש). Greek: 'cast into the lake of fire' (εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός). Hebrew has simply 'fire'; Greek has 'lake of fire.' The Hebrew never uses the 'lake' concept.

Greek adds: 'this is the second death, the lake of fire' (Οὗτος ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερός ἐστιν, ἡ λίμνη τοῦ πυρός) — an identification clause equating the second death WITH the lake of fire. Hebrew simply says 'this is a second death' — without the lake-of-fire identification.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Gehinnom' (valley of Hinnom — geographical). Greek: 'Hades' (Greek underworld — mythological). MOST significant divergence.
Hebrew: 'fire.' Greek: 'lake of fire.'
Greek adds interpretive identification: 'the second death IS the lake of fire.'
translation_notes: 'Gehinnom' is preserved untranslated — it is a specific geographical name (Valley of Hinnom) that became the Jewish term for the place of post-mortem judgment.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 7:31-32 — 'They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (גיא בן הנם), to burn their sons and daughters in the fire... therefore behold, days are coming when it shall no longer be called Topheth or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.' The geographical origin of Gehinnom as a place of judgment.

The Sheol/Gehinnom distinction: In v13, the Hebrew uses שאול (Sheol — the generic underworld where all dead reside). In v14, it switches to גיהנם (Gehinnom — the specific place of fiery judgment). This two-tier afterlife geography is standard in Jewish thought (see Mishnah, Avot 5:22; Tosefta, Sanhedrin 13:3) but does not exist in Greek thought, which has only Hades.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'cast into the fire' (באש). Greek: 'cast into the lake of fire' (εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός). Hebrew has 'fire'; Greek has 'lake of fire.' Consistent to the end.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'fire.' Greek: 'lake of fire.'
textual_notes: Psalm 69:28 — 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living (ספר חיים), and not be enrolled among the righteous.' The inverse of being found in the scroll of life.

21.summary: Revelation 21 in Hebrew draws massively from Isaiah 60 and the Torah's Tabernacle/priestly vocabulary. The Hebrew text preserves exact OT quotations (Isaiah 25:8, 60:11), uses Torah-specific terminology (mishkan, seh, nega'im, zar, qarav, sheluchim, ma'or), and shows linguistic self-awareness (marking foreign loanwords with בלעז). The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The most striking are: (1) 'the first and the last' vs. 'Alpha and Omega,' (2) the verbatim Isaiah 60:11 quote with 2nd person address, (3) 'fire of Sheol' vs. 'lake of fire,' (4) the בלעז foreign-word markers, and (5) the zar/qarav priestly terminology in verse 27.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah, H127 — 'ground/soil') for the NEW earth but אֶרֶץ (erets, H776) for the OLD earth. Greek uses γῆ (ge) for both. No translator going Greek→Hebrew would use two different words where Greek has one. The adamah echoes Genesis 2:7 — man formed from adamah returns to renewed adamah.

Uses יִגְוַע (yigva, H1478 — 'expired/died') — the verb used when patriarchs die (Gen 25:8, 25:17, 35:29, 49:33). The earth 'dies' like a person. Greek παρῆλθεν means merely 'passed away.' A back-translator would use עָבַר (avar — 'passed'), not the biological death verb גוע.
greek_deviations: Greek παρῆλθεν ('passed away') is far weaker than Hebrew יגוע ('expired/died'). The Hebrew verb implies biological death of the old creation.
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') to preserve the distinction from erets. The adamah/erets contrast is theologically loaded: adamah is the soil from which Adam was formed (Gen 2:7), the soil cursed for Adam's sake (Gen 3:17), now renewed.
'Expired' for yigva to capture the Hebrew verb's specific meaning of biological death, distinguishing it from merely 'passing away.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 65:17 prophesies 'new heavens and a new earth' using שָׁמַיִם חֲדָשִׁים וָאָרֶץ חֲדָשָׁה — with erets for both old and new. This Hebrew text's switch to adamah is a deliberate theological choice.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אִשָּׁה (ishah — 'woman/wife', H802) not כַּלָּה (kalah — 'bride'). Greek has νύμφην (bride). A back-translator from Greek would use kalah. The Hebrew author uses the more general 'woman' for the simile.

'From the heavens to the earth' (מִשָּׁמַיִם לָאָרֶץ) — Greek has 'from God out of heaven' (ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ). The Hebrew gives the trajectory (heaven→earth); the Greek gives the source (from God). These are different perspectives a translator would not interchange.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἡτοιμασμένην ('prepared') before 'adorned' — absent in Hebrew. The Hebrew has only 'adorned,' not 'prepared and adorned.'
Greek says 'from God' (ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ) which the Hebrew omits entirely.
translation_notes: 'Lord' for ba'al (H1167) captures the ownership/authority nuance. Ba'al means 'master/owner/lord' and is the standard Hebrew word for 'husband' that emphasizes his headship role.
מְקֻשָּׁט (mequshat) is from a root meaning 'adorn/decorate,' common in later Hebrew and Aramaic but not in the standard OT lexicon. No Strong's number assigned.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִשְׁכַּן (mishkan, H4908) — the specific word for the Tabernacle of Moses (Ex 25:9, 26:1ff). Greek σκηνή is generic 'tent.' A Hebrew author naturally reaches for the Torah's technical term; a back-translator might use אֹהֶל (ohel — tent) or just transliterate.

Uses singular הָאָדָם (ha-adam — 'the man/mankind', H120) with the definite article, echoing Genesis where God walked with 'the adam.' Greek has plural τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('men'). A back-translator from Greek would write אנשים (anashim — 'men'), not the Genesis-laden ha-adam.
Uses אֵצֶל (etsel, H681 — 'beside/next to') — a word expressing physical proximity. Greek μετά ('with') is far more generic. No back-translator would choose etsel from meta.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: voice 'from the throne' (מהכסא). Greek: voice 'from heaven' (ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ). Major difference in the source of the voice.

Greek adds σκηνώσει μετ' αὐτῶν ('he will dwell/tabernacle with them') and καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς ἔσται μετ' αὐτῶν θεὸς αὐτῶν ('and God himself will be with them, their God') — expanded clauses absent from the more concise Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Dwelling-place' for mishkan preserves the Tabernacle connection without anachronistically saying 'tabernacle.'
'Beside' for etsel captures the spatial intimacy — not merely 'with' but positioned right next to.
textual_notes: The covenant formula 'I will be their Elohim and they shall be my people' appears in Jer 31:33, Ezek 37:27, Zech 8:8. The Hebrew naturally uses the OT covenant language.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 25:8: וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים — 'And the Lord YHWH will wipe a tear from upon all faces.' The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact phrasing 'from upon all faces' (מעל כל פנים). Greek changes this to 'every tear from their eyes' (πᾶν δάκρυον ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν). A back-translator from Greek would write כל דמעה מעיניהם, not the Isaiah quote.

Uses יִמְשֹׁל (yimshol — 'shall rule/reign', H4910) for death. Greek has οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι ('shall be no more'). A back-translator from Greek would write לא יהיה עוד ('shall be no more'), using היה (to be), not משל (to rule). The Hebrew says death's REIGN ends — not that death ceases to exist.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a tear from upon all faces' (Isaiah 25:8 verbatim). Greek: 'every tear from their eyes' — a loose paraphrase that loses the Isaiah source.
Hebrew: 'death shall not rule anymore.' Greek: 'death shall be no more.' Fundamentally different claims — the end of death's dominion vs. the end of death's existence.
translation_notes: 'Rule' for yimshol is critical — this aligns with Romans 5:14,17 where death 'reigned' (ἐβασίλευσεν) and 1 Cor 15:26 where death is 'destroyed' (defeated) not annihilated.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — distress) and עִנּוּיִם (innuyim — afflictions) lack standard Strong's numbers; they are post-biblical Hebrew forms.
textual_notes: The Isaiah 25:8 parallel is the strongest OT connection in this verse. The Hebrew author quotes it verbatim; the Greek translator paraphrased it.

one_way_hebrew: Uses past tense עָשִׂיתִי (asiti — 'I have made', perfect tense). Greek has present tense ποιῶ ('I make/am making'). Hebrew perfect tense presents the renewal as already accomplished from God's perspective — a completed act. The Greek present tense suggests an ongoing process. These are fundamentally different theological perspectives that cannot be reconciled as translation variants.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'truth' (אֱמֶת, singular). Greek: 'true and faithful' (ἀληθινοὶ καὶ πιστοί). Greek adds 'faithful' (πιστοί) which is absent from the Hebrew.

Hebrew: אֱמֶת הִיא — 'truth she is' (feminine singular, referring to the collected words as a unit). Greek: ἀληθινοὶ καὶ πιστοί εἰσιν — 'true and faithful they are' (masculine plural). Different gender and number.
translation_notes: 'Have made' (past tense) for asiti — this is the Hebrew perfect, indicating completed action. The divine perspective sees the renewal as already done.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן ('the first and the last') — a direct quote from Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 where YHWH declares 'I am the first, and I am the last.' Greek has τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω ('the Alpha and the Omega') — Greek letters. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would write האלף והתו ('the Aleph and the Tav'). Instead, the Hebrew preserves the Isaiah quotation. The Greek translator converted the Hebrew concept to Greek letters. This is among the strongest one-way markers in all of Revelation.
