This is a uniquely Hebrew theological concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the light of the kingdom of God.' Greek: 'the kingdom of God come in power.' Entirely different: luminous kingdom vs. powerful kingdom.
translation_notes: מקצת (miqtsat) — from קצה (qatseh, H7097 — 'end/extremity'), used in later Hebrew for 'a portion/some.' Standard OT usage is spatial ('end of'), but post-biblical usage shifted to quantitative ('some of').

one_way_hebrew: Uses שנוי צורת הפנים ('change of the form of the face') — a concrete, physical Hebrew description. Greek μετεμορφώθη ('was transfigured/metamorphosed') is a Greek philosophical term. A Hebrew author describes what was visibly observed — the face changed form. A back-translator from Greek would struggle to find an equivalent for μεταμόρφωσις and would likely transliterate or use השתנה ('changed'), not the elaborate construct שנוי צורת הפנים.

Uses נהגם (nahagam, H5090 — 'led them'), the verb for leading/driving flocks (Gen 31:18, Isa 11:6). Greek has ἀναφέρει ('carries up'). A back-translator from Greek would use העלה ('brought up'), not the shepherd-leading verb נהג.
greek_deviations: Hebrew mentions only Keipha and Ya'aqov. Greek adds καὶ τὸν Ἰωάννην ('and Yochanan'). This may reflect a shorter Hebrew Vorlage.
Hebrew: 'change of the form of the face.' Greek: 'was transfigured' (μετεμορφώθη). Different conceptual frames — visible observation vs. abstract transformation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses על פני האדמה ('upon the face of the ground,' H127 — adamah). Greek has ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ('upon the earth'). The phrase פני האדמה is a specific Hebrew idiom appearing throughout the Torah (Gen 2:6, 4:14, 6:1, 7:3, 8:8). A back-translator from Greek would write על הארץ ('upon the earth'), not the idiomatic pnei ha'adamah.

Uses מזהירים (mazhirim, H2094 — 'shining/illuminating'), from the root זהר which carries dual meaning: 'to shine' AND 'to warn/enlighten' (Dan 12:3 — 'those who make wise shall shine'). Greek λευκά ('white') is purely visual. The Hebrew verb carries intellectual/spiritual connotation absent from Greek.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὡς χιών ('as snow') and a comparison to a fuller's whitening: γναφεύς. Hebrew mentions snow but not the fuller/launderer.
translation_notes: The bracket [ ] in the source indicates a gap or lacuna in the Hebrew manuscript.

greek_deviations: Hebrew order: Moshe and Eliyahu. Greek order: Ἠλίας σὺν Μωϋσεῖ (Elijah with Moses). Hebrew preserves chronological priority (Torah before Prophets); Greek reverses it.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אהלים (ohalim, H168 — 'tents'), the word for the Tabernacle dwelling-tents of Israel's wilderness period (Gen 12:8, 13:3; Ex 33:7ff). Greek σκηνάς ('booths') is the standard translation, but the Hebrew word naturally evokes the Sukkot festival and the wilderness Tabernacle tradition.

Uses עב (av, H5645 — 'thick cloud/dark cloud'), NOT ענן (anan — 'cloud'). The av is the specific theophany cloud — the thick dark cloud at Sinai (Ex 19:9 — הנה אנכי בא אליך בעב הענן, 'behold I come to you in the thick cloud'; Deut 4:11, 5:22). Greek νεφέλη ('cloud') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use ענן, not the Sinai-specific עב.

Uses צל (tsel, H6738 — 'shadow/shade'), connecting to Psalm 91:1 — 'in the shadow (צל) of the Almighty.' Greek ἐπισκιάζουσα ('overshadowing') is related but the Hebrew term evokes divine shelter and protection.

Uses יקר (yaqar, H3368 — 'precious/costly/rare') for the son, NOT אהוב (ahuv — 'beloved'). Greek has ἀγαπητός ('beloved'). A back-translator from Greek would use אהוב. The Hebrew says the son is 'precious/rare' (1 Sam 3:1 — the word of YHWH was yaqar). Different nuance: rarity and costliness vs. emotional affection.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'precious' (יקר). Greek: 'beloved' (ἀγαπητός). Different attributes of the son.
Hebrew: cloud 'making shadow.' Greek: cloud 'overshadowing.' The Hebrew is more concrete.
translation_notes: [שאמרת] is bracketed in the source, indicating editorial restoration.
textual_notes: The thick cloud (עב) with a voice speaking from it directly parallels the Sinai theophany (Ex 19:9, 24:15-18). The Transfiguration is portrayed as a second Sinai.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המראה (hamar'eh, H4758 — 'the vision/appearance'), the specific prophetic vision word used for Ezekiel's visions (Ezek 1:1, 8:3, 40:2) and Daniel's (Dan 10:7-8). Greek simply says μηδενὶ ἃ εἶδον διηγήσωνται ('should tell no one what they saw'). The Hebrew frames the Transfiguration as a מראה — a prophetic vision of the same class as Ezekiel's.

Uses יחזור חי ממות ('returns alive from death') — concrete Hebrew. Greek has ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ ('rise from the dead'). The Hebrew describes a journey: he goes to death and returns alive from it. A back-translator from Greek would write יקום מן המתים ('rise from the dead'), not 'return alive from death.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'this vision.' Greek: 'what they saw.' Hebrew uses a technical prophetic term; Greek is descriptive.
Hebrew: 'returns alive from death.' Greek: 'rise from the dead.' Different conceptual frame — return from a place vs. standing up from a state.

Greek has τὸν λόγον ἐκράτησαν ('they kept the word') — merely holding/retaining. Hebrew העלימוהו ('they concealed it') implies active hiding, from עלם (alam, H5956 — 'to hide/conceal'). Different implication: active concealment vs. passive retention.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הפרושים (haPerushim — 'the Perushim'), the native Hebrew name from פרש (parash, H6567 — 'to separate/distinguish'). Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes') is a functional title. A back-translator from Greek would NOT produce the internal Hebrew party name with its etymological transparency.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'and the scribes after them' — implying the scribes follow the Pharisees' teaching. Greek has only γραμματεῖς ('the scribes').
translation_notes: חוייב — a Hebrew legal term meaning 'obligated/required.' No standard Strong's number; a later Hebrew development from the root חוב.
textual_notes: References Malachi 4:5 (Hebrew 3:23) — 'Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of YHWH comes.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן האלוה (ben ha'Eloha — 'Son of God'). Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). The Hebrew consistently uses 'Son of God' where the Greek has 'Son of Man.' If this Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would faithfully render 'Son of Man' as בן אדם. The use of 'Son of God' points to an independent Hebrew tradition.

Uses נגישה (negishah — 'oppression/exaction'), from נגש (nagash, H5065). This is the word for the Egyptian taskmasters who oppressed Israel (Ex 3:7, 5:6,10,13,14). The Son of God's suffering is described with Exodus-slavery vocabulary. Greek has πάθῃ ('suffer') and ἐξουδενωθῇ ('be treated with contempt') — generic terms. A back-translator would NEVER reach for the Egyptian-oppression verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of God' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Major christological difference.
Hebrew: 'suffer oppression unto a shameful death.' Greek: 'suffer many things and be set at nought.' Different descriptions of the suffering.
translation_notes: מגונה ('shameful/disgraceful') — a later Hebrew moral term. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: The phrase 'as it is written' points to Isaiah 53 — the Suffering Servant who bears oppression.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הכתיבה (hak'tivah — 'the writing'), a characteristically Hebrew way of referring to Scripture. This later Hebrew noun form from כתב (katav, H3789) is a native linguistic development. Greek γέγραπται ('it is written') is the standard form.

Uses חכמים ומאותתים ('wise ones and lettered ones') — a Hebrew social description of the scribal class. Greek has γραμματεῖς ('scribes'). The Hebrew uses native categories: חכמים (learned/wise) and מאותתים (from אות — 'letter/sign,' meaning 'lettered/literate'). A back-translator from Greek would use סופרים (sofrim), not this descriptive Hebrew phrase.
translation_notes: מאותתים — from אות (ot — 'sign/letter'). Meaning 'lettered ones/scholars.' No standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שטן (satan, H7854 — 'adversary/accuser') — the Hebrew concept. Greek has πνεῦμα ἄλαλον ('mute spirit'). The Hebrew uses the uniquely Hebraic concept of a satan; the Greek uses the Hellenistic concept of a spirit (πνεῦμα). A back-translator from Greek would write רוח אלם ('mute spirit'), not שטן.
Locates the satan שבלבו ('in his heart') — the affliction is in the heart, a Hebrew anthropological concept. Greek mentions no location of the spirit within the body.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a satan in his heart.' Greek: 'a mute spirit.' Different entity and different location.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משפחה ממאנת ('refusing family'), from מאן (ma'an, H3985 — 'to refuse/be unwilling'). Greek has γενεὰ ἄπιστος ('faithless generation'). Hebrew ממאנת means active rebellion/refusal; Greek ἄπιστος means absence of faith. A back-translator would use חסרי אמונה ('lacking faith'), not the active-refusal verb מאן.
Uses משפחה (mishpachah, H4940 — 'family/clan') instead of דור (dor — 'generation'). Greek γενεά = 'generation.' The Hebrew addresses them as clan members — more intimate and more damning.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'refusing family.' Greek: 'faithless generation.' Different qualifier and different social unit.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בחסדך (b'chasdekha — 'with your lovingkindness/covenant-mercy,' H2617). Greek has σπλαγχνισθεὶς ἐφ' ἡμᾶς ('having compassion on us'). Hebrew חסד (chesed) is the untranslatable covenant-love word — God's steadfast loyal devotion. The father appeals to Yeshua's chesed, a concept far deeper than Greek σπλαγχνίζομαι ('compassion'). A back-translator from Greek would use רחם (racham — 'have compassion'), not the covenant-specific chesed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'help me with your lovingkindness.' Greek: 'have compassion on us, help us.' Different appeal: covenant loyalty vs. emotional compassion.
Hebrew: 'may it please you to help my faith.' Greek: 'help my unbelief' (βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ). Hebrew frames positively — strengthen my faith. Greek frames negatively — fix my unbelief.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שטן חזק ואלם ('mighty and mute satan'). Greek has τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἄλαλον καὶ κωφόν ('the mute and deaf spirit'). Hebrew uses חזק (chazaq, H2389 — 'strong/mighty') where Greek has κωφόν ('deaf'). Different attribute: 'mighty' vs. 'deaf.' Also, Hebrew addresses a 'satan'; Greek addresses a 'spirit' (πνεῦμα).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'mighty and mute satan.' Greek: 'mute and deaf spirit.' Different entity name and different attributes.
Hebrew: 'he returned alive' (חזר חי). Greek: 'he arose' (ἀνέστη). Hebrew uses the same 'returned alive' phrase used for resurrection predictions — creating a micro-resurrection pattern.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בסוד (b'sod, H5475 — 'in secret counsel/intimate council'). This is the Hebrew word for divine/prophetic council (Ps 25:14 — 'the sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'; Amos 3:7; Jer 23:18,22). Greek has κατ' ἰδίαν ('privately'). A back-translator would use בפרט ('privately'), not the theologically loaded סוד.

Uses מדת השטן ('this measure of satan'), from מדה (middah, H4060 — 'measure/dimension/standard'). Greek has τοῦτο τὸ γένος ('this kind/race'). Hebrew מדה implies graded classification — satans have different 'measures' or grades. A back-translator from Greek would write מין ('type/kind'), not the measurement/standard term מדה.

translation_notes: [ונסעו] is bracketed in the source, suggesting editorial restoration.

one_way_hebrew: Again בן האלוה ('Son of God') where Greek has υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). Consistent Hebrew pattern.

Uses נבגד ונמסר ('betrayed and delivered') — TWO distinct verbs. בגד (bagad, H898) means 'to act treacherously' (used of covenant-breaking in Jer 3:20, 5:11, Mal 2:10-16). מסר (masar, H4560) means 'to hand over/deliver.' Greek has only παραδίδοται ('is delivered') — one verb. The Hebrew separates treachery from the physical handover.
Uses ביד הרעים ('into the hand of the wicked') — Greek has εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων ('into the hands of men'). Hebrew specifies the moral character (wicked); Greek is neutral (men).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of God.' Greek: 'Son of Man.'
Hebrew: 'betrayed and delivered.' Greek: only 'delivered.'
Hebrew: 'the wicked.' Greek: 'men.'
Hebrew: 'return alive on the third day.' Greek: 'after three days rise again.' Different timing and different verb.
Greek adds ἐφοβοῦντο αὐτὸν ἐπερωτῆσαι ('they were afraid to ask him'). Hebrew says they 'began to question him' — no fear mentioned.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כפר נחום (Kfar Nachum — 'Village of Comfort'), preserving the full semantic meaning of the Hebrew place name. Greek Καφαρναούμ (Capernaum) is a transliteration that obscures the meaning.

Uses בינותינו ('among US') — first person plural, including himself in the group. Greek has πάντων ἔσχατος ('last of all'). The Hebrew includes Yeshua among those he addresses; the Greek has a different structure (last of all and servant of all).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall be a servant of all.' Greek: 'shall be last of all and servant of all.' Hebrew omits the 'last' concept.
translation_notes: Bracketed [שירצה] and [ ] in the source indicate editorial restorations.
Bracketed [אחד] and [יקבל] in the source indicate editorial restorations.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המשוטנים ('the satan-afflicted') — a Hebrew verbal form meaning 'those under the influence of satan,' from שטן. Greek has ἐκβάλλοντα δαιμόνια ('casting out demons'). The Hebrew does not separate the 'casting out' action — instead it describes the people as afflicted and the man as 'healing' them. Different conceptual frame: Hebrew sees illness under a satan; Greek sees separate demons being expelled.

Uses מחבורתינו (mechaburatenu — 'of our fellowship'), from חבורה (chavurah, H2267). This is a specific Hebrew term for an intimate study/fellowship group — a distinctly Jewish social structure. Greek has οὐκ ἀκολουθεῖ ἡμῖν ('does not follow us'). Different concept: belonging to a fellowship vs. following a person.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'healing the satan-afflicted.' Greek: 'casting out demons.' Different action and different affliction.
Hebrew: 'not of our fellowship.' Greek: 'does not follow us.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses נפלאות (nifla'ot, H6381 — 'wonders'), the OT word for God's miraculous acts (Ex 3:20, 15:11, Ps 77:12, 78:12). Greek has δύναμιν ('power/mighty work'). A back-translator from Greek would use גבורה ('power'), not the Exodus-vocabulary nifla'ot.

CRITICAL: Uses משיחים (meshichim — 'anointed ones,' H4899, plural of mashiach). Greek has ὅτι Χριστοῦ ἐστε ('because you are of Christ'). The Hebrew says the disciples ARE meshichim — anointed ones (plural, predicative). The Greek says they BELONG TO the Christ (singular, possessive). A back-translator from Greek would write של המשיח ('of the Messiah' — singular possessive), not 'you are meshichim' (anointed ones — plural). This reflects a Hebrew understanding where Messiah's followers share in his anointing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'you are anointed-ones' (plural identity). Greek: 'you are of Christ' (singular belonging). Fundamentally different: shared anointing vs. possessive relationship.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — GARDEN OF EDEN: Uses גן עדן (Gan Eden — 'Garden of Eden,' H1588 + H5731) where Greek has ζωήν ('life'). The Hebrew says 'enter the Garden of Eden' — the paradise of Genesis 2-3. Greek merely says 'enter into life.' A back-translator from Greek would write חיים (chayyim — 'life'), NEVER 'Garden of Eden.' The Hebrew preserves the native Jewish eschatological destination: return to the Garden of Eden. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire Gospel.

CRITICAL — GEI-HINNOM: Uses גיהנם (Gei-Hinnom — the Valley of Hinnom, H1516 + H2011). While Greek γέεννα is a transliteration of this, the crucial point is the PAIRING: Garden of Eden vs. Gei-Hinnom. In Hebrew, the eschatological contrast is native — Eden (paradise) vs. the valley where children were burned to Molech (2 Kings 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:6). In Greek, the pair is 'life' vs. 'Gehenna' — which loses the Edenic contrast entirely.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Garden of Eden.' Greek: 'life' (ζωήν). Entirely different destination concept.
Greek adds εἰς τὸ πῦρ τὸ ἄσβεστον ('into the unquenchable fire'). Hebrew has 'fire of Gei-Hinnom.'
translation_notes: The Garden of Eden / Gei-Hinnom contrast creates a Genesis-framed eschatology: humanity's choice is between returning to Eden or descending to the valley of burning.
textual_notes: Gei-Hinnom (the Valley of Hinnom) — south of Jerusalem, where Molech worship with child sacrifice occurred (2 Kings 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2-6, 32:35). It became the symbol of divine judgment in Jewish eschatology.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VENOMOUS THINGS: Uses הארסים (ha'arsim — 'the venomous things,' from ארס, eres — 'venom/poison'). Greek has ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν ('their worm'). The Hebrew does NOT say 'worm' — it says 'venomous things,' connecting to Numbers 21:6 where YHWH sent נחשים שרפים ('fiery/venomous serpents'). A back-translator from Greek 'worm' (σκώληξ) would use תולעת (tola'at — 'worm'), NEVER ארסים. The venomous things in Gei-Hinnom are serpent-like creatures of judgment — not common worms.

Uses אינו נח (eino nach — 'does not rest'), from נוח (nuach, H5117 — 'to rest'). This is the Sabbath-rest verb — the root of Noah's name. Greek has οὐ σβέννυται ('is not quenched'). The fire is described as anti-rest, anti-Sabbath — it finds no nuach. A back-translator from Greek would use לא תכבה ('is not extinguished'), not the theologically loaded 'does not rest.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'venomous things' (ארסים). Greek: 'worm' (σκώληξ). Entirely different creature.
Hebrew: 'the fire does not rest.' Greek: 'the fire is not quenched.' Different attribute: restlessness vs. unquenchability.
translation_notes: Both the 'venomous things' and the 'restless fire' quote Isaiah 66:24 — 'their worm (תולעתם) shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.' But the Hebrew here uses ארסים instead of Isaiah's תולעת, suggesting an independent interpretive tradition about the nature of these creatures.
textual_notes: Isaiah 66:24 is the source text. The Hebrew Gospels' use of ארסים instead of תולעת shows the Hebrew author is interpreting, not merely quoting — identifying Isaiah's 'worms' as venomous/serpentine creatures.

translation_notes: In this final repetition, the Hebrew uses נכבית (nikhbet — 'is extinguished,' H3518, from כבה) rather than the earlier נח ('rests'). The fire has two attributes across the three repetitions: it does not rest (v44,46) and it is not extinguished (v48).

greek_deviations: Greek: πᾶς γὰρ πυρὶ ἁλισθήσεται ('everyone shall be salted with fire'). Hebrew uses יתעלם — possibly from עלם ('hidden/concealed') or a corrupted form. The meanings diverge significantly. The Greek connects directly to the salt discussion in v50; the Hebrew is more obscure.
translation_notes: This verse is textually difficult. The verb יתעלם may be from עלם (alam — 'to conceal/hide') or could be a corruption. The second clause 'כל אדם מרוצח' could mean 'every slain offering' (from רצח). The verse seems to describe a refining/purifying process by fire.

one_way_hebrew: Pairs מלח (melach — 'salt') and שלום (shalom — 'peace'). In Hebrew, the 'salt covenant' (ברית מלח, Num 18:19, 2 Chr 13:5) is a covenant of perpetual peace/preservation. The closing 'let there be salt among you and peace among you' ties salt to covenant-peace — a Hebrew theology of salt invisible in Greek.

Uses נבשל (nevasherl, H1310 — 'shall we cook/season'), from בשל (bashal — 'to cook/boil'). Greek ἀρτύσετε ('will you season') is about general seasoning. The Hebrew word specifically refers to cooking — salt as a cooking ingredient for the Temple offerings (Lev 2:13 — 'with all your offerings you shall offer salt').
textual_notes: Leviticus 2:13 — 'You shall season with salt every offering of your grain offering; you shall not allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be absent from your grain offering.' The command links salt, covenant, and offerings.

10.summary: Mark 10 in Hebrew contains several major one-way markers. (1) נפילים (Nephilim, v33) replaces Greek 'gentiles' — the Hebrew author views the Romans as the biblical Nephilim, the violent fallen giants of Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33. No back-translator would replace 'gentiles' with 'Nephilim.' (2) ספר כריתות ('letter of cutting-off/divorce', v4) preserves the Deuteronomic legal terminology with its covenant-cutting metaphor. (3) בן האלוה/האל ('Son of God') again replaces 'Son of Man' in vv33 and 45. (4) יצר ('formed', v6) uses the Genesis 2:7 potter-verb rather than generic 'made.' (5) נחלות ('estates/inheritances', vv22,29) frames the rich man's wealth as tribal land-inheritance rather than generic possessions. (6) שפל ותמים ('humble and blameless', v15) adds two OT-loaded qualities absent from Greek. (7) משפחה ממאנת carries forward the 'refusing family' pattern. (8) באורך ('in your light', v37) again replaces Greek 'in your glory.' (9) Bar-Timai is described as יבש ('withered') not 'blind' — a completely different affliction. The chapter also preserves the Garden of Eden / Gei-Hinnom eschatological geography from chapter 9 by implication, and the פדיון ('ransom/redemption', v45) invokes the Torah's firstborn-redemption price for Yeshua's self-offering.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דורש (doresh — 'expounds/interprets', from דרש H1875 — 'to seek/inquire/expound'). This is the specific rabbinic term for Torah exposition — the same root as מדרש (midrash). Greek has ἐδίδασκεν ('he taught'). A back-translator from 'taught' would use לימד (limed), not the midrashic exposition verb.

Uses ספר כריתות (sefer keritut — 'letter of cutting-off/divorce', H5612 + H3748). The root כרת (karat — 'to cut') gives divorce its Hebrew meaning: a CUTTING of the covenant bond. Greek has βιβλίον ἀποστασίου ('certificate of standing-apart/abandonment'). The Hebrew frames divorce as cutting a covenant (like כרת ברית — 'cutting a covenant'); the Greek frames it as departure/standing apart. These are different conceptual metaphors that would not cross in translation.
This is a direct reference to Deuteronomy 24:1: 'he shall write her a letter of divorce (ספר כריתת).' The Hebrew preserves the Deuteronomic legal terminology verbatim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'letter of cutting-off' (כריתות — covenant-cutting). Greek: 'certificate of standing-apart' (ἀποστάσιον — departure/divorce). Different metaphors for the same legal act.
translation_notes: 'Letter of divorce' for sefer keritut — literally 'scroll of cutting.' The divorce document cuts the marriage covenant.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 24:1: 'When a man takes a wife and marries her, if she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some indecency in her, he shall write her a letter of divorce (ספר כריתת) and put it in her hand and send her out of his house.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses רוע לבבכם (ro'a levavkhem — 'the wickedness of your hearts'). Greek has πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ('for your hardness of heart'). Hebrew: the heart is WICKED (רע — evil/bad). Greek: the heart is HARD (σκληρός). Different moral diagnoses: moral corruption vs. emotional stubbornness.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'wickedness of your hearts' (רוע — moral evil). Greek: 'hardness of your hearts' (σκληροκαρδία — stubbornness). Different heart conditions.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יצר (yatzar — 'formed/fashioned', H3335) — the specific creation verb from Genesis 2:7 (ויצר יהוה אלהים את האדם — 'and YHWH God formed the man'). Greek has ἐποίησεν ('made'). A back-translator from 'made' would use עשה (asah — 'made'), not the potter-verb יצר. The Hebrew author reaches for the Genesis 2 formation vocabulary — God as the potter fashioning humanity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'formed' (יצר — potter's craft, Gen 2:7). Greek: 'made' (ἐποίησεν — general creation). Different creation vocabulary.
textual_notes: Genesis 1:27: 'male and female he created them.' Genesis 2:7: 'YHWH God formed (ויצר) man from the dust of the ground.' The Hebrew combines both Genesis accounts.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ויקח אשה (ve-yiqach ishah — 'and take a wife'). The OT Genesis 2:24 and the Greek both say 'and shall cleave to his wife' (ודבק באשתו / κολληθήσεται πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ). The Hebrew Gospel substitutes 'take' (לקח) for 'cleave' (דבק). A back-translator from Greek would preserve 'cleave.' The Hebrew uses the common OT idiom for marriage: לקח אשה ('to take a wife' — Gen 4:19, 6:2, 11:29, 12:19).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'and take a wife' (לקח — marriage idiom). Greek: 'and shall cleave to his wife' (κολλάω — adhesion). Different verbs, both expressing marriage but from different perspectives.

textual_notes: Genesis 2:24 verbatim: 'and they shall become one flesh' (והיו לבשר אחד).

one_way_hebrew: Uses יפריד (yafrid — 'shall separate', from פרד H6504 — the root of 'Pharisee' פרושים). Yeshua uses the Pharisee-root verb: 'No man shall pharisee-ize/separate what God has joined.' The irony: the Separatists ask about divorce (separation), and Yeshua says separation is forbidden — using their own root word against them.

Uses בעלה (ba'alah — 'her lord/husband', H1167). בעל (ba'al) means 'lord/master/owner' and is the standard Hebrew word for husband emphasizing authority. Greek has τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς ('her man/husband'). The Hebrew preserves the patriarchal marriage structure embedded in the language.

Uses דורון (doron — 'gift/present', H1890). Greek has προσέφερον αὐτῷ παιδία ('they brought children to him'). The Hebrew frames the children as a GIFT presented to the teacher — an offering of young souls. A back-translator from 'brought' would use הביאו (hevi'u — 'they brought'), not the gift-giving word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sent him a gift of youths' (דורון — gift/offering). Greek: 'they brought children to him' (προσφέρω — present/bring). Different framing: gift vs. presentation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חימה (chemah — 'wrath/fury', H2534) — the OT word for divine fury (Deut 29:27, 2 Kings 22:13, Isa 51:17, Jer 25:15). Greek has ἠγανάκτησεν ('was indignant/annoyed'). Hebrew: full of WRATH. Greek: indignant. The Hebrew emotion is far stronger — this is the anger of God, not mere annoyance. A back-translator from 'indignant' would use כעס (ka'as — 'vexed'), not the divine-fury word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'full of wrath' (חימה — divine fury). Greek: 'was indignant' (ἀγανακτέω — annoyed). Much stronger emotion in Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: Adds שפל ותמים (shafal ve-tamim — 'humble and blameless') — two qualities absent from Greek. Greek simply says 'whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child' (ὡς παιδίον). The Hebrew adds TWO specific moral qualities: שפל (shafal, H8217 — 'lowly/humble', the opposite of proud) and תמים (tamim, H8549 — 'blameless/whole/perfect' — the word used for Noah in Gen 6:9 and for sacrificial animals without blemish). A back-translator from Greek would not add these OT-loaded qualities.

תמים (tamim — 'blameless/complete', H8549) is the word YHWH uses for Abraham: 'Walk before me and be tamim' (Gen 17:1). Also the requirement for Passover lambs (Ex 12:5) and all sacrifices (Lev 1:3, 3:1). The kingdom requires the wholeness of a sacrificial lamb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'humble and blameless' (שפל ותמים) — absent from Greek, which only has the child comparison.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נעשה (na'aseh — 'shall WE do', first person plural). Greek has τί ποιήσω ('what shall I do', first person singular). The Hebrew man speaks inclusively — 'what shall WE do?' — whereas the Greek is individual. The Hebrew framing is communal.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'what shall we do to obtain the kingdom of heaven?' (communal, with 'kingdom of heaven'). Greek: 'what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' (individual, with 'eternal life'). Different goals and different scope.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לא תונה שום אדם (lo toneh shum adam — 'you shall not oppress any man', from ינה/הונה H3238 — 'to oppress/wrong/defraud'). This is the specific Torah verb for oppressing the stranger and the vulnerable (Ex 22:20 'You shall not oppress (לא תונה) a stranger'; Lev 19:33, 25:14,17; Deut 23:17). Greek has μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς ('do not defraud'). The Hebrew verb carries the full weight of Torah's protection of the weak; the Greek is narrower (financial fraud).

Uses נחלות (nachalot — 'estates/inheritances', H5159). This is the OT word for tribal land-inheritance — the allotted portions of the Promised Land (Josh 13-19, Num 26:53, 34:2, Deut 4:38). Greek has κτήματα πολλά ('many possessions'). A back-translator from 'possessions' would use קניינים or רכוש, not the land-inheritance word. The Hebrew implies the man's wealth is in ancestral land — the nachalah that belongs to the tribe.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'many estates/inheritances' (נחלות — tribal land). Greek: 'many possessions' (κτήματα — property). Different type of wealth.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבטח בעושרו (yivtach be-oshro — 'trusts in his riches', from בטח H982 — 'to trust/rely upon'). This is the OT language: Psalm 52:9 'the man who did not make God his refuge, but trusted (בטח) in the abundance of his riches'; Proverbs 11:28 'Whoever trusts (בוטח) in his riches shall fall.' Greek adds this in some manuscripts but the Hebrew's phrasing directly quotes the Psalms/Proverbs vocabulary.
textual_notes: Psalm 52:9: 'See the man who would not make God his stronghold, but trusted in the abundance of his riches.' Yeshua echoes this psalm precisely.
Genesis 18:14: 'Is anything too wonderful (הֲיִפָּלֵא) for YHWH?' The same theological principle.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אהבתי (ahavati — 'my love', H160). Greek has ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ ('for my sake'). The Hebrew says 'for the sake of my LOVE' — a more intimate and relational phrasing. A back-translator from 'for my sake' would write בעדי or למעני, not the love-language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'for the sake of my love' (אהבתי — personal love). Greek: 'for my sake' (ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ — on my account). More intimate in Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: Uses העולם הבא (ha-olam ha-ba — 'the world to come'). This is the standard rabbinic eschatological term for the age of resurrection and eternal life. Greek has ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τῷ ἐρχομένῳ ('in the coming age'). While similar, the Hebrew is the native rabbinic concept from which the Greek is derived.

CRITICAL: Uses נפילים (Nephilim, H5303) where Greek has τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ('the gentiles/nations'). The Nephilim are the fallen ones/giants of Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33 — the violent offspring of fallen beings who filled the earth with violence. A back-translator from Greek 'gentiles' would use גוים (goyim — 'nations'), NEVER Nephilim. The Hebrew author views the Romans through the lens of the biblical Nephilim — monstrous offspring of fallen powers who rule by brute force. This is one of the most striking one-way markers in the entire Gospel.
Again uses בן האל (ben ha-El — 'Son of God') where Greek has υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man').
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Nephilim' (נפילים — fallen giants of Gen 6:4). Greek: 'gentiles' (ἔθνεσιν — nations). Completely different characterization of the Romans.
Hebrew: 'Son of God.' Greek: 'Son of Man.' Consistent pattern.
translation_notes: 'Nephilim' — the fallen ones of Genesis 6:4. The Hebrew characterizes the Roman occupiers as the biblical Nephilim: violent, powerful, and the product of spiritual corruption.
textual_notes: Genesis 6:4: 'The Nephilim were on the earth in those days... they were the mighty men of old, men of renown.' Numbers 13:33: 'We saw the Nephilim... and we were like grasshoppers in our own sight.' The Hebrew author sees Rome as the Nephilim — the giants who make Israel feel like grasshoppers.

one_way_hebrew: Uses באורך (be-orekha — 'in your light', from אור H216 — 'light'). Greek has ἐν τῇ δόξῃ σου ('in your glory'). Same pattern as Mark 8:38 — 'light' where Greek has 'glory.' The Hebrew associates the kingdom with divine light (Gen 1:3, Ps 104:2 'wrapped in light as a garment'); the Greek associates it with glory/honor. A back-translator from 'glory' would use בכבודך.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in your light' (אור). Greek: 'in your glory' (δόξα). Consistent pattern.

Hebrew is extremely condensed — Greek has a fuller exchange: 'They said to him: We are able. And Yeshua said to them: You shall indeed drink of the cup... and be immersed.' The Hebrew preserves only Yeshua's concluding statement.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses חימה (chemah — 'wrath/fury', H2534) where Greek has ἠγανάκτησαν ('were indignant'). Same pattern as v14 — the Hebrew emotion is divine fury, not mere annoyance.
Again uses בן האלוה (ben ha-eloah — 'Son of God') where Greek has υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man').

Uses פדיון (pidyon — 'ransom/redemption', H6306). This is the specific Torah redemption price — the ransom for the firstborn (Num 3:46-49, 18:15-16), the ransom for a life (Ex 21:30). Greek has λύτρον ('ransom'). While equivalent, the Hebrew word carries the full firstborn-redemption theology of the Torah.
translation_notes: 'Ransom' for pidyon — the Torah's redemption price. Yeshua gives his soul as the pidyon — the firstborn-redemption price — for the many.
textual_notes: Numbers 18:15: 'Everything that opens the womb... you shall redeem (תפדה)... the redemption price (פדיון) you shall pay.' The Son of God pays the firstborn's redemption price.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבש (yavesh — 'withered/dried up', H3001). Greek has τυφλός ('blind'). The Hebrew says the man was WITHERED, not BLIND. Different affliction entirely. The verb יבש describes a dried/withered condition — like the withered hand in Mark 3:1 or Ezekiel's dry bones (Ezek 37:2). A back-translator from 'blind' would use עור (iver — 'blind'), not יבש.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'withered' (יבש — dried up). Greek: 'blind' (τυφλός). Different disability.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הושיעך (hoshi'akha — 'has saved you', from ישע H3467 — 'to save'). This is the root of Yeshua's own name (ישוע). The wordplay: Yeshua (ישוע) says 'your faith has SAVED (הושיע) you' — the salvation is embedded in the Savior's name.

11.summary: Mark 11 in Hebrew centers on the Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing. The strongest one-way markers are: (1) הושיענו מושיע ('Save us, O Savior!', v9) where Greek has the transliterated ὡσαννά — the Hebrew UNPACKS the Hosanna, making it both a prayer and a messianic title. No back-translator from the Greek transliteration would produce this expanded form. (2) המלך מושיע משמים ('the King, the Savior, from heaven', v10) vs. Greek's 'the coming kingdom of our father David' — completely different proclamations (a person vs. a system). (3) מגדול ('tower', v2) vs. Greek 'village' — a different place designation. (4) עיר (ayir — 'colt', v2) — the specific Zechariah 9:9 word for the donkey of the messianic entry. (5) גירש ('drove out/expelled', v15) — the Eden-expulsion verb applied to the Temple cleansing, framing it as a divine expulsion like Genesis 3:24. (6) עונותיכם ('your iniquities', v25) vs. Greek 'trespasses' — a heavier moral category. The chapter preserves both OT quotations (Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11) in their original Hebrew form.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'at the Mount of Olives' only. Greek: 'to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives' (πρὸς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν πρὸς τὸ ὄρος τῶν ἐλαιῶν). Hebrew omits Bethphage and Bethany.
textual_notes: Zechariah 14:4: 'On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives.' The Hebrew preserves the Zechariah eschatological connection.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגדול (migdol — 'tower', H4026) where Greek has κώμην ('village'). A back-translator from 'village' would use כפר (kfar) or עיר (ir — 'town'). The Hebrew calls the destination a 'tower' — possibly a watchtower settlement or fortified village. The word מגדל is used for the Tower of Babel (Gen 11:4), the tower in the vineyard (Isa 5:2), and watchtowers (2 Kings 9:17, 17:9).

Uses עיר (ayir — 'colt/young donkey', H5895). This is the specific OT word from Zechariah 9:9: 'humble and riding upon a donkey, upon a colt (עיר) the foal of a she-donkey.' Greek has πῶλον ('colt'). While both mean 'colt,' the Hebrew uses the exact Zechariah prophecy word. A back-translator could use several words for 'colt'; the Hebrew author specifically chose the prophetic term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tower' (מגדול). Greek: 'village' (κώμη). Different destination type.
textual_notes: Zechariah 9:9: 'Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion... your king comes to you, righteous and saved, humble and riding upon a donkey, upon a colt (עיר) the foal of a she-donkey.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הושיענו מושיע (hoshi'enu moshia — 'save us, O Savior!'). Greek has ὡσαννά ('Hosanna'). The Greek merely transliterates the Hebrew הושע נא (hosha na — 'save, please'). But the Hebrew text UNPACKS it: 'save us' (הושיענו) + 'O Savior' (מושיע) — making the cry both a prayer AND a title. The crowd calls him מושיע (Moshia — 'Savior'). A back-translator from the Greek transliteration ὡσαννά would write הושענא — the transliterated form — NOT the expanded 'save us, O Savior.' The Hebrew gives the FULL liturgical meaning.
Double ברוך ברוך (barukh barukh — 'blessed, blessed') — emphatic doubling not in Greek, which has only one ὡσαννά followed by εὐλογημένος. The doubling is a Hebrew intensification device.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Save us, O Savior!' (הושיענו מושיע — prayer + title). Greek: 'Hosanna!' (ὡσαννά — transliterated exclamation). Hebrew unpacks the meaning; Greek preserves the sound.
Hebrew doubles 'blessed, blessed.' Greek has single 'blessed.'
translation_notes: Psalm 118:25-26 is the source: 'Save us, please (הושיעה נא), YHWH! ... Blessed is the one who comes in the Name of YHWH.' The Hebrew preserves the psalmic prayer.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המלך מושיע משמים (ha-melekh moshia mi-shamayim — 'the King, the Savior, from the heavens'). Greek has ἡ ἐρχομένη βασιλεία τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Δαυΐδ ('the coming kingdom of our father David'). Completely different proclamations: Hebrew acclaims a PERSON (the King-Savior from heaven); Greek acclaims a THING (the coming kingdom of David). A back-translator would never convert 'the coming kingdom of our father David' into 'the King, the Savior, from heaven.'
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'blessed is the King, the Savior, from heaven' (a person). Greek: 'blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David' (a system). Entirely different objects of blessing.

translation_notes: בית עניה (Beit Aniyah — 'House of Poverty/Affliction'). The Hebrew place name is meaningful: the King-Savior lodges in the 'House of Affliction.'

textual_notes: The fig tree as a symbol of Israel: Jeremiah 8:13 'I will surely consume them, says YHWH: no grapes on the vine, no figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall wither.' Hosea 9:10 'I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers like the first fruit on the fig tree.' The fig tree's failure to produce fruit despite showing leaves symbolizes Israel's outward piety without inner fruit.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גירש (gerash — 'drove out/expelled', H1644). This is the verb God uses when expelling Adam from Eden (Gen 3:24: ויגרש את האדם — 'and he drove out the man') and when Israel drove out the Canaanites (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27, Josh 24:12,18). Greek has ἤρξατο ἐκβάλλειν ('began to cast out'). The Hebrew frames the Temple cleansing as an EXPULSION — the same act as the expulsion from Eden and the expulsion of the nations.

VERBATIM OT QUOTATIONS: (1) Isaiah 56:7 — בית תפלה לכל העמים ('a house of prayer for all the peoples'). The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact wording. (2) Jeremiah 7:11 — מערת גנבים (me'arat gannavim — 'a den of robbers'). Both prophetic quotations are preserved in their original Hebrew form. A back-translator from Greek would produce similar text, but the Hebrew IS the source text of both prophecies.
textual_notes: Isaiah 56:7: 'For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.' Jeremiah 7:11: 'Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?'

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Let there be good faith in HaShem.' Greek: ἔχετε πίστιν θεοῦ ('Have faith of/in God'). The Hebrew adds טובה ('good') — qualifying the faith.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אהבתכם (ahavatkhem — 'your love', H160). Greek has no equivalent phrasing — it simply says 'whatever you ask in prayer.' The Hebrew frames the teaching as motivated by love for the disciples.

Uses עונותיכם (avonoteikhem — 'your iniquities', H5771). Greek has τὰ παραπτώματα ὑμῶν ('your trespasses'). Hebrew עון (avon — 'iniquity') is heavier than Greek παράπτωμα ('trespass/misstep'). Avon implies deep moral twisting/perversion (Gen 4:13, 15:16, Ps 32:5, 51:4, Isa 53:5,6); trespass implies stepping over a boundary. A back-translator from 'trespass' would use פשע (pesha — 'transgression'), not the deeper עון.

Uses תרעומת (tar'omet — 'complaint/grievance', H8519). Greek has εἴ τι ἔχετε κατά τινος ('if you have anything against anyone'). The Hebrew uses a specific noun for the grievance; the Greek uses a general construction.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your iniquities' (עונות — deep moral failings). Greek: 'your trespasses' (παραπτώματα — boundary violations). Different severity.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נפלאות (nifla'ot — 'wonders', H6381) — the OT word for God's miraculous acts. Greek has ταῦτα ('these things'). The Hebrew specifies 'wonders'; the Greek says merely 'things.' The Hebrew frames the question in terms of divine wonder-working authority.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'these wonders' (נפלאות — miraculous acts). Greek: 'these things' (ταῦτα — generic). Hebrew is more specific.

12.summary: Mark 12 in Hebrew contains several critical one-way translation markers. The most significant are: (1) אטדים (thorns, v1) vs. Greek fence — the vineyard enclosed with thorns that foreshadow the sons crown of thorns, using the OT word from Judges 9:14-15; (2) עובדי אדמה (workers of the ground, v1) echoing Genesis 2-3 adam/adamah pattern; (3) תמונה (image, v16) — the Second Commandment word, framing Caesars coin as idolatry; (4) אמר האדון לאדוני (The Lord said to my lord, v36) — Psalm 110:1 preserving the distinction between YHWH (האדון) and the messianic lord (אדוני), invisible in Greek; (5) קרבן אנושי (human offering, v33); (6) ארון האוצר (treasury ark, v41) connecting to the Ark of the Covenant; (7) פרוטות (perutot, v42) using Jewish coins with no Roman equivalent.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses באטדים (ba'atadim, H329 'with thorns/brambles'). Greek has phragnon ('fence/hedge'). The Hebrew word atad appears in Judg 9:14-15 and Gen 50:10-11. A back-translator from Greek 'fence' would use geder, NOT atadim. The thorns foreshadow the crown of thorns placed on the son.
Uses עובדי אדמה (ovdei adamah 'workers of the ground'), echoing Genesis 2:5, 3:23. Greek has georgois ('farmers'). A back-translator would use ikkarim, not the Genesis-laden ovdei adamah.
Uses דמיונות (dimyonot 'likenesses/parables'), from damah ('to be like'). A natively developed Hebrew form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'enclosed with thorns' (באטדים). Greek: 'put a fence around it'. Different enclosure.
textual_notes: The parable draws from Isaiah 5:1-7, preserving the same vocabulary.

greek_deviations: Greek adds: 'and many others, beating some and killing some.' Hebrew is more concise.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יקר (yaqar, H3368 'precious/costly/rare'), consistent with 9:7. Greek has agapeton ('beloved'). Hebrew consistently uses 'precious' where Greek uses 'beloved.'
Uses ישאו כבוד ('shall bear honor'). Greek has entrapesontai ('will respect'). Hebrew: active honor-lifting. Greek: internal emotional response.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'very precious.' Greek: 'beloved.'
Hebrew: 'will bear honor.' Greek: 'will respect.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses יכלה (yekhaleh, H3615 'shall destroy/annihilate'). The word for total destruction (Gen 41:30, Deut 28:21). Greek apolesei ('shall destroy') is similar but lacks the annihilation weight.

Uses מונחת (munachat 'laid/resting'), from nuach (H5117). Greek egenthe ('became'). The stone 'rests' at the corner using the Sabbath-rest verb. A back-translator would use na'asetah, not the theologically loaded nuach.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'was laid for the corner.' Greek: 'became the head of the corner.' Hebrew lacks 'head.'
textual_notes: Quotes Psalm 118:22-23, a Hallel psalm sung at Passover and Sukkot.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'by our God.' Greek: 'from the Lord.' Hebrew uses personal possessive; Greek uses title.
textual_notes: Psalm 118:23 continuation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אנשי הורדוס ('men of Hordos'), a Hebrew construct. Greek has Herodianon ('Herodians') a Grecized party name. A back-translator would transliterate, not create the native Hebrew construct.
Uses אינך שופט לפי הפנים ('you do not judge by the face') the Deuteronomic impartiality idiom (Deut 1:17, 16:19).
Uses חוייבנו ('are we obligated') Hebrew legal obligation term. Greek exestin ('is it lawful') asks about permission. Different legal categories: duty vs. permission.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Are we obligated?' (duty). Greek: 'Is it lawful?' (permission).

one_way_hebrew: Uses פשוט (pashut 'a simple coin'), later Hebrew colloquial. Greek has denarion ('denarius'). A back-translator would transliterate dinar, not use Hebrew slang.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a coin' (generic). Greek: 'a denarius' (specific Roman coin).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תמונה (temunah, H8544), the EXACT word from the Second Commandment (Deut 5:8, Ex 20:4). Caesar's image on the coin is framed as violating the commandment against images. Greek eikon ('image/icon') lacks this resonance. A back-translator would use tselem, not the commandment-loaded temunah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'inscription upon the top.' Greek: epigraphe ('inscription'). Hebrew gives concrete physical description.
textual_notes: The use of תמונה creates ironic tension: religious leaders carry coins bearing a temunah while testing the Torah teacher.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תחייה (techiyyah 'revival'), from chayah (H2421 'to live'). Hebrew focuses on LIFE; Greek anastasin on RISING. Different conceptual frame.

textual_notes: References Deuteronomy 25:5-6 levirate marriage law.

one_way_hebrew: Uses השם (HaShem 'the Name'), the distinctly Jewish reverential substitute for the divine name. Greek has tou theou ('of God'). A back-translator would write ha'Elohim, never HaShem.
Uses בעלים (be'alim 'husbands/masters', H1167). Hebrew explicitly addresses BOTH directions: women shall not have husbands, men shall not have wives. Greek is gender-asymmetric.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'not have wives, nor husbands.' Greek: 'neither marry nor are given in marriage.'

textual_notes: Exodus 3:6: 'I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses העקרי (ha'iqari 'the principal/root'). Greek has prote panton ('first of all'). Hebrew seeks the root; Greek seeks the rank.
Adds בישראל ('in Yisrael'). Greek omits 'in Israel.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'which is the principal in Israel?' Greek: 'which is the first of all?'

one_way_hebrew: The Shema (Deut 6:4). Uses אלהיך ('your God' 2nd person) vs. standard אלהינו ('our God'). Greek preserves 1st person 'our'; the Hebrew shifts to 'your' a teaching adaptation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your God' (2nd person). Greek: 'our God' (1st person).
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 6:4: שמע ישראל יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד

one_way_hebrew: Adds מחשבך (machshavtekha 'your mind'). Original Deut 6:5 has three: heart, soul, might. Both Hebrew and Greek here have FOUR. Hebrew uses מחשבה ('thought/plan') while Greek uses dianoias ('intellect'). Different cognitive concepts.
textual_notes: Deut 6:5: heart (לבב), soul (נפש), might (מאד). The Hebrew Gospels replace מאד with כח and add מחשבה.
Leviticus 19:18: ואהבת לרעך כמוך.
Echoes Deuteronomy 4:35: 'YHWH, He is God; there is no other besides Him.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קרבן אנושי (qorban enoshi 'human offering'). Greek has holokautomaton kai thysion ('whole burnt offerings and sacrifices'). Hebrew has one compact phrase; Greek specifies two types. A back-translator would list two types, not compress to qorban enoshi.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'any human offering' (one phrase). Greek: 'whole burnt offerings and sacrifices' (two types).
textual_notes: Echoes Hosea 6:6 and 1 Samuel 15:22.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Whose son is he?' (open question). Greek specifies 'the Christ is the son of David.' Hebrew omits, leaving it open.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL - PSALM 110: Uses אמר האדון לאדוני ('The Lord said to my lord'). This preserves the crucial distinction: האדון (ha'Adon YHWH) vs. אדוני (adoni 'my lord,' the messianic king). Greek uses kurios for both, making the distinction INVISIBLE. Only Hebrew shows YHWH speaks to a human lord. This is a fundamental one-way marker.

Uses מתנבא (mitnabbe 'prophesying'). Greek has 'in the Holy Spirit.' Hebrew: prophetic act. Greek: spiritual inspiration. A back-translator would write b'ruach haqodesh, not the simple prophetic verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'David said, prophesying.' Greek: 'David said in the Holy Spirit.'
Hebrew: האדון / אדוני (two forms). Greek: kurios / kurio mou (same word). Distinction invisible in Greek.
translation_notes: אדוני (adoni 'my lord') is the KEY term. This is NOT Adonai (divine substitute) but adoni (human address). David calls the Messiah 'my lord,' distinguishing him from YHWH.
textual_notes: Psalm 110:1: Most-quoted OT verse in the NT.

one_way_hebrew: ברצון (b'ratzon 'with favor/delight'), from ratzon (H7522). Greek hedeos ('gladly'). Hebrew ratzon is the sacrificial acceptance term (Lev 1:3, Ps 19:15). A back-translator would use b'simchah, not the sacrificial term.
Uses יודעי ספר ('who know the book') native Hebrew scribal description. Greek has grammateon ('scribes').
Uses הסוחרים (hasocharim 'the merchants'). Greek has 'in the marketplaces.' Hebrew specifies WHO; Greek specifies WHERE. A back-translator would write bashvakim, not 'the merchants.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'merchants give greetings.' Greek: 'greetings in the marketplaces.' WHO vs. WHERE.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בתי כנסיות (batei knesiyot 'houses of assembly'), the native Hebrew term for synagogues.
Uses עוקרים (oqrim 'uproot'). Greek katesthiontes ('devour'). Hebrew: agricultural destruction. Greek: consumption. A back-translator would use okhlim, not oqer.
Adds ביום הדין ('day of judgment'). Greek has merely krima ('condemnation'). Hebrew adds eschatological Day.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'uproot houses.' Greek: 'devour houses.' Different imagery.
Hebrew: 'day of judgment.' Greek: 'greater condemnation.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses ארון האוצר ('treasury ark'), same word as the Ark of the Covenant. Greek has gazophulakion ('treasury'). A back-translator would use otsar, not aron.
Uses מתנדבים (mitnaddevim 'giving voluntarily'), from nadav (H5068). The freewill offering term (Lev 7:16, 22:21). Greek ballonta ('casting'). Hebrew emphasizes voluntary nature.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'treasury ark.' Greek: 'treasury.'
translation_notes: [ארון האוצר] is bracketed, indicating editorial restoration.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פרוטות (perutot), the smallest Jewish coin. Greek has lepta duo, ho estin kodrantes ('two lepta, which is a quadrans'). Greek gives BOTH Jewish and Roman equivalents. Hebrew uses only the Jewish denomination, no Roman conversion needed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'two perutot' (Jewish only). Greek: 'two lepta, which is a quadrans' (Jewish + Roman).

one_way_hebrew: Uses מאכלה (ma'akhalah 'her food'), from ma'akhal (H3978). Greek has holon ton bion ('her whole livelihood'). Hebrew is concrete, she gave her FOOD. Greek abstracts to 'livelihood.' A back-translator would use chayyah ('her life'), not 'food.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all her food' (concrete). Greek: 'all her livelihood' (abstract).

13.summary: Mark 13 in Hebrew presents the Olivet Discourse with several dramatic divergences from the Greek TR. The most striking one-way markers include: (1) שקוץ שומם (v14) — Daniel's EXACT participial phrase for the desolating abomination, which a back-translator would not reproduce; (2) בן האלוה (v26) — 'Son of God' where Greek has 'Son of Man,' an irreconcilable divergence representing independent traditions; (3) המלכות שממיי (v10) — 'kingdom of heaven' where Greek has 'the gospel,' entirely different objects of proclamation; (4) כנפות הארץ (v27) — 'wings of the earth' (Isaiah 11:12) where Greek has 'four winds'; (5) חלו פני האל (v18) — the specific OT prayer-idiom 'entreat the face of God' where Greek has merely 'pray'; (6) השם (vv19-20) — the reverential 'the Name' for God, a characteristically Jewish practice. The Hebrew also frames eschatology differently: the world will 'perish/rot' (ליפסד, v4) rather than be 'completed'; the fig tree signals 'the end' (v28) rather than 'summer'; kings fight kings (v8) rather than kingdoms fighting kingdoms. Throughout, the Hebrew draws on Daniel, Isaiah, and Micah in ways that could not derive from the Greek text.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המקדש (ha-miqdash, H4720 — 'the sanctuary') — the OT term for the sacred precinct (Ex 25:8, 1 Kgs 6:16, Ezek 37:26). Greek ἱερόν ('temple') is the broader term for the entire complex. A back-translator would more likely use בית המקדש ('house of the sanctuary'). The Hebrew uses the specific sacred-space word.
translation_notes: תלמידיו (talmidav — 'his disciples') is post-biblical Hebrew, from the root למד (lamad — 'to learn'). No standard Strong's number.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תהרס (tehares — 'shall be torn down', H2040) — the same verb used for the destruction of pagan altars (Judg 6:25, Ex 34:13) and the undoing of divine constructions (Jer 45:4). Greek καταλυθῇ ('shall be dissolved/destroyed') is more generic. A back-translator would use תחרב or תשחת, not the altar-demolition verb הרס.

Uses בסוד (be-sod, H5475 — 'in secret/counsel'). This is the OT term for intimate divine counsel (Jer 23:18,22 — 'who has stood in the sod of YHWH?'; Ps 25:14 — 'the sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'; Amos 3:7). Greek κατ' ἰδίαν ('privately') is merely spatial. The Hebrew frames this as a prophetic sod-session — the disciples entering Yeshua's inner counsel circle, just as prophets enter YHWH's sod. A back-translator from Greek would use בסתר or לבד, not the prophetic sod.
greek_deviations: Greek lists Peter, James, John, and Andrew (same four). No divergence in names, but the Hebrew's סוד framing is absent from Greek.
textual_notes: The four disciples mirror the first four called (Mark 1:16-20). The 'secret counsel' session on the Mount of Olives echoes Zechariah 14:4 where YHWH stands on the Mount of Olives.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ליפסד (le-yifased — 'to perish/spoil/decay') — a distinctly Hebraic verb from the root פסד ('to rot/corrupt'), used in rabbinic Hebrew for food spoiling and moral decay. Greek συντελεῖσθαι means 'to be completed/consummated.' These are OPPOSITE concepts — the Hebrew asks when things will ROT; the Greek asks when things will be COMPLETED. A back-translator from Greek would never produce פסד.

Uses הקץ (ha-qets — 'the end', H7093) — the eschatological term from Daniel 8:17, 11:35,40, 12:4,9,13. Greek συντέλεια ('completion') is related but distinct. The Hebrew directly invokes Daniel's apocalyptic vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the end of the world when all things shall begin to PERISH.' Greek: 'the sign of your coming and the COMPLETION of the age.' The Hebrew frames the eschaton as decay; the Greek as fulfillment. Entirely different eschatological perspectives.
Hebrew has a single question about the 'end of the world.' Greek has TWO distinct questions: (1) when shall these things be, and (2) what is the sign of the completion. The Hebrew conflates them.
translation_notes: 'Perish' for yifased — preserving the unique Hebrew concept of cosmic decay/rotting, absent from the Greek.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יונה (yoneh — 'oppress/deceive', H3238 from ינה) — the Torah verb for oppressing the stranger (Ex 22:20, Lev 19:33, 25:14,17). Greek πλανήσῃ ('lead astray') is about deception. The Hebrew warns against OPPRESSION, not mere deception — someone who would exploit and cheat them. A back-translator from Greek would use יתעה or ירמה, not the stranger-oppression verb.

Uses לעולם (la-olam — 'into the world/into eternity', H5769). Greek simply says ἐλεύσονται ('shall come'). The Hebrew adds 'into the world' — a characteristic Hebrew idiom for entering earthly existence, absent from the Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'saying that I am he' (שאני הוא). Greek: 'saying ἐγώ εἰμι (I AM).' Both preserve the echo of Exodus 3:14, but the Hebrew adds שאני ('that I') as a reporting clause.

Hebrew: 'many wars or BEGINNINGS of wars.' Greek: 'wars and RUMORS of wars' (ἀκοὰς πολέμων). Hebrew says 'beginnings' — wars starting; Greek says 'rumors' — reports about wars. Different concepts entirely.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מלך נגד מלך (melekh neged melekh — 'king against king', H4428 singular). Greek has βασιλεία ἐπὶ βασιλείαν ('kingdom against kingdom'). Hebrew speaks of KINGS (persons in conflict); Greek speaks of KINGDOMS (political entities at war). A back-translator from Greek 'kingdom' would write ממלכה נגד ממלכה, not 'king against king.' The Hebrew personalizes the conflict — wars originate from rulers, not abstractions.

Uses כאבים (ke'avim — 'sorrows/pains', H3511) — physical labor-pain language (Jer 22:23, Job 33:19). Greek ὠδίνων ('birth-pangs') shares the birth imagery but the Hebrew root כאב is broader, encompassing all physical suffering. Isaiah 13:8 uses חבלים for birth-pangs; this author chose a different pain word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'king against king.' Greek: 'kingdom against kingdom.' Singular vs. abstract.
Hebrew adds 'in the land' (בארץ) for earthquakes. Greek has 'in various places' (κατὰ τόπους).

one_way_hebrew: Uses בתי כנסיותיהם (batei kenisyoteihem — 'houses of their assemblies') — the compound Hebrew construction for synagogues using the native word כנסיה ('gathering/assembly'). Greek has συναγωγάς, a Greek calque of the same concept. The Hebrew uses a COMPOUND phrase ('houses of assembly') where the Greek has a single word. A back-translator would use בתי כנסת (the standard term), not this longer construction.

Uses שרים (sarim — 'rulers/princes', H8269) — the OT title for tribal/military/administrative leaders (Gen 12:15, Dan 10:13,20). Greek ἡγεμόνων ('governors') is a Roman administrative title. A back-translator from Greek would use פחות (pachot — 'governors') as in Ezra 8:36, not the Israelite sarim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to bring testimony OF ME in their witness.' Greek: 'as a testimony TO THEM' (εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς). The Hebrew says the testimony is ABOUT Yeshua; the Greek says it is directed AT them.
translation_notes: מועצותיהם (mo'atsoteihem — 'their councils') is post-biblical, from עצה (etsah — counsel, H6098).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses המלכות שממיי (ha-malkhut she-mi-shamayim — 'the kingdom of heaven', H4438+H8064). Greek has τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ('the gospel/good-news'). These are ENTIRELY different concepts. Hebrew says the KINGDOM OF HEAVEN must be proclaimed; Greek says the GOSPEL must be preached. A back-translator from Greek would write הבשורה ('the good-news'), not 'the kingdom of heaven.' This is among the strongest one-way markers in Mark 13 — the Hebrew author's concept of what must be spread to all nations is the REIGN OF HEAVEN, not a message about events.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the kingdom of heaven.' Greek: 'the gospel' (τὸ εὐαγγέλιον). Completely different object of proclamation.
Hebrew: 'to all the peoples' (לכל העמים). Greek: 'to all the nations' (εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη). Hebrew עמים and Greek ἔθνη overlap but עמים carries a more neutral 'peoples' connotation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הקדוש רוח (ha-qadosh ruach — 'the Holy Spirit') with adjective BEFORE noun — unusual Hebrew word order. The standard OT form is רוח הקדש (ruach ha-qodesh — 'spirit of holiness', Isa 63:10-11, Ps 51:13). Greek τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον follows standard Greek with article-noun-article-adjective. This reversed order is characteristic of later Sephardic Hebrew and could not derive from the Greek word order.

Uses יישרכם (yeyashrekhem — 'directs/guides you straight', H3474 from ישר). Greek δοθῇ ('shall be given'). The Hebrew says the Spirit will STRAIGHTEN/DIRECT them; the Greek says words will be GIVEN to them. Different models of inspiration — Hebrew: guidance; Greek: dictation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Holy Spirit directs you.' Greek: 'it is not you who speak but the Holy Spirit.' The Hebrew frames it as GUIDANCE; the Greek as REPLACEMENT of the speaker.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וינגשום (ve-yingshu-m — 'and shall oppress them', H5065) — the specific verb for tyrannical oppression of laborers and the downtrodden (Ex 3:7, Isa 3:12, 14:2). Greek θανατώσουσιν αὐτούς ('shall put them to death') simply means 'kill.' The Hebrew says they will OPPRESS them to death — a slow grinding persecution, not a quick execution. A back-translator from Greek would use ימיתום ('shall kill them').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall oppress them to death' (lingering persecution). Greek: 'shall put them to death' (execution).
Hebrew mentions 'mothers' (אמותם, plural). Greek has only 'parents' (γονεῖς). Hebrew specifies the maternal relationship.
textual_notes: Echoes Micah 7:6 — 'For the son treats the father with contempt, the daughter rises up against her mother.' The Hebrew preserves the Micah framework of familial betrayal.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יקציפו (yaqtsifu — 'shall rage/be furious', H7107) — the verb for divine and human wrath (Deut 1:34, 9:19; Eccl 5:5). Greek μισούμενοι ('being hated') is passive reception of hatred. Hebrew: the world will RAGE; Greek: you will be HATED. Active fury vs. passive endurance. A back-translator from Greek would write שנואים ('hated'), not the active wrath verb קצף.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all shall rage' (active). Greek: 'you shall be hated by all' (passive). Reversed grammatical perspective.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses השקוץ שומם (ha-shiquts shomem — 'the desolating abomination', H8251+H8074) — this is the EXACT phrase from Daniel 12:11 (שקוץ שומם) and closely parallels Daniel 9:27 (שקוצים משומם) and Daniel 11:31 (השקוץ משומם). Greek βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως ('the abomination of desolation') is a loose rendering that converts the Hebrew active participle שומם ('desolating') into a Greek genitive noun ('of desolation'). A back-translator from Greek would likely write תועבת השממה or שקוץ השממה — using a noun construct, not Daniel's exact participial form. The Hebrew preserves Daniel's precise grammar.

Uses עמוד (omod — 'standing', H5975) — a masculine participle. Greek ἑστηκότα is also masculine, but the Hebrew participle specifically echoes Daniel 12:11 where the abomination is SET UP (הנתן). The Hebrew envisions the abomination as a standing figure — possibly an idol or statue erected in sacred space.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'standing in a place that is not fitting' (שאין ראוי). Greek: 'standing where it ought not' (ὅπου οὐ δεῖ). Similar meaning but the Hebrew ראוי ('fitting/worthy') has a stronger moral/ritual valence than Greek δεῖ ('it is necessary').
translation_notes: 'Desolating abomination' preserves Daniel's participial grammar — the abomination actively desolates, it is not merely 'of desolation.'
textual_notes: Daniel 12:11: וּמֵעֵת הוּסַר הַתָּמִיד וְלָתֵת שִׁקּוּץ שֹׁמֵם — 'And from the time the continual offering is removed and the desolating abomination is set up.' The Hebrew Gospel preserves Daniel's exact phrase.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עלייה (aliyah, H5944 — 'upper room/roof chamber') — the specific architectural term for the rooftop room in Israelite houses (2 Kgs 4:10 — Elisha's upper room; Judg 3:20-25 — Eglon's upper room; 2 Sam 18:33 — David's upper room). Greek δώματος ('housetop/roof') is the external roof surface. Hebrew specifies a ROOM; Greek specifies a ROOF. A back-translator from Greek 'roof' would use גג (gag — 'roof'), not the upper-room term.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his garment' (בגדו, singular). Greek: 'his garments' (τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, singular also). Agreement here.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חלו פני האל (chalu penei ha-El — 'entreat the face of God', H2470+H6440+H410). This is a SPECIFIC OT idiom: חלה את פני ה' (Ex 32:11, 1 Sam 13:12, 1 Kgs 13:6, 2 Chr 33:12, Jer 26:19, Zech 8:21-22, Mal 1:9). Greek προσεύχεσθε ('pray') is generic. No back-translator from 'pray' would produce this specific three-word OT formula. The Hebrew author uses the covenantal prayer idiom — literally 'making God's face sweet.'

CRITICAL: Uses הקור (ha-qor — 'the cold', H7135). Greek χειμῶνος means 'winter' (the season). The Hebrew says 'the cold' — a weather condition, not a calendar season. Matthew's parallel adds 'nor on a Shabbat' (μηδὲ σαββάτῳ) which the Hebrew Mark lacks. The Hebrew concern is practical (cold weather for refugees in mountains) rather than calendrical.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'entreat the face of God' (specific OT prayer formula). Greek: 'pray' (generic).
Hebrew: 'in the time of the cold.' Greek: 'in winter.' Weather vs. season.
translation_notes: 'Entreat the face' preserves the OT idiom חלה פנים — literally to make the face sweet/favorable, the posture of supplication before a king or God.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses השם (ha-Shem — 'the Name') as a substitute for the divine name. This is a characteristically Jewish practice of reverential circumlocution (Lev 24:11,16). Greek has ὁ θεός ('God'). A back-translator from Greek would write אלהים ('God'), not the reverential השם. This substitution appears repeatedly in the Hebrew Mark and is a strong marker of Jewish authorial practice.

Uses שברא (she-bara — 'created', H1254) — the verb reserved exclusively for DIVINE creation in the OT (Gen 1:1,21,27, 2:3; Isa 40:26, 42:5). Greek ἔκτισεν is also 'created' but the Hebrew ברא carries the specific theological weight of creation ex nihilo. The combination 'the Name created the world' uses both Jewish reverential practice and Torah creation vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Name created the world' (השם). Greek: 'God created the creation' (ὁ θεὸς ἔκτισεν τὴν κτίσιν). The use of 'the Name' vs. 'God' is a fundamental divergence in divine reference.
Hebrew uses צרה (tsarah — 'distress/trouble', H6869). Greek uses θλῖψις ('tribulation/pressure'). The Hebrew term echoes 'the time of Jacob's trouble' (עֵת צָרָה, Jer 30:7; Dan 12:1).
textual_notes: Daniel 12:1: וְהָיְתָה עֵת צָרָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא נִהְיְתָה מִהְיוֹת גּוֹי עַד הָעֵת הַהִיא — 'And there shall be a time of distress such as never was since there was a nation until that time.' The Hebrew Mark echoes Daniel's exact language (עת צרה).

one_way_hebrew: Again uses השם (ha-Shem — 'the Name') for God — second occurrence in two verses, confirming this is the author's consistent practice, not a one-off choice.

Uses כל בשר (kol basar — 'all flesh', H3605+H1320) — the OT phrase for all living creatures (Gen 6:12,13,17,19; 7:15,16,21; 9:11,15,16,17; Isa 40:5,6, 49:26, 66:23). Greek πᾶσα σάρξ is a direct calque. Both traditions preserve the phrase, but the Hebrew is the original idiom.

Uses משיח (mashiach — 'anointed', H4899) — the OT term for one anointed with oil (1 Sam 2:10, 16:6, 24:7; Ps 2:2, 132:17; Dan 9:25-26). Greek Χριστός is a translation of this. Both converge here, but the Hebrew preserves the concrete physical meaning — 'smeared with oil' — while the Greek has become a proper name.

Uses שקרנים נביאים (shaqranim nevi'im — 'lying prophets') with the adjective BEFORE the noun. Greek has ψευδόχριστοι καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ('false-christs AND false-prophets'). The Hebrew has only 'lying prophets' — no mention of false anointed ones. Greek adds an entire category (false christs) absent from the Hebrew.

Uses אותות ונפלאות (otot u-mofetim/nifla'ot — 'signs and wonders', H226+H6382) — the standard OT pair from Deuteronomy 13:2-4 (the test of a false prophet) and Exodus 7:3 (the plagues). The Hebrew author frames the warning in Deuteronomy's false-prophet test language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'lying prophets' only. Greek: 'false-christs AND false-prophets.' Greek adds the 'false-christs' category.
Hebrew: 'to deceive' (לדמות). Greek: 'to deceive/lead astray' (πρὸς τὸ ἀποπλανᾶν). The Hebrew root דמה means 'to resemble/liken' — the false prophets make things SEEM like what they are not.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 13:2-4 — 'If a prophet arises among you and gives you a sign or wonder (אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵת), and the sign or wonder comes to pass... you shall not listen to that prophet.' The Hebrew Mark uses the exact Deuteronomy test language.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I say to you before it comes to pass.' Greek: 'I have told you all things beforehand' (προείρηκα ὑμῖν πάντα). Hebrew uses present tense; Greek uses perfect tense.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תזריח (tazriach — 'shall shine/rise', H2224 from זרח). Greek: οὐ δώσει τὸ φέγγος αὐτῆς ('shall not give its light'). Hebrew: the moon will not RISE/SHINE (active verb of luminescence); Greek: the moon will not GIVE its light (transitive). A back-translator would use תתן אורה ('give her light'), not the sunrise verb זרח.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the moon shall not shine.' Greek: 'the moon shall not give her light.' Different framing.
textual_notes: Isaiah 13:10: כִּי כוֹכְבֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וּכְסִילֵיהֶם לֹא יָהֵלּוּ אוֹרָם חָשַׁךְ הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בְּצֵאתוֹ וְיָרֵחַ לֹא יַגִּיהַּ אוֹרוֹ — 'The stars and their constellations shall not flash their light; the sun is darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not cause its light to shine.' Joel 2:31 also: 'The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses ינועו (yinu'u — 'shall shake/tremble/wander', H5128 from נוע) — the verb used for the shaking of trees (Isa 7:2), the trembling of the earth (1 Sam 14:15), and wandering of fugitives (Gen 4:12 — Cain's 'wandering'). Greek σαλευθήσονται ('shall be shaken') is seismic. The Hebrew verb encompasses both trembling AND dislocation — the heavenly powers not only shake but become displaced.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:4: וְנָמַקּוּ כָּל צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם — 'And all the host of heaven shall rot/dissolve.' The Hebrew Mark uses a different verb (נוע rather than מקק) but the same cosmic imagery.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן האלוה (ben ha-Eloah — 'Son of God', H1121+H433). Greek has τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of MAN'). This is an ENORMOUS divergence. The Hebrew says 'Son of God' where the Greek says 'Son of Man.' No back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would write 'Son of God.' These are different theological claims. The Hebrew author consistently uses בן האלוה as a messianic title, whereas the Greek preserves the Daniel 7:13 'Son of Man' language. This suggests the Hebrew and Greek represent INDEPENDENT traditions about Yeshua's self-designation.

Uses ואורה (ve-orah — 'and light', H219) where Greek has δόξης πολλῆς ('much glory'). Hebrew: power and LIGHT; Greek: power and GLORY. Light (אורה) connects to the theophany traditions — God appears in light (Ps 104:2, Hab 3:4, Ezek 1:4). Glory (δόξα) is a broader concept. A back-translator from Greek would write וכבוד רב ('and much glory').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of GOD' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of MAN' (υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Fundamentally different title.
Hebrew: 'power and light.' Greek: 'power and glory.' Different attributes.
Hebrew: 'coming FROM the heavens' (directional — FROM heaven downward). Greek: 'coming IN clouds' (ἐν νεφέλαις). Different imagery — descent vs. cloud-riding.
contradictions: The Son of God vs. Son of Man divergence cannot be resolved as a translation variant. It represents a fundamental difference in how the Hebrew and Greek traditions identify the eschatological figure.
translation_notes: אלוה (Eloah, H433) — the rare singular of Elohim, used primarily in Job and Deuteronomy 32. Its use here (rather than אלהים) matches the consistent pattern of the Hebrew Mark.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:13-14 (Greek context): 'One like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.' The Greek Mark quotes Daniel directly. The Hebrew Mark reinterprets the figure as 'Son of God' — identifying Daniel's 'son of man' with divine sonship.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כנפות הארץ (kanfot ha-aretz — 'wings of the earth', H3671+H776) — the specific OT idiom for the extremities of the earth (Isa 11:12 — 'the four wings of the earth'; Job 37:3, 38:13; Ezek 7:2). Greek τεσσάρων ἀνέμων ('four winds') is a completely different metaphor — winds vs. wings. A back-translator from Greek 'four winds' would write ארבע רוחות (arba ruchot), not כנפות הארץ. The Hebrew author thinks in Isaiah's geography of the earth as a garment with four corners/wings.

Uses ויקבץ (ve-yiqabets — 'and gather', H6908) — the specific verb for the regathering of Israel's exiles (Deut 30:3-4; Isa 11:12, 56:8; Jer 31:10; Ezek 20:34, 34:13, 36:24). Greek ἐπισυνάξει ('shall gather together') is adequate but lacks the exile-return resonance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'four wings of the earth' (כנפות הארץ). Greek: 'four winds' (τεσσάρων ἀνέμων). Entirely different metaphor.
Hebrew: 'his chosen' (נבחריו). Greek: 'his elect' (ἐκλεκτοὺς αὐτοῦ). Semantic overlap but Hebrew בחר carries covenant-election weight (Deut 7:6, 14:2).
translation_notes: 'Wings of the earth' preserves the Isaiah 11:12 image — the earth conceived as a garment with four corners (kanfot), the same word used for the corners of a prayer shawl (tsitsit on the kanfot, Num 15:38).
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:12: וְנָשָׂא נֵס לַגּוֹיִם וְאָסַף נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּנְפֻצוֹת יְהוּדָה יְקַבֵּץ מֵאַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת הָאָרֶץ — 'And he shall raise a signal for the nations, and gather the outcasts of Israel, and collect the scattered of Judah from the four wings of the earth.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses לחנוט (lachanot — 'to bud/put forth early fruit', H2590 from חנט). This rare verb appears in Song of Songs 2:13: הַתְּאֵנָה חָנְטָה פַגֶּיהָ — 'the fig tree puts forth her green figs.' Greek ἁπαλὸς γένηται ('becomes tender') describes a quality; the Hebrew verb describes a PROCESS of budding/fruiting. A back-translator from Greek 'tender' would use רך (rakh), not the Song of Songs fig-budding verb.

Uses הקץ (ha-qets — 'the end') where Greek has θέρος ('summer'). MAJOR divergence: the Hebrew fig tree signals the END; the Greek fig tree signals SUMMER. The Hebrew reads this as an eschatological parable; the Greek reads it as a seasonal analogy.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the end draws near.' Greek: 'summer is near.' Different referent — eschatological end vs. agricultural season.
textual_notes: Song of Songs 2:13: הַתְּאֵנָה חָנְטָה פַגֶּיהָ — 'The fig tree has budded her early figs.' The Hebrew Mark uses this exact verb, connecting the Olivet Discourse to the love-poetry of Song of Songs.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קץ העולם (qets ha-olam — 'end of the world') — explicitly eschatological. Greek has ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις ('it is near, at the doors'). The Hebrew specifies WHAT is near (the end of the world); the Greek leaves the subject ambiguous ('it/he is near').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the end of the world draws near to the door' (singular). Greek: 'it is near, at the doors' (plural θύραις). Hebrew makes the eschatological referent explicit.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אמת (emet — 'truth', H571) where Greek has ἀμήν ('amen'). Greek amen is a transliteration of Hebrew אמן. But the Hebrew text does NOT use אמן; it uses אמת — a different word from the same root. A back-translator from Greek ἀμήν would write אמן, not אמת. This is a consistent pattern in the Hebrew Mark.

textual_notes: Isaiah 40:8: וּדְבַר אֱלֹהֵינוּ יָקוּם לְעוֹלָם — 'But the word of our God shall stand forever.' Yeshua claims for his own words the permanence Isaiah attributes to YHWH's word.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלאכי השמים (malakhei ha-shamayim — 'messengers of the heavens') where Greek has οἱ ἄγγελοι οἱ ἐν οὐρανῷ ('the angels IN heaven'). Hebrew: messengers OF the heavens (possessive — they belong to heaven); Greek: angels IN heaven (locative — they are situated in heaven). Different prepositions signal different conceptions of angelic nature.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'guard yourselves and be awake and PRAY.' Greek: 'Watch, keep alert' (ἀγρυπνεῖτε). Greek omits 'pray' here (though some manuscripts add it). The Hebrew includes the full triad: guard-wake-pray.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יכולת (yekhólet — 'ability/authority') — a later Hebrew abstract noun. Greek ἐξουσίαν ('authority') is standard. The Hebrew uses the capacity/ability word rather than the authority/jurisdiction word — the servants receive CAPABILITY, not just PERMISSION.

Uses שיעור (shi'ur — 'measure/watch-period') — a specifically rabbinic Hebrew term for a measured quantity or defined period of duty. No Greek equivalent; Greek has τῷ θυρωρῷ ('to the doorkeeper'). The Hebrew frames the watchman's task as a measured duty-period.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'commands the watchman to watch a measured period.' Greek: 'commands the doorkeeper to keep watch' (τῷ θυρωρῷ ἵνα γρηγορῇ). Hebrew envisions a watchman (military); Greek envisions a doorkeeper (domestic).

one_way_hebrew: Uses the four-watch system: ערב (evening), חצי הלילה (midnight), תרנגול קורא (rooster's call), בקר (morning). Greek has ὀψὲ ἢ μεσονυκτίου ἢ ἀλεκτοροφωνίας ἢ πρωΐ — the same four Roman night-watches. Both traditions agree on the four-fold division, but the Hebrew uses natural-language descriptions while the Greek uses more technical watch terminology.
translation_notes: אדון הבית (adon ha-bayit — 'master of the house', H113+H1004) — the Hebrew patriarchal household title, used here for the returning lord.

14.summary: Mark 14 in Hebrew presents the Passion narrative with several extraordinary divergences from the Greek TR. The most striking one-way markers include: (1) בן האלוה / בן הבתולה (vv21,41,62) — 'Son of God' and 'Son of the Virgin' where Greek consistently has 'Son of Man,' representing an entirely different Christological vocabulary; (2) לבי (v22) — 'This is my HEART' at the Last Supper where Greek has 'This is my BODY,' reframing the eucharistic theology from physicality to interiority; (3) המימה (v36) — 'remove this DEATH from me' where Greek has 'remove this CUP,' replacing metaphor with raw directness; (4) גת שמני (v32) — 'oil-press,' preserving the transparent Hebrew meaning lost in the Greek transliteration; (5) מלבישן (v51) — a PROPER NAME for the anonymous young man, an inexplicable detail if translated from Greek; (6) סכינים (vv43,48) — 'knives' where Greek has 'swords,' domestic weapons vs. military ones; (7) שלום עליך (v45) — the peace blessing vs. Greek 'Hail!'; (8) בזכרוני (v9) — 'in MY memorial' vs. Greek 'as a memorial of HER'; (9) שאחזור חי (v28) — 'after I return alive' vs. Greek 'after I am raised.' The Hebrew omits the 'new covenant' formula (v24), names Barabbas 'Bar-Aven' (Ch15:7), and uses consistent reverential circumlocutions (השם, השם הברוך). These cannot be explained as back-translation from Greek.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הפסח ויום המצה (ha-Pesach ve-yom ha-Matsah — 'the Pesach and the day of the unleavened-bread', H6453+H4682) — preserving the DISTINCT Torah observances: the Pesach sacrifice (Ex 12:21,27) on the 14th of Nisan and the Festival of Matsot (Ex 12:17-20, Lev 23:6) beginning the 15th. Greek τὸ πάσχα καὶ τὰ ἄζυμα ('the Passover and the unleavened') uses pluralized Greek abstractions. The Hebrew preserves the precise liturgical calendar structure.
