Uses מאותתים מהדת (me'ot'tim me-ha-dat — 'scholars/signers of the law') — a distinctly Sephardic Hebrew compound term for those who authenticate legal tradition. Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes') is a single Greek word. No back-translator would produce this unusual two-word compound.
translation_notes: מאותתים (me'ot'tim) appears to derive from אות ('sign/letter') — those who deal with the signs/letters of the Torah, i.e., Torah scholars. This term recurs throughout the Hebrew Mark.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משיחה (meshichah — 'anointing/anointing-oil', H4888) — the SAME root as משיח (mashiach — 'anointed one/messiah'). The woman performs a MESSIANIC ANOINTING on Yeshua's head. Greek μύρον ('perfume/ointment') lacks this theological resonance. A Hebrew reader instantly connects this act to royal anointing (1 Sam 10:1, 16:13; 1 Kgs 1:39). A back-translator from Greek μύρον would use שמן (shemen — 'oil') or בשם (bosem — 'perfume'), not the messianic anointing term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: קאפסא אלבשטרי ('capsule of alabaster'). Greek: ἀλάβαστρον μύρου ('alabaster jar of ointment'). Hebrew uses a Romance loanword (capsa) for the vessel.
translation_notes: קאפסא (qafsa) is a loanword from Latin capsa ('box/case'). מרגלי (margali) is from Latin margarita/pearl, used here to mean 'precious/costly.' Both are markers of Sephardic Hebrew vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses האבדה (ha-avedah — 'the loss/waste', H6 from אבד) — the specific Hebrew legal term for lost property (Ex 22:8, Deut 22:3). Greek ἀπώλεια ('destruction/waste') is broader. The Hebrew frames the complaint in property-law terms — the anointing is 'lost property' that should have been recovered for the poor.

Uses פשיטין (peshitin) — a post-biblical Hebrew/Aramaic monetary unit meaning 'small coins/pennies.' Greek δηναρίων ('denarii') is the Roman monetary unit. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as דינרין. The Hebrew uses a Semitic monetary term, not a Roman one.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'peshitin' (Semitic coins). Greek: 'denarii' (Roman coins). Different monetary systems.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פעלה פעולה טובה (pa'alah pe'ulah tovah — 'she wrought a good work', H6466+H6468) — a cognate accusative construction (verb and noun from the same root). Greek καλὸν ἔργον εἰργάσατο ('she worked a good work') also has a cognate accusative. Both traditions preserve the rhetorical figure, but the Hebrew root פעל specifically means labor/wages (Lev 19:13, Deut 32:4, Isa 49:4) — connecting the woman's act to divinely-worthy labor.

translation_notes: Echoes Deuteronomy 15:11: כִּי לֹא יֶחְדַּל אֶבְיוֹן מִקֶּרֶב הָאָרֶץ — 'For the poor shall never cease from the midst of the land.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses עבדה (avdah — 'she served', H5647) where Greek has ἔσχεν ἐποίησεν ('she has done'). The Hebrew frames the anointing as SERVICE — the same verb used for serving God (Ex 3:12, Josh 24:15) and priestly service (Num 3:7-8). The woman SERVED Yeshua in a priestly/liturgical sense. Greek merely says she 'did' something.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she served me' (priestly/liturgical). Greek: 'she has done what she could' (practical). Different framing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בזכרוני (be-zikhroni — 'in my memorial', H2146 from זכר) — the word used for memorial offerings and remembrance rituals in the Torah (Lev 2:2,9,16 — the אזכרה, memorial portion of the grain offering). Greek εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς ('as a memorial of HER'). Hebrew: 'in MY memorial' — the act memorializes Yeshua. Greek: 'as a memorial of HER' — the act memorializes the woman. The possessive pronoun differs, and the Hebrew connects to the Torah's memorial-offering vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in MY memorial' (בזכרוני — Yeshua is memorialized). Greek: 'as a memorial of HER' (εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς — the woman is memorialized). Different referent.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אשקריות (Ashkeriot) — preserving a Semitic form. Greek Ἰσκαριώτης (Iscariot) is debated: from איש קריות ('man of Kerioth') or from שקריא ('liar/false one'). The Hebrew form אשקריות may derive from שקר ('deceit') — making it a descriptive epithet ('the deceitful one') rather than a geographic surname.

Uses נדרו (nadru — 'vowed', H5087 from נדר) — a religious vow, the same word for vows to God (Num 6:2, 21:2, 30:3; Judg 11:30). Greek ἐπηγγείλαντο ('promised') is a secular promise. The Hebrew frames the payment as a SACRED VOW — the priests make a religious commitment to pay for the betrayal. A back-translator from Greek 'promise' would use הבטיחו, not the religious vow term.

Uses מעות (ma'ot — 'coins/money', H3701 related to silver) — a post-biblical but Semitic monetary term. Greek ἀργύριον ('silver'). Both point to silver, but the Hebrew uses the common Jewish term for small coins.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'vowed' (religious). Greek: 'promised' (secular). Different nature of commitment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פת המצה (pat ha-matsah — 'bread of the unleavened', H6595+H4682). Greek: τῶν ἀζύμων ('of the unleavened'). The Hebrew adds פת ('bread/morsel'), specifying the physical food item, not just the abstract quality of unleavenedness. This is how a Hebrew speaker naturally refers to matzah — 'the bread of the unleavened.'
textual_notes: Exodus 12:8: וְאָכְלוּ אֶת הַבָּשָׂר... עַל מַצּוֹת — 'And they shall eat the flesh... with unleavened bread.' The Hebrew Mark naturally uses Torah Pesach vocabulary.

translation_notes: חבית (chavit — 'jar/barrel', H2789) — used in 1 Kings 17:12,14,16 for the widow of Zarephath's jar of oil. The same vessel-word.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ביתי (beiti — 'MY house'). Greek has τὸ κατάλυμά μου ('my guest-room/lodging'). Hebrew: Yeshua calls it 'my house'; Greek: Yeshua calls it 'my guest room.' The Hebrew claim is far bolder — ownership vs. temporary lodging. A back-translator from Greek 'lodging' would use מלוני or אכסניא, not ביתי ('my house').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'my house' (ביתי — ownership). Greek: 'my guest room' (τὸ κατάλυμα — temporary lodging). Different claim.
Greek adds ἐστρωμένον ἕτοιμον ('spread out, ready/furnished'). Hebrew has only 'a great house for eating' — no mention of furnishing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבגדני (yivgedeni — 'shall betray me', H898 from בגד) — the OT term for treacherous dealing and covenant violation (Jer 3:20, 12:1; Isa 24:16, 33:1; Mal 2:10-16). Greek παραδώσει με ('shall deliver me') is a neutral legal term. Hebrew: covenant TREACHERY; Greek: legal DELIVERY. A back-translator from Greek would use ימסרני ('shall deliver me'), not the covenant-betrayal term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall betray me' (בגד — covenant treachery). Greek: 'shall deliver me' (παραδίδωμι — hand over). Different moral framing.
textual_notes: Psalm 41:10 (9 in English): גַּם אִישׁ שְׁלוֹמִי אֲשֶׁר בָּטַחְתִּי בוֹ אוֹכֵל לַחְמִי הִגְדִּיל עָלַי עָקֵב — 'Even my close friend whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.' The 'one who eats with me' echoes this psalm of betrayal.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אדון (adon — 'master/lord', H113). Greek: μήτι ἐγώ ('surely not I?'). The Hebrew adds the ADDRESS 'Master' before the question, absent from the Greek. The disciples' grief is expressed with the deference of servants before their lord.
greek_deviations: Hebrew includes 'Master' (אדון) as a form of address. Greek has only the question 'surely not I?'

one_way_hebrew: Uses קערה (qe'arah — 'bowl/dish', H7086) — the same word used for the Tabernacle's golden bowls (Num 7:13,19,25,31 etc. — the offering bowls of the twelve tribal leaders). Greek τρύβλιον ('dish/bowl') is a common table vessel. The Pesach dish is described with Tabernacle vocabulary.

CRITICAL: Uses BOTH בן האלוה (ben ha-Eloah — 'Son of God') AND בן הבתולה (ben ha-Betulah — 'Son of the Virgin', H1330) IN THE SAME VERSE. Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man') for both references. This is the most dramatic divergence in the entire Hebrew Mark. The Hebrew author uses TWO DISTINCT Christological titles — one divine (Son of God) and one incarnational (Son of the Virgin) — where the Greek uses a single title (Son of Man) twice. No back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would produce EITHER 'Son of God' OR 'Son of the Virgin,' let alone both.

בן הבתולה (ben ha-Betulah — 'Son of the Virgin') echoes Isaiah 7:14: הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה — 'Behold, the young woman/virgin is with child.' The Hebrew Gospels use בתולה (betulah — 'virgin', the stronger virginity term) rather than Isaiah's עלמה (almah — 'young woman'). This title 'Son of the Virgin' has no Greek equivalent and appears to be a uniquely Hebrew Christological formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew first reference: 'Son of God' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of Man.' Different title entirely.
Hebrew second reference: 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה). Greek: 'Son of Man.' No Greek equivalent for this title.
translation_notes: 'Son of the Virgin' is translated literally to preserve this unique Hebrew Christological title. It combines incarnational theology (born of a virgin) with the messianic 'Son of' formula.
textual_notes: The dual-title structure 'Son of God... Son of the Virgin' encapsulates a two-nature Christology: divine origin (Son of God) and human entry (Son of the Virgin). This is theologically sophisticated in a way that 'Son of Man' (used twice in Greek) is not.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses לבי (libi — 'my heart', H3820). Greek has τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου ('this is my body'). MASSIVE divergence. Hebrew: 'This is my HEART.' Greek: 'This is my BODY.' A back-translator from Greek 'body' would write גופי (gufi) or בשרי (besari — 'my flesh'), NEVER לבי ('my heart'). The Hebrew makes the bread a symbol of Yeshua's INNER SELF — his will, love, and intent — rather than his physical body. This reframes the entire Last Supper theology.

The Hebrew לב (lev — 'heart') in the OT is the seat of thought, will, and moral decision (Deut 6:5 — 'love YHWH with all your heart'; 1 Kgs 3:9 — Solomon asks for a 'hearing heart'; Jer 31:33 — the Torah written on the 'heart'). Yeshua gives his disciples his HEART — his Torah-filled, God-directed inner self.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'my heart' (לבי). Greek: 'my body' (σῶμα). Irreconcilable divergence — inner self vs. physical form.
translation_notes: 'Heart' for libi — this must NOT be softened to 'body' or 'self.' The Hebrew word is unambiguously לב (heart), the OT seat of cognition and will.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 31:33: 'I will put my Torah in their inner parts, and write it on their HEART (לב).' Yeshua giving his 'heart' at Pesach echoes the New Covenant promise of Torah internalized.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גביע (gavia — 'cup/goblet', H1375) — the specific word for Joseph's silver divination cup (Gen 44:2,12,16,17) and the flower-cups of the Menorah (Ex 25:31,33,34). This is not the common כוס (kos — 'cup'). Greek ποτήριον is a generic drinking vessel. The Hebrew uses the ornamental, ceremonial cup-word.
translation_notes: חנות (chanot — 'thanks/favor') — from חן (chen — grace). The Hebrew blessing is an act of GRACE-giving, not merely 'giving thanks' (Greek εὐχαριστήσας).

one_way_hebrew: Uses ישפך (yishafekh — 'shall be poured out', H8210 from שפך) — the specific verb for the pouring of blood at the altar base (Lev 4:7,18,25,30,34 — the sin offering blood). Greek ἐκχυνόμενον ('being poured out') is also sacrificial but the Hebrew שפך specifically echoes the Levitical altar protocol. The Pesach cup IS the altar.

Hebrew OMITS the covenant formula. Greek has τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης ('this is my blood of the NEW COVENANT'). The Hebrew has simply 'my blood which for many shall be poured out' — no mention of covenant (ברית), new or old. This is a MAJOR omission that a back-translator would not produce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew OMITS 'of the new covenant' (τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης). The Hebrew gives the blood significance without invoking covenant language.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכות אבי (malkhut avi — 'kingdom of my Father'). Greek: ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ ('in the kingdom of GOD'). Hebrew: 'my Father'; Greek: 'God.' The Hebrew preserves the intimate filial address; the Greek uses the formal divine title.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'kingdom of my Father.' Greek: 'kingdom of God.' Different divine reference.
Hebrew: 'they gave thanks' (plural — all participants). Greek: ὑμνήσαντες ('having sung a hymn'). Hebrew: thanksgiving; Greek: hymn-singing. Different worship acts.
translation_notes: The Pesach Hallel (Psalms 113-118) was traditionally sung at the conclusion of the seder. Greek 'hymn' likely refers to this. Hebrew 'thanks' may be a more general description.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אני אכה (ani akeh — 'I shall strike', first person). This quotes Zechariah 13:7 where the MT has הַךְ (hakh — imperative 'strike!') addressed to the sword: 'Sword, awake against my shepherd... strike the shepherd.' The Hebrew Gospel changes the imperative to FIRST PERSON — 'I shall strike' — making GOD the direct agent. Greek πατάξω ('I will strike') also has first person. Both traditions agree against the MT imperative, but the Hebrew's אכה is a deliberate theological choice — God strikes his own shepherd.

Uses נכשלים (nikhshalim — 'stumbling', H3782 from כשל) — the word for spiritual stumbling and falling (Isa 8:15, 28:13, 31:3; Jer 6:21; Hos 4:5, 5:5, 14:2). Greek σκανδαλισθήσεσθε ('scandalized/offended'). Hebrew: they will STUMBLE (lose their footing); Greek: they will be SCANDALIZED (morally offended). A back-translator from Greek would use תתקלקלו or תתבלבלו.
textual_notes: Zechariah 13:7 MT: הַךְ אֶת הָרֹעֶה וּתְפוּצֶיןָ הַצֹּאן — 'Strike the shepherd, and the flock shall be scattered.' Both Hebrew Mark and Greek change the MT's imperative to first person, suggesting a shared pre-textual tradition.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שאחזור חי (she-achzor chai — 'after I return alive', H7725+H2416). Greek: μετὰ τὸ ἐγερθῆναί με ('after I am raised/resurrected'). Hebrew says 'RETURN ALIVE' — implying departure and return, not death and resurrection per se. Greek says 'BE RAISED' — passive, implying God raises him. These are fundamentally different resurrection concepts. The Hebrew frames it as COMING BACK to life (active return); the Greek frames it as BEING RAISED from death (passive divine act).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'after I return alive' (active — Yeshua returns). Greek: 'after I am raised' (passive — God raises him). Different agency.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כופר (kofer — 'denying', H3584 from כפר) — the specific verb for denying God and denying truth (Josh 24:27, Job 8:18, 31:28; Prov 30:9). Greek ἀπαρνήσῃ ('deny/disown') is also strong. But the Hebrew כפר in the denial sense carries the specific weight of denying what one knows to be true — a conscious, deliberate falsehood before God.

CRITICAL: Uses גת שמני (Gat Shemani — 'oil-press', H1660+H8081). גת (gat) means 'press/winepress' (Judg 6:11, Joel 4:13, Neh 13:15) and שמני (shemani) means 'of oil/oily' (from שמן, shemen — 'oil'). The Hebrew preserves the transparent meaning: this is an OIL-PRESS location. Greek Γεθσημανῆ is an opaque transliteration that conveys no meaning to Greek readers. A back-translator from Greek would just transliterate back. Only the Hebrew reveals the profound irony: Yeshua, the 'Anointed One' (מָשִׁיחַ, from שמן 'oil'), is PRESSED at the oil-press.

Calls the location a שדה (sadeh — 'field', H7704). Greek has χωρίον ('place/plot of ground'). Hebrew specifically says it is agricultural land — a field with an oil-press, not merely a 'garden' (κῆπος, as John calls it).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a field whose name is Gat Shemani.' Greek: 'a place named Gethsemane.' Hebrew reveals the meaning; Greek obscures it.
translation_notes: 'Gat Shemani' is left untranslated as a place name but its meaning ('oil-press') is crucial. The Anointed One (from oil) is pressed at the oil-press.

one_way_hebrew: Uses להתפלל ולהתפחד (le-hitpalel ve-le-hitpached — 'to pray and to be afraid'). Greek ἤρξατο ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν ('began to be greatly amazed and distressed'). Hebrew puts PRAYER first, then fear. Greek has amazement and distress but NO prayer at this point. The Hebrew shows Yeshua entering prayer as his FIRST response to the crisis; the Greek shows emotional reaction first.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to pray and to be afraid.' Greek: 'to be amazed and distressed.' Hebrew includes prayer; Greek has only emotional states.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT ECHO of Psalm 42:6,12 / 43:5: מַה תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי — 'Why are you cast down, O my soul?' and Jonah 4:9: 'I am grieved unto death' (כי טוב מותי מחיי). The Hebrew נפשי עצבה עד מות uses the OT soul-grief formula.
textual_notes: Psalm 42:6 (5): מַה תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי וַתֶּהֱמִי עָלָי — 'Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?' Yeshua's words echo the psalmist's lament.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כרע באפיו ארצה (kara be-apav artsah — 'fell on his face to the ground') — the standard OT prostration formula (Gen 17:3, Num 14:5, 16:4,22, 20:6; Josh 5:14, 7:6). Greek ἔπιπτεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ('fell upon the earth') is simpler. The Hebrew uses the full liturgical prostration language — face to the ground.
Uses לשם (la-Shem — 'to the Name') — praying TO the Name, again the reverential circumlocution for God.

CRITICAL: Uses המימה (ha-mimah — 'the death') where Greek has τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο ('this cup'). MASSIVE divergence. Hebrew: 'remove this DEATH from me.' Greek: 'remove this CUP from me.' A back-translator from Greek 'cup' would write הכוס or הגביע, NEVER המימה ('the death'). The Hebrew Yeshua asks directly for DEATH to be removed; the Greek Yeshua asks for the symbolic CUP to pass. The Hebrew is raw and concrete; the Greek is metaphorical.

Uses רצון (ratson — 'will/desire/favor', H7522) — the OT word for divine favor and human will (Ps 40:9, 103:21, 143:10; Prov 12:2, 14:9). Greek θέλημα ('will') is adequate but ratson carries the additional nuance of DELIGHT — 'not my delight but your delight.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'this death' (המימה). Greek: 'this cup' (τὸ ποτήριον). Concrete vs. metaphorical.
Hebrew: 'Father, who is able' (אב שהוא היכול). Greek: 'Abba, Father' (αββα ὁ πατήρ). Hebrew attributes ABILITY to God; Greek doubles the paternal address.
translation_notes: המימה (ha-mimah) is a later Hebrew form of מיתה (mitah — 'death'), from the root מות. Not 'cup,' not 'bitterness' — the word means DEATH.

one_way_hebrew: Addresses both כיפא (Kefa) and שמעון (Shimon) — using both names of the same person. Greek has only Σίμων (Simon). The Hebrew preserves BOTH the Aramaic nickname (Kefa/Rock) and the Hebrew birth name (Shimon), suggesting an author who knows him by both names.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to Kefa and to Shimon' (both names). Greek: only 'Simon' (Σίμωνι).

one_way_hebrew: Uses חולה (choleh — 'sick/weak', H2470 from חלה) for the flesh. Greek ἀσθενής ('weak') is generic weakness. The Hebrew says the flesh is SICK — a medical/disease metaphor. The body is not merely feeble but AILING. A back-translator from Greek 'weak' would use חלש (chalash), not the sickness term חולה.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the flesh is sick' (חולה). Greek: 'the flesh is weak' (ἀσθενής). Medical vs. generic.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלה (milah — 'word', H4405) — the Aramaic/poetic Hebrew word for 'word' found in Job (4:2, 12:11, 23:5, 32:11, 33:8, 34:16, 35:4, 36:2) and Daniel. Greek τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον ('the same word/saying'). Both traditions note the repetition, but the Hebrew uses the rare/poetic term for speech, not the common דבר.

Again uses בן הבתולה (ben ha-Betulah — 'Son of the Virgin', H1121+H1330). Greek again has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). Second occurrence of this unique Hebrew title in this chapter, confirming it is the author's consistent choice, not a scribal error.

Uses החוטאים (ha-chot'im — 'the sinners', H2400 from חטא) — the standard OT term for those who miss the mark of Torah (Num 32:14, 1 Sam 15:18, Isa 1:28, 33:14). Greek ἁμαρτωλῶν ('sinners') is a direct semantic equivalent. Both traditions agree here.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of the Virgin.' Greek: 'Son of Man.' Same divergence as v21.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סכינים (sakinim — 'knives') — a post-biblical Hebrew word for cutting implements. Greek μαχαιρῶν ('swords'). Hebrew: KNIVES (domestic/butchering tools); Greek: SWORDS (military weapons). A back-translator from Greek 'swords' would use חרבות (charavot). The Hebrew suggests a hastily-armed mob with kitchen/butchering knives, not a military detachment with swords.

Uses סגן הכהנים (segan ha-kohanim — 'deputy of the priests', H5461) — the OT title for the second-in-command of the Temple hierarchy (Neh 11:11, Jer 20:1, 2 Kgs 25:18). Greek ἀρχιερέων ('chief priests') is plural and more generic. The Hebrew preserves a specific Temple administrative title.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'knives' (domestic). Greek: 'swords' (military). Different weapons.
Hebrew: 'deputy of the priests' (specific rank). Greek: 'chief priests' (general).

one_way_hebrew: Uses בחכמה (be-chokhmah — 'with wisdom/carefully', H2451) — the OT wisdom word (Prov 1:2,7, 2:6; Ex 31:3). Greek ἀσφαλῶς ('safely/securely') is merely cautious. The Hebrew says bring him 'with wisdom' — implying cunning strategy, not just physical security.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'with wisdom' (בחכמה). Greek: 'safely' (ἀσφαλῶς). Wisdom vs. safety.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שלום עליך (shalom aleikha — 'peace be upon you', H7965) — the standard Hebrew greeting. Greek has χαῖρε ῥαββί ('Hail, Rabbi!'). Hebrew: a PEACE blessing; Greek: a HAIL/rejoice greeting. A back-translator from Greek χαῖρε would use ששון or שמח, not the שלום blessing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'peace upon you' (blessing). Greek: 'hail!' (greeting). Different speech acts.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וחתך (va-chatak — 'and cut off') — the Hebrew verb for cutting covenants (כרת ברית, Gen 15:18) is from this same root כרת (karat, H3772). Greek ἀφεῖλεν ('took away/cut off') is generic. The Hebrew verb for severing the ear is the COVENANT-CUTTING verb — a bitter irony at the moment of covenant betrayal.

Uses הכתיבות (ha-ketivot — 'the writings', from H3791 כתב) — a plural noun meaning 'written documents/scriptures.' Greek αἱ γραφαί ('the scriptures') is equivalent. The Hebrew uses a form that emphasizes the ACT of writing — these are things that were written down, documents. The focus is on the recorded, authored quality of scripture.

CRITICAL: Uses מלבישן (Malbishan) as a PROPER NAME. Greek has νεανίσκος τις ('a certain young man') — an anonymous figure. The Hebrew identifies this person BY NAME. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, why would the translator invent a name? The word מלביש (malbish) means 'one who clothes/dresser,' and with the suffix -ן it becomes a personal name: 'the Clothier' or 'the Well-Dressed One.' This is a Hebrew proper name that Greek readers would not recognize.

Uses סדין (sadin, H5466 — 'linen garment/sheet') — the same word from Judges 14:12-13 (Samson's riddle involving linen garments) and Proverbs 31:24 (the woman of valor who makes linen). Greek σινδόνα ('linen cloth/shroud') is a loanword FROM Semitic. The Hebrew is the original.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Malbishan' (named individual). Greek: 'a certain young man' (anonymous). The Hebrew identifies the person; Greek does not.
translation_notes: מלבישן (Malbishan) is preserved as a proper name. It derives from the root לבש (lavash — 'to wear/clothe'), suggesting a trade name — 'the Clothier' or 'Garment-maker.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses עידי שקר (edei sheqer — 'witnesses of falsehood', H5707+H8267). Greek μαρτυρίαν κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ('testimony against Jesus'). The Hebrew explicitly labels the witnesses as FALSE from the start. The Greek is neutral — just 'testimony against.' The Hebrew narrator editorializes, exposing the judicial corruption; the Greek presents the surface procedure.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'false witnesses' (editorial judgment). Greek: 'testimony against him' (procedural description).

one_way_hebrew: Uses חרש (charash — 'new/fresh') — a variant of חדש (chadash, H2319) reflecting later Hebrew pronunciation. The Hebrew testimony includes both 'made by hands' and 'NOT made by hands' — but note the Hebrew literally says 'another new one, made by hands of men, I shall build,' which may be a confused witness testimony or a textual corruption of 'NOT made by hands.'
greek_deviations: Greek explicitly has ἄλλον ἀχειροποίητον ('another, NOT made with hands'). The Hebrew text as it stands appears to say 'made by hands of men' for both, which may reflect the deliberate confusion of false testimony.

one_way_hebrew: Uses השם הברוך (ha-Shem ha-Barukh — 'the blessed Name') — a characteristically Jewish reverential circumlocution for God. Greek τοῦ εὐλογητοῦ ('the Blessed One') — a divine epithet without 'Name.' The Hebrew adds השם ('the Name') to the 'blessed' epithet, reflecting Jewish liturgical practice: God is referred to as 'the Name' and 'the Blessed Name' in prayer. A back-translator from Greek 'the Blessed' would write הברוך alone, without adding השם.
Echoes Isaiah 53:7: כַּשֶּׂה לַטֶּבַח יוּבָל... וְלֹא יִפְתַּח פִּיו — 'Like a lamb led to slaughter... he did not open his mouth.' Yeshua's silence fulfills the suffering servant prophecy.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of the blessed Name' (השם הברוך). Greek: 'Son of the Blessed' (τοῦ εὐλογητοῦ). Hebrew adds 'Name.'

one_way_hebrew: Again uses בן האלוה (ben ha-Eloah — 'Son of God') where Greek has τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). Before the highest Jewish court, Yeshua identifies himself as 'Son of God' in the Hebrew — a far more explosive claim than 'Son of Man.'

Uses בעבי השמים (be-avei ha-shamayim — 'in the clouds/thick clouds of the heavens', H5645). Greek ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν ('upon the clouds'). Hebrew עב (av — 'thick cloud') is the specific word for the cloud of God's presence (1 Kgs 18:44, Ps 18:12, 68:34). These are THEOPHANY clouds, not weather clouds.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of God.' Greek: 'Son of Man.' Same divergence as Mark 13:26.
Hebrew: 'in the thick-clouds of heaven' (theophany). Greek: 'upon the clouds of heaven' (generic).
textual_notes: Psalm 110:1: נְאֻם יְהוָה לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי — 'YHWH declares to my lord: Sit at my right hand.' Daniel 7:13: עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא — 'with the clouds of heaven.' Yeshua combines both passages.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כוספים (kosfim — 'yearning/desiring', H3700 from כסף) — the verb for intense longing and desire (Gen 31:30, Ps 17:12, 84:3). Greek χρείαν ἔχετε ('you have need'). Hebrew: do you still YEARN for witnesses? Greek: do you still NEED witnesses? The Hebrew is more emotionally charged — the desire for evidence after such a statement is absurd.
textual_notes: The high priest's tearing of garments is forbidden by Leviticus 21:10 for the high priest. The Hebrew narrates this violation of Torah without comment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קללה (qelalah — 'curse/blasphemy', H7043 from קלל) — the OT term for cursing God (Lev 24:11,14,23) and cursing a ruler (Ex 22:27). Greek βλασφημίαν ('blasphemy') is a Greek concept. The Hebrew uses the specific Levitical curse-word, invoking the death penalty of Leviticus 24:16.

Uses תפוחים (tapuchim — 'blows', lit. 'swellings/apples') — an unusual Hebrew term for physical strikes. Greek ῥαπίσμασιν ἔλαβον ('received slaps'). The Hebrew word can mean both 'apples' (Song 2:5) and 'swollen blows.' This ambiguity is impossible in Greek and marks a native Hebrew idiom.

UNIQUE DETAIL: שנועל נעלו (she-no'el na'alo — 'lacing his sandal'). This specific physical detail — Peter adjusting his shoe — is ABSENT from the Greek entirely. Greek says only 'warming himself' (θερμαινόμενον). A back-translator would not invent 'lacing his sandal.' This is a vivid eyewitness detail preserved only in the Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'lacing his sandal' — unique physical detail absent from Greek.
Greek adds 'your speech matches' (ἡ λαλιά σου ὁμοιάζει) — identifying the Galilean accent. Hebrew identifies him as 'Galilean' without specifying how he was recognized.
Greek adds ἐπιβαλὼν ἔκλαιεν ('having thrown himself on, he wept') — a physical gesture. Hebrew simply says 'he began to weep.' The Greek adds the prostration; the Hebrew focuses on the tears.

15.summary: Mark 15 in Hebrew presents the crucifixion with several extraordinary one-way markers. The most striking: (1) שתי וערב (shti va'erev — 'warp-and-woof') appears FOUR times (vv21,30,32,46) for the cross — a Torah textile metaphor from Leviticus 13 that no back-translator would invent from σταυρός; (2) ערפליות (arafiliyot, v33) — the theophanic thick-darkness of Sinai (Ex 20:21) and Solomon's Temple (1 Kgs 8:12) identifies God's presence at the cross; (3) המקדש נשבר (v38) — 'the sanctuary was BROKEN' where Greek has 'the veil was torn,' irreconcilable differences in both object and action; (4) הספדות (hespadot, v32) — 'funeral speeches' for the thieves' mockery, a uniquely Jewish cultural form; (5) בראבן/בר אבן (Bar-Aven — 'son of iniquity') vs. Barabbas ('son of the father'); (6) השם יושיעך (v18) — soldiers unknowingly pray YHWH's salvation upon Yeshua; (7) Psalm 22:1 quoted in pure Hebrew (v34) vs. Greek's Aramaic; (8) חג המצות (v42) — Torah festival dating vs. 'preparation day'; (9) נצרי (v26) — triple-wordplay title (Nazirite/Branch/Nazarene); (10) עושה המשפט (v45) — native Hebrew functional description vs. Latin title. The Hebrew places the crucifixion within Israel's sacred narrative through Torah vocabulary (talah, goralot, chag, mikdash, argaman, atarah, shti va'erev).

one_way_hebrew: Uses בקר בקר (boqer boqer — 'morning morning', H1242 doubled) — a Hebrew intensifying construction meaning 'very early in the morning' (cf. Isa 28:19, Ex 16:21). Greek has πρωΐ ('early'). A back-translator would use בבקר once, not the emphatic doubling.

Uses וקשרוהו (vayiqsheruhu — 'and they bound him', from H7194 qashar — 'to bind/conspire'). The root קשר carries a double meaning: to bind physically AND to conspire (1 Kgs 15:27, 16:9, 2 Kgs 15:10). The priests who conspired (qashar) against him now bind (qashar) him — a Hebrew wordplay invisible in Greek.
greek_deviations: Greek has the chief priests 'held a consultation' (συμβούλιον ποιήσαντες). Hebrew has them 'assembled to counsel' (נתאספו לעצה) — a formal gathering.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלך ישראל (melekh yisrael — 'king of Yisrael'). Greek has βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων ('king of the JEWS'). Hebrew preserves the covenantal title 'king of Yisrael'; Greek uses the Romanized 'king of the Jews.' A back-translator would use מלך היהודים.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'king of Yisrael.' Greek: 'king of the Jews.' Different political/theological framing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הלשינוהו (hilshinuhu — 'they informed against him', from H3960 lashan — 'to use the tongue/slander'). The root לשון means 'tongue.' Greek κατηγόρουν ('accused') is standard legal terminology. The Hebrew verb implies malicious speech.

textual_notes: Isaiah 53:7 — 'He was oppressed and afflicted, yet he did not open his mouth.' Yeshua's silence fulfills the Servant prophecy.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חג (chag, H2282 — 'feast/pilgrimage festival') — the specific Torah term for the three pilgrimage festivals (Ex 23:14-17, Deut 16:16). Greek ἑορτή is more generic.

CRITICAL: The name is בראבן (Bar-Aven). Greek has Βαραββᾶν (Barabbas — 'son of the father'). The Hebrew parses as בר-אבן (Bar-Aven — 'son of iniquity/wickedness'), from אָוֶן (aven, H205 — 'wickedness'). The released prisoner is 'the son of wickedness' while 'the Son of God' is condemned. A back-translator from Greek would write בר-אבא, not the morally loaded Bar-Aven.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: Bar-Aven ('son of iniquity'). Greek: Barabbas ('son of the father').
Hebrew: 'in a quarrel committed murder.' Greek: 'in the insurrection (στάσει) had committed murder.' Personal dispute vs. political uprising.
textual_notes: Hosea 10:8 calls idolatrous shrines אָוֶן (aven — 'wickedness'). The name Bar-Aven echoes prophetic condemnation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קנאה (qin'ah, H7068 — 'envy/jealousy/zeal'). The same word for God's jealousy (Ex 20:5, 34:14) and Phinehas's zeal (Num 25:11). Greek φθόνον is purely negative. Hebrew קנאה is morally ambiguous — the priests' 'zeal' leads them to kill God's son.

DIFFERENT AGENTS: Hebrew says ההגמונים (ha-hegmonim — 'the governors', Roman officials) stirred up the crowd. Greek has οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς ('the chief priests'). Hebrew blames Roman authorities; Greek blames Jewish leaders.
Uses הזהירו (hizhiru — 'warned/cautioned', from H2094 zahar — 'to warn/teach'). Greek ἀνέσεισαν ('stirred up'). Hebrew implies instruction; Greek implies mob agitation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the governors warned the people.' Greek: 'the chief priests stirred up the crowd.' Different agents and actions.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תלהו (talehu — 'hang him!', from H8518 talah — 'to hang'). Greek has σταύρωσον αὐτόν ('crucify him!'). The Hebrew uses the Torah term for execution by hanging (Deut 21:22-23, Gen 40:19,22, Esth 7:10). Deuteronomy 21:23 declares 'cursed of God is the hanged one' (קללת אלהים תלוי). A back-translator would transliterate or use צלב.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'hang him' (Torah vocabulary). Greek: 'crucify him' (Roman vocabulary).
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 21:22-23 — 'If a man has committed a sin worthy of death... and you hang him on a tree... for he who is hanged is cursed of God.'

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'what evil has he done TO YOU?' (לכם). Greek omits the personal element.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רצון העם (retson ha'am — 'the will of the people', H7522). רצון is the OT word for God's will/favor (Ps 40:8, 143:10). Irony: Pilat does the 'will' of the people where he should do God's will. Greek τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι ('to satisfy') lacks this theological irony.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'beaten' (מוכה). Greek: 'scourged' (φραγελλώσας, Roman loanword).
textual_notes: Isaiah 53:4-5 — 'smitten (מוכה) of God and afflicted.' The word מוכה echoes the Suffering Servant.

one_way_hebrew: Uses היכל השוטר (heikhal hashoter — 'the hall of the officer'). Greek has πραιτώριον ('Praetorium' — a Latin loanword). Hebrew uses native OT terms: היכל (H1964) and שוטר (H7860, the Israelite officer from Ex 5:6, Deut 16:18). A back-translator would transliterate 'Praetorium.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the people assembled' (העם). Greek: 'the whole cohort' (ὅλην τὴν σπεῖραν). Civilian crowd vs. military unit.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ארגמן (argaman, H713 — 'purple') — the specific Tabernacle/priestly purple (Ex 25:4, 26:1,31, 28:5,6). They mockingly dress him in the Tabernacle's own color.
Uses עטרה (atarah, H5850 — 'crown') — used for royal crowns (2 Sam 12:30, Esth 8:15) and glory (Prov 4:9, Isa 28:5, 62:3).
textual_notes: Genesis 3:18 — 'thorns and thistles (קוץ ודרדר) shall it bring forth for you.' The King wears the curse of the ground on his head.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses השם יושיעך (hashem yoshiakha — 'the Name save you!'). Greek has χαῖρε ('Hail!'). The Hebrew is a PRAYER FORMULA invoking YHWH. The root ישע (yasha — 'save') is the root of Yeshua's name. The mockers unknowingly pray for YHWH's salvation upon 'YHWH-saves.' A back-translator from χαῖρε would use שמח ('rejoice'), not a salvation prayer.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'The Name save you!' (prayer formula). Greek: 'Hail!' (Roman salutation).
textual_notes: Ironic wordplay: ישוע (Yeshua = 'YHWH saves') is mocked with יושיעך ('may [YHWH] save you').

one_way_hebrew: Uses ומתפללים (umitpalelim — 'and praying', from H6419 palal). Greek προσεκύνουν ('worshipped'). The Hebrew uses the PRAYER verb — they mockingly 'pray' to him. A back-translator would use משתחוים ('bowing down').
textual_notes: Isaiah 50:6 — 'I gave my back to the smiters... I did not hide my face from shame and spitting.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses הלעיגוהו (hil'iguhu — 'mocked him', from H3932 la'ag) — the word for mocking God's prophets (2 Chr 36:16).

CRITICAL: Uses שתי וערב (shti va'erev — 'warp and woof') for the cross. This is the Torah TEXTILE term for the vertical and horizontal threads of a loom (Lev 13:48,49,51,52,53,56,57,58,59). The cross is described through Levitical purity vocabulary. NO back-translator from σταυρός would EVER choose a weaving metaphor. This is one of the most distinctive one-way markers in the entire Hebrew Gospels.
Uses עבד (eved, H5650 — 'servant') for Simon. Greek has Κυρηναῖον ('a Cyrenian'). Hebrew identifies by social status; Greek by geography.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a servant who came from his city.' Greek: 'Simon a Cyrenian coming from the countryside.'
Hebrew: 'warp-and-woof' (שתי וערב). Greek: 'cross' (σταυρός).
translation_notes: 'Warp-and-woof' for shti va'erev — the interlocking perpendicular threads of fabric.
textual_notes: Leviticus 13:48-59 uses שתי and ערב repeatedly in the laws of skin/fabric affliction. The execution instrument is described in the language of Levitical cleansing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גולגולתא (Gulgolta) — from גלגלת (gulgolet, H1538 — 'skull'), used in the OT for census head-counts (Ex 16:16, Num 1:2,18). The Hebrew preserves the transparent meaning; Greek merely transliterates.
greek_deviations: Hebrew gloss: מון קולורי — Romance-language for 'Monte Calvario.' Greek gloss: Κρανίου Τόπος ('Place of the Skull'). The manuscript was used in a Sephardic community.

translation_notes: מור (mor, H4753 — 'myrrh') — the same spice in the Tabernacle anointing oil (Ex 30:23). The Anointed One is offered the anointing spice in suffering.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גורלות (goralot — 'lots', H1486 plural) — the Yom Kippur lot-casting word (Lev 16:8).
textual_notes: Psalm 22:18 — 'They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (יפילו גורל).'

one_way_hebrew: Uses נצרי (natsri) — connecting to three Hebrew roots: (1) נָזִיר (nazir, H5139 — 'consecrated one'); (2) נֵצֶר (netser, H5342 — 'branch' from Isa 11:1); (3) נצרת (Nazareth). Greek Ναζωραῖος captures only geography.
greek_deviations: Hebrew includes 'Yeshua Nazarite' in the inscription. Greek Mark 15:26 has only 'The King of the Jews.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:1 — 'A shoot (נֵצֶר) shall come forth from the stump of Jesse.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses גנבים (ganavim — 'thieves', H1590). Greek has λῃσταί ('bandits/insurrectionists'). Hebrew ganav is a petty thief (Ex 22:1-3); Greek lestes is a violent rebel.
From Isaiah 53:12. The Hebrew uses הרשעים ('the wicked', H7563) rather than Isaiah's פושעים ('transgressors'). Both native Hebrew, but the substitution suggests quoting from memory.
Uses נשלמת (nishlemet — 'fulfilled', from H7999 shalam — 'to complete/make peace'). Root שלם = שלום. Scripture is 'made-whole' by fulfillment.
textual_notes: Isaiah 53:12 — '...he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors (ואת פושעים נמנה).'

one_way_hebrew: Uses מקדש השם ('the sanctuary of the Name') — combining the Temple term with the reverential circumlocution for God. Greek just has τὸν ναόν ('the temple').
Uses מניעים ראשם ('shaking their head') — echoing Psalm 22:7 and Lamentations 2:15.
textual_notes: Psalm 22:7 — 'All who see me mock me... they shake the head (יניעו ראש).'

one_way_hebrew: The root ישע (yasha — 'save') is Yeshua's own name. The mockers demand that 'YHWH-saves' save himself.
Second occurrence of שתי וערב for the cross.
Uses מצחקים (metsachaqim — 'laughing', from H6711 tsachaq). Root of Isaac's name (יצחק). The priests 'laugh' at the true sacrifice — an ironic Genesis echo.

CRITICAL: Uses הספדות (hespadot — 'funeral speeches/eulogies', from H5594 safad — 'to mourn/eulogize'). Greek ὠνείδιζον ('reviled'). The thieves deliver MOCK FUNERAL ORATIONS for a man still alive — a uniquely Jewish form of mockery. A hesped is the formal eulogy at a funeral (Gen 23:2, 50:10; 2 Sam 1:12, 3:31; Zech 12:10). NO back-translator from 'reviled' would invent this.
Third occurrence of שתי וערב for the cross.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: thieves 'make funeral-speeches.' Greek: thieves 'reviled him.' Jewish mourning ritual vs. verbal abuse.
translation_notes: 'Funeral-speeches' for hespadot — the formal Jewish eulogy genre, performed here as mockery.
textual_notes: Zechariah 12:10 — 'they shall mourn (וספדו) for him as one mourns for an only son.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses ערפליות (arafiliyot — plural of ערפל, arafel, H6205 — 'thick fog/dense cloud'). This is the THEOPHANIC DARKNESS of Sinai. Exodus 20:21: 'Moses drew near to the arafel where God was.' Deuteronomy 4:11: 'darkness, cloud, and arafel.' 1 Kings 8:12: 'YHWH said he would dwell in the arafel.' The crucifixion darkness is GOD'S PRESENCE-CLOUD. Greek σκότος ('darkness') is generic. A back-translator would use חשך, NOT the Sinai theophany word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: ערפליות ('theophanic fog'). Greek: σκότος ('darkness'). Divine manifestation vs. natural phenomenon.
translation_notes: 'Thick-fog' for arafiliyot — the Sinai presence-cloud. God is present at the cross in the same form he appeared at Sinai.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:21 — 'Moses drew near to the arafel (ערפל) where God was.'
1 Kings 8:12 — 'YHWH said he would dwell in the arafel.'

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Psalm 22:1 in pure Hebrew: אלי אלי למה עזבתני. Greek Mark has the Aramaic form Ελωι Ελωι λαμα σαβαχθανι — from the Aramaic Targum. The Hebrew preserves the ORIGINAL PSALM; the Greek preserves an Aramaic paraphrase. A back-translator from the Greek Aramaic would reproduce Aramaic, NOT pure Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: pure Hebrew Psalm 22:1. Greek: Aramaic quotation. Different languages for the same Psalm.
textual_notes: Psalm 22:1 — 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (אלי אלי למה עזבתני).'

one_way_hebrew: The confusion between אלי ('my God') and אליהו ('Eliyahu') works naturally in Hebrew. This wordplay requires a Semitic language.

textual_notes: Psalm 69:21 — 'For my thirst they gave me vinegar (חמץ) to drink.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses נשף (nashaf — 'breathed out', from H5301). Echoes Genesis 2:7 where God 'breathed (ויפח) into his nostrils the breath of life.' The one into whom God breathed life now breathes out his spirit — a Genesis reversal.
Adds ברוחו ('his spirit', H7307). Greek simply says 'he expired.' Hebrew makes explicit that his ruach departed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'breathed out his spirit.' Greek: 'expired' (ἐξέπνευσεν). Hebrew is more theologically specific.
textual_notes: Genesis 2:7 — 'YHWH God breathed (ויפח) into his nostrils the breath of life.' Death reverses creation.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses המקדש נשבר ('the SANCTUARY was BROKEN'). Greek has τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ ἐσχίσθη ('the VEIL of the temple was TORN'). TWO irreconcilable differences: (1) Hebrew says the SANCTUARY ITSELF broke, not its veil; (2) Hebrew uses נשבר (nishbar — 'shattered', H7665 — for smashing pottery, Jer 19:11; breaking tablets, Ex 32:19; a broken heart, Ps 34:18, 51:17). Greek uses ἐσχίσθη ('was torn' — a fabric word).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the sanctuary was broken in two sides.' Greek: 'the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.' Different object, action, and manner.
translation_notes: 'Broken' for nishbar — the shattering verb. The sanctuary breaks like the covenant tablets (Ex 32:19).
textual_notes: Exodus 32:19 — Moses 'broke (וישבר) the tablets.' Same verb שבר for a covenant-ending act.
Psalm 51:17 — 'A broken (נשבר) and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses שר המאה (sar hame'ah — 'captain of the hundred', H8269+H3967) — the native Hebrew military title (2 Kgs 11:4,9). Greek κεντυρίων is a Latin loanword.
Uses בן האל (ben ha'El — 'Son of THE God'). The definite article makes the claim monotheistic.
Uses שלומי (Shlomi) — a Hebrew name meaning 'my peace.' Greek Σαλώμη (Salome) is a Hellenized form.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: women 'came from Yerushalayim.' Greek: women 'came up with him TO Jerusalem.' Opposite directions.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חג המצות (chag hamatsot — 'feast of the unleavened-bread', H2282+H4682). Greek has παρασκευή ('preparation day'). Hebrew identifies time by TORAH FESTIVAL (Lev 23:6, Ex 12:17); Greek uses civic terminology. A back-translator would write ערב שבת, NOT the Torah festival name.
The phrase נכנס כבר חג המצות ('the feast had already entered') uses the characteristically Jewish expression where festivals 'enter' at sunset.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the feast of Matzot entered.' Greek: 'it was preparation day.' Jewish liturgical vs. civic calendar.
textual_notes: Leviticus 23:6 — 'On the fifteenth day is the feast of unleavened bread (חג המצות) to YHWH.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses רמתים (Ramatayim) — the full Hebrew dual form. Greek Ἀριμαθαίας is Hellenized. Hebrew preserves the native name meaning 'the two heights' — Samuel's birthplace (1 Sam 1:1). A back-translator would transliterate.
Uses גבר נכבד ('honored man', H1397+H3513). Greek εὐσχήμων βουλευτής ('prominent council member'). Hebrew emphasizes character; Greek emphasizes position.
Uses מלכות שמים ('kingdom of heaven'). Greek: βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ('kingdom of God'). The Jewish circumlocution.
textual_notes: 1 Samuel 1:1 — 'a man from Ramatayim-Tsofim.' Joseph's hometown is Samuel's birthplace.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עושה המשפט ('the executor of judgment') — a FUNCTIONAL DESCRIPTION. Greek has κεντυρίων ('centurion'). Hebrew describes roles by function; a back-translator would transliterate the Latin title.
Uses אבן חצובה ('hewn stone', H68+H2672). חצב is the OT verb for quarrying (Isa 22:16 — a tomb 'hewn in the height').
Fourth occurrence of שתי וערב for the cross.
textual_notes: Isaiah 53:9 — 'He made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death.' Joseph of Ramatayim is the 'rich man.'

16.summary: Mark 16 in Hebrew presents the resurrection and commissioning with several distinctive one-way markers. The most striking: (1) חזר חי (chazar chai — 'returned alive') used THREE times (vv9,11,14) instead of any resurrection verb — framing death as departure and resurrection as return; (2) דבר מלך השמים (v15) — 'the word of the King of Heaven' where Greek has 'the gospel,' a royal-decree metaphor; (3) ימחה (v16) — 'shall be blotted out' (Book of Life erasure from Ex 32:32-33) where Greek has 'condemned' — ontological erasure vs. legal judgment; (4) בצורת גרים (v12) — Yeshua appears 'in the form of strangers' (the OT sojourner category) where Greek has 'in another form'; (5) בעזר השם (v20) — the Jewish prayer formula 'with the help of the Name'; (6) the mashiach/meshichah wordplay in v1; (7) four grief terms (v10) vs. Greek's two; (8) ירפאו (v17) — 'heal' the demonized vs. Greek 'cast out' demons; (9) consistent השם ('the Name') as reverential circumlocution. The chapter colophon confirms the manuscript's self-awareness as part of a canonical collection.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משיחה מרגליית (meshichah margaliit — 'costly ointment', H4888+H4030). The word משיחה is from the same root as משיח (mashiach — 'Messiah/Anointed'). The women come to 'anoint' (למשוח) the Anointed One (משיח). This wordplay is visible only in Hebrew. Greek ἀρώματα ('spices') has no connection to Christos.
translation_notes: The mashiach/meshichah wordplay: women bring anointing-oil (משיחה) to anoint (למשוח) the Anointed One (משיח).

one_way_hebrew: Uses לבקר (levaqer — 'to visit/inspect', from H1239 baqar). Greek ἔρχονται ('they come'). Hebrew adds a specific PURPOSE — an inspection visit. A back-translator would use באו alone.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the day after, in the morning.' Greek: λίαν πρωΐ ('very early'). Hebrew uses מחרת — a specific time reference.

one_way_hebrew: The source text merges Greek vv3-5 into a single verse. The women's question about the stone, seeing the young man, and their fear are compressed — a different narrative structure than the Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew compresses Greek vv3-5 into one unit. Greek separates these into distinct sequential actions (asking about stone, seeing it rolled, entering tomb, seeing young man).

one_way_hebrew: Uses שנתלה (shenitlah — 'who was hung', from H8518 talah). Greek ἐσταυρωμένον ('the crucified one'). Consistent Torah hanging vocabulary throughout Mark.
Uses נצרי (natsri — 'the Nazarite') — the triple-wordplay title (consecrated one / branch / Nazareth). Greek Ναζαρηνόν captures only geography.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἠγέρθη ('he is risen') — the explicit resurrection statement. Hebrew says only איננו פה ('he is not here'). The Hebrew is more enigmatic — absence rather than explicit resurrection.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תכף (tekhef — 'immediately'). Greek has no equivalent urgency word. The Hebrew adds immediacy absent from Greek.

Uses פחדתן (pachadtan — 'their dread', from H6343 pachad). This is the same word as פחד יצחק ('the Fear/Dread of Isaac', Gen 31:42,53) — a divine terror. Greek τρόμος και ἔκστασις ('trembling and astonishment'). The Hebrew echoes the patriarchal encounter with the divine.
textual_notes: Many scholars consider the original Greek Mark to end here at v8. The Hebrew continues with vv9-20.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חזר חי (chazar chai — 'returned alive', H7725+H2416). Greek ἀναστάς ('having risen'). Hebrew does NOT use a resurrection verb. It says he 'RETURNED ALIVE' — went away (died) and came back (alive). A back-translator from ἀναστάς would use קם ('rose') or נעור ('awakened'), NOT חזר חי.
Uses גורש (gorash — 'drove out/expelled', H1644) — the verb for expelling Adam from Eden (Gen 3:24) and driving out the Canaanites (Ex 23:28-31). Greek ἐκβεβλήκει ('had cast out') is more generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'returned alive' (חזר חי). Greek: 'having risen' (ἀναστάς). Return vs. resurrection.
translation_notes: 'Returned alive' for chazar chai — framing death as departure and resurrection as return.

one_way_hebrew: Uses FOUR grief terms: אנונים ('grieving'), אנוחים ('sighing', H585), בוכים ('weeping', H1058), מתאנחים ('groaning'). Greek has only πενθοῦσιν και κλαίουσιν ('mourning and weeping' — TWO terms). A back-translator would not expand two Greek terms to four Hebrew ones.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: four grief terms. Greek: two grief terms.

one_way_hebrew: Again חזר חי ('returned alive') — consistent with v9.

Uses בצורת גרים (b'tsurat gerim — 'in the form of strangers/sojourners', H6755+H1616). Greek ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ ('in another form'). Hebrew specifies גרים (gerim — 'resident aliens') — the OT category from Gen 23:4, Lev 19:33-34. The risen Yeshua appears as a ger — an alien in his own land, echoing Abraham's self-description (Gen 23:4). A back-translator from 'another form' would NOT specify 'strangers.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the form of strangers' (specific identity). Greek: 'in another form' (vague transformation).

one_way_hebrew: Uses מיאונם ('their refusal') — active refusal. Greek ἀπιστίαν ('unbelief'). Hebrew specifies willful refusal; Greek names a state.
Third use of חזר חי ('returned alive') for the resurrection.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'after the first day' (specific timing). Greek: ὕστερον ('afterward', vague).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses דבר מלך השמים (dvar melekh hashamayim — 'the word of the King of Heaven'). Greek τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ('the gospel'). The Hebrew uses a ROYAL DECREE metaphor — the message is a king's edict. A back-translator from 'gospel' would use בשורה ('good news'), NOT 'the word of the King of Heaven.'
Uses דרשו (dirshu — 'proclaim/seek', from H1875 darash). Root of מדרש (midrash). Greek κηρύξατε ('preach/herald'). A back-translator would use קראו or הכריזו, not darash.
Uses בריה (beriyah — 'creature', from H1254 bara — 'to create'). The Genesis 1 creation verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the word of the King of Heaven' (royal decree). Greek: 'the gospel' (good news). Different metaphors.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses ימחה (yimmacheh — 'shall be blotted out', from H4229 machah). This is the verb for blotting names from the Book of Life (Ex 32:32-33, Deut 9:14, 25:19, Ps 69:28). Greek κατακριθήσεται ('shall be condemned'). A back-translator would use יורשע ('condemned'), NOT the Book of Life erasure verb.
Uses טבול (tavul — 'immersed', from H2881 taval — 'to dip'). The OT verb for ritual immersion (Lev 14:6,16; 2 Kgs 5:14 — Naaman's immersion).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'blotted out' (ימחה, Book of Life). Greek: 'condemned' (κατακριθήσεται, legal). Erasure vs. judgment.
translation_notes: 'Blotted out' for yimmacheh — the Book of Life erasure verb, not mere condemnation.
'Immersed' for tavul — the OT ritual dipping verb.
textual_notes: Exodus 32:32-33 — 'blot me out (מחני) of your book... whoever has sinned, him will I blot out (אמחנו).'

one_way_hebrew: Uses ירפאו ('shall heal', H7495 rapha). Greek ἐκβαλοῦσιν ('shall cast out'). Hebrew: HEAL the demonized. Greek: CAST OUT the demons. Different approach — healing a person vs. expelling an entity.
Uses חלוף לשונות ('diverse/changed tongues', H2487+H3956). Greek γλώσσαις καιναῖς ('new tongues'). Hebrew: 'changed tongues' (transformed). Greek: 'new tongues' (additional).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'heal the demon-possessed.' Greek: 'cast out demons.'
Hebrew: 'diverse tongues.' Greek: 'new tongues.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses בהמות ונחשים ('beasts and serpents'). Greek mentions only ὄφεις ('serpents') and θανάσιμόν ('deadly poison'). Hebrew adds בהמות (behemot — 'beasts', H929) — the Genesis 1:24-25 and Job 40:15 word — absent from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'beasts and venomous serpents.' Greek: 'serpents and deadly poison.'
textual_notes: Genesis 3:15 — 'He shall crush your head, and you shall bruise his heel.' Victory over the serpent extends to believers.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לימין השם (limin hashem — 'at the right hand of the Name'). Greek ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ ('at the right hand of God'). Hebrew uses the reverential circumlocution 'the Name.' A back-translator would use אלהים, not the Jewish substitute.
Uses משיח (mashiach — 'Anointed', H4899) — the native Hebrew title. Greek Χριστός is the translation of this.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'right hand of the Name.' Greek: 'right hand of God.' Reverential circumlocution vs. direct naming.
textual_notes: Psalm 110:1 — 'YHWH said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand (שב לימיני).' The ascension fulfills the Psalm.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בעזר השם (b'ezer hashem — 'with the help of the Name') — a standard Jewish invocation formula still used today. Greek τοῦ κυρίου συνεργοῦντος ('the Lord working with them'). The Hebrew uses the liturgical formula; the Greek describes cooperation. A back-translator would not produce בעזר השם.
Uses דברים טובים (devarim tovim — 'good words', H1697+H2896). Greek τὸν λόγον βεβαιοῦντος ('confirming the word'). Different descriptions of apostolic activity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'with the help of the Name' (Jewish formula). Greek: 'the Lord working with them.'
Hebrew: 'good words and wonders.' Greek: 'confirming the word with signs.'
textual_notes: The colophon reads: 'Here end the chapters of Matthew 54 and the chapters of Mark 16.' This confirms the manuscript's self-awareness as part of a canonical collection.

1.summary: James 1 in Hebrew contains at least 10 clear one-way translation markers. The most extraordinary is the VERBATIM quotation of Job 5:17 in verse 12, using Job's three signature words (enosh, Eloah, Shaddai) completely absent from the Greek. The mar'ot hatsov'ot (mirrors of the serving-women, v22) from Exodus 38:8 is equally decisive. The dat hasimchah (law of joy, v24) reveals a fundamentally different framework from Greek's perfect law of liberty, with simchah (joy) as the epistle's keynote. Additional markers: moznayim (scales, v6) vs Greek wave; Job 14:2 shadow imagery (v11); or/choshekh creation vocabulary (v17) vs Greek astronomical abstraction; sivlut (Exodus burden-bearing, v3) vs patience; she'irut (priestly service, vv25-26) vs religion. YHWH appears throughout where Greek has God, and Greek v21 has no Hebrew counterpart.

one_way_hebrew: Uses simchah (joy, H8057) as the greeting. Greek has chairein, a stock epistolary formula meaning greetings. The Hebrew is a concrete declaration: Joy! A back-translator from Greek would use shalom, not simchah.
Uses YHWH (H3068) where Greek has theou (God). Throughout the epistle, Hebrew uses the divine name where Greek has the generic theos.
Uses mefuzarim (scattered, H6327). Greek has en te diaspora (in the dispersion). Hebrew uses a native verb; Greek uses a technical term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has mikkodem (beforehand) after simchah, absent from Greek.
Hebrew: in all the places. Greek: in the dispersion.
translation_notes: The greeting simchah mikkodem sets the thematic tone; joy recurs at the trial (v2) and characterizes the law itself (v24, dat hasimchah).

one_way_hebrew: Uses noflim (fall, H5307). Greek has peripesete (encounter). The Hebrew verb is more direct and physical.
greek_deviations: Greek adds various trials. Hebrew simply says trial (singular).

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says your faith, if it is COMPLETE (shelemah, H8003), produces endurance. Greek says the TESTING of your faith produces patience. Different mechanism: Hebrew conditions on faith quality; Greek conditions on the testing process.

Uses sivlut (endurance/bearing, H5450 from saval). This is the word for burden-bearing of Israelite slaves in Egypt (Ex 1:11, 6:6-7). Greek has hupomone (patience). No back-translator would choose the Exodus slavery word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: complete faith produces endurance. Greek: testing of faith produces patience.
Hebrew: in fullness (one concept). Greek: perfect and complete (two words).
translation_notes: Milu'ah (fullness) shares the root of milu'im (priestly ordination offerings, Ex 29:22, Lev 8:28).

one_way_hebrew: Uses litpallel (to pray, H6419, hitpael of palal), reflexive self-examination. Greek has aiteito (let him ask), a simple request.
greek_deviations: Greek adds without reproach, absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: from YHWH. Greek: from God.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses moznayim (scales/balance, H3976). Greek has a wave of the sea driven by wind. Entirely different imagery! The Hebrew pictures a set of scales placed on the sea, forever tipping one way then the other. A back-translator from Greek would write gal hayam (wave of the sea), NEVER the scales word moznayim. Connects to Job 6:2 and Proverbs 16:11.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: like scales upon the sea (static balance). Greek: like a wave of the sea driven by wind (dynamic wave).

one_way_hebrew: Uses ba'al (H1167, master/possessor). Greek has aner dipsuchos (double-minded man). Ba'al means owner, lord, husband. No back-translator would choose ba'al.
Uses beli yedi'at (without knowledge). Greek akatastatos means unstable. Hebrew: ignorance; Greek: instability.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: a doubting master. Greek: a double-minded man.

translation_notes: The shafal/govah contrast is a Hebrew word-pair (Isa 2:11, Ezek 17:24).

one_way_hebrew: Uses ketsits hasadeh (flower of the field), echoing Isaiah 40:6 verbatim. Greek has flower of grass (anthos chortou). Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact phrase; Greek changes field to grass.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: flower of the field (Isaiah 40:6). Greek: flower of grass.
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:6-8: All flesh is grass and all its beauty like the flower of the field.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: vayyivrach katsel velo ya'amod (flees like a shadow and does not stand) is from Job 14:2. Hebrew preserves BOTH halves of Job 14:2 (flower v10, shadow v11). Greek has in his journeys he shall wither, with no shadow imagery. A back-translator from Greek would never import Job 14:2.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: flees like a shadow (Job 14:2). Greek: shall wither in his pursuits. No shadow in Greek.
textual_notes: Job 14:1-2: Man born of woman comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and does not stand.

one_way_hebrew: STRONGEST ONE-WAY MARKER: First half is VERBATIM Job 5:17: ashrei enosh yokichenu Eloah umusar Shaddai al tim'as. Uses three Job-signature words: enosh (mortal, H582, 42x in Job), Eloah (H433, 41x in Job out of 57 OT total), Shaddai (H7706, 31x in Job out of 48 OT total). Greek James 1:12 says Blessed is the man who endures temptation with NO Job connection. No translator going Greek-to-Hebrew would compose a verbatim Job 5:17 quotation.
Uses keter (crown, H3804), the royal crown (Esther 1:11, 2:17). Greek has stephanon (athletic wreath). Different types of crown.
greek_deviations: The entire Job 5:17 quote is ABSENT from Greek.
Hebrew: keter (royal crown). Greek: stephanos (athletic wreath).
translation_notes: Mortal for enosh emphasizes frailty (from root meaning to be weak/sick).
Eloah and Shaddai preserved as distinct divine titles of Job and the patriarchal tradition (Gen 17:1, Ex 6:3).
textual_notes: Job 5:17 is spoken by Eliphaz. James recontextualizes his partial wisdom as complete gospel truth, promising the crown of life after suffering.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: YHWH does not test man for evil (purpose statement). Greek: God cannot be tempted by evil (nature statement). Different claims.
greek_deviations: Hebrew uses YHWH twice. Greek uses theos.

one_way_hebrew: Uses menatseach (overcomes, H5329 natsach), the root of the Psalm superscription lamenatseach (55 times). Greek says drawn away and enticed (passive luring). Hebrew is ACTIVE: desire CONQUERS the person.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: desire overcomes (active). Greek: drawn away and enticed (passive).
Greek uses birth imagery (desire conceived gives birth to sin). Hebrew uses causal language: desire produces sin. No birth metaphor in Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: Uses tit'u (go astray, H8582 ta'ah), the OT verb for wandering like lost sheep (Ps 119:176, Isa 53:6). Greek planasthe means be deceived. Hebrew: moral WANDERING; Greek: being MISLED.

Uses or/choshekh (light/darkness, H216/H2822), Genesis 1:3-4 creation vocabulary. Greek says no variation or shadow of turning (abstract astronomical language). Hebrew uses concrete primordial imagery.
Uses etslo (beside him, H681 etsel), the unusual spatial proximity word, same as Rev 21:3.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: no exchange from light and from darkness (concrete). Greek: no variation or shadow of turning (astronomical).
textual_notes: Genesis 1:3-4: God separated between the light (or) and the darkness (choshekh).

one_way_hebrew: Uses her'ah (showed, H7200). Greek has apekyesen (birthed). Hebrew: God SHOWED us; Greek: God BIRTHED us.
Uses bikkurim (firstfruits, H1061), the Temple/agricultural offering term (Ex 23:19, Lev 23:17), tied to Shavuot.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: he showed us (revelation). Greek: he brought us forth (generation).
translation_notes: The bikkurim connect to Shavuot; the community born at Pentecost is the firstfruits offering.

one_way_hebrew: Uses benei adam (sons of man/Adam, H1121/H120). Greek has every man. The Hebrew collective connects to the creation narrative.
translation_notes: Echoes Ecclesiastes 5:1-2: Be not rash with your mouth, let your words be few.

one_way_hebrew: Uses lifnei YHWH (before the face of YHWH). Greek: does not produce the righteousness of God. Hebrew: what is GOOD (moral quality). Greek: RIGHTEOUSNESS (legal standing).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: good before YHWH. Greek: the righteousness of God.

textual_notes: This is Hebrew v21 = Greek v22. Greek 1:21 (lay aside all filthiness and receive with meekness the implanted word, able to save your souls) is ENTIRELY ABSENT from the Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: AMONG THE STRONGEST ONE-WAY MARKERS: Uses mar'ot hatsov'ot (mirrors of the serving-women). This phrase appears ONLY in Exodus 38:8, describing bronze mirrors donated by women who served at the Tent of Meeting, melted into the priestly washing basin (laver). Greek has merely in a mirror (generic). NO back-translator would produce this Tabernacle reference. The metaphor: the man gazes into mirrors that should have become the laver of purification; he sees but never washes, never enters service.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: mirrors of the serving-women (plural, Tabernacle). Greek: a mirror (singular, generic).
translation_notes: Theological arc: mirrors for seeing; laver for washing/purification and priestly service. Hearing without doing is using the mirror but refusing the laver.
textual_notes: Exodus 38:8: The women's mirrors were melted into the kiyyor (laver) for priestly washing (Ex 30:17-21).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: dat hasimchah (the law of joy, H1881/H8057). Greek: the perfect law of liberty/freedom. Hebrew: JOY; Greek: FREEDOM. The law of joy connects to the greeting simchah (v1) and joy in trials (v2). No back-translator from liberty would substitute joy.
Uses dat (H1881) not torah for law. The author distinguishes dat (binding decree, Esther/Daniel) from torah (instruction). Greek has only nomos. This distinction cannot arise by back-translation.
Uses yihyeh kadosh (shall be HOLY, H6918). Greek: shall be BLESSED. Holiness (Lev 19:2) vs. blessedness. A back-translator would write ashrei, not kadosh.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: law of joy. Greek: perfect law of liberty.
Hebrew: shall be holy. Greek: shall be blessed.
translation_notes: Law of joy: the dat is not a burden but a source of joy. Psalm 19:8: The precepts of YHWH are right, rejoicing the heart.
textual_notes: Psalm 119:14,111,162 connects torah to simchah/joy.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses she'irut (service, from sharat H8334, priestly/Tabernacle service). Greek has threskeia (religion). Hebrew is concrete ministerial SERVICE, not abstract religion. A back-translator from threskeia would use avodah or dat, not she'irut.
Uses hissit (enticed, H5496 sut), the verb for the adversary inciting David (1 Chr 21:1) and regarding Job (Job 2:3). Greek apaton means deceiving.
Uses resen (bridle, H7448), connecting to horse/bridle imagery in 3:3. A structural thread through the epistle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: she'irut (service). Greek: threskeia (religion).
Hebrew: not good. Greek: worthless (mataios).
translation_notes: Service for she'irut captures priestly/ministerial meaning.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses she'irut (service, not religion). Pure service is defined solely by visiting orphans and widows.
greek_deviations: Hebrew ends here. Greek ADDS and to keep oneself unspotted from the world. Hebrew defines pure service solely as visiting orphans and widows.
translation_notes: tahor (H2889) is the Levitical purity term (Lev 11-15).
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 10:18, 14:29, 24:17 and Isaiah 1:17 mandate care for orphans and widows.

2.summary: James 2 in Hebrew is saturated with Torah vocabulary and direct OT quotations. The most striking feature is beit din (house of judgment, v2) where Greek has synagogue -- no back-translator from synagogue would produce a rabbinic court term. The chapter quotes Leviticus 19:18 verbatim (v8), uses torah directly alongside dat to distinguish instruction from binding decree (v8), and quotes Genesis 15:6 verbatim (v22). The dat besimchah (law in joy, v12) continues the joy-law theme from chapter 1. Faith without works cannot lekadesh (make holy, v14) -- not save as in Greek. The setanim (adversaries, PLURAL, v18) differs from Greek's demons. The Akeidah (binding of Isaac) uses korban (sacrifice) and mizbeach (altar) -- Temple vocabulary. Rahab's story uses meraglim (spies) and vatitmenem (she hid them), drawing directly from Joshua 2.

one_way_hebrew: Uses nose fanim (lifts faces, H5375/H6440) -- the classic OT idiom for showing partiality (Deut 10:17, 2 Chr 19:7, Job 13:10, Prov 18:5). Greek has prosopolempsiais, a word literally COINED from the Hebrew idiom (prosopon = face, lambano = take/lift). The Hebrew is the source idiom; the Greek is a derivative calque.
translation_notes: Nose fanim literally means lifting faces -- looking at someone's face/status rather than their case. The Torah forbids this in judgment (Lev 19:15, Deut 1:17).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses beit din (house of judgment, H1004/H1779) -- the standard term for a rabbinic court of law. Greek has sunagogen (synagogue). A back-translator from Greek would write beit knesset (house of assembly), NEVER beit din. The Hebrew author sees the community gathering as a judicial proceeding, not merely a worship assembly. This is a strong one-way marker.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: beit din (house of judgment). Greek: sunagoge (synagogue/assembly). Fundamentally different institutions.
translation_notes: Beit din is used throughout rabbinic literature for the local court. The scene is not a worship service but a legal proceeding where partiality is shown.

one_way_hebrew: Uses YHWH (H3068) where Greek has theos (God). Also uses yoreshim (heirs, from H3423 yarash) -- the verb for inheriting the Promised Land throughout Deuteronomy.

CRITICAL: Uses BOTH dat (H1881, law/decree) AND Torah (H8451, instruction/teaching) IN THE SAME VERSE, distinguishing them. The dat is what you DO; the Torah is where it is WRITTEN. Greek has only nomos (law) for both. This two-word legal distinction is impossible to produce by back-translation from Greek which has only one word.
Quotes Leviticus 19:18 VERBATIM: ve'ahavta lere'ekha kamokha (and you shall love your neighbor as yourself). This is the exact Hebrew of the Torah commandment.
translation_notes: The dat/Torah distinction: dat is the binding regulation you follow; Torah is the authoritative source text. Both translate to Greek nomos, losing the distinction.
textual_notes: Leviticus 19:18: lo tiqom velo titor et benei ammekha ve'ahavta lere'akha kamokha ani YHWH (You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge... you shall love your neighbor as yourself, I am YHWH).

one_way_hebrew: Uses kol hatorah kullah (all the Torah, all of it) -- emphatic double expression with the feminine kullah reinforcing totality. This is natural Hebrew emphasis impossible to derive from Greek's simple holon ton nomon (the whole law).
Quotes the Decalogue VERBATIM: lo tin'af (you shall not commit adultery, Ex 20:14) and lo tirtsach (you shall not murder, Ex 20:13). The Hebrew preserves the exact Torah wording.

Uses hadat besimchah (the law in joy, H1881/H8057) -- again linking law with joy, continuing the dat hasimchah theme from 1:24. Greek says nomon tes eleutherias (law of liberty/freedom). The Hebrew consistently pairs law with JOY; Greek consistently pairs it with FREEDOM.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: the law in joy. Greek: the law of liberty.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses lekadesh (to make holy, H6942) where Greek says sosai (to save). Hebrew: faith without works cannot make you HOLY (kadosh). Greek: faith without works cannot SAVE you (sozo). These are different claims -- holiness is about consecration/separation; salvation is about rescue/deliverance. The Hebrew continues the holiness theme from 1:24 (yihyeh kadosh).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: faith cannot lekadesh (make holy). Greek: faith cannot sosai (save). Holiness vs. salvation.
Hebrew combines Greek vv15-16 into one long verse.

one_way_hebrew: Uses setanim (adversaries, H7854, PLURAL). Greek has daimonia (demons). Different beings! Hebrew satan means adversary/accuser -- a legal/military opponent. Greek daimonion means demon -- a supernatural evil spirit. The Hebrew plural setanim suggests multiple adversarial beings; Greek's demons are a different category entirely.
Quotes the Shema framework: YHWH echad (YHWH is one). Greek has heis estin ho theos (God is one). The Hebrew preserves the core of the Shema (Deut 6:4) with the divine name YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: setanim (adversaries, plural). Greek: daimonia (demons).
Hebrew: YHWH echad. Greek: God is one.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 6:4: Shema Yisrael YHWH Eloheinu YHWH echad.

one_way_hebrew: Uses korban (sacrifice/offering, H7133) and mizbeach (altar, H4196) -- specific Temple/sacrificial vocabulary. Greek has anenenkas... epi to thusiasterion (offered... upon the altar). The Hebrew korban is the technical Torah term for offerings brought before YHWH (Lev 1:2-3, Num 5:15). The scene is framed as a priestly act, not merely an offering.
Uses avinu (our father) in brackets, suggesting editorial restoration. Greek has ho pater hemon (our father) without brackets.
translation_notes: The Akeidah (Binding of Isaac, Gen 22) is the quintessential Hebrew narrative of faith demonstrated through action.

one_way_hebrew: Quotes Genesis 15:6 VERBATIM: ve'Avraham he'emin be-YHWH vayyachsheveha lo tsedakah (and Avraham believed in YHWH and it was reckoned to him as righteousness). The Hebrew preserves the Torah's exact wording with YHWH. Greek has episteusen Abraam to theo (Abraham believed God) -- using theos where the Torah has YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew preserves YHWH from Gen 15:6. Greek substitutes theos (God).
textual_notes: Genesis 15:6: veHe'emin baYHWH vayyachsheveha lo tsedakah. This is the foundational OT text on faith and righteousness, quoted by Paul in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6.

one_way_hebrew: Uses meraglim (spies, H7270) and vatitmenem (and she hid them, H2934) -- vocabulary drawn directly from Joshua 2:1-4. Greek has kataskopous (spies) which is adequate, but vatitmenem is the specific biblical Hebrew verb for Rahab's hiding of the spies.
textual_notes: Joshua 2:4: vatikkach ha'ishah et shenei ha'anashim vatitspenom (and the woman took the two men and hid them).

one_way_hebrew: Uses ruach (spirit/breath, H7307) where Greek has pneuma (spirit). Both words can mean spirit or breath, but ruach carries specifically Hebrew connotations of the breath of life from Genesis 2:7 (nishmat chayyim). The body-ruach connection is the Genesis creation framework.

3.summary: James 3 addresses the power of the tongue using deeply Hebrew imagery. The resen (bridle, v3) connects back to 1:25, creating a structural thread. Gehinnom (v6) is the Hebrew topographical name for the Valley of Hinnom (Josh 15:8, 2 Ki 23:10, Jer 7:31), not a Greek theological concept. Tselem Elohim (image of God, v9) quotes Genesis 1:26-27 verbatim. The botanical imagery (palms, oil, vine, figs, v12) uses native Hebrew agricultural vocabulary. Sam hamavet (poison of death, v8) is a distinctly Hebrew idiom. The wisdom from above (v17) is described with Hebrew ethical vocabulary: naki (pure), shalom (peace), nachat (gentleness), rachamim (mercies). Me'ha-adamah (from the ground, v15) echoes the Genesis adam/adamah wordplay.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ba'al melamed (master teacher, H1167/H3925). Greek has didaskaloi (teachers). The Hebrew ba'al adds authority/ownership; melamed is from lamad (to teach/learn), the root of Talmud. No back-translator would add ba'al.
Uses ish kadosh (holy man, H376/H6918). Greek has teleios aner (perfect man). Again holy vs. perfect, as in 1:24.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: holy man. Greek: perfect man.

translation_notes: The bridle (resen, H7448) connects to 1:25 where the tongue is bridled. Same word, same metaphor.

one_way_hebrew: Uses malach for helmsman -- literally messenger (H4397). The same word used for angels. In context it means the sailor/pilot, but the word choice creates a double meaning absent from Greek's kubernon (pilot/steersman).

Uses ya'ar (forest, H3293) -- a common OT word for woodland (Josh 17:15,18; 1 Sam 14:25; 2 Ki 2:24; Isa 10:18-19). Greek has hulen (forest/wood). Both are adequate, but the Hebrew connects to Isaiah 10:18-19 where YHWH's fire consumes the forest -- a judgment metaphor.

Uses Gehinnom (H1516 gei + Hinnom) -- the Hebrew topographical name for the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem (Josh 15:8, 2 Ki 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2-6). This was the physical location of child sacrifice to Molech, later used as a burning garbage dump. Greek geennes is simply a transliteration of the Hebrew. The Hebrew author uses the native place name; the Greek preserves it as a loanword.
translation_notes: Gehinnom/Gehenna is not an abstract theological concept in Hebrew but a real valley with horrific historical associations.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 7:31-32: The Valley of Hinnom will be called the Valley of Slaughter. The tongue is said to be kindled from this place of judgment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses sam hamavet (poison of death) -- a strong Hebrew idiom. Greek has iou thanatephorou (deadly poison). The Hebrew phrasing is more visceral and concrete.

Uses tselem Elohim (image of Elohim, H6754/H430) -- VERBATIM from Genesis 1:26-27. Greek has kath homoiosin theou (according to the likeness of God). Hebrew tselem means image/likeness (concrete -- a statue, representation); Greek homoiosis means abstract likeness/resemblance. A back-translator from Greek would write demut (likeness), not the Genesis-specific tselem.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: tselem Elohim (image, Gen 1:27). Greek: homoiosin theou (likeness of God).
textual_notes: Genesis 1:27: vayyivra Elohim et ha'adam betsalmo betselem Elohim bara oto.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ma'yan (spring, H4599) -- the specific Hebrew word for a natural water spring (Gen 16:7, Lev 11:36, Ps 87:7, Prov 25:26). Greek has pege (spring/fountain).

Uses native Hebrew agricultural terms: temarim (palms, H8558), shemen (oil, H8081), gefen (vine, H1612), te'enim (figs, H8384). Greek has suke (fig tree), elaias (olives), ampelos (vine). The Hebrew mixes the items differently: palm+oil, vine+figs. Greek has fig tree+olives, vine+figs. Different combinations suggest independent tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: palm tree producing oil, vine producing figs. Greek: fig tree producing olives, vine producing figs. Different plant-fruit pairings.

one_way_hebrew: Uses sin'ah (hatred, H8135) where Greek has eritheian (selfish ambition). Hebrew sin'ah is the strong emotion of hatred (Gen 37:4-5); Greek eritheia is a political term for party rivalry. Different emotions.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: jealousy and hatred. Greek: jealousy and selfish ambition.

one_way_hebrew: Uses me'ha-adamah (from the ground, H127). Greek has epigeios (earthly). The Hebrew adamah echoes Genesis 2-3 where adam was formed from adamah. A back-translator from the abstract Greek epigeios would use ertsit (earthly, from erets), not the creation-narrative adamah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: from the adamah (ground, Genesis term). Greek: earthly (epigeios, abstract).

one_way_hebrew: Uses lechatchilah (at first/from the beginning) -- a rabbinic Hebrew term. Also lists Hebrew ethical virtues: naki (clean/innocent), shalom (peace), nachat (gentleness), rachamim (mercies). These are deeply rooted Hebrew concepts with no exact Greek equivalents.
Uses massa'ui fanim (lifting of faces, H5375/H6440) for partiality -- same idiom as 2:1 (nose fanim), using the Deuteronomy 10:17 language.
Uses niz'ra'at (is sown, H2232) -- agricultural language. The righteous life is described as planting seeds that grow into fruit. This agricultural metaphor is deeply Hebrew.
textual_notes: Isaiah 32:17: And the work of righteousness shall be peace, and the effect of righteousness, quietness and assurance forever.

4.summary: James 4 is saturated with Torah allusions. The most striking one-way marker is rachil (gossip/slander, v11) from Leviticus 19:16 (lo telekh rachil -- do not go about as a slanderer). Greek has katalalein (speak against), a generic word with no Torah connection. The plural setanim (adversaries, v7) again differs from Greek's singular diabolos (the devil). Torah (v5) is used directly for the authoritative source. The chapter uses nokem venoter (avenging and bearing grudges, v2) -- the exact two prohibitions from Leviticus 19:18. Masa umatan (buying and selling/commerce, v13) is a Hebrew idiom with no Greek equivalent. Ruach (breath/spirit/wind, v14) for human life echoes Genesis, where Greek has atmos (vapor/mist).
